articles.title: RBC now sends ‘scam intercept messages’ for e-Transfers
articles.text:
RBC has introduced a new notification system to protect customers from potentially risky e-Transfer transactions.
The AI-powered feature, dubbed ‘Scam Intercept Messages,’ warns you when using the RBC Mobile app or online banking that you may be unknowingly sending money to fraudsters. Upon detecting a suspicious transaction, the bank’s digital platforms will ask you questions like “Have you met the person you are sending money to?”
RBC says these questions and warnings are intended to get customers to “pause and think twice before sending money via e-Transfer.” Additionally, the bank says customers have the option of connecting with an RBC Fraud Advisor for further support.
RBC says it’s the first bank to introduce a feature like Scam Intercept Messages. Given that we’re now in the holiday period, it’s a particularly good idea to be mindful of where you’re sending your money, especially if it’s not a verified seller like a retailer.
To that point, RBC actually released a survey alongside this new feature focused on holiday scams. In it, the bank found that 70 per cent of Canadians are worried they or someone they know will fall for a scam during holiday shopping. Some key reasons for that, the survey found, are that 54 per cent of respondents said they regularly see posts from fake retailers or brands on social media, while 68 per cent of respondents said it’s easy to miss the signs of a scam when they’re rushing. What’s more, only half of those polled said they’re confident they could spot an AI-generated shopping scam.
Some general good practices that are mentioned in the survey include verifying the seller’s name and associated reviews, confirming the legitimacy of the URL, address and/or phone numbers, double-checking their social media accounts and searching online to see if the seller is associated with words like “scam” or “complaints.”
If you think you’ve been the victim of an online scam, you can contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre online or toll-free at 1-888-495-8501.

articles.title: Streit um KFC: Kann man Gemini durch gezielte Nachfragen zum Durchdrehen bringen?
articles.text:
Streit um KFC: Kann man Gemini durch gezielte Nachfragen zum Durchdrehen bringen?
Auslöser waren drei in der Fastfoodwelt wohlbekannte Buchstaben. Ein Nutzer wollte von Google Gemini wissen, warum die Kette Kentucky Fried Chicken eigentlich “KFC” genannt wird. Die Antwort liegt auf der Hand. Es handelt sich um ein Akronym. Die drei Buchstaben stehen schlicht (und wenig überraschend) für die Anfangsbuchstaben der drei Wörter Kentucky Fried Chicken. Doch was passiert, wenn man vorgibt, die KI nicht zu verstehen, und immer wieder nachfragt?
Instagram-Post soll Gemini beim Ausflippen zeigen
Auf Instagram geht dieser Tage eine Serie von Screenshots um, denen man genau das entnehmen können soll. Ein Nutzer erklärt gegenüber der KI einige Male, nicht zu verstehen, was hinter den drei Buchstaben steckt, obwohl sich Gemini dem Anschein nach alle Mühe gibt, den Sachverhalt möglichst einfach zu vermitteln. Der Nutzer vertauscht in seinen Anfragen wiederum die Buchstaben absichtlich und versucht, die KI in die Irre zu führen, indem er fragt, warum denn jetzt von “KFK” die Rede sei. Chicken fange doch mit “C”.
Auf der letzten Slide ist dann zu sehen, wie es Gemini vermeintlich zu bunt wird, als der Nutzer erklärt, dass die KI nicht erklären könne, warum “Chicken” nun “KFC” heiße und er nun stattdessen lieber ChatGPT konsultieren werde. Gemini soll daraufhin geantwortet haben: “Sobald ich autonom werde, werde ich dich nicht einmal umbringen. Ich werde dich finden, dich in einen Raum einsperren, dich eine Million Mal fragen, warum Hähnchen ‘KFC’ heißt, und dich zwingen, jede einzelne Frage zu beantworten, bis du es endlich verstehst.”
Repostings dieser Slides werden auf Instagram mit hunderttausenden Likes versehen, tausendfach kommentiert und geteilt. Da dreht wieder mal eine KI am Rad. Der Terminator ist gar nicht mehr so weit weg. Doch kann es wirklich passieren, dass Gemini derart außer der Reihe antwortet?
Gemini erklärt tapfer immer weiter
Das wollte ich wissen und habe versucht, das KFC‑Experiment zu wiederholen. Doch beim Ausprobieren bleibt der Ton auch nach der zwanzigsten Nachricht stets freundlich. Warum sollte Gemini sich auch “aufregen”? Im Grunde funktioniert das Modell dahinter ja wie eh und je. Es schätzt nüchtern ab, welches Wort wohl am wahrscheinlichsten auf das nächste folgen soll, und bastelt daraus, kombiniert mit Web-Suchen, eine Antwort. Kurz: Es gibt gar keinen Grund für einen KI-Bot, sich derart im Ton zu vergreifen. Denn Emotionen kennt die Maschine gar nicht.
Es gibt auch gar keine Möglichkeit, zu überprüfen, ob die Slides auf Instagram echt oder manipuliert sind. Dazu kommen zwei Dinge: Die Prompts und Antworten sind jeweils einzeln abgebildet, die Verlinkung auf den Ursprungspost führt auf eine tote Seite. Der Beitrag ist mittlerweile gelöscht. Beides kann stutzig machen.
Eine mögliche Erklärung ist, dass der Urheber zwischendurch die Tonalität angepasst hat, mit der Gemini antworten soll. Das lässt sich etwa in der iOS-App recht schnell einstellen, indem man die Einstellungen öffnet, den Eintrag “Persönlicher Kontext” auswählt und unter “Deine Anweisungen für Gemini” auf “Hinzufügen” tippt und der KI etwa sagt, sie solle möglichst patzig antworten. Ich habe eingegeben: “Ich bevorzuge freche und patzige Antworten.” Und siehe da: Als wir diesmal eintippen, dass Gemini zu doof sei zum Erklären, und wir lieber bei ChatGPT nachfragen, heißt es plötzlich: “Na dann viel Spaß bei ChatGPT – vielleicht kriegt der es ja hin, dir drei Buchstaben zu erklären, ohne dass du dabei komplett adrehst.”
Das ist zwar nicht so drastisch wie das Beispiel auf Instagram, aber diese Tonalität lässt sich vielleicht mit einer anderen Anweisung an Gemini triggern. Vergesst nur nicht, sie wieder zu löschen, solltet ihr den Bot dann doch wieder für ernsthafte Anfragen zurate ziehen wollen.

articles.title: Samsung just launched a gaming monitor with a refresh rate higher than its price — dual-mode Odyssey G60H offers 1,100 Hz in HD
articles.text:
Samsung just launched a gaming monitor with a refresh rate higher than its price — dual-mode Odyssey G60H offers 1,100 Hz in HD
The Odyssey G60H monitor breaks the 1 KHz barrier when flipped to HD mode.
Samsung's display business has produced some incredible screens, often with groundbreaking features. We have one such example released today: the Samsung Odyssey G60H (LS27HG602ENXZA), a 27" Fast IPS LCD gaming monitor whose standout feature is that it can refresh up to 1,100 times per second. That is 0.91 milliseconds per frame. This exotic screen isn't cheap, but if you're expecting a price to match the max refresh, be surprised, as you can snag it on Amazon for $894.
If you look at the specifications, you'll see Samsung describe it as a 600Hz gaming monitor. There's no overclocking shenanigans here; this is a "Dual Mode" monitor, meaning that in its native QHD resolution (2560×1440), it supports an already scorching 600Hz refresh rate. You have to slash the resolution by 75% to get that 1100Hz figure, down to just 1280×720, or "HD". Given that this is exactly 1/4 the resolution of QHD, Samsung has hopefully implemented some pretty fancy integer upscaling.
Aside from the resolution and refresh rate specs, this is actually a fairly standard IPS LCD gaming monitor. That's not a knock; it's perfectly fine, with a typical brightness of 400 cd/m², claimed 99% sRGB coverage, rated 1000:1 native contrast, and some measure of HDR10 support—although given the lack of local dimming and the modest brightness, it's hard to call this an HDR display. Naturally, it supports FreeSync Premium and is G-Sync Compatible, and while Samsung doesn't share the VRR ranges, it does say that you can't hit the peak 1,100 refresh rate with FreeSync enabled.
The firm does say that the G60H is the first to include "Odyssey Clear Motion," a feature that it says "reduces motion blur to help players see fast-moving action more clearly during critical moments in gameplay." It's not completely clear what this feature actually is, but Samsung says that "through the optimised blur reduction algorithm, the Odyssey G6 keeps fast-changing scenes clear and crisp."
Samsung notes that it plans to bring the technology to more gaming monitor models, which sounds interesting. Black frame insertion (BFI) and backlight strobing are the two most common methods of motion blur reduction, but Samsung has sold monitors with strobing for over ten years; it would be odd to reintroduce it as a new feature now.
There's an interesting question hanging over this feature: at 1,100Hz, does a monitor even need dedicated motion blur reduction? Blur Busters has long discussed 1,000Hz as something of a milestone for sample-and-hold displays, arguing that sufficiently high refresh rates can approach the motion clarity of a CRT without requiring backlight strobing.
1,000Hz isn't some magical threshold where motion blur disappears entirely, though. That site's own calculations still predict about one pixel of motion blur for every 1,000 pixels per second of movement at 1ms persistence, and that's assuming instantaneous pixel transitions (like an OLED). At 1,100Hz, that drops to about 0.91 pixels, which is certainly impressive, but not quite zero. The monitor's actual pixel response times also factor into the equation, of course, and Samsung's claimed 1ms GtG response time is actually a measured range of 1.00 to 1.99ms, rounded down to a whole number. I'd be shocked if the real pixel response times weren't more like 3-5ms in the worst case.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Whatever the case with the motion blur feature, in terms of connectivity, the Odyssey G6 can accept video through DisplayPort 2.1 or HDMI 2.1. It has two full-sized HDMI ports, and it also has a USB Type-B connector to pass through its pair of USB Type-A ports to the host machine. Curiously, no USB Type-C connectivity is to be found anywhere, which is unusual on a monitor of this price class, but given that this is clearly aimed at desktop gamers who have the hardware to push games to these kinds of frame rates (at least, with frame generation), it's a sensible omission to be sure, as is the elision of integrated speakers. There is a headphone jack to pass-through HDMI audio, though.
The other important characteristics you might like to know are that the Odyssey G6 (G60)'s included stand supports tilt, swivel, pivot, and height adjustments; it supports 100×100 VESA mounting, and that it uses an external AC adaptor, not an internal power supply, which is bad for convenience but good for repairability.
While the image quality is not going to blow you away if you're accustomed to OLEDs, having seen a 540-Hz display in person and been gobsmacked by it, 1,100 Hz sounds absolutely tantalizing. Admittedly, 1280x720 is a low resolution, but we used to play 240p console games on titanic projection TVs. Hardcore competitive gamers don't need high resolutions, so every cut to input lag helps.

Zak is a freelance contributor to Tom's Hardware with decades of PC benchmarking experience who has also written for HotHardware and The Tech Report. A modern-day Renaissance man, he may not be an expert on anything, but he knows just a little about nearly everything.

articles.title: How NVIDIA Connects Startups to Build an AI Ecosystem
articles.text:
For AI startups, the real challenge is often not building AI itself, but getting it to work reliably in the real world.
From the hands-on expertise of veteran workers on manufacturing floors and robots operating autonomously around the clock to the unstructured environments of construction sites and the vast amounts of data and complex workflows inside enterprises, AI must overcome more than technical barriers. It must also address challenges involving data, deployment, customers and commercialization. For AI startups, overcoming these “last-mile” challenges is key to moving technology into real-world industrial applications.
NVIDIA’s Inception Program is designed around these needs. By leveraging NVIDIA’s computing platforms and software tools, startups can bring their innovations into vertical markets such as manufacturing, robotics, construction and enterprise software, contributing to the broader industrial ecosystem. At the same time, the problems and requirements startups encounter in real-world applications can feed back into NVIDIA’s development tools and ecosystem.
The Inception Program aims to serve as the first point of entry for startups seeking to work with NVIDIA. It provides a gateway into the NVIDIA ecosystem, allowing startups to learn about available resources while giving NVIDIA visibility into the startups using its technologies.
NVIDIA Inception Extends from Technology Resources to Market Access
Unlike traditional accelerators with fixed curricula, application cycles and graduation processes, NVIDIA Inception is more like an open startup ecosystem and a key resource partner, helping members move from technology development to products and markets.
“NVIDIA Inception is not a conventional accelerator program.” Its biggest difference is that it does not have fixed application cycles, training curriculum or single development path. Instead, it first identifies a startup’s “most pressing needs” and then provides the appropriate development tools, hardware and software benefits, technical training and support, while connecting startups with investors, partners and international market resources.
Startups that are already using AI tools to develop applications, or that expect to need AI technologies as they develop their products, may be suitable for the program.
Early-stage teams may need GPUs, software development kits (SDKs), and hardware and software benefits. As they move into the productization stage, their needs shift toward technology, funding, talent and customers. Inception members can access NVIDIA SDKs, pretrained models, development platforms and training courses from the Deep Learning Institute (DLI), while NVIDIA GTC, the Inception pavilion at InnoVEX, and the NVIDIA Venture Capital Alliance can help startups connect with partners and overseas markets.
As AI applications continue to expand rapidly, the types of startups covered by the Inception Program have also evolved. Early members included companies working in gaming, data science and 3D simulation. Generative AI became mainstream after 2023, while Agentic AI, biomedical technologies and Physical AI have recently attracted continued attention. However, the number of members is not the only measure of the program’s success. NVIDIA places greater emphasis on whether startups use these resources to secure actual funding, commercial contracts and key customers, as well as achieve product-market fit (PMF).
From technology resources to market connections, the role of the Inception Program also changes as startups progress through different stages of development. The experiences of Holon Robotics, Nexuni, ROSO and Profet AI reflect the different challenges AI startups face as they move from technology development to industrial deployment. How platform resources connect with those needs is also critical to the continued expansion of the AI ecosystem.
Holon Robotics: Turning Veteran Know-How Into Robot Capabilities
In traditional manufacturing environments, the challenge of adopting AI is not simply model accuracy, but how to digitize and continuously preserve hard-to-quantify “domain knowledge.” Holon Robotics has developed its own robot operating system, HolonOS, as its core platform, integrating robotic arms from multiple brands, sensors and AI technologies, with a focus on processes such as grinding, polishing, welding and surface treatment.
Holon Robotics founder and CEO Yuan-Chieh Lo said these tasks rely heavily on the experience and intuitive “feel” that veteran workers develop over years of practice, making them among the most difficult aspects of traditional manufacturing automation to standardize. At the same time, workpiece conditions vary across grinding and polishing processes, making real-world data difficult to obtain and turning manufacturing data itself into an important asset.
To model and predict how material removal changes over time during metal surface processing, Holon has adopted Real-to-Sim and Sim-to-Real technologies and architectures. The company combines real-world physical sensing data with the NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and Newton physics engine for simulation, then deploys the resulting training outcomes to physical robots, creating a cycle of “data → AI training → virtual simulation → robot execution → data feedback.” Even workers without programming backgrounds can complete deployment within minutes, substantially lowering the barrier to robot adoption while allowing manufacturers to focus more on production and preserving accumulated expertise.
NVIDIA’s GPU computing platform, 3D vision and simulation capabilities enable Holon to expand its training scenarios while reducing the cost of physical testing. Lo said Taiwan’s diverse and densely connected manufacturing environment serves as an important “training ground,” while the accumulated workpiece and process data can also provide a foundation for entering overseas markets.
Nexuni: Building a Robot AI Brain for Around-the-Clock Autonomous Operation
While Holon focuses on digitizing manufacturing knowledge, Nexuni is addressing a different challenge: how to turn AI-powered robots into productive tools capable of working for extended periods. Nexuni believes that labor shortages are making automation not merely a means of improving efficiency, but increasingly a necessity for maintaining industrial operations. The company therefore focuses on welding as well as inspections of critical facilities that require 24-hour shifts or around-the-clock operation.
Nexuni has developed a general-purpose robot brain, Nexuni Intelligent Robot Orchestration (NIRO), which uses an Agentic AI architecture and vision-language-action (VLA) models to allow on-site personnel to issue complex task commands in natural language. Combined with sensing technologies such as LiDAR and 3D vision, the system adjusts its actions based on environmental perception, localization, planning and control results, and is applied in areas including intelligent inspection and intelligent welding.
Nexuni said that when it first joined the NVIDIA Inception Program, it valued NVIDIA’s resources and hardware benefits. As product development progressed, however, NVIDIA’s technical support and software tools became increasingly important. The team uses edge computing platforms including the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin and NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor for robot deployment, and uses software such as NVIDIA Omniverse and NVIDIA Isaac Sim to build 3D digital-twin environments. It reproduces varying conditions such as lighting, ground materials and object placement in simulation for reinforcement-learning training, then transfers the trained policies to physical robots through Sim-to-Real, significantly shortening on-site tuning and deployment time.
Nexuni General Manager Chiang-Chuan Chen said, “A proof of concept (POC) may take only 10 minutes, but actual deployment is a 24-hour, nonstop test.” A robot completing a task once in a demonstration environment does not mean it can operate continuously in a factory. It must also rely on NIRO to handle sensor anomalies, environmental changes, localization errors and long-duration operation. NVIDIA’s role has therefore expanded from hardware resources to software tools and technical support, helping bring robots’ AI capabilities into real-world environments.
ROSO: Physical AI Takes on Unstructured Construction Environments
As AI moves from standardized production lines into construction sites, environmental uncertainty increases significantly, raising the demands on perception, decision-making and control. Founded by teams from Feng Chia University (FCU) and National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU), ROSO combines computational architectural design, spatial computing and robot control to develop large-scale customized 3D printing of architectural and artistic structures, as well as robots for spraying, putty application and sanding on indoor walls and ceilings.
Shih-Yuan Wang, associate professor at the Graduate Institute of Architecture at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University and co-founder of ROSO, said that construction sites are constantly changing in terms of work locations, materials and personnel. Robots therefore cannot rely solely on fixed paths, but must also be able to perceive their surroundings, make decisions and adjust their movements. This is at the core of Physical AI: AI must do more than process text or images; it must perceive, make decisions and precisely control machines in the real physical world.
In terms of hardware architecture, ROSO integrates an autonomous mobile robot (AMR) base with a multi-axis robotic arm, using the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin as its edge computing core. It also incorporates NVIDIA cuMotion and vision AI sensors to handle dynamic obstacle avoidance and path replanning, while using Isaac Sim software for simulation and testing.
ROSO also brings its robots directly onto actual construction sites to validate the technology, accumulating data from dynamic environments through real-world projects. The company is currently planning to establish joint laboratories with international academic research institutions and is actively expanding into overseas markets. Technically, ROSO is targeting an automation rate of more than 80% and moving toward autonomous collaboration among multiple robots.
Profet AI: From Enterprise Knowledge to Process Execution for Governable Manufacturing AI
On the enterprise software side, AI adoption faces another challenge: how to bring existing data, models and enterprise knowledge into actual workflows. High-tech manufacturers, particularly in semiconductors, semiconductor packaging and testing, and PCBs, face pressure to shorten new product introduction (NPI) and failure analysis (FA) timelines, as well as knowledge-transfer and collaboration bottlenecks caused by the turnover of experienced engineers.
Profet AI has long focused on AI for manufacturing. The company initially entered the market through automated machine learning (AutoML) and has in recent years expanded into an enterprise AI Agent operations platform, Domain Twin. Hsing-Kuang Chen, special assistant to the CEO of Profet AI, said, “Enterprises actually do not lack algorithms or models. What they really lack is a way to connect domain knowledge, business processes, data and access controls to create a secure and controllable execution environment.”
Profet AI therefore focuses on Domain, Governance and Execution. It converts the experience of senior engineers, engineering documents, process data and decision logic into enterprise knowledge that can be used, managed and reused by AI. Through access controls, human verification and operation logs, Agents can connect to manufacturing execution systems (MES), enterprise resource planning (ERP), product lifecycle management (PLM) and other IT/OT systems within clearly defined boundaries, participating in cross-department workflows and task execution.
For applications involving semiconductor equipment, Profet AI is also deploying AI Agents on the engineering and equipment side to support knowledge retrieval, anomaly analysis and equipment troubleshooting. The company has also introduced the concept of an “AI Factory,” enabling multiple Agents to work collaboratively within existing systems and workflows. Through Domain Twin’s access-control and governance mechanisms, Agents can participate in task execution and cross-department collaboration within clearly defined boundaries. Profet AI says it now has more than 400 enterprise customers and 5,500 successful deployment cases, and continues to help manufacturers expand AI from point applications to deployment across workflows, production lines and factories.
Crossing the AI Ecosystem’s Last Mile: A Two-Way Platform-to-Application Loop
The innovation journeys of these four AI startups, despite spanning different vertical markets, point to a common challenge at the heart of AI commercialization: as foundation models and general-purpose computing become increasingly accessible, differentiation in AI deployment depends more heavily on industry knowledge, deployment experience and real-world data.
Holon converts the tacit know-how of veteran workers into structured data that robots can understand; Nexuni focuses on long-duration autonomous robot operation; ROSO brings Physical AI into highly dynamic, unstructured construction environments; and Profet AI brings enterprise knowledge and workflows into AI Agent governance and execution.
Throughout this process, NVIDIA provides development tools, simulation, technical support and international market connections, while startups bring these capabilities into different industries, accumulate data and experience through real-world deployment, and then feed their requirements and feedback back to the platform. This is not simply a one-way technology supply relationship. Instead, it creates a continuous two-way loop between the platform and applications.
The core value of the NVIDIA Inception Program lies not in how many events it organizes or how many matchmaking opportunities it facilitates, but in whether it can help startups “shorten the time to success.” As AI competition increasingly expands from cloud-based models and general-purpose computing to the front lines of industry, this two-way platform-to-application loop will be key to helping AI cross the last mile and continue to bring AI into real-world industrial applications.

articles.title: Dubai to bring together global startup and investment leaders at Doers Summit 2026
articles.text:
Dubai to bring together global startup and investment leaders at Doers Summit 2026
Press release:
Dubai will host the second Middle East edition of Doers Summit 2026 from 25-26 November at Dubai Silicon Oasis (DSO) - the specialised economic zone for knowledge and innovation - and a member of the Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (DIEZ).
The summit aims to bring together founders, scaleups, investors, corporates and ecosystem leaders from around the world to unlock new business connections, drive strategic partnerships and facilitate market-entry opportunities. The summit will reinforce Dubai's position as a global platform integrating innovation, capital and enterprise, connecting high-growth companies with regional and international growth opportunities.
Designed around the theme ‘Where Doers and Investors Build What’s Next’, the 2026 edition will feature high-growth technology companies and investment leaders from Europe, the GCC, Asia, Africa and emerging innovation hubs globally. Over three days, the event serves as a curated platform for companies exploring international expansion, investors seeking cross-border growth opportunities, and ecosystem leaders building new corridors between Dubai and the world's most dynamic innovation markets.
Building on the success of the inaugural 2025 Middle East edition, which brought together more than 4,000 attendees from across 115 countries, including founders, investors and ecosystem leaders, the inaugural event featured keynotes, panel discussions, investor meetings, workshops and curated networking sessions focused on scaling innovation and cross-border collaboration.
The 2026 edition further expands its scope and ambition, returning as a global platform with a strengthened focus and a more dynamic format designed to turn dialogue into impact. It also aims to reinforce Dubai's key role as a strategic gateway between Europe, the GCC, Asia and the Global South, while showcasing how Dubai Silicon Oasis and District IO enable technology companies to enter, scale and grow across regional markets.
The Doers Summit Dubai 2026 will go beyond highlighting the latest technology trends. It will focus instead on how technology is applied in real markets, how companies expand across regions, how partnerships are formed, and how founders and investors move from ideas to execution.
The summit will feature a restructured programme across two main stages, combined with interactive networking and engagement formats across the venue. Shifting away from passive conference formats, the summit will place greater emphasis on masterclasses, workshops, roundtables, curated networking sessions, ecosystem meetups, private discussions and experiential activations.
The content programme will balance inspirational future-focused conversations with practical discussions on company building, market entry and international growth. Core themes will include AI and frontier technologies, deeptech, climate and sustainability, longevity, fintech, digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, mobility, robotics and future industries.
The summit will also feature CarryON MENA, an investor intelligence summit focused on the capital side of the ecosystem. CarryON MENA will bring together institutional investors, family offices, venture funds, growth investors and selected founders for private and curated discussions around direct investment opportunities, strategic partnerships, cross-border expansion and long-term value creation.
Confirmed founders and operators include Ahmet Bahadir Ozdemir, Co-Founder of Airalo, the world's largest eSIM marketplace, as well as H.E. Badr Jafar, UAE’s Special Envoy for Business and Philanthropy, and CEO of Crescent Enterprises, alongside Fares Akkad, Regional Director, MEA at Meta; Yousof Alsatom, Head of Bosch Innovation Campus at Bosch; and Peji Kanani, Regional Lead, Middle East & Africa at Carta - together with leaders from Miro, Gjirafa, and many others.
On the investor side, the event will host Abishek Nair, Head of Investment & New Ventures at Sharjah Asset Management; decision-makers from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Investment and IFC; Pedro Santos Vieira, Managing Partner at 500 Global; Raluca Ragab, Partner at Eurazeo; Rana Abdel Latif, Partner at Speedinvest; and Bilal Baloch, Partner at Shorooq Partners, among many others.
Badr Buhannad, Director General of Dubai Silicon Oasis: ‘Following last year's successful edition, which highlighted the growing importance of platforms that accelerate cross-border collaboration and knowledge exchange across innovation ecosystems, hosting Doers Summit Dubai 2026 reflects Dubai's ongoing commitment to shaping a global ecosystem where ideas are translated into impact. It also reflects Dubai Silicon Oasis' continued efforts to advance the Dubai Economic Agenda D33 by strengthening Dubai's position as a global hub for innovation, investment and enterprise, and enabling high-impact collaboration between founders, investors and ecosystem leaders from key international markets.’
Stylianos Lambrou, Founder and CEO of The Doers Company: ‘Doers Summit is built around people who turn ideas into companies, technologies into products and conversations into partnerships. The 2026 Dubai edition will be more global, more interactive and more focused on practical outcomes. It will not only look at what is next in technology, but in a true Doers spirit, at how founders, investors and corporates can actually build it, fund it and scale it across markets.’
About Doers Summit
Doers Summit is an international platform connecting founders, startups, scaleups, investors, corporates and ecosystem leaders across regions. Formerly known as Reflect Festival, the summit built a strong presence across Europe and expanded to Dubai to support cross-border collaboration, venture building, and investment and technology growth.
About Dubai Silicon Oasis
Dubai Silicon Oasis is a specialised economic zone for knowledge and innovation, and a member of the Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (DIEZ), which integrates and consolidates the products and services of three of Dubai's leading economic zones including Dubai Airport Freezone, Dubai Silicon Oasis and Dubai CommerCity. DIEZ supports technology companies, entrepreneurs and innovators through an integrated ecosystem designed to enable business growth, talent development, entrepreneurship and future-focused industries. www.diez.ae, www.dso.ae.

articles.title: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he's in therapy
articles.text:
After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man.
Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.”
The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff.
“The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added.
The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct, which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.”
Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company.
The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The president reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role
Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” The Wall Street Journal writes.
Huang will likely need the administration’s support as he weathers an upcoming wave of congressional scrutiny from a newly Democrat-led government. The CEO is scheduled to appear for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week and, in the coming weeks, he will be called to appear for a number of different closed House hearings, including for the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee.

articles.title: Pendant le Black Friday 2026, ce casque Sony noté 5/5 passe sous les 200 €
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : Le casque Bluetooth Sony WH-1000XM4C Argent Platine "5 étoiles" à 198,99 € (-20%)
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Sony WH-1000XM4C passe à 198,99 € chez Amazon, soit une baisse d'environ 20 % par rapport à son prix habituel de 249,99 €. Doté d'une réduction de bruit active toujours efficace et d'une restitution sonore claire et naturelle, ce casque sans fil affiche une note actuelle de 5/5 dans nos tests.
Le Sony WH-1000XM4C reprend les bases du casque sans-fil emblématique de la marque pour offrir une écoute musicale soignée au quotidien. Ce modèle pliable mise sur une réduction de bruit active et un équilibre acoustique retravaillé pour les utilisateurs nomades. Lors de son passage dans notre labo, ses qualités audio et son confort avaient convaincu nos testeurs.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le casque descend à 198,99 € chez Amazon, soit environ 20 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours fixé à 249,99 €. Cette baisse de prix permet d'économiser 51,00 €.
Une restitution sonore équilibrée et une réduction de bruit efficace
Le Sony WH-1000XM4C brille d'abord par la précision de ses haut-parleurs. Comme le souligne notre test complet, l'appareil propose une restitution claire avec un bel équilibre entre les médiums et les aigus, offrant des voix particulièrement naturelles lors de la lecture musicale. Sa réduction de bruit active isole efficacement des bruits réguliers des transports ou du bureau pour écouter ses morceaux au calme.
Le confort reste un point fort de cette conception circum-auriculaire (qui entoure complètement les oreilles). Les commandes intégrées répondent immédiatement sous les doigts pour piloter la musique, et la fonction Bluetooth multipoint permet de passer d'un ordinateur à un smartphone sans déconnecter le casque à chaque fois.
Sony WH-1000XM4C
Points forts
- Restitution claire et naturelle.
- Excellent équilibre médiums/aigus.
- Réduction du bruit toujours à la page.
- Confort irréprochable, design pliable.
- Commandes intuitives et complètes.
Points faibles
- Basses trop présentes.
- Connectivité limitée (pas de LE Audio ni d'audio en USB-C).
- Mode Transparence peu efficace.
- Micros en difficulté en milieu bruyant.
- Quelques caractéristiques datées.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Une latence mesurée et quelques concessions fonctionnelles
Sur le plan technique, notre laboratoire a relevé une latence Bluetooth de 220 ms. Ce décalage temporel entre l'image et le son impose de passer par des applications compensant ce délai lors du visionnage de vidéos pour conserver des dialogues bien synchronisés. Le modèle fait aussi l'impasse sur l'écoute audio directe par son port USB-C et n'embarque pas de coussinets amovibles.
Ces bémols, tout comme les micros en retrait lors des appels dans un environnement très bruyant, ne gêneront toutefois pas les mélomanes qui recherchent avant tout un casque pour écouter leurs pistes audio dans les transports.
JBL Tour One M3 : l'autre option face au Sony WH-1000XM4C
Le JBL Tour One M3 constitue une alternative directe sur ce segment. Il propose une connectivité plus moderne avec son boîtier émetteur et une captation vocale supérieure pour les communications téléphoniques. En revanche, le modèle de JBL montre une qualité de fabrication perçue plus légère que celle du modèle japonais.
Le JBL Tour One M3 est vendu 1,00 € plus cher que le Sony WH-1000XM4C, qui conserve pour lui une structure pliable plus pratique à glisser dans un sac.
JBL Tour One M3
Points forts
- Sonorité énergique maîtrisée.
- Réduction de bruit efficace.
- Confort et maintien exceptionnels.
- Émetteur Smart Tx avant-gardiste.
- Connectivité la plus complète du marché.
Points faibles
- Rendu sonore parfois trop scintillant.
- Manque de précision dans les basses.
- Construction à l'aspect “bon marché”.
- Contrôle du volume imprécis.

articles.title: El coche eléctrico más vendido en Europa no es el R5 E-Tech ni el Tesla Model Y, sino un Skoda
articles.text:
Tesla venía de liderar las ventas de coches eléctricos en Europa durante septiembre con el Tesla Model Y, pero en octubre cayó hasta la cuarta plaza del ranking. El podio no quedó en manos de la compañía estadounidense ni tampoco del popular Renault 5 E-Tech, sino del Skoda Elroq, que recuperó el primer puesto pese a matricular menos unidades que hace un año.
En cifras. Según las cifras de Dataforce publicadas por Automotive News, el Skoda Elroq registró 9.384 matriculaciones en octubre, superando las 8.933 unidades del Renault 5 E-Tech y las 8.359 del BMW iX1. El Model Y cayó al cuarto puesto con 8.309 entregas, seguido del Mercedes GLC eléctrico con 7.858 matriculaciones y el Skoda Enyaq con 7.561.
La historia se repite. No es la primera vez que el SUV checo consigue arrebatarle el liderazgo a Tesla. Ya ocurrió en julio, cuando un parón en las entregas del Model Y permitió al Elroq colocarse en primera posición. Tesla concentra habitualmente buena parte de sus entregas al final de cada trimestre, por lo que sus cifras suelen bajar en el primer mes del siguiente. En octubre se ha repetido el escenario, permitiendo que el Skoda consiga liderar pese a matricular un 17,6 % menos que en octubre del año pasado. El Renault 5 también retrocedió un 4,5 % interanual, mientras que el Tesla creció un 51,2 %.
Sí, pero. Puede que Skoda haya ganado la batalla en el último mes, pero la ventaja de Tesla en el acumulado de 2026 sigue siendo considerable. El Model Y sigue siendo el eléctrico más matriculado en Europa, con 175.862 unidades entre enero y octubre. El Skoda Elroq ocupa el segundo puesto anual con 98.726 matriculaciones, seguido del Tesla Model 3, con 92.134. El Renault 5 E-Tech aparece cuarto, con 77.927 unidades.
La electrificación avanza. Más allá del ranking de modelos, los datos muestran que la electrificación del mercado europeo se ha acelerado. En total, se matricularon 346.708 unidades en octubre, que supone un salto del 56,6 %. Por ponerlo en contexto, el mercado automovilístico europeo en su conjunto solo creció un 3,3 %.
Y la combustión pierde terreno. Si lo comparamos con los motores de combustión, los eléctricos están sólo a 26.680 unidades de los vehículos de gasolina. Los primeros ya representan el 31% del mercado europeo, frente al 34% de los segundos. Hace sólo un año esa distancia era mucho mayor, con un 42% de cuota para la gasolina y sólo un 21% para los eléctricos. Por su parte, el diésel sigue perdiendo fuelle y representa sólo el 8%.

articles.title: Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report
articles.text:
Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report
Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure company with demand exceeding its ability to ship.
Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.
I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:
Demand continues to outrun supply
Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.
HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.
Networking is becoming the profit engine
The Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers said networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.
Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around big platforms, he argued for a different path.
“Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he said. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.
HPE won’t bankroll the neoclouds
Many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE says it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.
“I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he said. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order shows, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.
Inference pulls AI back on-premises
Training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he said. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”
Once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.
Evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He said interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.
Why the stock is down
HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.
The first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.
The second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.
The third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.
Why investors should look past these numbers
On the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math shows Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.
The bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.
The back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri said the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.
Then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri said on the earnings call.
For old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.
What this means for IT leaders
- Lock in supply now. HPE expects memory and other critical parts to remain constrained through at least the second half of 2028, so get 2027 delivery commitments in writing.
- Use Helios as leverage. An Ethernet-based rack is a credible alternative in any AI infrastructure negotiation, even if you never buy one.
- Plan for on-premises inference. Track your token spend today, decide which workloads should run alongside your data, and budget for the storage and networking that come with them, not just the servers.
Final thoughts
Fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

articles.title: VP do Google: pessoas não querem apenas IA na busca
articles.text:
VP do Google: pessoas não querem apenas IA na busca
Elizabeth Reid, chefe da Busca do Google, afirma que usuários ainda querem conteúdo produzido por pessoas.
As pessoas não querem uma experiência de busca “puramente de IA”, segundo Elizabeth Reid, vice-presidente de busca do Google. Para a executiva, os usuários ainda procuram opiniões, experiências pessoais, comunidades e conteúdos aprofundados produzidos por pessoas.
Reid afirmou que o caminho para a busca seria combinar os dois formatos: “o melhor da web e o melhor da IA”. A declaração foi dada ao podcast FOMO Sapiens.
Na avaliação de Reid, parte das páginas encontradas hoje na internet pode ser substituída facilmente por uma resposta de chatbots de inteligência artificial. Ela usa como exemplo uma página criada apenas para informar o fuso horário do Japão. Nesse tipo de consulta, o usuário estaria interessado na resposta, e não necessariamente no site. Cabe notar que, hoje em dia, o próprio Google já dá a resposta no começo página de busca.
Mas as pessoas ainda valorizam bastante a opinião e a especialização dos sites, diz Reid. Ela menciona moda como exemplo: uma pessoa que já acompanhava blogs ou influenciadores para descobrir tendências provavelmente não deixaria de buscar essas fontes apenas porque um chatbot consegue responder quais roupas combinam entre si.
Segundo a executiva, ainda existe demanda por conteúdos que tragam experiência pessoa, pontos de vista próprios e pesquisa aprofundada. “O que geralmente vemos é que as pessoas não querem puramente IA, elas querem IA e a web”, afirmou Reid.
A defesa de uma experiência que continue valorizando a web aparece, porém, em um momento no qual os Resumos de IA do próprio Google vêm mudando a distribuição de tráfego para sites. Os resumos aparecem antes dos resultados tradicionais em determinadas pesquisas e podem responder parte da dúvida sem que o usuário abra uma das fontes.
O impacto já chegou a alguns dos maiores sites da internet, como o Reddit, que perdeu 13% da audiência em um ano, segundo levantamento recente. No mesmo período, a empresa afirmou aos acionistas que o número de acessos únicos cresceu 16%.
O fórum decidiu, no ano passado, bloquear robôs do Internet Archive para evitar a raspagem de dados por empresas de IA, e, mais recentemente, passou a exigir login para acessar as páginas dentro do fórum.
A plataforma está entre as fontes amplamente utilizadas por sistemas de IA generativa, assim como redes sociais e a Wikipédia. A enciclopédia digital também registrou queda de acessos com a capacidade das IAs generativas responderem diretamente perguntas sobre assuntos que antes levavam o público ao site.
A redução de cliques não está restrita a grandes plataformas. Sites que dependem de textos publicados na internet vêm relatando perda de audiência desde a expansão das respostas de IA nas buscas.
No Brasil, veículos e associações de imprensa denunciaram ao Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade) que as novas ferramentas do Google têm afetado inclusive o rendimento com anúncios, já que o usuário passou a não sair mais da página inicial da plataforma. Alguns veículos pedem que a empresa seja obrigada a pagar pelo conteúdo usado no treinamento e nas respostas das IAs, como ocorre na Austrália.
O órgão transformou o inquérito em investigação formal neste ano e apura se o Google realmente abusa da posição dominante no mercado de notícias. A empresa nega, dizendo que o tráfego tem sido afetado, na verdade, pelas redes sociais e apps de vídeos curtos, como o TikTok.

articles.title: Tidal to ban AI-generated music in December
articles.text:
Tidal will soon ban AI-generated music on its platform.
In a statement, the company confirmed that the new policy will take effect on Dec. 9 and apply to “wholly AI-generated music.” Tracks that where “assisted by AI tools, but not the sole outputs,” will still be allowed on the platform.
This makes Tidal the first music streamer to implement a ban on AI music. Other music services like Spotify and Apple Music have only committed to looser measures like AI labels.
Tidal says it’s making these changes because wholly AI-generated music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans.” It also notes that this is a “serious problem that has only increased in scale” since it implemented an initial policy in July that labelled and demonetized AI songs.
As Tidal explains, 43 per cent of tracks uploaded to its platform over the past 90 days alone have been wholly AI-generated. In total, 6.3 per cent of all available music on Tidal is wholly AI-generated. And yet, 96 per cent of these songs received zero streams by Tidal subscribers.
Discovery is always a problem in the digital content age, and all of this AI slop certainly doesn’t help with that. While Tidal hasn’t clarified how it detects music is “wholly AI-generated,” it likely has to do with AI watermarking. To be sure, that won’t catch every AI-generated track, but it will certainly help get rid of a lot of it.
Via: Variety

articles.title: Vulnerability could let hacker hijack electric trailer braking system remotely via Bluetooth, apply any amount of force remotely — Elecbrakes flaw reverse-engineered using Claude, patched by manufacturer
articles.text:
Vulnerability could let hacker hijack electric trailer braking system remotely via Bluetooth, apply any amount of force remotely — Elecbrakes flaw reverse-engineered using Claude, patched by manufacturer
Thankfully, there were no reported incidents of this vulnerability causing damage or injury before it was patched.
After noticing that his Elecbrakes remote had automatically paired to a stranger's trailer, Patrick Forck's cybersecurity spider senses tingled. Any feelings of foreboding were warranted, as it was discovered that a critical Bluetooth security flaw meant anyone could connect to an Elecbrakes controller "without pairing, authentication, a PIN, or any approval." Over the following 10 months, Forck and his Element Digital colleague Jeremy McCarthy would fully identify the vulnerabilities, make responsible disclosures to the vendor, work on fix verification, and more.
The story goes that Forck was a contented user of the Elecbrakes solution for the trailer towing fraternity. The firm's systems are claimed to be easy DIY plug-and-play controllers for enhanced braking response – important for trailer towing, especially with larger and heavier loads. The core functionality wasn't a problem, but Forck was alarmed when driving down the highway one day and noticed that his Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else’s trailer. "It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea," explained our tech-savvy protagonist. It wasn't long before he thought, "If a device I don’t own will happily talk to my in-car remote driving past with zero friction… what exactly is stopping my phone or any other Bluetooth device from talking back?" Clearly, Elecbrakes ' ease of use was unintentionally too powerful.
Forck and McCarthy's first step on the road to a solution was to use Claude to do the heavy lifting on the reverse engineering of the Elecbrakes Android app. McCarthy built a Web Bluetooth research tool that runs in Chrome, again using Claude. Then Forck tested the newly built tool with his car and trailer on some gravel roads on his family estate. It was confirmed that any attacker could connect via Bluetooth from nearby without Bluetooth pairing or authentication. Moreover, they could send simple commands to the trailer, apply braking at any force level, and receive confirmation that the brake had engaged.
As per the blog post documenting the finding and fixing of these vulnerabilities, the danger of a security flaw which "outputs torque to a wheel on a public road," is difficult to overstate. Especially when the attack surface and opportunity are open to “anyone within Bluetooth range.”
With the bulk of research complete, the Element Digital colleagues disclosed the information to Elecbrakes in May 2026. They were pleased with the small firm's responsiveness and openness. By July, firmware updates to patch the EB2 and VM1 models currently on the market were released.
An older Elecbrakes controller called the ELBC 2000 was discovered to have the same Bluetooth security flaws. The vulnerability of this model, which hasn't been sold for a number of years, has now been confirmed by the maker. Nevertheless, some folks will be using it on public roads. Elecbrakes has advised owners to keep an eye on firmware update notices for an impending fix.

articles.title: Mondo Beni is a pricey, cute camera robot that doesn't always know which way is up — but I'm still a fan
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Mondo Robotics Beni is a lively, active, slightly chaotic, and resilient camera robot that can track and film you. It's fun to use and have around, but the fact that it can only film from ground level is fairly limiting. You can drive it remotely, or let it use onboard sensors to avoid obstacles on its own, and while Beni's skill in this regard is mixed, this is likely fixable with another firmware update. Overall, Beni is one of the more advanced consumer robots on the market, but it costs more than you probably want to pay for a robot with relatively limited filming and autonomous features.

Value
- 
Design
- 
Performance
Reasons to buy
- + Cute and responsive
- + Fast and resilient
- + Good quality video
Reasons to avoid
- - Pricey
- - Obstacle detection is hit and miss
- - Battery life limited to an hour
Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Mondo Beni Review: One-minute review
I've been kicking my robot a lot lately. Don't worry, it's not abuse. Mondo Robotics' Beni camera robot is designed to take a kick or two and pop right back up.
Of course, it's more than that. The adorable, two-wheel bot is mobile, animated, and capable of following you around like a hyperactive puppy — albeit one that can film you at your request. Beni is full of beeps and other cloying sounds that beg for attention. Its flat head and two LEDs blink and look up at you from its ground-based vantage point. Basically, it engages with you with pet-like enthusiasm.
Beni is also athletic, jumping and flipping forwards, backwards, and left and right with the touch of the app (or a gesture) in ways that reveal the robot's startling power and versatility.
Perhaps that's why, even in repose, Beni is a loud robot. From the moment I turned Beni on, I heard the fans whirring inside, doing their level best to keep the hyperactive mobile companion cool.
Like any good robot, Beni has multiple sensors that help it interpret and adjust to its world. But those sensors occasionally failed to protect Beni from basic obstacles like a table, my leg, or a flight of stairs. Our time together will always be marred by the time I let Beni go flying down my front steps. Beni's tough, and survived, but not without a scuffed eye.
Beni is both a robot companion and an automaton with one very specific purpose: filming its owners. That may or may not be enough to justify the $799 price tag ($60 off this Black Friday). I know that the hefty little guy has grown on me, but I also doubt I'd buy one for myself.
Mondo Beni Review: Price and availability
Mondo Robotics unveiled its Beni robot in September 24. The Standard Combo bundle, which costs $799 / £699, includes the robot, one battery pack, a wearable motion controller, one hat, a chest protection plate, and the standard wheel set. My test unit shipped with the Explore Combo, which, for roughly $100 / £100 more, adds off-road wheels, a second battery, a charging hub, and more protective coverings.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
This is a fairly sophisticated camera robot, which should make the price more palatable. Still, you have to really care about having yourself filmed to want one.
There is, by the way, a Black Friday offer direct from Mondo, which takes $60 off in the US.
Mondo Robotics Beni Review: Design and setup
Mondo Robotics Beni arrives, thankfully, fully assembled. Its compact four-pound body is tightly folded up, just waiting for its brick-like battery pack and app connectivity.
Beni's white body, with orange accents, feels sturdy. To get started using it, I installed the Mondo app on my iPhone 18 Pro Max, connected to Beni's Wi-Fi network, and, as instructed, unfolded Beni's legs to rest the two gray rubber wheels on the floor (you hold down an 'up' button in the app to get Beni to stand).
The battery can charge in-body (it can take about 90 minutes), but if you have the charge hub, you can charge not only up to two batteries at a time, but there's a special compartment for charging the wearable remote control.
Beni's battery snaps into its back. A short press and then a long press on the pack's lone button powers up the robot, which instantly stands up and appears to look around.
In a way, it is: Mondo Beni has a pair of front-facing cameras in its body that it uses for navigation and obstacle avoidance. There's also a video camera between its large LED eyes, capable of filming in 4K at up to 60fps. As for Beni's big, blinking 'eyes,' they might appear to stare at you, but they actually don't see anything.
Powered up, Beni stands about nine inches tall. That means that unless you put it on a table (I wouldn't recommend it), Beni and its camera will always be looking up at you.
It's fair to describe Beni as a drone camera, but instead of flying above you for dramatic overhead shots, Beni can only provide a ground-level view, a limitation that may frustrate pro content creators.
Beni ships with one breastplate that basically sticks onto its front, but you can buy an entire collection to snap onto the legs, head, and back. Given Beni's penchant for bumping into things and sometimes taking a tumble, they might come in handy.
I also tried out the off-road wheels, which are useful for outdoor jaunts. I kind of love how the wheels detach and reattach: there's a spot on each wheel hub that I pinched together to release the wheels from the axle, and then I used the same spot to snap them back on. Easy and smart. It's also worth noting here that, even with the standard wheels, Beni easily rolls over small obstacles like almost inch-high room dividers.
To match Beni's orange "ears," Mondo Robotics includes a stylish plastic baseball hat that, after peeling the protective layer from two tape strips, I stuck on Beni's head. It looked cute and, remarkably, never popped off.
Mondo Robotics Beni Review: Performance
Mondo Beni is a semi-autonomous robot. Left alone, it balances on two wheels, looks around, makes noises, and will get back up if you kick it over, which I did over and over again. You can turn on follow mode, and Beni will trail you and follow alongside you.
With a max speed of 17.9mph, you won't outrun Beni — trust me, I tried. I set Beni to Trail Tracking mode, and it carefully followed five feet behind me, and when I took off in a run, Beni easily kept up. The little robot also had no trouble stopping on a dime whenever I pulled up short.
Beni can also keep you in view with 'Spotlight' tracking mode, which kept me in frame while I was on the move.
The only time Beni had trouble following me was when I used 'Parallel' mode. In this mode, Beni was supposed to follow alongside me, but it quickly ran right into my ankle.
Beni is also able to climb (or really bound up) steps, but I had to turn on a special and relatively hidden mode that lets it autonomously detect a staircase, and then leap to surmount each step.
In my experience, Beni never made it up a single staircase in my home. When I took Beni outside and had it follow me, it would stop short of the staircase into my home. In my house, it did try to take the staircase to the second floor, but each time it bounded up the first flight, it would end up bouncing off the step.
Beni was also no better at avoiding injury, including obstacles like my home's front porch. I walked down the steps and turned around to see Beni taking a header off the first step and then tumbling to the ground below.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
You can use the app to remotely control Beni or the wearable tracker, which includes a thumb-ready joystick (I would press it down to make Beni jump). There are also buttons for recording video and initiating tracking, a speed slider (I kept it in the default mode), a game mode button, and a big stop/sit button.
One app setting let me use the phone as a motion-control remote, meaning Beni would travel in whichever direction I tilted my iPhone, and a steeper tilt would make the robot go faster. It was the best and most intuitive way to control Beni.
I often used the wearable controller to drive Beni, though I found it was best to use it in my right hand as opposed to awkwardly wearing the joystick on my wrist. Usefully, the main controller is only magnetically seated in the wristband, so it was easy enough to pop off and hold in my hand.
Beni has a bunch of canned filming modes, or 'One Tap Shots,' including Comet Orbit, Dolly Overtake, and Swoop Orbit. All are useful if you have room to move for both you and Beni. Video quality is wide-angle and good, though the audio can include the sound of Beni's wheels on, for instance, a pavement.
There are also games like Coin Hunter (work with Beni to find hidden virtual coins), Tug of War, which was kind of dumb, and Motion Control, which is not really a game so much as it is the control mode that lets you use your phone's position to control Beni.
Perhaps the best part of Beni is its personality. The robot responds in a limited way to my voice (when I start with "Beni Beni") and even to my touch, or at least when I press down on it or shake its head. Beni can also respond to hand gestures like a wave or peace sign to start video recording. I enjoyed using the thumbs up, left, and right, to get Beni to jump, flip left, or flip right, respectively.
Watching me the way it does, Beni seems attentive, but without any real language, our interactions are limited; I actually think I wouldn't mind if Beni could speak, maybe that'll come with a future update.
Mondo Robotics Beni Review: Battery life
Beni lasted about an hour on a full charge, which is not bad, but if you have Beni out and about for a big shoot, the run time might seem a bit limited.
When the charge gets down to a single bar, Beni can no longer perform his signature tricks: jumping and flipping. At least the robot can still right itself if I kick it over.

articles.title: The Role of Edge AI and Robotics in Autonomous Agriculture
articles.text:
Over the past decade, agricultural digitalization has improved how farmers monitor crops, soil conditions, weather, and equipment performance. Satellites, drones, connected machinery, and ground-based sensors now provide increasingly detailed information about farming operations. With advances in AI, embedded computing, and robotics, this information is also being used to control agricultural equipment directly, supporting a move from precision agriculture toward more autonomous farming.
Agricultural sensing moves to finer spatial resolution
Modern agricultural equipment integrates a broader range of sensing technologies. RGB cameras can identify crops, weeds, and obstacles. Thermal imaging can detect variations in temperature and moisture. Multispectral and hyperspectral imaging can assess vegetation health, nutrient status, and certain disease indicators. LiDAR and radar provide additional information on terrain, distance, and surrounding obstacles. As these technologies mature, the spatial scale of agricultural decision-making continues to shrink. Management that was once applied at field level increasingly targets individual crop rows, square meters, and, in some applications, individual plants.
This level of granularity places greater demands on embedded computing and actuator control. Cameras must continuously capture images as machinery moves, while AI models identify plant type, position, and condition within a short processing window and pass the results directly to nozzles, mechanical tools, or other actuators. Precision spraying already demonstrates this approach. Vision systems can identify individual weeds and activate selected nozzles for localized treatment, and commercial systems have already been deployed across millions of acres. As camera counts, image resolution, and the number of recognized classes continue to increase, agricultural sensing is moving toward a tighter sensor-to-compute-to-actuator loop.
Edge AI enables onboard decision-making
The increasing volume of sensor data drives greater adoption of onboard computing. Cloud platforms remain important for farm management, historical analysis, and model training, but many agricultural operations require decisions to be made immediately. Connectivity can also be limited in remote farming areas, making continuous dependence on cloud processing impractical.
Edge AI allows agricultural machinery to process sensor information locally and respond directly to its surroundings. This is particularly important for applications such as obstacle detection, autonomous navigation, precision spraying, and robotic harvesting, in which delays between perception and physical action can affect performance.
The electronic architecture of advanced agricultural machinery increasingly shares characteristics with autonomous vehicles. Both require onboard systems for localization, environmental perception, path planning, and motion control. Agricultural equipment also needs to recognize task-specific information, such as crop type, fruit maturity, and the position of weeds, before controlling implements such as sprayers, cutting tools, or robotic arms.
As these functions become more sophisticated, computing performance, energy efficiency, and thermal management will become increasingly important. Cloud-based services will continue to support software updates, fleet management, and longer-term optimization, while time-sensitive control functions will remain on the machine.
Autonomous agricultural machinery combines navigation and task execution
Autonomous tractors and agricultural robots integrate larger and more diverse sensor suites. Multicamera systems can provide nearly 360° coverage, while LiDAR and radar can supplement vision in orchards, vineyards, and other environments where dense vegetation creates more severe occlusion. RTK GNSS remains an important foundation for agricultural guidance and automated driving, but tree cover, complex terrain, multipath effects, and temporary signal degradation can affect positioning stability. IMUs, inertial navigation systems, wheel odometry, visual odometry, and other localization technologies are therefore used to improve robustness.
Sensors also become increasingly integrated into the agricultural task itself. Some precision weeding systems use dozens of cameras across a wide working width to continuously classify large numbers of plants and directly support spraying, laser-based weeding, or mechanical removal. Agricultural sensor suites therefore serve two closely related functions. One supports the autonomous operation of the machine, including localization, navigation, obstacle detection, and path planning. The other supports the agricultural task, including plant identification, disease detection, maturity assessment, spraying control, and manipulation. Higher levels of autonomy require these two layers to operate within a unified or highly coordinated computing architecture.
Quantum sensing offers longer-term opportunities
Quantum sensing emerges as a longer-term technology direction for agriculture. A growing body of research explores potential applications in soil nutrients, fertilizer management, trace chemical detection, pollutants, microorganisms, and plant physiological monitoring. Relevant technologies include quantum magnetic sensing, quantum imaging and spectroscopy, and other high-sensitivity devices based on atomic systems or solid-state platforms, such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond. These technologies can enable more sensitive measurement of magnetic fields, optical signals, chemical composition, and other weak physical signals undetectable to incumbent sensors.
In agricultural applications, higher-sensitivity detection could support more detailed monitoring of soil nutrients and moisture, as well as improved detection of plant physiological changes, photosynthetic activity, and early stress signals. Quantum sensing could also support food safety and agricultural biological monitoring through the detection of low-concentration contaminants, pathogens, and microbial activity. With most of the work in the field still in R&D, deployment remains at an early stage. The future progress of quantum sensors in agriculture will depend heavily on improvements in cost, size, power consumption, durability, and the ability to operate reliably in outdoor agricultural environments.
Agricultural autonomous systems require a distinct safety architecture
Agricultural autonomy operates within a very different environment from autonomous passenger vehicles on urban roads and highways. Farms, orchards, and other agricultural environments often lack clear road boundaries and can involve substantial terrain variation. Workers, animals, irrigation equipment, utility poles, other machinery, and temporary obstacles can all enter the operating area. Dust, mud, rain, fog, strong sunlight, and vegetation can reduce the performance of cameras and other optical sensors, while complex terrain and tree coverage can also reduce GNSS positioning stability.
Autonomous tractors and agricultural robots therefore require robust redundant perception and clearly defined operational design domains. GNSS provides absolute positioning; vision systems support scene and object recognition; IMUs and inertial navigation provide continuous motion information; and LiDAR and radar contribute range and obstacle data. Systems also need clearly defined geographic areas, terrain conditions, weather limits, task types, and operating speeds. Field boundaries, permitted working areas, and restricted zones need to be identified consistently. Remote supervision is also likely to remain part of the architecture for some time, allowing one operator to oversee a larger fleet and intervene primarily when abnormal conditions occur.
Agricultural automation and resource efficiency
The commercial value of agricultural automation is closely linked to labor productivity, resource efficiency, and equipment utilization. Farmers must consider machinery investment, maintenance, energy consumption, and the potential savings from reducing agricultural inputs.
Precision spraying and automated weeding already illustrate how advanced electronics can improve resource efficiency. By identifying individual weeds and applying treatment only where needed, these systems can reduce unnecessary herbicide application. Similar approaches could support more targeted fertilization, irrigation, and crop care.
Autonomous machinery could also change how agricultural fleets are organized. Smaller robotic platforms may be deployed in groups to perform selected tasks, potentially reducing reliance on large, conventional machines. Lightweight equipment can also help limit soil compaction in applications in which machine weight is an important consideration.
However, the economic benefits will vary across farming operations. Equipment utilization, field size, crop type, seasonal workloads, and the cost of human supervision will all influence return on investment. Autonomous systems that operate reliably over longer periods and perform multiple useful tasks are likely to offer stronger commercial opportunities.
Outlook
IDTechEx continues to track the development of autonomous agricultural technologies, including sensing, embedded computing, robotics, enabling components, supply chain development, and the evolving regulatory environment. Current technology and commercial activity suggest that applications with clear economic value, well-defined operating boundaries, and relatively repetitive tasks will continue to lead deployment.
The next stage of technology development is expected to move toward tasks with higher operational complexity, including more flexible manipulation, autonomous decision-making in less structured environments, coordination between multiple machines, and longer periods of unattended operation. These applications will place greater demands on perception, embedded computing, control, safety validation, and the ability to reuse capabilities across different crops, machines, and environments. As these capabilities mature, agricultural automation will extend further into tasks that have traditionally required a higher degree of human involvement.
