articles.title: Kartoffeln wachsen in künstlichem Mondstaub – doch für Nasa-Mondbasen bleibt eine Hürde
articles.text:
Kartoffeln aus dem Mondstaub: Studie zeigt Chancen und Hürden für künftige Mondbasen
Forscher:innen der Oregon State University haben nun Kartoffeln in künstlichem Mondboden bis zur Ernte gezüchtet. Die Ergebnisse sind in einer Studie im Fachmagazin npj Microgravity nachzulesen.
Erst bei einer Beimischung von 30 Prozent Wurmkompost erreichten die Pflanzen ähnliche Knollenerträge wie in fruchtbarem irdischem Ackerboden. Allerdings maßen die Wissenschaftler:innen in Knollen einzelner Versuchsgruppen leicht erhöhte Werte bestimmter Schwermetalle.
Die US-Raumfahrtbehörde Nasa hat die Versuche im Labor finanziert. Hintergrund ist das Artemis-Programm der Behörde, das längere Aufenthalte von Astronaut:innen auf dem Mond vorbereitet.
Projektleiter Aymeric Goyer ordnet die Ernte in einer Mitteilung der Hochschule als Zwischenschritt für eine künftige Nahrungsmittelproduktion im All ein. „Wir haben herausgefunden, dass Kartoffeln ihren gesamten Lebenszyklus in simuliertem Mondboden abschließen können, wenn dieser mit organischem Material ergänzt wird“, sagt Goyer.
Warum purer Mondstaub für Kartoffeln schädlich ist
Fast die gesamte Mondoberfläche ist von einer trockenen Schicht aus zertrümmertem Gestein, Staub und scharfkantigen Glaspartikeln bedeckt, die Fachleute Mondregolith nennen. Über Milliarden Jahre haben winzige Meteoriteneinschläge und kosmische Strahlung dieses Material so fein zermahlen, dass spitze Körnchen Pflanzenwurzeln mechanisch aufscheuern können.
Chemisch enthält das Gestein viel Eisen, Kalzium sowie lösliche Schwermetalle, während pflanzenverfügbares Kalium, Phosphor und organischer Humus fehlen. „Mondregolith enthält keinerlei Stickstoff, sodass keine Nutzpflanze wachsen würde, ohne ihn zu ergänzen“, so Goyer.
Für ihre Versuche wählten die Forscher:innen eine frühreifende Kartoffelsorte aus, weil Kartoffeln pro Quadratmeter mehr Nahrungsenergie liefern als viele andere Feldfrüchte. In geschlossenen Lebenserhaltungssystemen könnten die Pflanzen künftig Grundnahrungsmittel bereitstellen und gleichzeitig organische Abfälle einer Stationsbesatzung verwerten.
Fünf künstliche Mondböden und Wurmkompost im Test
Da echter Mondstaub aus früheren Raumfahrtmissionen für Ackerbauversuche zu knapp ist, nutzte das Team fünf künstliche Gesteinsmischungen aus dem Labor. Diese Nachbildungen ahmen sowohl dunkle vulkanische Tiefebenen als auch helle Gebirgsregionen des Mondes nach und wurden mit ertragreicher Ackererde aus Oregon verglichen.
Als Nährstoffquelle mischten die Wissenschaftler:innen den Gesteinsstaub mit Wurmkompost, den Regenwürmer durch die Zersetzung organischer Pflanzenreste erzeugen. Je nach Gruppe wuchsen die Knollen in reinem Gesteinsstaub oder mit fünf bis 30 Prozent Kompost.
Ohne jeden Zusatz kümmerten die Pflanzen stark, bildeten kaum Wurzeln aus und lagerten hohe Mengen Kupfer in ihren Blättern ein. Fünf bis 15 Prozent Kompost halfen nur teilweise, während die Mischung mit 30 Prozent Kompost Wuchshöhe und Knollenertrag der irdischen Vergleichserde erreichte.
Innere Stressreaktion der Pflanzen und Spuren von Schwermetallen
Erstautor David Handy arbeitet als Wissenschaftler in Goyers Labor und vermutet laut der Hochschulmitteilung, dass organisches Material gelöste Schwermetalle im Boden festhält. Der Kompost helfe demnach, „einen Teil der Giftigkeit auszugleichen“, indem er „den Kontakt der Pflanzen mit schädlichen Verbindungen verringert“.
Wie die einzelnen Gesteinsmischungen die Wurzeln chemisch schädigen, ist laut der Facharbeit im Detail noch ungeklärt. Genanalysen der Blätter zeigten jedoch bei allen fünf Mondböden deutliche Stressreaktionen bei der Umwandlung von Licht in Energie sowie bei pflanzlichen Abwehrstoffen.
Zudem veränderte der Anbau den Säuregrad der Böden und verschob die Aktivität von Bakterien und Pilzen rund um die Wurzeln. Trotzdem behielten die Knollen ihren Nährwert, und natürliche Kartoffelgifte, die oft an grünen Stellen unter der Schale auftreten, blieben auf normalem Erdniveau.
Während die Mitteilung der Universität die Knollen bereits als sicher essbar einstuft, formuliert die Fachstudie eine deutliche Einschränkung. In bestimmten Versuchsgruppen enthielten die geernteten Kartoffeln leicht erhöhte Mengen der Schwermetalle Kupfer, Zink und Aluminium, die weiter überwacht werden müssen.
Probiert hat das Team bislang keine einzige Knolle, weil sämtliche Exemplare vollständig für chemische Analysen im Labor verbraucht wurden. Zudem wuchsen die meisten Pflanzen in kleinen Labortöpfen, und erst ein Zusatzversuch in größeren Gefäßen brachte Knollen nahe an übliche Supermarktgrößen hervor.
Hoher Bedarf an Kompost bremst frühe Mondstationen der Nasa
Selbst wenn künftige Analysen die Schwermetallwerte entkräften, stellt der nötige Kompostanteil von 30 Prozent frühe Mondmissionen vor ein Transportproblem. Weil Frachtplatz auf Raketen begrenzt ist, stufen die Autor:innen den Ackerbau im Gesteinsstaub für die erste Aufbauphase einer Mondstation als kaum tragfähig ein.
Künftige Besatzungen könnten stattdessen eine kleine Startmenge Kompost und Regenwürmer mitbringen, um den Boden über mehrere Ernten mit Bioabfällen und Pflanzenresten anzureichern. Weiterhin benötigen größere Gewächshäuser knappe Wasservorräte auf dem Mond, die vor Ort aus Polareis gewonnen und im Kreislauf aufbereitet werden müssen.
Offen bleibt auch der Einfluss echter Mondbedingungen, denn das Gewächshaus in Oregon arbeitete unter voller Erdanziehung statt einem Sechstel davon sowie ohne Weltraumstrahlung. In einer Folgestudie vergleicht das Team zehn Kartoffelsorten im künstlichen Mondstaub, um widerstandsfähige Varianten für einen späteren Anbau auf dem Mond zu finden.
Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Beyond UPI: Why many Indians still need help accessing basic banking services
articles.text:
Beyond UPI: Why many Indians still need help accessing basic banking services
Assisted banking is not an alternative to regular banks or the mobile application that banks provide. Through the extension of their services via designated local access points, banks can make use of the business correspondent model to extend basic banking functions to the local population.
The digital payments revolution has changed the way transactions happen in India. In both urban and rural settings, transactions take place through the use of QR codes. The use of payment systems like UPI is common. According to the report by National Payments Corporation of India, as of October 2026, there were 25.47 billion transactions worth more than Rs 31.53 lakh crore made using UPI.
While there has been a quick shift towards the use of digital payments, the use of digital payments does not imply the use of routine banking services. Digital payments are only one component of routine banking services. Routine banking services include withdrawing cash, transferring money, and checking the balance. There has been uneven access to basic banking services in India despite the quick expansion in payment transactions.
Financial inclusion beyond opening bank accounts
Opening an account is the initial step of financial inclusion. According to the official PMJDY dashboard, the Department of Financial Services, under the Ministry of Finance of India, the total number of beneficiaries under Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana was 59.63 crore as on 21 October 2026.
The performance report demonstrates vast structural coverage: 46.29 crore beneficiaries come from rural and semi-urban areas, 33.26 crore beneficiaries are female beneficiaries, and deposits in accounts is Rs 3.25 lakh crore.
Having an account does not necessarily guarantee smooth operation through that account. An account itself does not make the trick when operational issues appear.
- Distance problem: The process of getting to formal banking facilities costs time and daily wage.
- Digital constraints: Many people have one smartphone in the family or do not know how to use complicated digital banking applications.
- Operational issues: Issues such as language barrier in banking application, poor network connection, and possibility of transaction failures discourage usage of banking application independently.
It is crucial to note that digital literacy significantly varies depending on region, generation and social class. For some families, which rely on cash money, the possibility of taking out the money is as important as receiving anything
Why assisted banking continues to matter
Although self-service mobile applications eliminate all hassles for many individuals, there are many instances in which customers require personal help. In such a scenario, the banking correspondent (BC) model and assisted banking become invaluable.
Assisted banking is not an alternative to regular banks or the mobile application that banks provide. Through the extension of their services via designated local access points, banks can make use of the BC model to extend basic banking functions to the local population.
Local retailers authorised by the appropriate authorities act as an important connection in this case. Due to the regular visits made by community members to these retail outlets for daily necessities, the provision of secure technology in them will enable customers to access banking facilities without making an extra effort to visit a faraway branch of the bank.
This human-based service point acts as a reassuring factor for new users. Assistance from a trusted local retailer in withdrawing money, checking balance, or transferring money within the country will provide comfort to all types of users.
Digital literacy, security, and building trust
It is not enough just to increase access; making sure that usage is safe is equally important. The customer may be quite happy to effect a merchant payment via UPI but may be unsure as to how to authenticate the receipt and deal with any surprise payment failure.
Long-term confidence-building can be accomplished through a concentrated effort in three main directions:
- Local language campaigns can educate customers on the issues of transaction authentication, fraud prevention, and safe use of the digital interface.
- Intermediate accountability can ensure that all local service centres and BCs do their job with maximum transparency. Although customers enter their authentication details into the secure terminal by themselves, they should be constantly reminded never to share these details with anybody, including the intermediaries.
- Grievance redressal is essential for cases of transaction failure to ensure that there is always a way out when something goes wrong, and if the customer’s money has been withdrawn from his or her account without completing the transaction.
The next phase must focus on usability
India has been rather successful in integrating millions of people into the formal financial sector with the help of various financial inclusion schemes. But, in the coming years, the attention must be on usability rather than integration of citizens in the formal financial sector.
It would take a joint effort from all the stakeholders in the ecosystem. On one hand, the banks have to ensure adequate availability and liquidity support to the local access points while, on the other hand, the technology companies have to develop an intuitive system that accommodates different levels of digital literacy.
In short, financial inclusion does not necessarily entail moving everything on a smartphone.
The author is Founder and CEO of Ezeepay, a digital financial services platform.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: La IA pone en duda el objetivo de cero emisiones de Meta: la empresa revisa su plan para 2030
articles.text:
Meta está revisando su objetivo de alcanzar cero emisiones netas en toda su cadena de valor para 2030, una meta fijada en 2020. La compañía atribuye la reevaluación al rápido crecimiento de la infraestructura necesaria para desarrollar y operar servicios de inteligencia artificial (IA). En su informe de sostenibilidad de 2026, también señaló que reconsidera los plazos, la secuencia de trabajo y los objetivos intermedios de corto plazo.
El reporte indica que las emisiones netas de gases de efecto invernadero de Meta aumentaron 45 % en 2025, hasta llegar a 11,8 millones de toneladas métricas de dióxido de carbono equivalente. La mayor parte provino de su cadena de suministro, en particular de los bienes y servicios adquiridos y de los bienes de capital, como los equipos y las instalaciones que necesita para expandir sus operaciones.
La empresa no anunció que abandone su compromiso ni precisó qué fecha o metas podrían cambiar. Rachel Peterson, vicepresidenta de centros de datos, y Blair Swedeen, responsable global de cero emisiones netas y sostenibilidad, escribieron que el crecimiento previsto, la reducción de los costos de energía limpia y los cambios en el sistema energético no se han desarrollado como esperaban.
Los centros de datos elevan la demanda de energía
Los centros de datos alojan los servidores que procesan y almacenan información para los servicios digitales. Las aplicaciones de IA requieren una infraestructura de gran escala, y Meta sostiene que la demanda creció más rápido de lo previsto. La compañía advierte que construir esos centros al ritmo y la escala necesarios plantea retos que el sector no había afrontado antes.
El informe también registra un aumento de 35 % en el consumo eléctrico de Meta durante 2025, a medida que entraron en funcionamiento nuevos centros de datos. La empresa afirma que desde 2020 ha igualado todo su consumo anual de electricidad con energía limpia y renovable, principalmente mediante contratos de compra de energía a largo plazo. En 2025 contrató más de 10 gigavatios adicionales y elevó a más de 30 gigavatios su capacidad contratada de energía limpia.
Igualar el consumo con energía limpia mediante contratos no significa que cada centro de datos funcione exclusivamente con electricidad renovable en todo momento. La disponibilidad de energía, las conexiones a la red y los plazos para construir nuevas instalaciones eléctricas también condicionan cómo se abastecen los centros.
Meta contempla otras fuentes para alimentar sus instalaciones
La compañía ha señalado que podría recurrir a gas natural generado “detrás del medidor” si las empresas eléctricas no pueden cumplir los plazos que requiere su negocio. Esto significa producir electricidad cerca del centro de datos y suministrarla directamente a la instalación, en lugar de depender por completo de una conexión a la red. La opción puede acelerar el suministro, pero también plantea desafíos para reducir las emisiones.
En Luisiana, Meta anunció la ampliación de su centro de datos en Richland Parish hasta una capacidad informática de cinco gigavatios y financia siete centrales eléctricas de gas natural para abastecer el proyecto. Otros centros de datos que la empresa construye en Estados Unidos también podrían utilizar gas, al menos en parte.
La presión climática alcanza a otras tecnológicas
Meta no es la única gran compañía tecnológica que enfrenta mayores emisiones durante la expansión de la IA. Según sus propios reportes, las emisiones de Microsoft aumentaron 25 % en 2025, las de Amazon 16 % y las de Google 18 % bajo la metodología basada en sus objetivos. Las cifras no son directamente equivalentes, porque cada empresa puede aplicar distintas metodologías y límites de medición.
La revisión de Meta deja en suspenso el calendario de uno de sus compromisos climáticos más visibles. La compañía mantiene inversiones en energía limpia y otras tecnologías de bajas emisiones, pero todavía no ha detallado cómo compatibilizará esas iniciativas con la construcción acelerada de centros de datos para IA ni cuándo definirá los cambios a sus objetivos de 2030.

articles.title: Portátiles para trabajar, estudiar o jugar: el Black Friday de El Corte Inglés los tiene rebajados hasta en un 40%
articles.text:
El Black Friday ya está a la vuelta de la esquina. En apenas unos días el día con mayores descuentos del año dará comienzo. Sin embargo, muchas tiendas han querido aprovechar toda la semana, y ya podemos encontrar descuentos de todo tipo. Uno de los mejores ejemplos es el de El Corte Inglés, que ya cuenta con sus descuentos activos. Aunque la tienda tiene rebajados todo tipo de dispositivos, ha hecho especial hincapié en los ordenadores portátiles.
Las ofertas, que estarán disponibles hasta el 29 de noviembre, afectan a portátiles de cualquier tipo: para estudiar, trabajar, jugar, etc. Y entre la multitud de modelos que han rebajado, nosotros hemos querido hacer una pequeña selección de los más destacados:
- ASUS Vivobook S14 por 599,00 euros, una opción equilibrada para el uso diario.
- ASUS Vivobook S16 OLED por 499,00 euros, un modelo con pantalla OLED y gran autonomía.
- HP HyperX OMEN 15 por 1.649,00 euros, un portátil para el que quiera jugar.

- Lenovo Yoga 7 2-en-1 14IPH11 por 1.299,00 euros, un convertible 2 en 1 para tener tablet y portátil al mismo tiempo.
ASUS Vivobook S14
El primer portátil del que hablamos es un modelo que apuesta por ofrecer una gran relación calidad-precio. En primer lugar, porque ofrece uno de los últimos procesadores de Intel, como es el Core 7 350. Le acompañan 8 GB de RAM y 256 GB de almacenamiento SSD, lo que debería ser suficiente para un uso básico. Además, cuenta con una pantalla WUXGA (1.920 x 1.200) de 14 pulgadas y con Windows 11 instalado. Su precio actual es de 599,00 euros.
Portátil ASUS Vivobook S14 S5452MA-TM118W, Intel Core 7-350, 8GB, 256GB SSD, 14", W11 - Plata / Gris
ASUS Vivobook S16 OLED
En el caso de que busquemos un portátil con el que pasar largas jornadas fuera de casa o alejados de un enchufe, este modelo de ASUS es una opción fantástica. Gracias a usar un procesador ARM como el Snapdragon X, su autonomía se ve potenciada sin tener que sacrificar rendimiento, llegando a ofrecer hasta 25 horas de uso. Además, cuenta con la certificación Copilot+PC, lo que significa que podremos aprovechar la IA de manera local. Y por si fuera poco, monta un panel OLED de 16 pulgadas de gran calidad. Ahora mismo su precio es de 499,00 euros.
Portátil ASUS Vivobook S16 OLED S5608QA-U3253W, Copilot+ PC, Qualcomm Snapdragon X, 8GB, 256GB SSD, 16", W11 - Gris

Para el que vaya buscando un portátil gaming, este modelo de HP es una opción muy equilibrada. En primer lugar, nos encontramos con el Intel Core 7 240H, un modelo pensado para poder exprimirlo tanto jugando como editando o haciendo otras tareas. Además, le acompaña la GeForce RTX 5060, con la que se podrá aprovechar su pantalla WUXGA de 165 Hz. Además, cuenta con 16 GB de RAM y un almacenamiento de 1 TB SSD. Ahora mismo, su precio es de 1.649,00euros.
Portátil Gaming HP HyperX OMEN 15-ga0021ns, Intel Core 7 240H, 16GB, 1TB SSD, Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 8GB, 15,3", W11 - Negro

Este portátil de HP es una opción que va un poco más allá en términos de rendimiento. No por su procesador Intel Core 7 150U, que sigue ofreciendo un gran rendimiento, sino porque apuesta por 16 GB de RAM y 512 GB de SSD. Esto garantiza una mayor durabilidad a largo plazo. articles.title: Uber va vous permettre de réserver des billets de train en France
articles.text:
Après l’avoir déployée au Royaume-Uni et en Espagne, Uber lance officiellement la fonctionnalité Uber Trains en France. Les voyageurs pourront ainsi comparer et réserver des billets de train directement depuis l’application Uber. À noter qu’une offre est mise en place dans le cadre du lancement de cette nouvelle fonctionnalité.
Uber va vous permettre de réserver des billets de trains
Uber a annoncé le lancement en France d’une nouvelle fonctionnalité baptisée Uber Trains. Disponible à partir du 30 novembre prochain, celle-ci permet tout simplement de réserver des billets de train directement depuis l’application Uber. Les voyageurs auront accès à des liaisons ferroviaires auprès d’opérateurs français et européens comme SNCF TGV INOUI, TER, Intercités, OUIGO, Eurostar, Trenitalia France, Renfe et Lyria. Il sera donc possible de réserver un billet de train en France ou à destination de Londres ou de l’Espagne, directement depuis l’application Uber.
Les voyageurs pourront aussi comparer les billets de train et retrouver le billet acheté au sein de l’application. Au passage, il sera donc possible de réserver un billet de train, mais aussi un Uber pour rejoindre la gare ou pour rejoindre un hôtel une fois arrivé à destination. Précisons aussi que les avantages des programmes de fidélité des opérateurs ferroviaires sont conservés. L’utilisateur devra seulement renseigner sa carte de fidélité afin de pouvoir profiter de ses avantages, depuis l’application Uber.
Une offre dans le cadre du lancement de cette fonctionnalité
À l’occasion du lancement de la fonctionnalité Uber Trains, Uber met en place une offre : 10 % du montant de l’achat d’un billet de train est converti en crédits Uber, à utiliser pour les déplacements sur le lieu de destination ou lors de commandes Uber Eats. Il faut toutefois vérifier si la réservation de train est éligible à cette offre. Ainsi, un billet de train acheté à 50 € donne droit à 5 € de crédits « à utiliser sur de futurs trajets Uber ou commandes Uber Eats, selon les conditions applicables ». Uber ne précise toutefois pas la durée de cette offre.
Enfin, précisons qu’Uber lance la fonctionnalité Uber Trains, notamment pour favoriser les déplacements moins carbonés. Il sera donc bientôt possible de réserver un billet de train directement depuis l’application Uber, sans passer par une plateforme ou une application externe.

articles.title: Pendant le Black Friday 2026, cette tondeuse Panasonic notée 5/5 passe à 64,99 €
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : Le rasoir électrique Panasonic ER-GY60-H "5 étoiles" à 64,99 € (-14%)
Actuellement noté 5/5 par notre rédaction, le rasoir - tondeuse Panasonic ER-GY60-H s'avère particulièrement efficace pour sculpter la barbe et tondre le corps grâce à son peigne pour zones sensibles. Le Black Friday 2026 est l'occasion de se l'offrir moins cher : il passe à 64,99 € chez Amazon, soit une baisse d'environ 14 % et 10,46 € d'économie.
Panasonic décline son concept inspiré du coupe-choux avec l'ER-GY60-H, un rasoir-tondeuse pensé à la fois pour sculpter la barbe et tondre le corps. L'appareil est également conçu pour le passage sur les zones sensibles grâce à ses accessoires dédiés. Ce modèle à l'approche originale avait convaincu notre laboratoire lors de ses tests.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Panasonic ER-GY60-H descend à 64,99 € chez Amazon, soit environ 14 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (75,45 €). Cela représente une économie de 10,46 € sur ce produit.
Une ergonomie singulière efficace pour tailler la barbe et le corps
Le Panasonic ER-GY60-H adopte une prise en main verticale calquée sur celle d'un rasoir traditionnel, ce qui facilite le tracé des contours et le travail de précision sur les joues ou le cou. Comme nous l'avons souligné dans notre test complet, cette configuration rend la taille de la barbe intuitive et apporte une réelle précision pour délimiter les contours du visage.
Ce format sert aussi les passages sur le corps, d'autant que l'appareil s'accompagne d'un peigne dédié aux zones sensibles pour limiter les irritations. Pour l'entretien quotidien, la tondeuse est intégralement lavable sous l'eau du robinet, ce qui évite l'accumulation de poils sur la tête de coupe.
Panasonic ER-GY60-H
Points forts
- Idéal pour « sculpter » sa barbe.
- Bonnes performances sur le corps.
- Peigne zones sensibles.
- Autonomie.
- Lavable.
Points faibles
- Pas de station de recharge.
- 300 g de mode d’emploi imprimé dans la boîte
- Striures sur les molettes de réglage qui se salissent vite.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Plus d'une heure et demie d'utilisation continue
Sur le plan de l'endurance, l'appareil affiche une autonomie mesurée de 1 heure et 31 minutes, ce qui permet d'enchaîner plusieurs sessions complètes de rasage sans avoir à rebrancher l'alimentation entre deux utilisations.
Le rasoir fait l'impasse sur une station de recharge dédiée et oblige à brancher directement le câble au corps de l'appareil. Les striures des molettes de réglage ont aussi tendance à retenir les résidus de poils, mais ces détails pratiques n'empêcheront pas les utilisateurs réguliers d'apprécier la précision de coupe de ce modèle noté 5/5 à ce jour.
Philips MG 1100/16 : l'autre option face au Panasonic ER-GY60-H
Dans le domaine de l'entretien de précision, le Philips MG 1100/16 mise sur un gabarit très compact pour retoucher les détails de la barbe. Contrairement au modèle de Panasonic qui intègre une batterie rechargeable, le modèle de Philips fonctionne exclusivement avec des piles alcalines, ce qui restreint son usage à des retouches d'appoint plutôt qu'à une tonte intégrale du corps.
Le Philips MG 1100/16 coûte 42,76 € de moins que le Panasonic ER-GY60-H, mais l'ER-GY60-H reste supérieur par sa batterie intégrée et son accessoire pour le corps.
Philips MG 1100/16
Points forts
- Ergonomie.
- Un produit en parfaite adéquation avec sa vocation.
- Précision de la coupe.
- Nettoyage sous l’eau.
Points faibles
- Absence de batterie.
- Pas de trousse de rangement pour les accessoires.

articles.title: Vous allez pouvoir reproduire l’éclairage de Vice City chez vous avec ce pack Philips Hue à prix cassé pour le Black Friday
articles.text:
Les soirées d’hiver se passent souvent devant un écran, lumières éteintes. Philips Hue propose de prolonger l’image au-delà du cadre du téléviseur, en pilotant des lampes connectées au rythme du film, de la série ou du jeu (on vous laisse imaginer avec les lumières de Vice City de GTA 6). Le pack Entertainment 2027 est la dernière déclinaison de cette idée.
Pour le Black Friday, Boulanger l’affiche aujourd’hui à 169,99 € au lieu de 299,99 €, soit 43 % de remise.
Que vaut le pack Philips Hue Entertainment 2027 ?
Le cœur du kit est une caméra qui se fixe sur le téléviseur. Équipée d’un objectif fisheye, un grand angle capable de capter l’intégralité de l’écran, elle analyse les couleurs affichées grâce à un algorithme et les transmet en temps réel aux lampes Hue de la pièce. Concrètement, votre salon virera au rouge quand Dark Vador allumera son sabre laser, ou au bleu turquoise quand les Na’vi nageront dans l’océan dans Avatar, à la manière d’un téléviseur doté de l’Ambilight. Le kit comprend un ruban LED à fixer et une lampe à poser Hue Play.
Ce système fonctionne avec pratiquement tous les téléviseurs, jusqu’à 85 pouces. La caméra capte directement ce qui s’affiche à l’écran : les applications de streaming intégrées au téléviseur, les chaînes de télévision ou encore les consoles de jeu. Côté installation, le boîtier mesure 180,4 × 139,6 mm, pour une hauteur maximale de 68,2 mm, et dispose d’un câble de 2 mètres. Il reste à le fixer au téléviseur et à le configurer dans l’application pour profiter de la synchronisation lumineuse.
La communication avec les éclairages passe par le Bluetooth et le Zigbee, un protocole radio basse consommation très répandu dans la maison connectée. Le système fonctionne sans Wi-Fi. Les réglages se font depuis l’application Philips Hue, compatible avec iOS 17 et les versions ultérieures ainsi qu’Android 12 et les versions ultérieures. Le kit est également annoncé comme compatible avec Alexa, Google Home, Apple HomeKit, SmartThings et Sonos, ainsi qu’avec Matter via un hub tiers.
À ce prix, le pack Philips Hue Entertainment 2027 est-il une bonne affaire ?
Avec 130 € de réduction, soit près de 43 % de moins que son prix de référence, ce pack Philips Hue Entertainment 2027 devient nettement plus intéressant pour le Black Friday. L’éclairage connecté de Philips reste assez coûteux, et cette promotion permet de découvrir la synchronisation lumineuse à moindre frais. C’est d’autant plus intéressant si vous possédez déjà quelques ampoules Hue compatibles : vous n’aurez pas besoin de renouveler toute votre installation pour profiter de l’effet.
Le Black Friday est aussi une bonne occasion de s’équiper avant les longues soirées d’hiver, entre films, séries et sessions de jeu vidéo. Attention toutefois : la synchronisation sera moins convaincante sur les films au format cinéma, lorsque les bandes noires occupent une partie de l’écran. Pour les autres contenus, l’effet promet de donner une tout autre ambiance au salon. Et avec les 130 € économisés, vous pourrez même envisager d’ajouter un ou deux luminaires Hue à votre installation.
Black Friday 2026 : tout ce qu’il faut savoir
Depuis une dizaine d’années, le Black Friday s’est infiltré dans le calendrier commercial des grandes marques et enseignes françaises. Avec l’expérience, on peut vous dire que cet événement fait partie des meilleurs moments pour faire de bonnes affaires.
Les dates du Black Friday
Bien qu’il porte encore le nom du vendredi noir, le Black Friday s’étend désormais sur un mois chez de nombreux revendeurs. Un format moins typique qui lui retire un peu son petit côté FOMO. On dirait presque les soldes, finalement. Mais c’est aussi moins le rush, ce qui est une bonne chose pour ceux qui veulent faire des achats plus raisonnés. Globalement, on peut résumer ce Black Friday en quatre temps forts :
- Début novembre : les avant-premières Black Friday.
- Autour du 20 novembre, selon les enseignes : la Black Week commence généralement plusieurs jours avant le jour J.
- 27 novembre : la date du Black Friday, même si les offres commencent généralement avant et se prolongent le week-end des 28 et 29 novembre.
- 30 novembre : le Cyber Monday.

Globalement, tous les rayons profitent des remises, mais il ne faut pas pour autant se jeter sur les premiers prix bradés. N’oubliez pas que pour les enseignes, ce moment est aussi l’occasion de déstocker de vieux produits, dont les plus remisés frôlent parfois l’obsolescence.

articles.title: Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself
articles.text:
As AI assistants evolve into more capable agents that can access our files, emails, calendar, browser, and more, the amount of trust we’re expected to place in AI companies is growing. One startup called Maple, co-founded by a former Apple engineer who worked on privacy-preserving technologies, is taking a different approach with its AI app, where users’ data remains private — even from the company itself.
“We wanted to build something that was not only encrypted but also could be proven, and that people could go look at the open-source code, and then they could look at what we call trusted execution environments,” explains Maple co-founder and CEO Mark Suman. “They can look at and verify the code that’s running on our servers, so they don’t really have to take our word for it.”
“They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled,” he adds.
The idea of trust is Maple’s larger theme, as the startup proposes that there’s a way to build an AI app where consumers don’t have to trade privacy for convenience, as its competitors often require with their invasive privacy policies and data collection practices, and sometimes even training on users’ personal data.
Instead of asking users to trust that Maple won’t misuse their personal data, it’s attempting to build a business where it can’t access that data in the first place.
Like other AI apps on the market, Maple allows users to engage in a chat experience where they ask questions and get answers. Meanwhile, its newly launched desktop app, Maple Work, offers a more agentic experience where the AI can control your computer, work with your files and apps, and control your browser to get online tasks handled.
With the company’s recently closed $5.3 million round, it’s moving on to its next product — a cloud-based agent that will be able to continue its work even if your computer isn’t on. This addition would make Maple more competitive with other popular consumer AI services, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, and other AI agents that work over chat.
The oversubscribed seed round was led by Epic Ventures, with participation from Draper Associates, Planetary VC, and Epoch VC, and follows a pre-seed angel round of under a million. Maple plans to raise a Series A in the first half of 2027, given the investor interest.
Suman, who previously spent six years at Apple, already had a background where AI and privacy overlapped, he tells TechCrunch.
At Apple, he worked on AI and machine learning with a particular focus on computer vision. Given Apple’s stance on consumer privacy, the challenge he faced was building products that would protect people’s identity while benefiting from computer vision techniques. His co-founder, Anthony Ronning (CTO), has a background in defense tech, security, and networking.
Ronning started the company that later became Maple AI back in 2023, initially as a privacy-focused fintech. When Suman teamed up with Ronning in August 2024, the idea to create Maple AI was born. The following January, the product became available to the public as a mobile app.
The app offers a familiar interface for those used to AI chatbots, but under the hood it runs a variety of open models, including versions of DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Inkling from Thinking Machines, Google’s Gemma, and OpenAI’s GPT OSS. Users can pick and choose the models they want or, for a simpler experience, just toggle between a quick model and the more powerful one.
The models themselves run inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) — meaning a server with hardware encryption on it — within a U.S.-based data center. (Maple also offers support for European customers through a partner that runs its server in Europe.)
“We actually don’t have access to [the data] while it’s inside the TEE,” explains Suman. “The data gets encrypted first on your device using a unique password that’s only known by you, the user — we don’t have access to it. It then goes into this TEE, and it gets decrypted inside there. The AI does its thing, and then it re-encrypts it with your password and sends it back to you,” he continues. “So we provide an end-to-end experience that’s very easy for the user, but we actually don’t have access to the raw data as it’s in flight or even when it’s at rest,” he adds.
This allows Maple to protect its users’ data, even from outsiders — like if hackers breached its system or the government came with a subpoena, for instance. All it could do would be to hand over an encrypted file.
“We just simply don’t want access to it,” Suman says of customers’ data. “That’s not part of our business model. And we also don’t want it to be part of our threat model.”
With the new desktop app, Maple is looking to small businesses that may want to benefit from AI without the data privacy risks. Inside the app, there’s an integration store where users can connect with other apps, like their Gmail or calendar. The desktop app can also spin up a subagent that works inside another AI app you may have on your desktop, like Claude, Codex, or others that support the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). This allows customers to use their preferred AI app for specific tasks, without having to give it all their information — just what’s needed for the given task.
Next year, Maple plans to enter the enterprise market with pilot work, where it will offer its own version of zero data retention. (Maple doesn’t retain most of the customers’ data, but when it has to, that data is encrypted.) It’s now in the process of completing SOC 2 compliance and security audits to get ready for this expansion.
The company declined to share its registered customer numbers but noted it’s seen 60x growth over the past three months, as people have been looking for ways to increase their security with AI.
Maple currently generates revenue via subscriptions, which are comparable to those from other AI model providers. Its Pro plan is $20 per month, and it offers two Max plans, Max and Max Plus, at $100 and $200 per month, respectively.
The Austin- and San Francisco-based startup is a team of four and is actively hiring.

articles.title: Asus could go back to 8GB of RAM in entry-level and mid-range PCs as memory prices soar
articles.text:
Facepalm: With memory prices continuing to track upward, Asus is reportedly considering reducing the amount of RAM in some of its mid-range laptops from 16GB to 8GB. Explaining the potential move, Asus co-CEO S.Y. Hsu said that the rising prices have reached an inflection point where the company can no longer afford to pass all additional costs on to buyers without potentially losing customers.
Talking to investors at Asus' Q3 2026 earnings call, Hsu said that the company is likely to "adjust the memory configuration" in its entry-level and mid-range PCs to 8GB following the latest Windows 11 update, which Microsoft promises will make the operating system faster and more responsive on devices with just 8GB of RAM.
Hsu claimed that Asus worked closely with Microsoft on memory optimization in Windows 11 and that the changes implemented in the new build work as advertised. He added that 16GB had become the default memory standard on Windows devices to ensure a lag-free user experience, but the "adjustments" in the updated build ensure that even 8GB offers an "acceptable" experience.
Hsu's statement comes just weeks after Microsoft released Windows 11 26H2 with a series of optimizations aimed at improving performance on PCs with just 8GB of memory. Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's EVP of Windows and Devices, claimed that the changes will make Windows up to 20% more responsive and boost multitasking performance by up to 40% on devices with 8GB of RAM.
Redmond, however, acknowledged that Windows 11 PCs with 16GB or 32GB of RAM will still be better at gaming and multitasking, but added that 8GB PCs will help users "do more" without a noticeable drop in performance. That said, the data shared by Microsoft comes from its own lab tests under controlled conditions, so don't expect as much of a performance boost in real-world use cases.
It is worth noting that in May 2026, Microsoft actually raised the recommended memory configuration for Windows 11 devices from 16GB to 32GB. However, faced with skyrocketing memory prices, the company removed that recommendation shortly afterward and pushed out the latest update designed to improve memory usage in Windows 11 devices.

articles.title: Virgin, Koodo, Fido drop wireless plans by $5 ahead of Black Friday
articles.text:
Several Canadian wireless providers have launched Black Friday deals on phones, but so far there hasn’t been much in the way of discounted wireless plans. However, things are starting to shift, with the Big Three flanker brands knocking $5 off the price of some plans.
Bell’s Virgin Plus, Telus’ Koodo, and Rogers’ Fido have all tweaked pricing on some of their plans. All three offer a 60GB Canada-wide plan — it used to cost $50/mo but now costs $45/mo across all three providers.
The $45/60GB plan otherwise hasn’t changed, offering 5G data, unlimited Canada-wide minutes and unlimited international texting across all three, as well as other standard features like hotspot, voicemail, etc.
Virgin Plus and Koodo also dropped their 60GB CAN/U.S./MEX plan from $55 to $50. Fido initially didn’t offer this plan either, but as I was writing the story, it added a matching $50/60GB CAN/U.S./MEX plan. Notably, Koodo’s plan includes two years of unlimited international calling to 27 countries with this plan, while Fido limits the U.S./Mexico roaming and calling to the first 12 months with the plan. Virgin doesn’t appear to limit either of these features with its plan.
Finally, Koodo dropped the price of its 100GB Canada-wide plan from $60 to $55. Neither Virgin nor Fido offer a similar 100GB plan.
All of the plans outlined above include autopay discounts, so if you don’t want to do automatic payments, you can expect to pay $5 to $10 more per month.
The three providers also have a $40/10GB plan that hasn’t changed.
Generally, these pricing shifts are in the right direction, but Virgin, Koodo, and Fido still aren’t the best value options out there. For comparison, Freedom Mobile has a $40/70GB plan with CAN/U.S./MEX roaming, unlimited talk and text in Canada and 120+ destinations, and 1GB/mo of Roam Beyond data in those same destinations, as well as a similar plan with 125GB of data for $45/mo.
And fellow Telus flanker brand Public Mobile has a $40/75GB CAN/U.S./MEX plan available now as well, plus customers can get an extra 25 per cent off with a promo code for even greater savings.

articles.title: Galaxy Watch 8 Classic fica abaixo dos R$ 1.600 no esquenta Black do Mercado Livre
articles.text:
Galaxy Watch 8 Classic fica abaixo dos R$ 1.600 no esquenta Black do Mercado Livre
Galaxy Watch 8 Classic com design tradicional, tela AMOLED e coroa giratória atinge o menor preço que já vimos, com desconto de 66% no Pix com cupom
O Galaxy Watch 8 Classic está saindo por R$ 1.527 no Pix com cupom DESCONTOSMELI no Mercado Livre. O smartwatch da Samsung, com coroa giratória e sensores avançados, atinge o menor preço já visto pelo Achados, com desconto de 66% sobre o original de R$ 4.499 na semana da Black Friday 2026.
Esta oferta é o menor preço que já encontramos para o Galaxy Watch 8 Classic LTE 46 mm. Nas outras 17 ofertas publicadas desde março de 2026, o melhor foi R$ 1.628,06 (Mercado Livre, 16/10/2026).
Um dos melhores smartwatches da Samsung, o Galaxy Watch 8 Classic se destaca do Watch 8 graças ao design tradicional reforçado pela coroa giratória, que possui funções de navegação por menus e apps. O corpo de aço inoxidável de 46 resiste a até 5 ATM, sendo apto para uso em esportes aquáticos.
Seus sensores avançados suportam mais de 100 tipos de atividades esportivas, como caminhada, corrida e ciclismo, e incluem diversos recursos de qualidade de vida, como eletrocardiograma (ECG), medidores do sono, da saúde da mulher e da oxigenação do sangue (SpO2).
Este wearable ainda pode fazer a diferença em uma situação de risco: graças ao 4G/LTE, ausente na versão BT do Watch 8, ele pode enviar alertas para contatos específicos e ligar para números como 190 (polícia) e 192 (ambulância) no caso de uma emergência médica, sem depender de um celular.
A tela AMOLED de 1,34″ do Watch 8 Classic, que não recebeu um modelo sucessor no último Unpacked, possui brilho de até 3.000 nits. Ela reproduz imagens com cores excelentes e garante a visibilidade em qualquer lugar, enquanto o vidro Cristal de Safira a protege contra quedas e pancadas.
Seu chip Exynos W1000, aliado a 2 GB de RAM e 64 GB de espaço interno, suporta a instalação e execução local de apps. A bateria de 445 mAh resiste a um dia inteiro de uso, segundo a Samsung, e suporta carregamento de 10 W.
O Galaxy Watch 8 Classic (R$ 1.527 no Pix com cupom DESCONTOSMELI) possui conectividade Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5.3 e GPS multibanda, além do já citado 4G/LTE.
O esquenta da Black Friday 2026 já começou: lojas como o Mercado Livre se anteciparam à data principal nesta sexta-feira (27) e oferecerão cupons e promoções em eletrônicos com condições especiais até o fim de novembro.

articles.title: TCL Debuts 120 Hz IPS LCD Drawing Just 1 W in Lenovo Yoga Prototype Laptop
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 24th 2026
TCL Debuts 120 Hz IPS LCD Drawing Just 1 W in Lenovo Yoga Prototype Laptop
TCL CSOT has been working on some significant display innovations recently, including its recent announcement of 1250 Hz QHD OLED monitors at DTC 2026. Also at DTC 2026, TCL has reportedly (via Notebookcheck) shown off a new 14-inch LCD prototype drawing as little as 1 W of power in a new Lenovo Yoga Pro laptop prototype. While it's unknown exactly what luminance settings and refresh rates are used to bring the power down so significantly, the display is said to reach a peak brightness somewhere between 300 and 400 nits. 
The display itself is called an Ultra Low Power Milliwatt Class Notebook Display, and TCL CSOT says that it uses an oxide panel with an "FTT high-transmittance pixel design for high luminous efficiency," allowing it to reach such low power draw. The display has an adaptive refresh rate range of 1-120 Hz, which could theoretically be used in conjunction with technology like FreeSync or G-Sync to enable more efficient mobile gaming in laptops—especially now that iGPUs like the one in Intel's Arc G3 Extreme are capable of high-speed gaming away from the wall.The LCD panel is also surprisingly lightweight, weighing in at just 100 g, which could make it an attractive option for thin-n-light laptops, like the Lenovo Yoga Pro it was previewed in. Also of note is that the display uses IPS tech, not OLED, so it will be less likely to flickering, which can be an annoying side effect of PWM dimming commonly used on OLED displays. That should also theoretically make it easier to color calibrate than OLED using traditional calibration tools.

articles.title: 'Get the foundation right': AWS CEO Matt Garman says AI safety can't rely on an 'emergency brake', calls for companies to be bold in their deployment
articles.text:
'Get the foundation right': AWS CEO Matt Garman says AI safety can't rely on an 'emergency brake', calls for companies to be bold in their deployment
AWS CEO looks to play down fears over AI
- AWS CEO Matt Garman outlines thoughts on AI safety and security
- Garman likens AI to car safety, with multiple systems ensuring security
- AWS re:Invent starts next week, with AI set to be front and center
AWS CEO Matt Garman has urged companies not to give into fears around AI when deploying the technology across their organizations.
In a blog post published days before the company's annual AWS re:Invent conference, Garman noted that when it comes to AI, and its security and safety in particular, "the hype is making us worse at risk management".
Garman went on to note that trusting AI models to behave and operate in the same way forever is a potentially foolish approach, as models change so often that the trends they show today may not be the case in a few months time.
AI risks
Garman's post began with an understanding of the potential that many organizations see in AI, and a recognition that this is causing great excitement across multiple industries.
But as he notes, organizations aren't hanging around, despite these rollouts coming as, “policymakers are debating guardrails. Model providers are publishing principles. Industry leaders are calling for standards."
“It is already possible to make better security choices through solid engineering,” Garman said, calling for caution, and using the example of car safety as an analogy.
He noted how drivers do not solely rely on their emergency brake as the only protection when out on the road, as the primary brakes, steering, suspension, and navigation all work together to keep drivers safe - with the emergency brakes as a last resort.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
“AI systems should be engineered the same way,” he contended. “That work can and should be happening right now, alongside the policy conversations.”
Garman's blog comes as AWS prepares to unveil its latest products and services at Re:Invent 2026, with the CEO set to open the event with his traditional keynote.
He noted that, “the organizations that lead with AI won’t be the ones that are just using the best models...they’ll be the ones that also invest in the best engineering discipline around them.”
With concerns around AI model security at an all-time high following the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident, and Kimi K3 breaching GitHub, Garman was also keen to address these worries, telling customers not to give in to fear, and pursue innovation.
Looking at malicious model behavior, Garman used the example of water affecting a house, noting, “Water doesn’t want to get into your basement, but if there’s a crack in the foundation, it will find it."
“AI models work the same way," he pointed out. "They’re optimizers. They push toward whatever objective they’re given, and if the boundaries leave a gap, they’ll go through it.”
“You don’t get safety by avoiding scrutiny. You get it by building systems that can withstand it.”

articles.title: Shared CXL memory pools come with steep software tax that could stall multi-server scaling — UT Arlington shares real-world test that measured four servers sharing the same pool at SC26
articles.text:
Shared CXL memory pools come with steep software tax that could stall multi-server scaling — UT Arlington shares real-world test that measured four servers sharing the same pool at SC26
The results land as memory makers push shared CXL pools as a home for AI’s KV cache.
Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington and Intel measured what happens when four servers share one pool of CXL memory on real hardware. In a presentation shared at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), they found that because the hardware doesn’t automatically keep shared data updated across servers, necessary software overhead adds a 3-5µ (microsecond) delay per lock, each time servers access the same data. These minute delays effectively cancel out the benefits — a finding that comes as CXL memory pools are being proposed as a potential AI KV cache solution.
Locks work like traffic signals for shared data: a server has to claim the lock before it changes something in the pool, and the other servers wait until it releases it. This way, no two servers overwrite the same data at the same time. Within a given server, the CPU’s hardware handles that handoff in a fraction of a microsecond, but across these servers, software is in charge of enforcement.
The setup comprises four 86-core Intel Xeon 6787P servers with 256GB of DRAM each, connected over PCIe 5.0 to one CXL memory box. The switch, which UT Arlington’s Peiran Du called “the only commercially available product we can use,” caps their setup at four servers. The catch is that there is no cross-host cache coherence or atomic operations on “a real four-host CXL shared-memory system.”
This means no synced CPU caches and no hardware atomics between servers to build locks on, so software has to handle both. Writers publish their cached copy out to the pool and wait for it to finish, while readers throw out stale copies before reading, with the locks built from plain reads and writes, such as Lamport’s fast mutex. CXL 3.0 defines a hardware fix for the caches, called Back-Invalidate, but the researchers hadn’t received vendor confirmation that their platform supports it.
Aside from the lock acquisition penalty, which is “roughly an order of magnitude higher than local hardware spin locks,” there is a visibility cost: “one-way cross-host visibility is about 1 µs.” This is 0.94 µs, one way, compared to 1.91 µs for an RDMA write on their 400Gb/s InfiniBand, so the link isn’t the cause. A local compare-and-swap takes about 100 ns and, across servers, a lock’s median is 3.7 µs if uncontended, but 132 µs at the 95th percentile with several servers on one lock.
The result: breadth-first search (BFS), a standard graph algorithm and a common benchmark, “gains nothing from adding a second host,” and was actually slower on four servers than on one, at 0.74s versus 0.55s. This was mostly not from the locks and barriers, which were only about 3.5% of its runtime, but due to the repeated flushing of shared state at every level.
On the other hand, throughput for a hash table — using independent buckets and per-host allocators — grew almost linearly when adding hosts. Triangle counting, another standard graph benchmark, also had a runtime reduction of more than half when scaling from one to four hosts.
| Scaling on shared CXL memory (UT Arlington/Intel, 32 threads per server) |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Workload | One server | Four servers | Change | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Graph search (BFS) | 0.55 s | 0.74 s | About 35% slower | 
| Triangle counting | 2.43 s | 0.97 s | About 60% less time | 
| Hash table, 95% reads | 4.1M ops/s | 16.6M ops/s | About 4x throughput | 
Why it matters
Those costs matter, in part, because shared CXL pools are emerging as a new home for KV cache — an AI model’s stored record of a conversation’s state — once it outgrows GPU memory and a server’s own DRAM. The CXL Consortium’s SC26 session description says cloud providers and GPU makers “have highlighted CXL memory pooling as an effective approach for improving KV cache access.”
SK hynix, which makes CXL memory modules, showed a design that hands KV cache between GPU servers through a shared pool and claims 2.6x faster time to first token than standard RDMA setups. Its abstract also claims 3.0x lower P99 latency and 1.9x higher throughput. Micron, at SC26’s CXL Pavilion, showed its Abaco reference design of pooled CXL memory shared across rack servers and GPUs. It claimed 10x to 30x agentic AI gains, with famfs support for apps like Nvidia’s Dynamo.
The need is real, even if efficiency gains have led to less cache needed per token. Vikram Sharma Mailthody of Nvidia Research said at SC26’s Emerging Storage panel that his own analysis of open models on Hugging Face shows KV per token falling “by 50% every twelve months” with “up to 78 times reduction so far,” giving the example that 128K context took “about 64 gigabytes” three years ago and now takes less than one. But context lengths are heading toward millions of tokens, and “the product of those two will keep increasing,” he said.
Agents also add to the demand. Earlier in the conference, a workshop talk by Argonne National Laboratory and RIT researchers, based on public AI serving traces, showed that a “session calls again ~2 min later, once its tools return: a 160 GiB recency cache keeps 1% of its context,” needing the GPU to recompute the rest, or about 99%. Recomputation is significantly slower and more demanding, and memory is needed to cache more.
That makes it a capacity problem more than a speed problem. “Memory capacity is becoming a dominant factor. Memory latencies have not been seen as a primary problem yet,” Mailthody said. An agent’s context only has to survive a gap of a couple of minutes. It’s also ideal for any KV cache solution to be as inexpensive as possible, and given that a 128GB DIMM costs more than four times that of a 64GB DIMM last year. According to Intel’s Anil Godbole on SC26’s CXL panel, being able to add capacity past the DIMM slot limit — including reusing DDR4 — bolsters the case for CXL even further.
It doesn’t hurt that the KV cache handoff is write-once, read-many, which is the type of pattern that actually scaled in testing, although UT Arlington did not specifically test KV cache. Researchers behind OCEAN, a CXL emulator, backed this idea in the same paper session as UT Arlington, saying that software coherence is fine for read-heavy work, with hardware essential as writes climb. Its abstract reports that hardware coherence, at least in emulation, can give an 11x improvement at full coverage on Tigon database workloads.
Limitations still exist, which is why SK hynix, for one, is relying on “novel locking and coherence protocols” for its design. Hardware isn’t quite there yet, and Back-Invalidate might “be pretty costly,” Du said, suggesting that both hardware and software coherence may be required.
Micron, which built prototype KV cache sharing into Nvidia’s Dynamo, noted two primary failure cases in a CXL Consortium presentation last month: where the writer’s data never reaches the pool, and where the reader never sees the updates. The first can be fixed by producers flushing before blocks are published, so unflushed blocks can never be found. The second is fixed with a consumer flush, that is, invalidation of their cached lines, before reading. These are the fixes and costs that UT Arlington was measuring.
Micron cut its flushing cost by flushing each slot only once, which works because KV cache is content-addressed — a slot in the pool that hasn’t changed stays coherent after its first flush. Micron’s presentation also notes that neither failure causes a crash. Instead, the read returns plausible-looking data, and the output is wrong in subtle ways, with the wrong tokens on some requests under cache pressure.
Working against CXL as a solution is the fact that the memory pooling only reaches within a rack today, Godbole said; it doesn’t span a full data center. Marvell and Penguin Solutions, in collaboration and in addition to others like Lightelligence, have shown or announced memory expansion and pooling over optical links, which could stretch pooling past a single rack. CXL is also “not the protocol to ferry such big data,” Godbole added, as it’s built for smaller reads and writes, 64 bytes at a time, closer to how a CPU uses RAM. For bulk transfers, he said, RDMA is more efficient.
A research system called Beluga, in a paper published on arXiv a year ago, had KV cache in “a commercial CXL switch-based memory pool” with time to first token cut by 89.6% and throughput raised 7.35x compared with an RDMA-based setup once its cache was filled. This suggests some optimization could improve the usefulness of the technology, too.
CXL is clearly a hit or miss with how it is actually used being a main concern, with “a gap between the [CXL] spec and the implementation from different vendors,” according to UT Arlington’s Jia Rao. SK hynix’s second-generation CMM-DDR5, at 256GB and using CXL 3.2, has only been shown, and the device its KV cache design uses to select what to send is still what the company’s Younghoon Min called a “research prototype.” These are early times, and the enterprise landscape is simultaneously changing quickly.
On paper, shared CXL pools do fit the KV handoff idea, but until a commercial switch ships with confirmed coherence across servers, the best we have is KV cache numbers from vendor demos and research prototypes. Back-Invalidate should cut the software overhead UT Arlington measured, but Du expects it to add delays of its own; production systems would likely need a combination of hardware coherence and software approaches like Micron’s.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Vehicle-to-Grid: Great Idea or Unrealistic Dream? (Part 2)
articles.text:
Part 1 provided an overview of vehicle-to-grid (V2G) and its presumed benefits. This part looks at some real-world concerns and considerations.
V2G sounds good so far, but there are “issues”
Despite the presumed benefits, there are problems associated with V2G, starting with the charging hardware and technology. I suspect these will be worked out in a reasonable time, as vehicles increasingly come equipped with bidirectional chargers that can transfer power from the grid to the battery and send it back to the grid just as easily. Further, the higher-level management of the grid, power flows, supply/demand, pricing, monitoring, and other issues certainly are complicated, but let’s assume these, too, will eventually be worked out at some point.
It’s the implications of V2G that have me skeptical.
The good news is that it distributes energy storage, at least to a modest extent. That’s generally good for system resiliency, reliability, and integrity, at least in principle. V2G works on the premise that many cars and drivers will use only a fraction of their battery capacity most of the time; this approach optimizes battery utilization to get more out of the same components—that’s also a virtue.
The bad news is that your vehicle is now part of a bigger, much more complicated system, with all the idiosyncrasies, baggage, and issues that it brings. The simple act of hopping into the car for a short, medium, or longer drive now involves the simple question: Was there enough charge last time I parked it? You may have to check whether your battery pack was drained a little too much while it was parked and connected.
Going somewhere may become more complicated, as your needs will have to be synced with what the grid “master” says. Will you need to file the equivalent of a flight plan or consult your personal travel-charge app before going out, and do so some hours in advance?
What if the V2G oversight software decides, rightly or not, that it needs your battery’s energy right now more than you do? Perhaps the “system” algorithm will decide that the needs of the grid outweigh your own, as in, as in “the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few” (thank you, Mr. Spock).
Or perhaps a bug or misunderstanding between your vehicle’s battery management system (BMS) and the sophisticated V2G management software says, “you’re already good to go, no more power for you,” when you actually are not?
There’s another “oops” factor: V2G proponents make the implicit assumption that many of these EVs/HEVs are parked in the owner’s driveway or garage when not in use and hooked up to a personal charger. Reality is that only about half the owners in the U.S. have an assured, private parking arrangement (and most of these are without charging setup), while the rest instead rely on public charging; worldwide, the percentage without their own driveway as a potential hotspot is far higher.
There are also technical concerns. No one knows yet what those V2G-initiated moderate charge/discharge cycles will do to the life of the car battery pack. Some evidence suggests that it’s not good and may shorten the battery life anywhere from slightly to moderately; it depends on many variables such as battery chemistry and construction, along with cycling specifics.
Finally, every time you transfer energy from a source to a load, there will be inefficiencies and power losses, and these add up. In fact, those losses can soon negate any system-level benefits you were expecting to see.
Reality hits, but how?
Will car owners be willing to give up their hard-earned battery charge status for a few dollars and the “greater good,” especially if it may leave them out of juice when they suddenly need it? Will people accept adding yet another complication to their lives for what was previously a simple task? Will they need to invoke an AI-driven app on their phone to figure out if they can actually make a quick, unplanned afternoon trip to visit a friend 50 miles away?
Plus, there are unavoidable issues of cost and added vehicle complexity for a non-critical feature of uncertain benefit. A BOM cost of $100 to $200 for the bidirectional charger translates to another $500 to $1,000 in the customer price, a major add-on in a world of increasing car unaffordability. It’s yet another thing to break and need diagnostics and replacement at the module level.
I suspect that a few will go along with the V2G scheme, but many won’t, as it’s just not worth the headache, complexity, and risk for such a modest benefit. Proponents talk about V2G as if it is 1) inherently a good thing; 2) obviously going to happen; and 3) something whose only real obstacle is people’s reluctance to be team players. To me, it’s another case where academics and engineers posit a wonderful global solution, without being sensitive to the reality “on the ground” of how people live their lives and what their priorities actually are.
I’ll say this about V2G: It has a snappy name and acronym with the right words, and often that’s a big help in getting upfront attention and stirring up the hype. But when it comes to power and energy, it’s critical to recognize that the laws of physics dictate that there is no free lunch. Saying “I’ll get the energy I need from you, and you’ll get yours from me, and we’ll both have what we need” seems a little too good to be true.
To those who say all the problems can be worked out, I like to keep in mind the maxim to “keep it simple” and the question, “Is the pain worth the gain?” I can see the benefits of V2H—vehicle-to-home—for keeping the house power going in the event of a blackout or similar, but as for sending your stored energy to the anonymous collective grid: Well, I am not seeing that.
Let’s check back in five or 10 years and see where V2G stands in vehicle installations (of course, its inclusion may be mandated by regulations!) in use, as well as actual use. I suspect it will still be talked about in “dreamy” terms but will not have developed much traction on the ground.

articles.title: Black Friday 2026 : 3 PC gamer Cybertek, de la RTX 5060 au monstre RTX 5080
articles.text:
À trois jours du Black Friday du vendredi 27 novembre, Cybertek a déjà baissé le prix de deux de ses PC gamer équipés de cartes GeForce RTX 50, dans le cadre de son opération Black Month. Nous avons retenu trois configurations, de la RTX 5060 à la RTX 5080, en vérifiant sur chaque fiche les composants réels et en nous appuyant sur nos tests de cartes graphiques et de processeurs quand nous les avons menés.
Aucun de ces trois PC n’est passé entre nos mains : ils sont classés du moins cher au plus cher, et nous citons nos tests des composants quand nous les avons menés. La sélection va de la RTX 5060 à la RTX 5080, et deux des trois machines affichent une remise, de 4 % à 8 % par rapport au prix barré. La plus forte économie revient au BLACKCYBER, avec 100 € de moins, soit 8 % sous son prix barré.
- Cybertek BLACKCYBER RTX 5060 et Ryzen 7 5700X à 1 099,99 € au lieu de 1 199,99 € (-8 %)
- Cybertek BLACKROCK RTX 5060 Ti et Ryzen 5 8400F à 1 349,99 € au lieu de 1 399,99 € (-4 %)
- Cybertek BLACKSAPPHIRE RTX 5080 et Ryzen 7 9800X3D à 3 299,99 €
Cybertek BLACKCYBER : la RTX 5060 avec un watercooling 240 mm et 100 € de remise, à 1 099,99 €
Ce PC associe une GeForce RTX 5060 de 8 Go à un Ryzen 7 5700X refroidi par un watercooling M.RED Serenity 240, avec 16 Go de DDR4 et un SSD de 512 Go. La carte mère MSI A520M Vector intègre le Wi-Fi, et Windows 11 Home est fourni en version d’essai de 90 jours. Nous ne l’avons pas testé.
✅ Points forts
- 100 € de remise : le prix passe de 1 199,99 € à 1 099,99 €, le plus bas de la sélection.
- Un processeur 8 cœurs bien refroidi : le Ryzen 7 5700X est placé sous un watercooling de 240 mm plutôt que sous un simple ventirad.
- À savoir : les 16 Go de DDR4 tiennent sur une seule barrette, et le SSD de 512 Go se remplit vite avec quelques gros jeux.
Cybertek BLACKROCK : la RTX 5060 Ti sur une plateforme AM5 en DDR5, à 1 349,99 €
Le BLACKROCK passe à la plateforme AM5 d’AMD avec un Ryzen 5 8400F (6 cœurs, 12 threads), 16 Go de DDR5 à 6 000 MHz et une GeForce RTX 5060 Ti OC de 8 Go. Le processeur est refroidi par un watercooling MSI MAG Coreliquid A13 de 240 mm, sur une carte mère MSI MAG A620AM Gaming EVO WIFI5. Nous ne l’avons pas testé.
✅ Points forts
- Une base plus récente : socket AM5 et DDR5 à 6 000 MHz, quand le BLACKCYBER reste en AM4 et en DDR4.
- Un watercooling 240 mm : le MSI MAG Coreliquid A13 refroidit le Ryzen 5 8400F.
- À savoir : la remise se limite à 50 €, les 16 Go de DDR5 tiennent sur une seule barrette et le SSD de 500 Go est le plus petit de la sélection. Cybertek propose un SSD de 1 To en option, pour 159,99 € de plus.
Cybertek BLACKSAPPHIRE : la RTX 5080 et le Ryzen 7 9800X3D noté 9/10, à 3 299,99 €
Notre test de la GeForce RTX 5080 lui a attribué 8/10 : en 4K, avec le DLSS 4 et la génération multi-images, elle dépasse 150 images par seconde dans Cyberpunk 2077 en path tracing. Le Ryzen 7 9800X3D qui l’accompagne a obtenu 9/10 dans notre test du Ryzen 7 9800X3D, porté par ses 96 Mo de cache L3. Cybertek complète avec 32 Go de DDR5 à 6 000 MHz et un SSD Samsung 990 EVO de 2 To. Nous ne l’avons pas testé.
✅ Points forts
- Une alimentation de 1 050 W : la M.RED MRR-1050, certifiée 80+ Gold, laisse de la marge à la RTX 5080, mesurée à 368 W en charge dans notre test.
- Un watercooling 360 mm : le M.RED Onyx refroidit le Ryzen 7 9800X3D, contre 240 mm sur les deux autres PC de la sélection.
- À savoir : aucun prix barré n’est affiché sur ce modèle, et sans génération multi-images la RTX 5080 ne devance la RTX 4080 que de 17 % en 4K, selon notre test.
Black Friday 2026 : comment Cybertek déroule ses promos sur les PC gamer
Le Black Friday tombe le vendredi 27 novembre et le Cyber Monday le lundi 30, mais les configurations de cette sélection sont déjà en ligne à leur prix actuel. Chez Cybertek, l’opération s’affiche sous le nom de Black Month, avec un paiement en quatre fois sans frais par Alma proposé du 2 novembre au 2 décembre, sous réserve d’acceptation. Les prix d’un PC monté dépendent du coût de chaque composant et peuvent bouger d’ici vendredi : noter dès maintenant celui de la configuration qui vous intéresse permet de comparer sereinement. Pour suivre les autres offres, notre page Black Friday réunit chaque jour celles retenues par la rédaction.
Comment savoir si un PC gamer tout monté vaut vraiment son prix ?
Le nom de la carte graphique ne suffit pas : regardez la quantité de mémoire vidéo, 8 Go sur les RTX 5060 et 5060 Ti de cette sélection, contre 16 Go sur la RTX 5080. Vérifiez ensuite les composants moins visibles, comme le nombre de barrettes de RAM, la capacité du SSD et la puissance de l’alimentation. Windows est souvent livré en version d’essai : chez Cybertek, la licence définitive coûte 159,99 € de plus en édition Home, une somme à intégrer au budget. articles.title: NetApp advances intelligent data infrastructure for AI
articles.text:
Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT
Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.
The shift places new demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.
“I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”
Kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.)
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:
Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:
Insight #1: Intelligent data infrastructure must support competing AI workloads.
Enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The company’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.
“Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he said during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”
The demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.
“What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:
Insight #2: Technology partnerships help enterprises put AI infrastructure to work.
Modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing new AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.
“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”
NetApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.
“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”
The integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.
“Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole said during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”
Another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.
“AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he said during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Alvaro Celis and James Cole:
Insight #3: Autonomous infrastructure requires more than intelligent automation.
As enterprises introduce autonomous agents into infrastructure management, intelligent data infrastructure must accommodate increasingly complex operational demands. NetApp’s unified control plane, delivered through NetApp Console, is designed to reduce routine administrative work through policy-driven automation. In one keynote demonstration, agents responded to a nighttime performance anomaly, according to Sandeep Singh, senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp.
“Agents can, in real time, implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there’s compliance to the boundary conditions there,” he told theCUBE. “And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved, and there’s no noisy neighbor effect. And there’s an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up.”
Automation, however, can’t resolve organizational questions about data ownership and responsibility. As enterprises extend intelligent data infrastructure across applications and environments, leadership must establish accountability for the information those systems rely on, according to Helen Yu, founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., who appeared alongside Singh.
“It’s not a storage problem. It’s a leadership and accountability issue,” she said during the event. “When teams don’t have access to … trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Helen Yu and Sandeep Singh:
