articles.title: Google prepara nuevas restricciones para frenar a los agentes de IA que navegan solos en Chrome
articles.text:
Google explora un sistema de permisos para limitar lo que los agentes de inteligencia artificial pueden hacer al navegar por internet. La propuesta busca que el navegador establezca esos límites: el usuario podría autorizar a un agente a visitar ciertas páginas, pero restringir otras direcciones y acciones, como completar formularios o pulsar botones.
La iniciativa se plantea como una extensión del protocolo WebDriver BiDi, utilizado para automatizar navegadores. Ingenieros de Google publicaron en Chromium una intención de crear un prototipo , por lo que la idea aún está en una etapa experimental. No hay una fecha anunciada para su llegada a Chrome.
Los agentes de IA pueden ejecutar tareas en línea siguiendo instrucciones, desde buscar productos hasta navegar entre páginas. Para hacerlo, interactúan con el navegador: abren sitios, leen su contenido y realizan acciones. La propuesta de Google plantea que Chrome participe en la definición y aplicación de los permisos, en lugar de dejar esos controles únicamente en manos de cada desarrollador de agentes.
El usuario podría limitar sitios y acciones
Según el modelo descrito, un agente empezaría con permisos restringidos y tendría que solicitar acceso a páginas o funciones específicas. El usuario o el propio navegador decidiría qué autorizar. Por ejemplo, alguien podría permitir que la IA revise una tienda en línea y compare productos, pero bloquear el acceso a una web externa de pagos.
Los permisos también podrían definir qué acciones están habilitadas. Una persona podría dejar que el agente visite una página sin permitirle hacer clic en sus botones ni escribir en los campos de texto. Así, el asistente podría recopilar información sin tener autorización para iniciar sesión, enviar un formulario o completar una compra.
La propuesta incluye la posibilidad de interrumpir una sesión activa y retirar permisos. Si el usuario cambia de opinión mientras el agente navega, podría detenerlo o revocar el acceso concedido. Además, Chrome podría señalar visualmente cuáles pestañas están bajo control del agente para que la persona pueda seguir sus movimientos.
Google Chrome tendría un papel en la seguridad
WebDriver BiDi fue diseñado para automatizar tareas en navegadores, como pruebas de sitios web. La propuesta busca extender el protocolo para contemplar agentes de IA que navegan por cuenta del usuario. En la actualidad, estas herramientas pueden recibir amplios permisos de automatización; los desarrolladores suelen crear sus propios límites.
Si el navegador aplicara las restricciones, estas podrían seguir vigentes aunque el agente no tuviera sus propias medidas de seguridad. En otras palabras, Chrome actuaría como una capa adicional para controlar qué páginas y operaciones están permitidas durante una tarea.
Google también plantea que el trabajo pueda incorporarse más adelante al estándar WebDriver BiDi. Si el protocolo evoluciona en esa dirección, otros navegadores podrían adoptar mecanismos similares. Por ahora, se trata de un objetivo de la propuesta, no de una función confirmada para otros productos.
La propuesta todavía tiene límites
El control por tipo de acción no distingue necesariamente la intención detrás de cada botón. Si un usuario permite que el agente haga clic en una página autorizada, el sistema podría no diferenciar entre un botón para avanzar y otro que elimine información. Por eso, los permisos generales no eliminarían todos los riesgos de una acción equivocada.
La idea tampoco detalla cómo sería la interfaz de autorización ni qué nivel de precisión tendría el control de cada permiso. Esos aspectos deberán definirse durante el desarrollo y las pruebas del prototipo.
La iniciativa apunta a que las personas tengan más control mientras los agentes realizan tareas en Chrome. Sin embargo, Google aún no ha confirmado cuándo, ni si, estas herramientas llegarán al navegador. Por ahora, el plan sirve como una propuesta para debatir cómo dar autonomía a la IA sin dejar que navegue sin límites establecidos por el usuario.

articles.title: New Inception extortion gang launches large-scale vishing campaign
articles.text:
A newly formed data extortion group named ‘Inception’ has been linked to a large-scale campaign that targets single sign-on (SSO) credentials of multiple global brands and firms.
The gang surfaced on November 17, claiming seven victims on its extortion site, including chip maker AMD, PepsiCo, Cigna Healthcare, AutoZone, and Lucid Motors, but none of them have publicly confirmed a data breach.
However, cybersecurity company ReversingLabs has been tracking Inception gang's activity and says that it has been operating since late October.
The security firm has confirmed the existence of 21 domains used for SSO phishing, 41 domains believed to be used in campaign infrastructure, and 4 other domains with suspected use.
The researchers identified an extensive phishing infrastructure impersonating dozens of major corporations, including Dropbox, Duolingo, Western Union, Indeed, Activision Blizzard, Riot Games, Twitch, Reddit, Nestlé, Anthropic, Nintendo, Starbucks, McDonald's, Paramount, and NBCUniversal.
The existence of these domains is not proof that those firms have been breached, or even targeted yet, and none have recently disclosed cyberattacks or other related incidents.
The campaign appears to rely on phone-based social engineering rather than email phishing, strongly resembling the tactics used by the infamous ShinyHunters extortion group.
Inception is using legal-themed websites that imitate corporate authentication services, primarily Okta but also NetIQ/OpenText Access Manager.
ShinyHunters link and denial
One of those authentication providers, Okta, published a report yesterday linking Inception to O-UNC-053, a threat cluster it previously associated with ShinyHunters, which has been active since March.
According to Okta, after law enforcement disrupted the ShinyHunters extortion group following the arrest of suspected members [1, 2], and the shutdown of the leak site, O-UNC-053 continued to register new phishing domains.
In late October, the activity cluster launched its legal-themed campaign, and in mid-November, the Inception leak site went live, announcing victims that matched previous targeting.
“This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” describes Okta.
“Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation.”
Inception was quick to respond and dispute the alleged links to other threat actors in an announcement on their extortion page.
The threat actors claimed to operate independently and with no affiliation to any previous group, arguing that overlapping targets and the use of common domain registration and CDN services did not establish operational links.
They also acknowledged that private tooling is circulating among independent threat actors, and using it does not prove affiliation.
To defend against the latest Inception campaign, ReversingLabs recommends enforcing phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, and strengthening help desk identity verification procedures.
DNS, proxy, and identity provider logs dating back to October 21, 2026, should be carefully reviewed for signs of suspicious activity.

articles.title: La barre de son Samsung HW-Q800H passe à 449 € à l'occasion du Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : La barre de son Samsung HW-Q800H à 449,00 € (-10%)
À l'occasion du Black Friday, la Samsung HW-Q800H passe à 449,00 € chez Boulanger.com, soit 50,00 € d'économie et une baisse d'environ 10 %. Dotée d'une restitution sonore équilibrée et d'une large scène frontale, cette barre de son affiche une note actuelle de 4,5/5 dans nos tests.
Avec la barre de son Samsung HW-Q800H, le fabricant coréen reprend les bases de sa gamme audio avec une configuration 5.1.2 canaux accompagnée d'un caisson sans fil compact. L'ensemble s'adresse à ceux qui cherchent à dynamiser le son de leur téléviseur sans encombrer leur salon avec de multiples enceintes physiques. Cet ensemble audio avait convaincu notre laboratoire lors de son passage sur le banc d'essai.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, la Samsung HW-Q800H descend à 449,00 € chez Boulanger.com, soit environ 10 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (499,00 €). Cela représente une économie de 50,00 €.
Une scène sonore frontale ample avec 11 haut-parleurs
Pour diffuser le son dans la pièce, la Samsung HW-Q800H embarque un ensemble de 11 haut-parleurs configurés en 5.1.2 canaux. Les haut-parleurs orientés vers le haut et les côtés créent une scène sonore frontale particulièrement large, tandis que le caisson sans fil assure un registre de graves généreux sans nécessiter de câblage à travers le salon. Comme l'a souligné notre test complet, la barre restitue une signature audio équilibrée qui met en valeur aussi bien les voix des dialogues que les bandes-son énergiques des films.
Samsung HW-Q800H
Points forts
- Signature sonore équilibrée.
- Effets surround excellents en frontal.
- Large scène sonore.
- Caisson de basses compact et puissant.
Points faibles
- Effets Dolby Atmos perfectibles.
- Entrée HDMI non compatible 4K/120 Hz, VRR et ALLM.
- Non prise en charge des formats DTS.
- Nouveautés 2026 anecdotiques.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
L'absence de compatibilité DTS et les limites du passthrough vidéo
Ce modèle fait en revanche l'impasse sur le décodage des formats DTS et n'embarque pas d'entrée HDMI compatible avec la 4K à 120 Hz, le VRR ou l'ALLM. Les amateurs de disques Blu-ray encodés en DTS et les joueurs équipés de consoles de dernière génération devront donc privilégier un branchement direct sur le téléviseur en eARC, alors que les cinéphiles adeptes de streaming Dolby Atmos profiteront pleinement du système sans contrainte.
Sony Bravia Theatre Bar 8 : l'autre option face au Samsung HW-Q800H
La Sony Bravia Theatre Bar 8 propose une approche différente en concentrant l'ensemble de ses transducteurs dans un châssis unique et discret, là où la Samsung HW-Q800H est livrée de série avec un caisson de basses dédié. La barre de Sony offre une bonne immersion sonore, mais elle souffre d'une connectique plus restreinte et d'une partie connectée simplifiée à l'extrême.
L'alternative de Sony s'affiche à un tarif identique à celui du système Samsung à son prix du jour. Face à la Sony Bravia Theatre Bar 8 notée 4/5, la Samsung HW-Q800H garde l'avantage grâce à sa note actuelle de 4,5/5 et son caisson de basses séparé qui renforce l'impact sonore pour le même prix.
Sony Bravia Theatre Bar 8
Points forts
- Son équilibré et polyvalent.
- Dimension Surround excellente.
- Compatibilité avec l’immense majorité des formats audio.
- Intuitivité de l’app Bravia Connect.
- Qualité de construction et compacité.
Points faibles
- Pas de miracle dans les basses fréquences.
- Connectique rachitique.
- Assez peu de réglages disponibles.
- Pas de commandes sur la barre, afficheur très limité.
- Disparition de la compatibilité Chromecast.

articles.title: El resurgir de Jensen Huang en Nvidia con apoyo de Trump tiene un precio: a China no le van a pasar ni una
articles.text:
Nvidia ha repuesto a Jensen Huang como consejero delegado apenas once días después de su dimisión, y todo tras una intervención directa de Donald Trump que no tardó en atribuirse la decisión (desde el primer día fue muy vocal). Su vuelta ha disparado las acciones de Nvidia, pero no todos parecen estar contentos porque también coincide con el momento en el que Washington estudia limitar aún más la venta de chips de Nvidia a China.
Y no sólo buscan frenar la evolución de la IA china, sino toda su tecnología: la de consumo, la de los coches y la de los robots humanoides.
Vaya viaje, niño. Es complicado no haber seguido el hilo de la historia, pero por si lo necesitas, ayer publicamos una cronología de todo el lío de Jensen Huang y Nvidia. Aunque, para líos, los que ha tenido él no sólo con la supuesta espía china, sino con varias empleadas de Nvidia (y cada día más), hecho que llevó a su dimisión el pasado 12 de noviembre.
Sin embargo, este lunes 23, la junta de Nvidia lo readmitió. La compañía dijo que lo hacía tras recibir aportaciones de altos niveles del Gobierno de Estados Unidos y, como digo, Trump salió a la palestra a decir que había sido gracias a él al no ver en Huang una amenaza para la seguridad nacional. The Washington Post va más allá, afirmando que Trump orquestó personalmente la operación.
Nvidia en China. De la manera que sea, Huang vuelve a ocupar el trono de la compañía que es la columna vertebral de la IA y ahora toca preguntarse... qué va a pasar en China. El motivo es que Huang es una pieza clave para la IA china sin poder ser, oficialmente, una pieza clave para la IA china. Me explico: Nvidia no vende en China sus procesadores más potentes, ya que esos están vetados por la guerra comercial y tecnológica que mantienen ambos países.
Lo que pueden vender es gamas inferiores o recortadas como GPUs para ordenadores de juego, PCs profesionales, chips para robótica y otros como los H20 que pueden usarse tanto para entrenar como para ejecutar modelos de IA. Sin embargo, y más allá del asunto del contrabando y de que los chips más potentes sí han terminado llegando a China, está el hecho de que Huang se tiró meses intentando convencer a Trump de que le dejaran vender los H200.
Estos H200 no son los chips punteros de Nvidia para la IA, ya que esos son exclusivos para los socios estadounidenses, pero sí una plataforma muy capaz que era de las que estaba vetada en China y que, por la insistencia del mandamás de Nvidia, Trump accedió a vender en el gigante asiático. La lógica era impepinable: China va a llegar en algún momento a tener chips similares, así que lo mejor es vendérselos directamente para ganar dinero y, además, hacer que sigan dependiendo de tu tecnología.
Lupa. El problema viene cuando llevamos años de restricciones y, realmente, no se ha vigilado prácticamente nada, o eso consideran algunos en Estados Unidos. En la cúpula del Gobierno se han mantenido dos velocidades estos últimos meses. Por un lado, los que abogaban por seguir vendiendo a China para lo mencionado: que China dependa de tecnología estadounidense a la vez que empresas de EEUU se llevan un buen dinero. Por otro, los que querían cerrar el grifo directamente para no beneficiar a las tecnológicas chinas ni un poco.
Durante los escándalos de Huang, el Departamento de Comercio dio un paso para regular de una mejor forma hacia dónde van los chips. Hasta ahora, parecía que las propias empresas que vendían los chips tenían que cerciorarse de que sus chips llegaban al destino adecuado. Eso abría el agujero de que se podían vender a Singapur o Malasia, pero luego los chips podían terminar llegando a China. Además, las empresas chinas no podían comprar chips directamente, pero sí alquilar computación en la nube a las neoclouds.
Con la nueva regla entre manos se busca que esas restricciones de acceso no puedan eludirse, ya que el propio Gobierno va a estar mucho más encima.
Problemas. De hecho, y como publicó mi compañera Laura hace unas horas, el propio Departamento de Comercio de EEUU ha dado un golpe más a China al endurecer los mecanismos de control sobre circuitos integrados más antiguos que se seguían usando en dispositivos como móviles, coches o electrodomésticos, entre otros. Esos chips maduros son esenciales para la industria tecnológica china, y EEUU acaba de poner un palo en las ruedas de la bici.
Todo esto ya está teniendo consecuencias en la industria china. Como leemos en Reuters, hay clientes que han comenzado a cancelar pedidos de una GPU muy concreta: la RTX Pro 5500. Se trata de una GPU diseñada para ordenadores profesionales, pero puede ejecutar modelos de IA y, aunque no está vetada, hay quien asume que lo estará en algún momento y no quieren que el dinero y los pedidos se queden en el limbo.
Hay un temor, según las fuentes de Reuters, de que ese mayor escrutinio se extienda a las ventas legales de chips de Nvidia. Antes de la salida de Huang, esas empresas chinas pidieron más de seis millones de RTX Pro 5500 por valor de unos 70.000 millones de dólares, siendo ByteDance, Alibaba y Tencent los tres máximos compradores. Con la salida de Huang, esos clientes frenaron o cancelaron los pedidos por si la tarjeta no podía entrar en el país.
Reacciones. Dos días después de que la Cámara de Comercio hiciera públicos sus planes, Tencent comentó que la norma tiene el potencial como para hacer retroceder a todos en China debido a que el proceso de entrenamiento de sus próximos modelos se verán afectados.
Huang ligado a la Casa Blanca. Pero claro, que ahora Huang haya vuelto (y por la puerta grande) no implica que la situación vuelva a ser la que era. Estados Unidos parece que se va a poner las pilas con los controles de exportación tanto a China como a Singapur, Malasia, Tailandia, Indonesia o Brasil y se estima que el Congreso empezará a presionar de forma más activa para que se cierre el grifo tras dos años de supervisión casi nula.
Lo que parece claro es que Nvidia, ese pegamento de la industria de la IA, va a estar algo más controlado porque el apoyo de Trump implica que Huang está mucho más ligado a la Casa Blanca y no se puede dar ni un traspiés más, sobre todo en un clima político en el que el Congreso tendrá mayoría demócrata en enero.
Si Jensen ya era una pieza política antes, ahora lo es aún más. Sólo queda ver cómo evoluciona la industria china y si sus alternativas patrias (Cambricon y Huawei) dan con la tecla para llenar ese posible hueco de Nvidia. Y el problema no es tanto tecnológico como de producción: no dan abasto.

articles.title: Zipher lands $53M to put AI agents, not data engineers, in charge of data workloads
articles.text:
Zipher lands $53M to put AI agents, not data engineers, in charge of data workloads
Data infrastructure startup Zipher Technologies Ltd. today announced that it has raised $53 million in funding for a platform where artificial intelligence agents, not data engineers, decide how enterprise data workloads run.
Founded in 2024, Zipher takes over the day-to-day running of enterprise data workloads, from resource allocation to framework selection and scheduling. Customers set performance targets and budgets, leaving the rest to the company’s agents. The platform runs on Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, with support for data tools including Databricks Workflows, Apache Airflow, dbt and Azure Data Factory.
The company already manages production workloads for a number of Fortune 500 enterprises in sectors including financial services, travel, consumer packaged goods and energy. Those customers see cost-efficiency gains of 40% to 60%, it says, with service-level agreement adherence improving by as much as 80%.
Among them is Hertz Global Holdings Inc. Gaurav Rastogi, senior director of enterprise data analytics and BI platforms at Hertz, said the car rental company has seen compute cost reductions of 25% to 40% depending on the workload while “supporting consistent performance through seasonal peaks.”
Behind the numbers is an argument that AI agents have changed the way enterprises use their data platforms, with anyone in an organization now able to spin up a data workload in seconds. Zipher’s agents learn each of those workloads, dependencies included, and then pick the engine each one runs on based on capacity and load at the time.
The agents can go as far as rewriting a workload’s framework, code and syntax. Dan Coster, Zipher’s co-founder and chief executive, said that as agents create more workloads, the infrastructure needs to “make its own decisions.”
The funding is intended to support research and development along with go-to-market work. Zipher plans to build out its U.S. enterprise sales team and expand across Latin America, Asia-Pacific and the Europe, Middle East and Africa region.
Zipher was founded by Coster and Chief Technology Officer Yoav Gill Ben Ephraim, both alumni of Unit 8200, the Israel Defense Forces’ intelligence technology unit. Ben Ephraim previously served as director of data platform at Payoneer Global Inc. and held a senior data role at Microsoft Corp. The company is headquartered in New York, with offices in Tel Aviv.
The $53 million, which covers both Zipher’s seed and Series A rounds, came from TLV Partners, Maor Investments and Glilot Capital Partners. Angel investors and advisers include Dremio Corp. co-founder Tomer Shiran, Monte Carlo AI Inc. co-founders Barr Moses and Lior Gavish and Cribl Inc. co-founder Clint Sharp.
According to TLV Partners Managing Partner Shahar Tzafrir, enterprises in an agentic world need a platform that decides where and how each workload runs. The Zipher team, he added, has “proven it in production with Fortune 500 customers who keep expanding their use of the platform.”

articles.title: 3,5 milliards de données personnelles en libre accès : des pirates laissent à leur tour fuiter leurs fichiers
articles.text:
Deux chercheurs en cybersécurité ont découvert d'immenses bases de données accessibles sur Internet sans la moindre authentification. Identifiants, mots de passe, données administratives et cookies de session y côtoyaient des dossiers permettant de reconstituer la vie numérique de leurs victimes.
Les cybercriminels ne sont pas à l'abri des erreurs de sécurité qu'ils exploitent chez les autres. Comme le rapporte WIRED, deux chercheurs ont découvert, à peu près au même moment, deux bases de données sans lien apparent entre elles, qui totalisaient plus de 3,5 milliards d'enregistrements. Tout porte à croire qu'elles servaient à centraliser et à exploiter des informations personnelles dérobées au fil des ans.
Des milliards de données volées, collectées et triées
La première base, découverte par Greg Pollock, directeur de la recherche chez UpGuard, regroupait 1,64 milliard de documents concernant en grande majorité la population chinoise. Le chercheur y a recensé au moins 840 millions de numéros d'identité nationale distincts, près de 300 millions de numéros de téléphone associés à des données vraisemblablement collectées auprès d'Alipay, quelque 11 millions de dossiers d'inscription scolaire et près de 8 millions d'enregistrements d'entreprises. Loin d'avoir été stockées en vrac, ces informations, issues de sources distinctes, avaient fait l'objet d'un important travail de recoupement et de structuration.
La seconde base, découverte par Jeremiah Fowler, chercheur chez Black Hills Information Security dont les travaux ont été publiés par ExpressVPN, contenait près de 2 milliards d'identifiants et de données de connexion, répartis dans plus de 8 400 dossiers, dont plusieurs classés par pays, France comprise. Cette fois, les informations semblent en grande partie issues d'infostealers, ces logiciels malveillants capables de siphonner les données stockées sur les appareils infectés. Des centaines de millions de comptes de messagerie, plus de 100 millions de comptes de réseaux sociaux et des dizaines de millions de comptes de commerce en ligne figuraient dans les fichiers, sans que rien ne laisse penser que les plateformes concernées aient elles-mêmes été piratées.
Les deux bases ne sont désormais plus accessibles au public, la première ayant disparu au cours des investigations de Greg Pollock, qui soupçonne une attaque par ransomware ou une opération de destruction de données, et l'accès à la seconde ayant été restreint par son hébergeur après un signalement de Jeremiah Fowler.
Les chercheurs n'ont toutefois pas été en mesure d'en identifier les propriétaires, Jeremiah Fowler n'excluant d'ailleurs pas que la seconde base ait été constituée à des fins de recherche en cybersécurité, ni de vérifier l'intégralité de leur contenu ou d'en éliminer tous les doublons. Impossible, donc, d'établir le nombre exact de victimes, la proportion de données inédites ou encore de savoir si d'autres personnes ont profité de leur exposition.
Quand les pirates en savent assez pour prendre possession de votre vie numérique
Outre le volume d'informations exposées, les chercheurs s'inquiètent de la complémentarité des données collectées. Un numéro de téléphone, une adresse mail ou un numéro d'identité nationale prennent une tout autre valeur aux yeux d'un escroc dès lors qu'il peut les rattacher à un même individu. En accumulant et en croisant les informations issues de vols successifs, les cybercriminels peuvent ainsi affiner leurs campagnes de phishing, usurper votre identité ou se faire passer pour un organisme avec lequel vous entretenez déjà des relations.
Plus préoccupant encore, Jeremiah Fowler a mis la main sur quelque 400 000 documents qui associaient aux identifiants de connexion des informations sur les appareils infectés, des données de navigation, des cookies et des fichiers récupérés sur les machines. Or, lorsqu'ils sont encore valides et réutilisables, les cookies d'authentification peuvent permettre aux pirates de détourner une session déjà ouverte, sans avoir à saisir votre mot de passe ni à franchir l'étape de la double authentification.
On rappellera donc que, si l'utilisation de mots de passe uniques et l'activation de la double authentification vous protègent contre une grande partie des tentatives de piratage de comptes, ces précautions ne vous mettent pas à l'abri d'un détournement de session. En cas d'infection par un infostealer, il vous faudra aussi révoquer vos sessions actives et renouveler vos mots de passe depuis un appareil sain, en prenant soin de désinfecter la machine compromise avant de vous y reconnecter.

articles.title: Ist der Anthropic-Boom schon wieder vorbei? Aktie fällt unter den Ausgabepreis
articles.text:
Ist der Anthropic-Boom schon wieder vorbei? Aktie fällt unter den Ausgabepreis
Die Aktie der KI-Firma Anthropic ist wenige Tage nach ihrem Rekord-Börsengang unter den Ausgabepreis gefallen. Im frühen US-Handel notierte sie nach einem Minus von mehr als acht Prozent an der Marke von 80 US-Dollar.
Den Ausgabepreis hatte Anthropic zum Börsendebüt am 19. November auf 83 Dollar festgesetzt – angesichts einer hohen Nachfrage von Interessenten deutlich über der zuvor festgelegten Spanne von 70 bis 78 Dollar. Zudem bot Anthropic mehr als 150 Millionen Aktien mehr zum Kauf an als ursprünglich geplant. Damit machte die KI-Firma richtig Kasse und legte mit einem Erlös von 107,3 Milliarden Dollar den bisher größten Börsengang hin.
Abwärts nach starkem Start
Am ersten Tag schien der Erfolgslauf zunächst weiterzugehen: Der erste Kurs lag mit 111,50 Dollar um 34 Prozent über dem Ausgabepreis. Danach ging es abwärts. Aus dem regulären US-Handel ging das Papier am ersten Tag mit einem Kurs von 97,17 Dollar. Das war immer noch ein Aufschlag von gut 17 Prozent auf den Ausgabepreis.
Schon am 20. November aber waren Technologie-Aktien auf breiter Front unter Druck. Auch die Hoffnung, dass der Anthropic-Börsengang zu einem Stimmungswandel bei KI-Aktien führen könnte, verpuffte damit. Am Markt waren zuletzt abermals Sorgen größer geworden, ob die gewaltigen Investitionen in Rechenzentren für Künstliche Intelligenz zurückverdient werden können. Allein Anthropic veranschlagte für die kommenden Jahre Ausgaben von fast 900 Milliarden Dollar für Rechenleistung.
Huang-Euphorie für KI-Aktien verpufft?
Am 23. November dann sorgte die von Präsident Donald Trump durchgesetzte Rückkehr von Jensen Huang an die Spitze des Chip-Riesen Nvidia für einen Auftrieb bei Tech-Aktien. Doch schon einen Tag später stand der Markt wieder unter Druck.
Bei Anthropic muss man als Investor daran glauben, dass die Zukunftsversprechen aufgehen – denn bisher gibt es vor allem hohe Verluste, wenn auch das Geschäft schnell wächst. Ab dem Börsendebüt konnten zudem auch viele Anthropic-Mitarbeiter Aktien verkaufen. Es ist allerdings unklar, ob das zu der Talfahrt beigetragen haben könnte.
)) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Four SA students build fintech to fix bursary pay problems
articles.text:
Four university students have experienced the frustrations of accessing bursary money firsthand. Now, they are building CampusFit, a fintech platform that aims to change how students access, manage and track their allowances. PHATHISANI MOYO writes.
Imagine standing at a supermarket till on a Friday with a basket of groceries, only to discover that your allowance has not cleared, leaving you stranded until Monday.
It is a frustration Brian Mbana, co-founder of student fintech platform CampusFit, says many university students know all too well. Across South Africa, receiving a bursary allowance rarely guarantees immediate access to the funds. Delays in transferring disbursements into bank accounts often leave students borrowing money for groceries or queuing at retailers to withdraw cash.
Mbana, 24, and his co-founders—Aaron Matsemela, 21; Cliff Kaela, 21; and Simanye Sobekwa, 23—are building CampusFit to solve a problem they have personally experienced.
The four founders want to address what they call the “mailbox effect”, where money enters an account only to be withdrawn almost immediately because it offers little convenience for everyday transactions.
The issue is particularly acute in South Africa’s student funding ecosystem, where receiving financial support and accessing it when needed are not always the same thing. The National Student Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) (NSFAS) has faced recurring challenges with allowance payments and its disbursement model, highlighting the administrative complexities students can encounter.
For four founders still navigating university themselves, CampusFit is an attempt to turn those frustrations into financial infrastructure. But building a product that works for students and the institutions funding them will require more than a promising idea.
From a university hackathon to a fintech idea
CampusFit took shape at a hackathon in East London, the Eastern Cape’s second-largest city, where the four founders met after being assigned to the same team. Challenged to develop a solution to a financial services problem, they focused on students and the disconnect between receiving money and being able to use it conveniently.
“We realised that students have a similar relationship with their accounts, particularly when it comes to NSFAS funding. As soon as money enters their wallets, many students withdraw it and take it to supermarkets such as Boxer and Shoprite,” Sobekwa told TechCabal in an interview on Saturday.
CampusFit wants to change that behaviour by making digital financial services more useful to students. Its proposed platform includes instant peer-to-peer transfers, budgeting tools and a unified dashboard that allows users to connect their bank accounts and view transactions in one place.
Matsemela believes the idea is rooted in his own experience with student funding. Having recently received a bursary, he encountered delays and uncertainty when accessing his money through Intellimali, a student allowance management platform. He said students also turn to social media to share complaints about payment delays and difficulties accessing their allowances.
“I hold three bank accounts. Having a platform that allows me to link all my accounts in one place and view transactions from all those different accounts would be very helpful,” he said.
The balance between financial oversight and privacy
CampusFit emerges amid growing scrutiny over how students spend educational allowances. NSFAS and the National Gambling Board recently joined forces to curb student gambling following reports that recipients were using their allowances to bet online.
While the founders see an opportunity to give both students and bursary providers clearer visibility into spending, they stress that any form of financial oversight must respect students’ privacy.
That concern has shaped the team’s approach to regulation. Kaela said the founders had considered the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) and other regulatory requirements from the outset. The team is also pursuing a system operator licence, which they say is necessary for the platform’s intended payment activities.
“We are not simply holding people’s data. We are also enabling transactions, and there are specific licences involved in that process,” Kaela said.
The regulatory process is part of the groundwork the founders must complete before taking the platform to market and pursuing partnerships with financial institutions and funding providers.
Turning an MVP into a business
The founders have developed a minimum viable product (MVP) and expect to begin onboarding students in the coming months. They are part of the Genesis Block cohort, a fintech startup incubation programme backed by FNB and the University of Cape Town Financial Innovation Hub. The programme provides mentorship and exposure to the financial services industry.
Mbana’s motivation remains close to home. He wants CampusFit to be built around the everyday difficulties students face, rather than assumptions about how they manage their money.
“Imagine going to buy groceries on a Friday, only to discover at the till that you cannot access your money because there is no cash available. You then have to wait until after the weekend to get your money,” he said.
The founders say their immediate challenge is proving that students will use the platform and that its technology can support a growing user base. They are building in backups and using containerisation to improve reliability, while exploring partnerships that could drive expansion.
Their ambition is to build South Africa’s leading student financial wellness platform. That will mean earning students’ trust, meeting regulatory requirements and persuading financial institutions that the model can work at scale.
“We want students to have more control over their money, rather than spending their time figuring out how to access it,” Sobekwa said.

articles.title: Entrará en vigor: el Gobierno aprueba que los autónomos declaren el IVA una vez al año si facturan menos de 85.000 euros
articles.text:
Los autónomos que facturen menos de 85.000 euros al año podrán dejar de hacer la declaración trimestral del impuesto sobre el valor añadido (IVA). El Consejo de Ministros ha aprobado un régimen voluntario que la sustituye por una declaración anual. El paquete también incluye descuentos en el impuesto sobre la renta de las personas físicas (IRPF) y cambios en los pagos por adelantado que los trabajadores por cuenta propia ingresan a Hacienda.
Después de la reunión del Ejecutivo, el ministro de Hacienda, Arcadi España, ha presentado las medidas. En la nota sobre las medidas para los autónomos, el ministerio cuantifica la rebaja fiscal en 465 millones de euros. Los cálculos que ha presentado España dicen que son beneficiados 2,6 millones de contribuyentes. A la rebaja fiscal suma un efecto distinto: hasta 1.800 millones de impuestos que podrán aplazarse con las simplificaciones y los cambios en los pagos fraccionados.
Una declaración anual, con pagos de abril, julio y octubre
El nuevo régimen del IVA permitirá cambiar las cuatro autoliquidaciones trimestrales por una única declaración anual. En el transcurso del ejercicio se producirán tres pagos a cuenta, en los meses de abril, julio y octubre. La Agencia Tributaria calculará cada uno, dividiendo entre cuatro la cuota de la autoliquidación anual del ejercicio anterior, y pondrá esa información a disposición del contribuyente.
El sistema, según Hacienda, puede beneficiar a unos 1,1 millones de autónomos y permitir que estos tengan en caja 577 millones de euros más. Es una previsión de liquidez: el impuesto continuará existiendo y se tendrá que liquidar.
Este cambio hay que diferenciarlo bien del IVA franquiciado que se plantea para los pequeños comercios. El acuerdo adoptado cambia la forma de declaración y pago a cuenta del impuesto; no introduce una exención general para los que facturen menos de 85.000 euros.
Más deducción del impuesto sobre la renta y cambios en los pagos por adelantado
A los tributantes en estimación directa simplificada, la reforma aprobada eleva del 5 al 10 por ciento el porcentaje de gastos y provisiones de difícil justificación, y el límite anual sube de 2.000 a 3.000 euros. La mejora se aplicará para el ejercicio 2026. El Ministerio de Hacienda calcula que beneficiará a 1,6 millones de trabajadores autónomos, lo que supondrá un ahorro conjunto de 362 millones de euros en este aspecto. Ese tope es el importe que se puede deducir, no un reembolso automático de 3.000 euros.
A los que tributan por módulos, la reducción del rendimiento neto pasa del 5 % al 10 % en 2026, un 15 % en las actividades agrícolas. Según los cálculos del ministerio, un millón de contribuyentes se verán favorecidos por la mejora en módulos. El paquete también amplía hasta 2027 los límites para permanecer en el sistema de módulos.
De otra manera, cambian los pagos fraccionados del IRPF. El ejemplo puesto por Hacienda es el de un autónomo en estimación directa que facture menos de 85.000 euros y cuya declaración de 2025 haya sido negativa porque pagó por adelantado más de lo que le correspondía pagar. Bajo ese supuesto, señala, podría dejar de hacer pagos fraccionados en 2027.
Para los que deban seguir haciéndolos y facturen menos de 250.000 euros, el tipo anunciado baja del 20 % al 19 %. También se contempla una alternativa de cálculo que tenga como referencia el rendimiento neto de 2025. Con esta opción, la Agencia Tributaria realizará los cálculos de los pagos y el contribuyente podrá domiciliarlos, sin necesidad de presentar las declaraciones trimestrales del IRPF correspondientes.
Hacienda estima que la exención de los pagos fraccionados, la reducción del tipo y el nuevo cálculo permitirán diferir hasta 1.200 millones de euros. Esa cantidad corresponde a impuestos cuyo pago se difiere y que afectan a la disponibilidad de dinero durante el ejercicio.
El paquete también incluye el aplazamiento de Verifactu, el sistema de facturación verificable, hasta octubre de 2028. El Boletín Oficial del Estado, al publicar el real decreto-ley, deberá especificar la fecha de entrada en vigor y las condiciones de aplicación de cada uno de los cambios.

articles.title: OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando
articles.text:
OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches.
Pando now powers all development in OpenAI's monorepo and is serving nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. OpenAI attributes the increased load to Codex-driven development, and each push can in turn trigger multiple CI jobs that all fetch the same history. Pando went into production in April 2026.
Rather than replace Git's client and protocol, OpenAI has changed how the backend coordinates reference updates and stores and transfers objects. On a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it's being streamed to immutable blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. A metadata transaction records the reference version (containing the new branch tip, the packfile and its dependencies on earlier reference versions) and atomically updates the reference pointer. Updates to unrelated references can proceed independently of one another; updates to the same reference still need to be coordinated.
OpenAI refers to this as causal consistency with serialisable updates to individual references and read-your-own-write consistency. A reader gets the history needed for the requested revision, but fetching a number of branches won't provide a repository-wide snapshot. Two clients can see different combinations of branch versions during concurrent updates. The trade-off removes a shared coordination point for unrelated pushes.
Pando also changes how Git decides which objects to transfer. By default, when a client pushes a new feature branch, the server will advertise only a designated trunk branch as its base. That constrains the dependencies of the resulting packfile, which in turn allows Pando to reuse it for readers who already have that trunk history. Repeated or stacked branch pushes can resend objects outside trunk, trading some additional bandwidth for the benefit of reusable packs.
Pando’s topic-branch packs depend on advertised trunk history and can repeat objects from earlier pushes (source)
For fetches, Pando maps the client's existing and requested commits to reference versions and picks out the appropriate stored packs to cover the missing history. Git's packfile-uri capability allows the server to return download links rather than generate a bespoke pack for each client. Express, a regional pack-delivery cache, serves those downloads. OpenAI reports cache-hit rates in excess of 99% and tests in which clone and fetch operations saturated 10 Gbps network links.
Background compaction groups packs into larger, geometrically sized covers, resembling compaction in a log-structured merge-tree. The covers provide better compression and act as a skip-list-like index for fetch planning. Pando keeps packs at every level so that clients with different histories can still be served.
Pando groups successive packs into larger covers to improve compression and fetch planning, retaining packs at every level (source)
The design contrasts with Anthropic's Scion, previously covered by InfoQ. Scion replaces Git's underlying model with changesets recording files changed relative to their first parent and content-addressed pointers to compressed file contents; commits, merges, rebases and history queries run server-side. Its clients retrieve missing immutable trees and blobs, rather than negotiate Git packfiles, and use bounded local caches and sparse or virtualised checkouts.
Both systems make use of immutable data and regional caches to reduce repeated computation. The way in which they draw the compatibility line is very different, though. Pando preserves Git's object model and client-side workflows and changes the backend coordination and delivery. Scion, on the other hand, assumes an online client and moves the repository operations into a dedicated service. The improvements they report are not directly comparable. OpenAI reports on push latency, whereas Anthropic reports on checkout speedups and infrastructure reductions compared with its previous Git-based setup.
Git compatibility did not eliminate migration work. OpenAI initially deployed Pando as a read- and write-through proxy, moved clients in phases, and migrated hundreds of integrations using legacy APIs, webhooks and repository downloads. It also distributed its own Git build, which supports parallel downloading and indexing of independent packs. OpenAI says some client improvements are already upstream, with others available in its public repository.
For the architects, it's a case of two separate decisions: which source control operations go on the server and which of the consistency and transfer guarantees do the workloads actually need. Pando retains the Git workflows but dispenses with the repository-wide snapshot across branches and accepts redundant transfers in order to reduce the amount of coordination and per-fetch computation.

articles.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
articles.text:
AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  University of Plymouth
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.
- Share:
Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.
Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.
The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.
AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records
Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.
Confirming bladder cancer currently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.
To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.
The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.
AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases
The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.
The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.
Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.
The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.
For example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.
These findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.
Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.
Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.
A New Approach to Early Cancer Screening
Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).
This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.
For example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.
PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022."
"Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods."
Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?
The potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.
Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.
"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.
"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved."
Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.
"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.
"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages."
More Research Needed Before Clinical Use
Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.
All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.
Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.
"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.
"But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions."
The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.
The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.
The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Plymouth. Original written by Mrs. Amy King. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xu Wang, Andrea Preston, Jonathan Aning, Michael Loizou, Shang-Ming Zhou. Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs. IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering, 2026; 73 (11): 3680 DOI: 10.1109/TBME.2026.3658230

articles.title: Australia threatens US tech giants with fines of up to 5% of global revenue over online safety
articles.text:
Winners & losers: Australia is threatening to slam US tech giants with penalties that could reach into the billions of dollars. The country says that unless these companies take reasonable steps to protect users from harmful content and addictive features on their platforms, they could be fined up to 5% of their global revenue.
Australia's Labor government struck a deal with the Greens on Tuesday that gives its Digital Duty of Care bill the support it needs to pass the Senate. The original proposal capped fines at A$109.2 million, or about US$72 million. But even that amount looks modest next to what a company the size of Meta could face under the revised bill.
In Meta's case, that would be around $10 billion based on its 2025 revenue, while the same calculation for Google parent Alphabet comes to about $20 billion.
The changes would also give Australians who suffer harm the right to sue a platform directly, opening the door to class actions. For someone with a smaller claim, going to court might be more trouble than it's worth. The deal would let the government set up an independent ombudsman to handle those complaints.
For users, anyone aged 16 or older could turn off algorithmic recommendations and see posts only from accounts they follow. The bill would also require platforms to tackle risks to children, including bullying and material promoting eating disorders. For adults, the list includes stalking, threats of violence, and the familiar problem of intimate images being shared without consent.
In addition to its impact on social media, the proposal would replace separate industry codes covering everything from search engines to AI chatbots and messaging apps. Google warned earlier this month that the bill's age-check provisions could force it to block under-18s from Gmail. Australia's opposition Coalition has a different concern. With billions of dollars potentially on the line, platforms might simply decide it's safer to take down perfectly legal posts.
Australia already requires major social media sites to take reasonable steps to keep under-16s from holding accounts, with mixed results. An April survey found that 61% of Australian 12- to 15-year-olds who had accounts before the ban could still access at least one of them.
For an idea of how those potential penalties stack up, the European Commission fined Apple €500 million and Meta €200 million in April 2025, the first fines it handed out under the Digital Markets Act. Add the two together (~$767 million) and they still come to less than a tenth of what 5% of Meta's 2025 annual revenue would represent.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Unpatched Flaw in Defunct Idunno AntiCsrf Library
articles.text:
Threat actors are exploiting an unpatched vulnerability in the open source anti-CSRF library Idunno AntiCsrf for remote code execution (RCE), security researchers warn.
AntiCsrf is a legacy ASP.NET module for WebForms applications that has no active maintainer and is no longer actively supported. The most recent version, 0.9.1 Beta, was released in December 2008.
Tracked as CVE-2026-131914 (CVSS score of 9.3), the exploited security defect is described as an insecure deserialization bug in the processing of HTTP POST requests to ASP.NET WebForms endpoints.
“Exploitation requires only a single HTTP POST request with no prior authentication or valid CSRF token. Active exploitation in the wild has been observed,” Google Cloud’s Mandiant warned on November 18.
The flaw allows an attacker to supply any non-empty value in the CSRF cookie along with a Base64-encoded gadget chain to gain RCE in the context of the IIS worker process, Mandiant notes.
According to preemptive cybersecurity firm WatchTowr, the issue exists because AntiCsrf does not perform sufficient checks on data from incoming form submissions before reconstructing it into program objects.
“The vulnerable check runs before the application’s own page logic, so it can affect many pages on an affected site, not just ones that use a login form. A successful attack gives the attacker control over the process that runs the website, which can lead to full compromise of the server,” WatchTowr says.
On Tuesday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2026-131914 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list, urging federal agencies to address it within three days.
As no official patch is available for the vulnerability, all organizations relying on the 18-year-old AntiCsrf to validate anti-CSRF tokens on form submissions should immediately discontinue the module and transition to an actively supported solution.
“WatchTowr Intel detected exploit probes across our honeypots that used creative .NET compiled gadget payloads to confirm if a given system is vulnerable. We validated the exploit and confirmed that, if the host was vulnerable, the server would be tricked into redirecting to a unique URL that would discreetly confirm control of the web server to the attacker,” WatchTowr principal threat intelligence specialist Yordan Ganchev told SecurityWeek.
“There is no patch, and likely there won’t be one. Defenders should audit ASP.NET products to identify ones packaging the Idunno.AntiCSRF library and review their audit logs for signs of exploitation. Where possible, the library should be replaced in affected applications. Where that’s not possible, apply WAF rules until alternative workarounds are identified,” Ganchev added.
