articles.title: What’s going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
articles.text:
Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.
It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.
Tackling Riemann
The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”
The proof of the hypothesis was announced by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.
But it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.
The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.
Proof factories
It’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.
But AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.
When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.
AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.
The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.
Deriving worries
Mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter. We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.
Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.
But that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever issues they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.
By contrast, the internal workings of large neural networks are notoriously opaque. Asking an AI to explain its reasoning runs into the same problems that asking it anything else does: Since the software has only been selected for producing decent-sounding text, it’s likely to make something up that sounds good when asked about its own internal processes. So, an AI-generated proof has little to offer the field in terms of new ideas or unexpected advances, at least on its own.
Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce new insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.
How mathematicians are expected to identify new challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.
This is all new and progressing incredibly quickly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.
But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.
John is Ars Technica's science editor. He has a Bachelor of Arts in Biochemistry from Columbia University, and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. When physically separated from his keyboard, he tends to seek out a bicycle, or a scenic location for communing with his hiking boots.
Yep, it has! Imagining just such a situation, or perhaps one where a human was the one to prove it, there's a longstanding statement of the Riemann Hypothesis in the standard Mathlib library. It's been confirmed that Alpoge's proof (Claude's proof?) aligns to it. 
There's a confirmation from the Mathlib initiative here, which gives more detail.

articles.title: Chatr rolls out new, pricier six- and 12-month plans
articles.text:
Rogers’ Chatr brand rolled out new six-month and yearly plans that are more expensive than previous offers.
First up is the new six-month plan. It costs $150 and includes 90GB of 4G data — that works out to about $25 and 15GB of data per month.
The other plan is a 12-month plan. It costs $199 for the year and includes 60GB of data. That’s about $16.58 and 5GB of data per month.
Unfortunately, this plan is more expensive than Chatr’s previous yearly offer. The old $159/year 40GB plan is no longer available.
Both plans include unlimited Canada-wide talk, unlimited Canada, U.S., and international texting, and voicemail. Chatr offers 4G data speeds up to 150Mbps.
On the one hand, I like to see more multi-month plans like this, as they’re often good value for people who don’t need a crazy phone plan. I could see these plans being good for a kid’s first phone, or perhaps for an elderly family member who just needs a cellphone for emergencies. On the other, I don’t like to see Chatr pushing the price up on these plans.
It’s worth noting, however, that there are a few other carriers offering multi-month plans. Freedom Mobile, for example, has several six- and 12-month plans. On the six-month side, Freedom has a $90 talk and text plan, a $150/90GB plan, and a $180/180GB plan. And for the 12-month options, Freedom has a$129/20GB and $159/40GB plans.
Telus’ Koodo also offers a couple of yearly plans, including a $100 plan with 400 minutes and 400 texts, and a $159/40GB plan.
In other words, if you really liked Chatr’s $159/40GB plan, there are some other carriers out there worth considering now that Chatr no longer offers it. But if the new six- and 12-month plans call to you, you can check them out on Chatr’s website.

articles.title: Electric truck startup Harbinger gets financing boost from Palmer Luckey's bank
articles.text:
Harbinger has tapped Palmer Luckey’s Erebor Bank as a new source of capital as the electric truck startup looks to diversify how it funds its growth and an expanding portfolio of products spanning autonomous vehicles, energy storage, and defense.
Los Angeles-based Harbinger said Tuesday it secured more than $100 million in financing, including a convertible note from Pinegrove Venture Partners and senior debt from Erebor Bank, which launched in February 2026 and recently surpassed $1 billion in loans, according to the Financial Times.
The new financing comes less than three weeks after Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D funding round co-led by Tiger Global, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline. FedEx, which ordered 2,000 trucks from Harbinger, also participated.
Harbinger co-founder and chief executive John Harris explained in a statement that building an industrial technology company at scale requires a “different financing approach,” adding that the capital needed to ramp up production and deliver vehicles to customers shouldn’t have to come entirely from equity. Harris noted that major vehicle and aerospace manufacturers have long relied on debt financing to support their production operations.
Erebor is now Harbinger’s primary banking partner. In a statement, Luckey said traditional lenders have struggled to support the unique capital needs of businesses developing real technology and creating U.S. jobs.
“Harbinger is exactly the kind of business we built Erebor to back: an American manufacturer building world-class technology,” he said.

articles.title: MTN’s proposed Telkom takeover comes with a competition cost
articles.text:
South Africa’s telecoms industry may be heading for a major restructuring, with MTN, Africa’s largest mobile network operator, and Telkom, a major telecommunications provider, revisiting acquisition talks four years after previous negotiations collapsed. A deal could combine two major mobile businesses and one of the country’s largest fibre networks.
While a larger operator could pool infrastructure, reduce duplicated investment and strengthen its capacity to finance expensive next-generation networks, absorbing Telkom would also remove an independent infrastructure competitor. This could potentially weaken competition and limit choices for smaller operators, internet service providers and consumers.
The talks’ outcome will determine how smaller operators negotiate network access, whether internet service providers retain competitive wholesale options and, ultimately, whether consumers continue benefiting from affordable connectivity. 
Consolidation may strengthen network operators’ balance sheets, but without meaningful regulatory safeguards, it could also concentrate control over the infrastructure on which much of the digital economy depends.
The economics of getting bigger
MTN Group chief executive officer (CEO) Ralph Mupita has consistently argued that South Africa has too many mobile network operators competing for a limited pool of industry profits. In a 2023 interview with McKinsey, a global management consulting firm, he explained why the group believes consolidation is necessary.
“Most markets still have four or more operators licensed to operate and provide full infrastructure and services to their customers,” Mupita said, asserting that the capital required to maintain independent networks makes returns difficult to sustain. He added that some markets would move towards two operators, while others would settle at three.
Mupita’s argument reflects the economics of telecommunications. Building and maintaining mobile networks requires substantial investment in spectrum, base stations, fibre backhaul, electricity and technology upgrades. Operators must continually spend to improve coverage and capacity while competing to attract and retain subscribers.
Combining MTN and Telkom could therefore o eliminate duplicated infrastructure spending, improve network utilisation and direct more capital towards 5G and fibre expansion. MTN would also gain access to Telkom’s established fixed-line and enterprise businesses.
Consolidation also has potential consumer benefits. A larger operator could spread investment across more subscribers, reduce duplicated infrastructure costs and make network expansion into underserved areas more viable.
If these efficiencies translate to lower costs, better network quality and more affordable services, consumers could benefit. Fewer operators do not necessarily mean weaker competition, particularly where fibre providers, internet service providers (ISPs) and mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs) offer alternatives to traditional mobile networks.
For instance, Telkom’s group revenue increased 2% to R22.5 billion ($1.3 billion), according to its latest interim results. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation rose 5.8% to R6.4 billion ($377 million).
Its mobile business generated R13.3 billion ($764 million) in revenue, with mobile data subscribers increasing 13.6% to 21 million. Openserve, Telkom’s fibre business, meanwhile, recorded 15.1% growth in connected homes to 870,856.
“The next phase of Telkom’s transformation is not simply about proving that our business can withstand a changing market. It is about demonstrating that we can consistently convert our customer relationships, infrastructure and capabilities into sustainable earnings, cash generation and long-term value,” Telkom chief executive (CEO) Serame Taukobong said in a statement on November 17.
Telkom’s growth makes it an attractive acquisition target beyond its infrastructure assets. Its expanding mobile subscriber base would give MTN additional scale, while Openserve’s fibre footprint would strengthen its fixed broadband offering.
MTN would gain established revenue streams, a growing mobile competitor and an established wholesale fibre network, making the deal both a growth opportunity and a potential competition concern.
The regulatory test
The concern is who controls rivals’ networks. Cell C, an independent South African mobile operator, no longer operates its own radio access network, relying on roaming arrangements with MTN and Vodacom. Many MVNOs depend on host networks, letting banks, retailers and other brands sell mobile services without building infrastructure.
But their competitiveness depends on wholesale prices, coverage and service terms set by network owners. If MTN absorbs Telkom, smaller operators could face a larger supplier that also competes for their customers. Internet service providers buying wholesale fibre could face similar risks with fewer independent networks.
Following its Data Services Market Inquiry, whose final report was released in December 2019, the Competition Commission secured settlements with MTN and Vodacom in 2020. These included substantial reductions in prepaid data prices, daily free data and zero-rated access to educational and government services. The Commission subsequently estimated that the interventions saved consumers approximately R4 billion ($230 million) in the first year. Its recommendations also contributed to Openserve wholesale fibre price reductions and measures supporting MVNO competition.
Any transaction would face scrutiny from the Competition Commission and Tribunal. The Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (ICASA), the country’s telecommunications regulator, would consider licencing and spectrum implications. The state and Public Investment Corporation, South Africa’s largest asset manager, which together own 51.6% of Telkom, are pivotal shareholders.
Regulators will need to weigh the potential investment benefits against the risk of weaker competition, particularly in mobile and wholesale broadband markets. The deal’s impact will depend on whether consumers and smaller operators benefit or face greater dependence on a combined business controlling more essential network infrastructure.
Ultimately, businesses and consumers will feel the real test. A stronger operator may benefit the industry, but not if consumers end up paying for it through weaker competition.

articles.title: Back-to-back measles deaths is our new reality; US tally now at 14
articles.text:
Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.
The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.
Deaths and transmission
On November 23, Pennsylvania’s health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death, an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child. New York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby. On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4.
The virus isn’t slowing down. Measles is the most contagious virus known; it can linger in the air for up to two hours. Up to 90 percent of people who are not immune will fall ill after an exposure. People are considered immune if they’ve been vaccinated or previously infected. With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, the number of susceptible people is only growing.
To keep measles from getting a foothold in a community, vaccination rates need to be 95 percent or higher. According to the latest data, only 92.4 percent of US kindergartners were vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year. Only 10 states have MMR vaccination rates at or above the 95 percent threshold. But even in those states, there are pockets and communities that are undervaccinated.

articles.title: Why AI Struggles To Reuse Chip Designs
articles.text:
AI can accelerate derivative designs, but physical constraints and incomplete data limit how much can be automated.
Key Takeaways:
- AI can accelerate derivative chip design, but those derivatives may not be physically viable or cost-effective.
- AI-assisted reuse depends on the availability of accurate design data, engineering knowledge, and proven methodologies.
- End-to-end automation is limited by gaps in multi-physics simulation, implementation, and verification.
Chipmakers are seeing mixed results when they apply AI to derivative and new chip designs, finding that AI-generated solutions can be substantially different and more costly than expected, and that AI-driven designs introduce new manufacturing and verification challenges.
Several key problems have emerged when incorporating AI in chip design. Among them:
- The data needed to ensure that follow-on designs will function as expected may not be complete because some of that data resides in other companies, such as foundries, OSATs, and various equipment and process providers;
- Integrating rapidly evolving AI capabilities into established EDA flows remains challenging, especially where predictability, traceability, and silicon-proven results are required.
- Many organizations have customized tools for their own chips, markets, and expertise, and AI tools have not yet adapted to those changes.
“There’s the engineer in me that says if AI can take us to brave new worlds where humans haven’t yet gone, that’s an exciting thing,” said Nilesh Kamdar, general manager of Keysight EDA. “But I’ve seen it run into problems. For example, I had a low-pass filter, which we call a pixelated model, and it looks like a QR code in the middle. There’s a high-frequency part running at about 2 GHz. If I want to change it to 2.5 GHz, a human would look it up in a textbook. There are traditional ways to do it, and they would create something that any other human would recognize. AI looks at this, says, ‘I don’t understand your textbook, so I’m going to just turn on and off any single part of this grid, and I’ll come up with something.’ It does sort of work, but there are constraints. Is this manufacturable? Is this cost-effective? Did I learn anything out of this? Yes, AI solved a problem for me, but as a human, I had intuition about what worked at 2 GHz. Now, if I want to shift to 2.5 GHz, that same intuition will change the design.”
Instead of making an incremental change to account for a new spec, AI may come up with something completely different, with no correlation between versions, Kamdar explained. “There’s a cost of letting AI do all of these things.”
Reusing designs across multiple generations of chips has long been the go-to strategy as a way of amortizing non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs and reducing development time. Using AI agents to come up with derivatives adds a whole different way of looking at the problem. AI agents can assess existing architectures and RTL to identify potential bottlenecks, explore design modifications, optimize EDA tool settings, and automate portions of verification and debugging. And they can orchestrate workflows across multiple tools, reducing the manual effort required to adapt existing IP to new specifications.
But the resulting AI-generated design is not necessarily ready to be implemented in a follow-on chip. Engineers must determine whether proposed changes are physically feasible, manufacturable, cost-effective, and compatible with the new design’s requirements. That, in turn, will determine where AI can and cannot be used, and where EDA tools need to evolve in order to close that gap.
Software reuse easier than hardware reuse
Despite AI’s promise, a lot of human effort is still needed in today’s designs. Working with natural language interfaces is a big plus, but minor differences in queries can result in very different answers.
“We were rapidly adapting the automotive solution to robotics because there’s a lot of commonality,” said Baaziz Achour, CTO of Qualcomm. [1] “Many of the key functions are similar, such as perception, path planning, and foundational technologies like sensor fusion, object recognition, location, and control. We were able to take the full automotive solution and apply it to robotics. We have very effective solutions for scaling the software. However, hardware IP scaling and SoC integration still require significant human effort.”
Those differences can also be significant across domains. for example, developers may increase the number of cores in an NPU and use tools to analyze bottlenecks as application workloads shift. But this type of scaling is very different with mobile multimedia, such as a camera, Achour explained. “Across a lot of this AI spectrum of products, the basic camera and display blocks are similar, but the requirements are very different in camera count, speed, and power.”
Fig. 1: Designers can use tools to adapt common IP, but there is still a non-recurring engineering cost for SoC implementation. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
While designers can leverage core IP blocks, such as an image signal processor, every processing core, camera, and display across these devices must meet diverse requirements and cost targets. “Currently, we often create separate architectures and hardware design variants for each case,” said Achour. “Can EDA help us build one flexible architecture that adapts to these diverse requirements instead of manually customizing for each time?”
The answer? Maybe. Ensuring that a chip design will function flawlessly requires an ecosystem. Automating some steps in the design flow can help, but how much automation and which steps are still being explored. Nevertheless, there are plenty of places where engineers would welcome more flexibility and automation, such as iteratively tuning EDA tools to meet design targets.
“Three months were spent in recipe tuning of EDA tools,” said Achour. “Neither the RTL nor the floorplan were changed in these iterations, so this is a huge source of inefficiency. EDA tool companies have AI-aided fine-tuning, but that consumes a lot of compute. Further innovation is needed for this.”
Fig. 2: EDA tools to help designers reuse IP need to account for area, thermal, PDN, and much more. Source: Qualcomm/DAC
The overall goal for engineers is to reduce runtime and compute, shortening time to market, increasing coverage and improving confidence at sign-off, and enabling engineers to be more productive. “We need innovation in GenAI, including GenAI that can create design input for the EDA tools, like a human designer, to drive fast convergence, and agents that can orchestrate design flows to reduce human effort for iteratively running tools to refine and optimize the design,” said Achour. “These are critical technologies to rapidly adapt common hardware to evolving AI product demand. We need innovation in AI for SoC design.”
Capturing IP data and design knowledge
Before AI can effectively help engineers adapt existing designs to new requirements, it needs access to accurate, organized information about the IP already available, including its configurations, constraints, dependencies, and previous implementations. Capturing and managing that information, along with the engineering knowledge and methodologies used to develop it, is essential to making AI-assisted derivative design scalable.
To help solve these challenges, established EDA vendors and startups are releasing physics-based, assistive AI co-pilot technology to speed up design exploration, PPA optimization, RTL generation, and verification.
However, before deploying an AI tool to create a brand-new design or a derivative design from existing IP, engineering teams must first collect the knowledge already inside the organization. After that, IP lifecycle management software is needed to connect engineering data, automate workflows, improve traceability, and make valuable IP easier to find and reuse.
“How do you pull different IPs, and where is information about that IP?” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “You could have information that says this IP works great for certain power levels. If you are developing an earbud, the available power may be much lower, so you know which IP will not be suitable. You have to look for a different source of IP from the finished product. You can create a software bill of materials (SBOM) or hardware bill of materials (HBOM) that lists all the IP you used, and you can confirm whether that was the latest and greatest version of the IP. Were there other variants of the IP? There are all kinds of different ways to do IP management.”
Teams also need a way to share the AI prompts, skills, and workflows they develop so that everyone can benefit from communal wisdom. “We invested in a platform and innovation store that allows our people to share prompts, plugins, check-ins, and solutions across teams,” said Ram Narayan, senior director of engineering at Arm. [2] “That was done primarily with the vision that teams can share skills and upskill themselves through that exchange. They can use the platform to upskill teams across the company, as well. This is an opportunity to bring people together around common ways of working and common learnings, which may have been lost over the years because we have acquisitions of groups, and groups going off and doing things differently. This is a real opportunity to enable these practices.”
An organization’s specific workflows need to be captured to get the best results from agentic AI-based design exploration tools.
“A company’s methodology is as important as the design, and the methodology they have used for the last 20 years to be able to tape out their chip has brought a lot of learning,” said Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents. “For example, ‘Use this cell/ don’t use this cell. Optimize for PPA that way. Don’t do this. Don’t do that. Or, do this.’ When you are in the ECO stage, and you have crosstalk, you can talk to the customer, and they say, ‘Oh, for crosstalk at this modem company, I have a very specific way of solving it. I have done the same thing for the last 10 years, and I am able to solve the crosstalk.’ That’s what we call the ontology.”
This is a very promising use case for agentic AI. A common approach from EDA tool providers today is to have an agentic collaboration platform sit with the customer, allowing sharing between users while also feeding data, methodology information, and design information back into agentic workflows so they can do the best possible job and deliver the best possible outcome. In ChipAgent’s approach, all proprietary customer data stays on-prem. “This belongs to the customer,” Rahim noted. “It is not something that comes back to us.”
Automating interconnect design
While organizations wrestle with how to apply AI, they also are leveraging improvements in algorithmic optimization, software-driven simulation, and deterministic EDA. This is especially important when it comes to data movement, which is one of the key performance bottlenecks, along with moving data in and out of memories and processors. A tiled, algorithmic fabric is easier to scale up or down for derivatives than crossbars.
“For our switch customers who have been working with crossbars in the past, and have had deep, lived experience over decades, it is still a very hands-on experience with hand-coding RTL to build huge custom networks, and almost hand-wiring things,” said Saurabh Gayen, chief solutions architect at Baya Systems. “They say, ‘When this wire comes in, it’s going to come in here, then this other data is going to come from there, and we’re going to make it like an arbiter. This is a painstaking process where the whole design just gets bigger and more difficult by an n-squared factor. This is super painful for engineers, companies, and project managers, as well. It’s an incredible source of risk for them, because it’s iterative. It’s manual. They don’t know if they’re going to find surprises later.”
Massive parallelism and other techniques have transformed what previously looked like a complex engineering project into a very manageable math problem. “Suddenly, this becomes an algorithmic construct that says mathematically we will give you the exact performance properties you need,” Gayen explained. “This will create, literally, a grid of identical tiles. Top-down, you get that guarantee that it meets the performance needs ahead of time. Then in terms of implementation, when it’s the physical design, you actually build it and harden those designs, then figure out how to put it within a chip.”
In today’s landscape, a software-first approach is needed to build hardware, adapt it to new use cases and better products, and reduce customer cost, pain, engineering effort, and time to tape out. “It’s all built step by step,” Gayen observed. “For example, when I came in, we already had a really good software-defined flow, which is new for hardware. People don’t like writing software. They like getting their hands dirty and writing RTL. Having that software perspective of coming in and generating RTL is something that unlocks a different type of thinking and allows breakthroughs like this to happen. Companies are happy, and the engineers are happy because they don’t have to do the painstaking manual work anymore.”
Multi-physics optimization limits
However, for design exploration or reusing IP, no tool yet optimizes timing, IR, and thermal together at the RTL or architecture level.
“Today, we don’t have anything that helps the RTL designer all the way,” said Vinay Patwardhan, senior director, product management at Cadence. [3] “We have something that can help customers from the netlist stage. We have a vision for going all the way to architectural, but right now it’s either timing-based improvement, IR-based improvement, or thermal-based improvement — not all three together as a multi-physics problem. If you want improvement at the RTL stage, you have to incorporate all of them into the source code, which isn’t available because thermal analysis works on layout layers. IR needs the locations of the power sources. At the RTL stage, there is no physical awareness of any of this, so it is a difficult problem. However, if we can find correct ways to model and abstract all those effects at that early stage, then it will be possible. There is some work going on in that phase, but to answer clearly, we don’t have anything in the RTL today. We can optimize the netlist continuously with feedback.”
Tool providers are addressing the challenge from many angles. For example, ChipAgents developed Build-A-Chip-Bench to evaluate AI agents from workload spec and RTL generation through synthesis, physical implementation, and layout verification.
Fig. 3: Key steps from workload specification to GDS. Dashed arrows show problems found downstream that send the agent back to revise an earlier step. Source: ChipAgents
While these advances show AI’s potential to automate increasingly complex design workflows, generating a design is only part of the challenge. Each stage of implementation introduces physical constraints and interdependencies that can affect decisions made earlier in the process. Changes intended to improve one aspect of a design may create problems elsewhere, requiring tools to account for the interactions among electrical, thermal, mechanical, and other physical effects.
The need for agentic tools to be grounded in fundamental physics is one reason why end-to-end solutions are still under development.
“The limiting problems are no longer inside the chip,” said Hardik Kabaria, CEO of Vinci. “They’re physical problems that live at the boundaries — heat moving from die to package to board to enclosure, thermo-mechanical stress across heterogeneous material stacks, power density interacting with cooling strategy at the system level. The physical world doesn’t respect the organizational boundaries the industry has drawn around it, and neither do the failures.”
Others agree. “EDA tools must expand beyond single-die optimization to system-level design, including multi-die integration, packaging, and software-hardware co-design, evolving toward intent-centric platforms rather than collections of disconnected point tools,” said Insaf Meliane, director of product management and marketing at Arteris. “One major gap is verification, where rising design complexity continues to outpace engineering productivity despite significant AI advances.”
These challenges become even more complex as designs move beyond the chip and package to the board level, where reused IP and previously verified components must operate within new electrical and physical environments. While reusing proven designs can reduce engineering effort, changes in placement, connectivity, and surrounding circuitry can introduce interactions that were not present in the original implementation. This makes verification a critical part of derivative design, even when the underlying components have already been validated.
Verification at the board level
As with SoC IP data management, a robust data management foundation enables teams to reuse known good blocks on the board.
“They verified them in the past, and they could say, ‘This block doesn’t need to be verified,'” said David Wiens, product marketing manager at Siemens EDA. “If they use that block more than once, they only need to verify it once. But in reality, blocks of data and blocks of designs can and will behave differently depending on what’s around them. It’s a step toward simpler verification, but you still have to be careful. You have this one circuit, and you place it on the top layer of the design, but whatever’s running underneath it that’s native to that, that’s custom to that design and may in fact interact with it. You could put a shield around it if you wanted to really trust it and really make sure that it’s not impacted. But particularly with signal integrity, that’s a bit of a scary proposition to say, ‘I’m just going to trust that it’s more than likely to pass by itself.’ It’s a question of what it interacts with on the board.”
Fig. 4: Data management is a key component of using AI tools to speed up any part of the design flow. Source: Siemens EDA
Agentic AI tools can now shrink verification time. Siemens reported that its HyperLynx Agentic Toolkit reduced the design analysis for 112 high-speed channels from several weeks to a couple hours. “In a manual process, engineers would first need to figure out the signaling protocol,” Wiens explained. “What SerDes protocol is it using? I’ve got to dig up the manual, which can be hundreds of pages long. I’ve got to find the rules within that, and the conditions to set up my simulator. Then I’ve got to push the button and wait for it, and then when I get it back, I’ve got to visualize. I’ve got to look at the results one waveform at a time. Did it pass? Did it fail? And if not, I’ve got to figure out why, and I’ve got to iterate.”
With new agentic solutions, the AI can inspect the database itself. “It can identify potential issues off the bat before it even simulates,” he said. “Then it automates the workflow. That’s a big thing because it’s part of what democratizes the tool. Specialists understand both the workflow and the results. Democratizing that automation, simplifying it, means anybody can push the button. With visualization, when you’ve got a ton of data, you don’t want to look at it one at a time. We can use AI to take that data and visualize it to produce different types of results that aren’t just simple waveforms. The AI can diagnose where the problem is. ‘This eye [diagram] is failing. Here’s where I think the problem is, and here’s what we recommend you do next.’ It takes the engineers through that entire path.”
The speedup doesn’t come only from AI and software capabilities. “It’s about leveraging hardware horsepower, GPU horsepower, CPU cluster horsepower,” said Wiens. “That’s what gets us the speed. But there are also areas of AI that help us explore the design space faster without brute-force simulation. Agentic AI accelerates the steps, mostly through smarter execution, and then delivers trusted outcomes because it’s physics-based. It’s leveraging known good simulation engines, and IP can be managed in a safe way on-prem.”
Leveraging GPUs and CPUs comes with computational costs, a concern raised by Qualcomm’s Achour. Moreover, engineers still must manually implement many of the changes recommended by agentic AI tools.
“What engineers do next is go back to the design, the actual layout or schematic, and make the changes that were recommended,” said Wiens. “Today, that’s still largely a manual process. Watch this space. Automating the actual place and route and things like that is a lot harder than automating workflow.”
What AI still can’t automate
AI-based design tools are advancing rapidly, with vendors introducing new capabilities for RTL generation, design exploration, physical optimization, and verification. These advances are reducing engineering effort in individual stages of the design process, but efficiently adapting existing hardware IP to new applications remains a much broader challenge.
Making derivative chip design more scalable will require more than increasingly capable AI models. Design teams need organized, accessible IP data; reusable engineering methodologies; tools that can evaluate architectural and physical trade-offs; and verification workflows that account for changes in configuration, implementation, and operating environment. Agentic AI may help connect and automate these processes, but the underlying tools must still produce results grounded in physical reality.
At the most fundamental level, many AI tools are text-based LLMs. “They are really, really good at predicting the next word, the next phrase, the next line, then the next paragraph, and that means AI can be used to write text-based chip design specs or chip design documents like RTL design,” said Keysight’s Kamdar. “AI can be used to write verification scripts that will test RTL and prove it’s good RTL or not, or find flaws in it. AI can read a long series of debug logs that could be gigabytes long, and humans will take forever to go through that. AI can quickly say, ‘Hey, did you go to line 79? That’s where I see a major issue.’ Largely, that’s what AI is helping with. There are so many other aspects of chip design that are not text-based, not suitable for words, and they still need humans actively.”
For chip architects and design teams, the opportunity is not simply to generate new designs faster, but to reduce the engineering effort required to turn proven IP into new products. Achieving that goal will depend on how effectively AI-driven automation can work with established EDA tools, engineering knowledge, and physics-based verification to identify what can be reused, determine what must change, and validate the resulting design. The real measure of AI’s success in derivative chip design will not be how quickly it generates new RTL, but how reliably it can help engineers transform existing IP into verified, physically viable designs with less manual effort.

articles.title: Rockstar le cierra la puerta a Hollywood con ‘GTA’, pero podría llevar ‘Red Dead Redemption’ al cine
articles.text:
Con GTA 6 en boca de todos gracias a su exitoso lanzamiento, el interés de Hollywood por las propiedades intelectuales de Rockstar Games se ha revitalizado. Según un nuevo reporte de The Ankler, el estudio no está dispuesto a desarrollar una adaptación basada en Grand Theft Auto, pero no vería con malos ojos la posibilidad de una película o serie de Red Dead Redemption.
La citada publicación indica abiertamente que a Rockstar no le interesa expandir GTA al mundo del cine o la TV. Tiene todo el sentido que así sea, considerando que la franquicia ya tiene el hype y la anticipación suficiente por parte del público como para no requerir ningún tipo de adaptación. Los casi 3.800 millones de dólares que generó al cierre de su primer día a disposición son prueba cabal de ello.
En el caso de la saga Red Dead, la historia sería diferente; en especial, con las dos entregas de Red Dead Redemption. Según se menciona, Rockstar Games estaría abierta a escuchar ofertas para convertirla en películas o en una serie de televisión. Esto no necesariamente implica que el estudio termine aceptando alguna propuesta, pero sí que las posibilidades de que la IP dé el salto más allá de los videojuegos no son nulas.
Eso sí, los que quieran poner sus manos sobre Red Dead Redemption tienen que estar dispuestos a desembolsar en grande. El reporte indica que Rockstar quiere un mínimo de 100 millones de dólares para cualquier acuerdo de licencia.
Rockstar estaría dispuesta a adaptar Red Dead Redemption en películas o series
Desde Rockstar saben que tienen entre manos algunas de las propiedades intelectuales más buscadas de Hollywood. No es ilógico pensar que los pesos pesados del cine y la TV no tendrán problemas en desembolsar cuanto se les pida por licenciar Red Dead Redemption. En especial, considerando el empuje que en los últimos años han tenido las adaptaciones basadas en videojuegos.
The Last of Us (HBO) y Fallout (Amazon) son dos de los ejemplos más exitosos de esta movida. A estos hay que sumarle otras apuestas como God of War, Tomb Raider, Far Cry, Metal Gear Solid y Assassin's Creed. The Ankler sostiene que algunos de estos proyectos están destinando entre 15 y 25 millones de dólares por episodio, lo cual deja en claro que hay grandes expectativas detrás de este tipo de títulos.
Si una película o serie de Red Dead Redemption termina viendo la luz, aún es un misterio si podría tratarse de una adaptación fiel de los juegos, o una historia original que se inspire en estos. Sea como sea, todo el ruido por GTA 6 podría ayudar a darle más empuje a la iniciativa, para que Rockstar y Take-Two inflen todavía más sus cuentas bancarias.

articles.title: 9 startups picked for 1st Africa Ignite climate adaptation cohort
articles.text:
The United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) and BFA Global have selected nine climate adaptation startups from eight African countries for the first cohort of the Africa Ignite programme.
Funded by the Adaptation Fund Climate Innovation Accelerator (AFCIA) and run under the Adaptation SME Innovation Facility (ASIF), Ignite targets early-stage startups that have built a working prototype but are yet to validate it with users. The nine were chosen from 453 applications.
Over eight weeks, founders will test their solutions with farmers, cooperatives and agribusinesses. Weekly live sessions, specialist office hours, AI training and real-world user testing will help them gather evidence of demand and impact, sharpen their business models, and prepare to land customers and raise investment.
“Every founder in this cohort has a working prototype. The next step is often the hardest: putting it in front of a cassava farmer, a coffee cooperative or a poultry producer and learning what they will use and pay for,” said Rasima Swarup, ASIF lead at BFA Global.
The cohort includes Benin’s ALLO VETO, which helps poultry farmers formulate affordable feed from local ingredients when drought disrupts supply; Angolan biodigester maker EcoBioGás; and Tanzania’s GeoVLUP Adaptation Services, which turns farm and climate data into practical guidance for coffee farmers.
Also selected are Ugandan circular savings platform Ghala Circular Solutions; Zimbabwe’s Global Vision Impact, which captures and stores runoff water for households during dry spells; and Kenyan agritech Kilimora, whose AgriKonnekt platform delivers localised climate intelligence to cooperatives.
Rounding out the cohort are Zambia’s LinkBridge, which builds shared solar-powered irrigation for clusters of smallholder farmers; Malawian food traceability startup MTENGO wa Mizu; and Kenya’s North Coast Innovators, which cuts post-harvest losses for cassava farmers through solar drying and milling.
More than half of the startups are founded or co-founded by women, and seven of the nine have a woman in a leadership position.
The programme kicked off on November 11, pauses in December and resumes in January, with the startups set to present their results at a Founder Showcase and Feedback Forum in late February 2027.

articles.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
articles.text:
AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  York University
- Summary:
  AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.
For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.
But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."
A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI
The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.
If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.
"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.
The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.
Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.
AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story
The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.
AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.
This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.
"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.
The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.
Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.
That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.
"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.
Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior
The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.
If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.
"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.
Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.
The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.
Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain
Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.
By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.
"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."
A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.
To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.
Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.
The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.
Story Source:
Materials provided by York University. Original written by Sandra McLean. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sabine Muzellec, Kohitij Kar. Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains. Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; 8 (3): 474 DOI: 10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0

articles.title: Exein launches Ray AI agent to show manufacturers which firmware weaknesses to fix first
articles.text:
Exein launches Ray AI agent to show manufacturers which firmware weaknesses to fix first
Italian physical artificial intelligence cybersecurity company Exein SpA today launched an AI agent called Ray that it claims can help manufacturers find the security weaknesses that matter most in their connected-device firmware.
Ray is built into Exein Analyzer, the company’s firmware security platform, which examines firmware for vulnerabilities, security weaknesses and compliance issues. Engineers can then use Ray to explore those findings in a conversational way, looking at the security posture of a single product or an entire fleet.
The new offering is designed to address a growing security gap for manufacturers. Some connected products contain thousands of software components, and a single scan of one can flag hundreds of potential issues, Exein said. Which of those weaknesses actually needs to be fixed first is said to be the harder question.
Rather than working through separate vulnerability lists, security scores, trackers and compliance reports, engineers can put questions to Ray about Analyzer’s findings. Among the questions engineers can ask are what is driving a product’s security score, which vulnerabilities need attention first and which compliance issues affect a firmware image.
To pick out the small number of issues that pose the greatest risk, Ray draws on Analyzer’s scan results, vulnerability reachability data and compliance findings. An explanation of why each issue matters is provided alongside the results. In cases where the same weakness appears across multiple products, Ray is said to help teams see when addressing one issue could improve security across an entire product line.
Exein is launching Ray after a run of attacks on connected infrastructure across Europe, including cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems that disrupted stores in several countries in October and November. Similar risks extend to industrial equipment, healthcare, energy and transport systems, according to the company.
“Europe is connecting more of the physical world to software,” co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Giovanni Falcione said, “but too many products were never designed for the threat environment we have today. The recent attacks on refrigeration systems are a reminder that a weakness buried inside firmware can have consequences far beyond IT.”
The rate at which those weaknesses can be found and exploited is being “dramatically” accelerated by AI, Falcione said. With Ray, he said, engineering teams get a clearer way to work out what needs fixing before products reach the field, without every firmware engineer having to become a cybersecurity expert.
Also included in Ray is support for reading Analyzer’s findings against regulatory requirements such as the European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act. Reporting obligations under the act for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents have applied since September, with the wider requirements taking effect in December 2027.
Founded in 2018, Exein offers technology that is distributed across more than 2 billion connected devices in sectors including industrial automation, automotive, energy, healthcare and robotics. The company’s other offerings include Photon, which provides runtime security for connected devices, physical AI and autonomous AI agents. It raised $270 million at a $1.7 billion valuation in September.

articles.title: Galaxy Watch 8 fica mais em conta na pré-Black Friday do Magalu
articles.text:
Galaxy Watch 8 fica mais em conta na pré-Black Friday do Magalu
Galaxy Watch 8 oferece configurações avançadas para esportes e academia; smartwatch atinge 61% OFF histórico graças a cupom no app
O Galaxy Watch 8 BT de 40 mm está saindo por apenas R$ 1.079,10 no Pix no Magazine Luiza. Este é um dos menores preço que já vimos pelo smartwatch para treinos e esportes da Samsung, com uma redução significativa sobre o preço oficial mais recente (R$ 2.499).
Esta oferta é o menor preço que já encontramos para o Galaxy Watch 8 BT 40 mm. Nas outras 15 ofertas publicadas desde janeiro de 2026, o melhor foi R$ 1.169 (Magalu, 16/7/2026).
O Galaxy Watch 8 oferece recursos avançados de saúde, como monitor de pressão arterial, eletrocardiograma e o sensor BioActive. Essas tecnologias permitem acompanhar sua frequência cardíaca e composição corporal com alta precisão, ajudando a manter melhores hábitos de vida.
O Galaxy AI integrado, por sua vez, otimiza a análise desses dados oferecendo uma leitura mais completa da qualidade do sono e dos níveis de energia corporal. Essas características justificam a presença do Galaxy Watch 8 entre no ranking de melhores smartwatches para treinos segundo o Tecnoblog.
Vale pontuar que a queda de preços recente se dá pelo lançamento do Galaxy Watch 9 no mercado, que pode ser encontrado em promoção por cerca de R$ 1,5 mil (50% acima do antecessor). Entre uma geração e outra, bastante coisa mudou: processador mais novo, bateria maior, recursos de IA a mais e design mais leve.
Porém, isso não significa que o Galaxy Watch 8 tenha ficado obsoleto, nem que ficará tão cedo. O sistema operacional do relógio deve continuar recebendo atualizações até 2029, incluindo novas funcionalidades, melhorias, e segurança em dia — especialmente importante para um wearable com NFC disponível.

articles.title: Meta brings its Muse AI assistant directly into Instagram DMs
articles.text:
Instagram users can now chat with Meta’s AI agent Muse in a DM thread, the company announced on Tuesday. The social media network says users can chat with Muse to get more context about a post, place, or product they come across, or catch up on conversations they may have missed in their other DMs.
The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent. It also reflects the growing competition among tech companies to make AI assistants a part of users’ everyday digital lives. By embedding Muse directly into Instagram, Meta is making it easier for users to access the AI agent, while also giving Muse access to a platform where users already discover products, places, and content.
Users can share Instagram posts with Muse and ask it to take action, such as adding a coffee shop to their Mexico City itinerary or finding a Black Friday deal on a pair of shoes.
Meta notes that conversations with Muse on Instagram will appear as a side chat in the main Muse app.
Muse in Instagram DMs will begin rolling out on Tuesday for iOS and Android users in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore.
Meta also announced that users can now do more with the posts and reels they’ve bookmarked on Instagram. For example, they can ask Muse to organize their saved content into custom folders, known as Collections. They could also ask Muse to turn a recipe video into a grocery list, turn the travel content from their favorite travel creators into an itinerary for an upcoming trip, or have Muse send them outfit ideas based on fashion reels they’ve collected.
Starting Tuesday, when users save a post on Instagram, they will see a prompt for Muse to organize it for them. This feature is launching in the U.S. and Canada.
Meta says that users remain in control of their Muse experience on Instagram. Nothing is shared, published, or sent without their approval, and they can ask Muse to forget information or undo actions at any time.

Cell C, the South African telecoms operator, has acquired Melon Group, the owner of Melon Mobile, a South African mobile virtual network operator (MVNO). The companies did not disclose the financial terms, and Melon will continue operating as a separate business under its existing management.
Explain like I’m new here: Cell C has played the infrastructure-provider role for many mobile brands by providing network access that other companies use to sell their own mobile services. It hosts 5.71 million MVNO lines, including Capitec Connect, the mobile service offered by South African bank Capitec, and FNB Connect, the equivalent offering from First National Bank. Cell C estimates that it serves 80–85% of South Africa’s MVNO market.
What does Cell C get out of this? Melon brings more than 100,000 customers to the deal. It was also among the early South African MVNOs to offer eSIMs, which let users activate mobile services without inserting a physical SIM card. Cell C also gets Melon’s technology. In March 2025, Melon launched Melon Digital, a mobile virtual network enabler (MVNE) that allows other companies to launch and manage their own mobile services without building the systems themselves.
What’s interesting: Melon originally launched using MTN’s network and will remain a multi-network operator after the acquisition. Customers currently using MTN will not automatically move to Cell C. So, Cell C now owns a mobile business that still relies partly on its biggest rival’s infrastructure.

Vodafone records $3.3 billion gain from Safaricom deal
Vodafone’s latest Safaricom deal has produced two eye-catching figures: KES 272.4 billion ($2.1 billion) spent and KES 430.2 billion ($3.3 billion) gained. But there’s a catch. The second amount isn’t money that landed in Vodafone’s bank account.
The British telecoms giant recorded the KES 430.2 billion ($3.3 billion) accounting gain after its South African subsidiary, Vodacom, increased its stake in Kenya’s Safaricom from 35% to approximately 55%. 
Explain like I’m new here: In June, Vodacom bought 15% of Safaricom from the Kenyan government for KES 204.3 billion ($1.57 billion) and another 5% from its parent company, Vodafone, for KES 68.1 billion ($524 million). The purchases gave Vodacom control of Safaricom. And in accounting, gaining control changes how a company reports an investment. 
Previously, Vodacom treated Safaricom as an associate, recording its share of the Kenyan company’s profits. Now, it can include Safaricom’s full financial results in its group accounts. Accounting rules also required Vodafone to reassess the value of its existing investment, producing the KES 430.2 billion gain. 
Between the lines: This was a one-off gain on paper, not profit from selling airtime or processing M-Pesa transactions. Vodacom separately reported a KES 181.8 billion ($1.4 billion) accounting gain from the same takeover. Even with its larger gain, Vodafone recorded an overall €3.6 billion ($4 billion) loss for the six months ended September, weighed down by charges elsewhere in its business. 
State of play: There’s also a legal complication. In September, Kenya’s High Court nullified the government’s 15% stake sale, ruling that the transaction’s effect on Safaricom’s ownership and control had not been adequately disclosed. The decision is under appeal, and Vodacom retains control while the case continues. 
Zoom out: The bigger prize is control of Safaricom’s telecoms business, M-PESA operations, and Ethiopian expansion. Vodafone has booked its accounting gain, but the ownership battle isn’t over. A favourable balance sheet entry is one thing; keeping control of the business behind it is another.

MultiChoice wants ISPs to block pirate streams
Imagine paying for a football match on a streaming website, only to discover later that the service is illegal. Some pirate platforms look so legitimate that customers don’t even realise they’re paying the wrong people.
South African broadcaster MultiChoice wants to make those services harder to access. The DStv owner is lobbying the Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (ICASA), the country’s telecom regulator, to require Internet service providers (ISPs) to block websites distributing pirated content.
Explain like I’m new here: MultiChoice has been fighting online piracy for years. The problem is that many illegal streaming services operate outside South Africa, where local copyright enforcement has limited reach. Even when one website disappears, its operators can simply move to another address.
How would it work? MultiChoice wants dynamic site-blocking. Instead of pursuing a fresh court order each time a pirate website changes its address, ISPs could update their blocklists to stop customers from reaching the replacement site.
State of play: South Africa’s existing laws don’t clearly require ISPs to block access to these websites. Parliamentary advisers raised the issue last week, suggesting that ICASA explore interim regulations while lawmakers consider changes to existing legislation. No new blocking requirement has been approved.
Between the lines: MultiChoice is changing where it applies pressure. If a pirate operator overseas ignores a takedown request, a South African ISP is much easier for local regulators to reach.
But ISPs have concerns of their own. Blocking an IP address can accidentally cut off legitimate websites sharing that address. Industry body ISPA wants clear laws and judicial oversight before providers are required to decide what customers can access.
Zoom out: An industry-backed study on piracy’s economic impact is due on December 7. Its findings could strengthen the case for tougher enforcement, but stopping piracy without blocking innocent websites will require more than a list of addresses.

Botswana Telecommunications Corporation (BTC), the country’s state-owned telecoms operator, plans to launch BTC Satellite in partnership with Starlink, the satellite internet business owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, in early 2027. Explain like I’m new here: Starlink already has a presence in Botswana. The Botswana Communications Regulatory Authority granted the company a commercial operating licence in May 2024, and it launched its broadband service in August that year. BTC Satellite will extend that relationship into mobile connectivity.
BTC says the service will target gaps in places such as the Central Kalahari, wildlife conservation corridors and remote border areas. Users are expected to access services such as SMS, maps, WhatsApp calls and light browsing.
Africa is embracing direct-to-phone: Airtel Africa and Starlink launched Starlink Mobile in the Democratic Republic of Congo in August. The service reached Uganda in September, granting eligible Airtel customers access through a free introductory trial and qualifying data bundles.
In 2023, satellite company Lynk Global signed an agreement with Vodafone Ghana to extend mobile coverage to subscribers using its satellites. Vodacom is also eyeing a 2027 launch of direct-to-phone services in South Africa.
Although direct-to-phone services could help telecoms operators reach people in remote locations without the cost of building mobile towers across difficult terrain, it depends on compatible smartphones and operator integration. Not every phone will work, and users may need to update their devices to access it.
