articles.title: Apiary Therapeutics raises $7.3 million for engineered stem cell therapies
articles.text:
A biotechnology startup seeking to make more effective stem cell-derived therapies has announced its first round of venture funding.
The news: Apiary Therapeutics, co-founded by two Canadian entrepreneurial academics, announced on Monday that it had secured $7.3 million CAD to advance its stem-cell therapy technology toward pre-clinical trials. The seed round was co-led by Genesys Capital and BDC Capital’s Life Sciences Venture Fund, with participation from InBC and Mission BioCapital.
From the source: “A medicine that the body makes for itself, at the right level, in a durable manner, from one dose would change what treatment looks like for people who today depend on frequent infusions,” Apiary co-founder Yale Michaels, an assistant professor at the University of Manitoba, said in a statement.
The context: Apiary was co-founded by Michaels and University of British Columbia biomedical engineering professor Peter Zandstra, who has previously founded three biotech startups. Its technology turns stem cells, instead of a patient’s blood, into B cells (white blood cells that make antibodies) that can create proteins that fend off diseases, which could have applications across protein deficiencies, autoimmune diseases, and fighting cancers.
The startup is looking to validate its technique in preclinical trials, meaning in model animals like mice, before testing in humans. Apiary also hopes to expand its teams in Vancouver and Toronto.
Final thought: The funding announcement is the second from BDC Capital’s Life Sciences Venture Fund, a new direct investment vehicle that the Crown corporation announced after admitting it had pulled back too early from life sciences investing. The wider industry is seeing a funding crunch, as the medtech industry is on track to see its lowest financing activity in a decade.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by Trnava University.

articles.title: AI Vs. High-Level Synthesis
articles.text:
AI promises to automate chip design from spec to implementation, but can it match HLS in productivity, verification, and quality of results?
Key Takeaways:
- The main advantage provided by HLS is productivity, but those gains diminish if not accompanied by a robust verification methodology.
- AI agents around current HLS tools will allow more exploration and build on existing trust but full AI potential may want to work outside those bounds.
- Producing RTL is the easy part. HLS has to generate RTL that is implementable, that meets power, performance and area constraints, within a defined context. AI struggles with this today.
High-level synthesis (HLS) initially struggled to find a market, but eventually it became a valuable tool for certain kinds of design. It is now threatened by the promise of AI, which some predict will allow engineers to go from specification to finished silicon while avoiding many EDA tools, including HLS.
Most developers of HLS solutions are not troubled by this today, though they do see many changes on the horizon.
HLS has been most valuable for algorithmic accelerators, although that could change. “When I have something that is too slow or power hungry to run on a CPU, I may want to look at custom silicon,” says Stuart Clubb, technical product management director at Siemens EDA. “I might choose to go the path of IP reuse, and that is the most likely answer for a bus interface or peripheral. HLS got shoved off to the new blocks — things that hadn’t been done before and needed some smart architectural hardware design, and solving problems that hadn’t been tackled before.”
The main advantage of HLS is productivity. “HLS handles complex control logic and data path equally well, with 10 to 20 times less code than RTL,” says Badru Agarwala, CEO and co-founder at Rise Design Automation. “Less code is easier to review, so you can trust what you’re shipping, and easier to edit when the specification changes. That is what lets a design scale from a single block to a large subsystem, whether an engineer or an AI writes it.”
Those productivity gains can be significant (see figure 1, below.) “When we talk about HLS, the goal is not to do everything using HLS, or when we attempt LLM to RTL, the goal is not to do everything on LLM to RTL,” said Diptesh Nandi, senior product marketing manager at Microchip. “There will be a certain portion that requires time to market, or faster processing that will not be optimized. If you use HLS, it’s probably going to consume more power because it’s not going to be optimized (compared to hand-crafted RTL). If you take the LLM-to-RTL route — where you focus on time to market and then apply it on the development time, the training time that you require where you’re creating the whole tools flow, or creating the whole design — then you will spend less time developing the whole solution, less time training the whole solution, thereby saving power.”
Fig. 1: An HLS flow for FPGA designs. Source: Microchip
The real challenge is that chip complexity is growing faster than engineering productivity. “Writing RTL was never the biggest bottleneck,” says Rise DA’s Agarwala. “Amdahl’s law applies here. Making one relatively small part of the development process dramatically faster doesn’t help much if the rest of the process remains unchanged. Most of the schedule is spent on verification and the iterations needed to meet performance, power, and area targets.”
This does play into one aspect of HLS, which is that verification time of C code is orders of magnitude faster than RTL. Given that HLS can synthesize designs quickly, and those can be verified at the abstract level, it enables an AI agent to evaluate a lot of alternatives in a small amount of time. This coupling may be the big winner, but we are not there yet.
“Software is leading the pack,” says Tom De Muer, fellow at Keysight EDA. “Digital design is coming next, followed by mixed analog, and then the full physics. High-level synthesis sits at that digital part. It’s lagging software. In addition, we have the problem in the semiconductor world that you cannot prompt something very vague and expect something to come out that’s production-ready.”
To see widespread adoption, it has to solve a real problem. “For 50 years, EDA progress meant climbing abstraction,” says Mehir Arora, head of engineering at ChipAgents. “We built RTL, then HLS, because the human mind cannot hold the full design space. Abstraction narrows the potential design space for an engineer, making it possible for them to reason about it. But it is a loss of potential QoR. HLS was never about better hardware, but a price of designing for human capacity.”
Still, trust must be gained for any new tool or abstraction. “When we talk about AI doing this, there is some resistance from people like us because we have been burnt by things that we didn’t understand,” says Keysight’s De Muer. “For instance, if you have a design that works, that’s great, but it works under the test conditions that you know that you tested it with. But we all had our tape outs that went into production. We had full 100% regression test, but in the field something failed, and then you need to understand how it works to fix it.”
It took a long time before HLS was trusted. “HLS is now providing significant value for a specific segment of designs,” says Dave Kelf, CEO at Breker Verification Systems. “One of the most significant barriers to entry for the technology, and indeed logic synthesis originally, was the disconnect between the abstract model, especially regarding circuit timing, and the final design output. Engineers had trouble making that connection, making them nervous about trusting the results.”
What is stopping AI from doing the synthesis itself? “The rules for the synthesizable subset of C++, and by extension SystemC, have remained relatively constant for probably the last 10 to 15 years,” says Siemens’ Clubb. “In the C+ world, modeling streaming interfaces needed some level of IP to be able to represent that in an untimed sequential language, versus trying to model the explicit concurrency. We created AC channel and bit-accurate data types. A designer, or AI, needs to write out code that understands these. There’s just not a lot of training material.”
Verification
No new abstraction is going to be successful if you don’t have both a development and a verification methodology that work together. The widespread adoption of RTL required both RTL simulation and static timing verification. ESL required C and SystemC simulation and equivalence checking.
“On the verification side for HLS, people have clamored for sequential equivalent checking,” says Clubb. “It is slowly improving, but as with any formal verification challenge, there are limitations, capacity issues, things associated with latency and throughput. There’s still a lot of RTL verification required.”
Building trust takes time. “We already trust synthesis tools to perform complicated transformations without inspecting every gate,” says Agarwala. “That trust comes from verification, not from how the implementation was generated. Coverage-driven verification is equally important. Requirements can be mapped to assertions and functional coverage points, showing which parts of the specification have been exercised and which still need attention. Formal verification adds another level of confidence by checking RTL properties exhaustively within the assumptions of the formal model. The goal is to make verification faster and more complete, not simply generate RTL faster.”
The need to perform simulation on the output slows down performance and adoption. “The issue that arises, especially with analog and RF, is that you need to verify them against a physical oracle, a high-frequency simulator,” says De Muer. “Those take a long time to simulate. An agent typically needs multiple runs, and if that run takes you two or three hours, it naturally limits how much exploration can be done. Comparing it to software, you can produce a program, compile it, test it, and it stands up. In a fraction of a second, you have a data point to learn from. That’s not the case when you’re doing a 200 or 300 gigahertz design. Many runs are required so that models can improve.”
AI’s potential
In a similar manner, the primary advantage that AI can provide is productivity. By finding better architectures through a process of trial and error, it may eventually get to better designs, but that is not the case today. “The next leap in engineering productivity won’t come from doing the same work faster,” says Agarwala. “It will come from fundamentally changing how work gets done. The biggest productivity gains will come from shortening the time between an idea, an implementation, and a verified result. The teams that succeed will be the ones that can explore, measure, and verify the best architectures fastest.”
But that is not going to happen with agents. “Somebody once said that AI is a really good cover band,” says Clubb. “It’s seen the sheet music. It knows all the lyrics, and it will give you a variation on a theme. But for something completely new, maybe not so much. AI is still a way off, and it’s still very reliant on skill files that somebody else has to put together to guide how to do it. There’s not enough volume of training material. Even with these trillions of parameters and all of this input to these frontier models, they’re still not there yet.”
In addition, agents are built around existing tools, which may not be the best idea. “An LLM is much more acceptive for lower-level abstractions,” says ChipAgents’ Arora. “Give it verification and fast feedback and it can skip abstraction layers. Taking CUDA kernel generation as an example, we’ve seen LLMs write CUDA or even lower-level PTX without traditional compiler optimizations, but generate better output. Similar trends are happening in EDA and the IC flow. While humans are well suited to microarchitecture => HLS => RTL => netlist, we already see that LLMs are better at producing RTL directly when equipped with physics surrogates to predict PPA. Indeed, in the future, we may see LLMs directly generate netlists, eliminating another layer of indirection.”
Many people point to a context issue today. “If I say, ‘Design me an inductor for some IC design,’ my agent will do this, but it probably didn’t care about how well it will perform in situ in a bigger context,” says De Muer. “Does it even select the process I’m allowed to use? All of those things are missing. AI is helping to translate those intents. But you still need to be very specific because where the engineering matters, for the semiconductor pieces, all of these things need to be specified. They are not coming out of thin air.”
This is an opportunity to bring more of the context together for some problem domains. “Engineers can develop and verify the design within a TLM-based system simulation environment, alongside processors, memories, and other components, and then synthesize that same description into RTL,” says Agarwala. “This avoids maintaining separate functional models that can gradually diverge from the hardware implementation. Software development and system-level verification can also begin before RTL is available.”
That context is the ultimate shift left as well. “HLS historically, and most RTL designers, have striven to produce RTL that closes timing because if it doesn’t close timing, it’s useless,” says Clubb. “In HLS we do a lot of algorithmic, arithmetic stuff that has cascading wavefronts. When you get to a gate-level netlist, and in order to close timing, it’s not just a nice bunch of fast adders and AND gates or multipliers. There is a benefit to making sure that you don’t put too many operators between registers, because then your glitch power starts to get unmanageable. Even though your area goes down, if you over-pipeline, you’ve got too many registers. That puts your switching power up and puts your clock tree power up. You can do design exploration to hone in on the local saddle for power, or the local saddle for area, or — and this sounds like a prompt — find me the lowest power that doesn’t exceed the smallest area by 5%.”
One of the concerns is design stability. “With AI-generated RTL, changing the pipeline, resource allocation, or memory architecture often means generating a new implementation and verifying it again,” says Agarwala. “Every rewrite creates another opportunity for subtle bugs. HLS takes a different approach. We can keep the functional description unchanged while using synthesis constraints to control pipelining, parallelism, resource sharing, and memory organization. This allows AI to explore hundreds of implementations without regenerating thousands of lines of RTL. Some architectural changes still require modification of the source, but those changes are generally easier to make and verify at a higher level.”
Reality
The big question is exactly how well can AI do this today? “It does really badly, mainly because the type of code that we are handling in HLS does not usually have an easy one-to-one mapping for RTL,” says Clubb. “Once you start the process of scheduling and laying out a data path, you need to understand the process technology and the frequency that you are aiming for. What interfacing do you want? Is this a single-ported memory as an array? Is it a dual-ported memory that has memory bandwidth limitations? Can I split that up? Can I re-architect that? There are things you can do as microarchitectural constraints in HLS because they’re programmatic, but for the interfacing things like stalling, flushing, bubble compression, AI is not good.”
Still, if you have productivity gains, is it good enough? “If you need a small widget and you don’t care too much about performance, you don’t care too much about power consumption, if all of those things are irrelevant to you, AI can produce something reasonable for digital or even analog design,” says De Muer. “But even if we reduce that time to zero, the end-to-end results or gains are pretty modest. We need to look one step further, but that’s a long journey, and it comes from changing the workflows.”
Some of the gains are consumed by additional verification demands. “There was a recent paper out of Harvard talking about how AI-generated code in general is pushing more effort into verification of that code,” says Clubb. “That means the ROI for many companies is becoming questionable.”
For now, AI appears more likely to augment HLS than replace it. While AI can accelerate RTL generation and architectural exploration, producing silicon-ready designs still requires verification, implementation awareness, and careful optimization for power, performance, and area. Whether AI ultimately replaces existing abstraction layers may depend less on its ability to generate code than on its ability to produce predictable, verifiable results.

Los dos candidatos perfectos para el 75% de la población. Dos teléfonos de gama media, con un precio muy ajustado y que puede usar cualquier tipo de persona. El segundo modelo es uno de Motorola, sí, la mítica Motorola. La que todos recordamos, que se acabó yendo pero que regresó hace unos años más fuerte que nunca y manteniendo todos sus valores de ofrecer buena tecnología y un precio ajustado. El Moto G77 tiene una pantalla AMOLED de 6,8 pulgadas, un procesador Dimensity 6400, una cámara principal de 108 megapíxeles y una capacidad de almacenamiento de 512 GB. Cuesta menos de 250 euros.
Bonus: el teléfono con la mejor cámara del año

Los dos ofrecen la mejor experiencia en fotografía tanto en hardware como en software, respetando a la perfección lo que vemos, sin retocar de manera excesiva nada, con un zoom increíble al que le puedes acoplar un teleconvertidor. Pero es que además son dos teléfonos potentes, con las mejores especificaciones del mercado. articles.title: CRA, AI Robotics, Motor Control, Digital Energy at electronica 2026
articles.text:
The Singapore-based MCU and security-IC supplier showed 35 applications and solutions in Munich and argued that European buying decisions now turn on three things: evidence a chip can survive a Cyber Resilience Act audit, real-time response in AI robotics, and efficient power conversion for digital energy.
NSING Technologies, the Singapore-based fabless semiconductor arm of NSING Group (300077.SZ; 02701.HK), has concluded its participation in electronica 2026, which closed on 13 November at Messe München, after displaying 35 applications and reference designs on its Hall C2 stand (Booth 741), grouped around the questions European OEMs brought to the show: how to prove a product is cyber-secure before the EU Cyber Resilience Act becomes fully binding in December 2027, how to make a robot joint respond in real time, and how to convert power efficiently in digital-energy systems.
The show’s official themes — artificial intelligence, network resilience and energy efficiency — ran through the booth. What tied them together, according to the company, was a shift in where the difficulty now sits: less in any single chip’s peak specification, more in the compliance file, at the joint and in the power stage.
CRA: reporting obligations are already live; the deadline is next December
A sizeable share of the booth went to the EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847), which is less about features than about evidence. The regulation entered into force on 10 December 2024. Reporting obligations for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents took effect on 11 September 2026. The main obligations — conformity assessment and CE marking — apply from 11 December 2027.
For procurement teams, that sequence mattered more than the headline date. The reporting duty is already enforceable, and the design changes plus documentation needed to pass assessment have roughly a year to land. “Future compliance” is no longer an accurate description of the situation.
NSING maps its portfolio onto the regulation’s classes. N32S security ICs and TPM devices at CC EAL4+ support third-party assessment for Critical-class products. Cortex-M4 and Cortex-M7 MCUs, including the N32H and N32G4 families, are positioned for Class 2, with chip-level SESIP certification in progress. Cortex-M0 parts such as the N32G0 and N32WB fit the Class 1 self-declaration route.
Beyond the silicon, the company packages what an OEM has to put in the file: an ECR (essential cybersecurity requirements) mapping table, a software bill of materials, a compliance support pack and introductions to notified bodies. These are organised around a five-step route — classification and threat modelling, secure development practice, validation and bill-of-materials control, system documentation with a vulnerability reporting channel, and assessment plus CE archiving.
Post-quantum migration sits on the same axis. NSING’s MCUs integrate ML-KEM (512/768/1024) and ML-DSA (44/65/87), starting with the N32H4xx and N32H7xx and extending across its Cortex-M4-and-above N32 line, covering key establishment, device identity, firmware update and secure boot, and data integrity checks. The implementations coexist with RSA, ECC, SHA, and ship with drivers, a crypto abstraction layer, example code and a porting guide — the building blocks for an assessment, hybrid-verify, migrate and evolve sequence.
Digital energy: power conversion and battery management
On the power-conversion side, the pitch is topology coverage rather than a single headline number. The N32DP474 runs PFC, LLC resonant conversion and multiphase interleaved topologies from one device; NSING characterises peak efficiency at up to 99% under rated load, and says a reference design built on it is already in volume production with server-power customers. For energy storage, the NB1802 analog front end monitors 18 series-connected cells, covering 1500 V container systems and residential packs.
Humanoid robots: a three-tier architecture from joint to machine
The bottleneck in humanoid robots is not the model. It is the joint — torque, speed and position loops that have to close deterministically while the rest of the machine stays synchronised — and the coordination above it.
NSING splits that work across cores. The N32H785EC pairs a Cortex-M7 at 600 MHz, dedicated to field-oriented control across torque, speed and position loops plus dual absolute-encoder decoding, with a Cortex-M4F at 300 MHz handling CAN FD and EtherCAT. A 100 ps high-resolution timer and hardware CORDIC/FMAC units support multi-axis synchronisation on high-load joints. Secondary joints at the wrist, ankle and torso use the N32MD473, which integrates a three-phase gate driver. Dexterous hands move to a distributed arrangement of a main controller plus per-channel drivers, so wiring and heat dissipation stop setting the size of a finger.
Around the joints, the company supplies NB1802 battery management ICs, N32WB BLE SoCs and NS350 TPM rated CC EAL4+. NSING says these designs are shipping in volume as part of complete humanoid, quadruped, collaborative-arm and dexterous-hand platforms.
The same control IP appeared elsewhere on the stand: the VIGX π6 exoskeleton uses the N32H49x for high-precision position control; 3D printers run real-time motion planning and stepper drive on the N32G45x with the N32G003 handling housekeeping; collaborative arms implement multi-axis interpolation on the N32H78x.
Industrial, automotive and motor control: the revenue base underneath
Underneath the headline demonstrations sat the business NSING earns today. The N32H7 family serves servo drives, PLCs, inverters and integrated motion controllers. The N32H785EC includes a Beckhoff-licensed EtherCAT slave controller and holds multi-axis synchronisation jitter to the microsecond range; the N32H47x and N32H48x carry IEC 61508 SIL 2 and SIL 3 functional-safety certification. The stand also showed a servo drive controller built on the N32ZH785EC, an industrial I/O module based on the N32H760, and an industrial gateway that pairs an N32S032 security IC with the main controller.
On the automotive side, the N32A455, N32A052 and N32A003 are AEC-Q100 qualified and specified from −40 °C to 125 °C. NSING says they are in volume production with body-radar designs at major Chinese EV makers, and that applications are moving outward from body control into on-board chargers, T-Boxes and smart-cockpit functions. A body control module, a reversing-radar design on the N32A455 and a headlight design on the N32G435 were on display.
Motor control is where the portfolio’s integration showed most clearly. The company’s matrix spans Cortex-M7, M4 and M0 cores and can drive one, two, four or six motors from a single MCU, cutting bill-of-materials cost for appliance and power-tool designs. Three parts carried the demonstration: the N32M016, which integrates a 150 V three-phase 6N gate driver, LDO and differential PGA in a 5×5 mm package to deliver 800 W at 90,000 rpm for drills and handheld vacuums, with back-EMF sensing and three-level overcurrent protection; the N32M012, with a 3P3N driver covering 6–40 V and sensorless sinusoidal FOC for ceiling and pedestal fans that runs stably from 200 rpm; and the N32G033K8Q7-1, a 64 MHz M0 part with three op-amps and a 25 µs current loop that supports 120,000 rpm hair dryers and adaptive-start refrigerator compressors.
One silicon platform across four kinds of building device
The building-automation demonstration was organized around a single data chain rather than individual products. Smart locks and access control pair the N32WB Bluetooth SoC with a security IC, so identification and unlock authorisation happen on the endpoint. The N32G45x drives elevator-car human-machine interfaces. Occupancy and daylight sensing dimming built on the N32G45x, N32G03x and N32WB connects lighting control to energy monitoring. The N32L43x smart breaker folds circuit-level metering, protection and remote control into the same link. For an OEM, the reusable part is that one silicon platform, one provisioning method and one back-end data format can cover all four device classes in an office building.
Why Europe, and what comes next
During the show the NSING team met global end customers, distributors and trade press, and continued talks on distributor coverage and joint reference designs. The company framed electronica 2026 as a live test of its global strategy: compliance, functional safety, long-term supply and local support — the four things European customers ask about first — are the areas it has been investing in for several years.
NSING said it will keep investing in global product development and ecosystem partnerships, with AI computing infrastructure, embodied intelligence and edge AI as its stated priorities, alongside security, SoC, RF and power management as established strengths.
About NSING Technologies
NSING Technologies, an NSING Group member founded in Singapore in 2018, delivers high-performance semiconductor solutions for the global industry. Its expertise spans general MCU, secure IC (TPM), BLE and BMS, with advanced capabilities in Arm/GPU multi-core architectures, low-power design and secure-zone IP. Its solutions power a wide range of applications, including AI, robotics, industrial automation, consumer electronics, smart home, automotive electronics, IoT devices, medical equipment, energy storage systems and wearable technology, enabling customers to innovate with confidence. articles.title: Why Y Combinator is backing fewer African startups
articles.text:
Four years after African founders made up roughly one in 17 companies in a Y Combinator batch, the continent has become a footnote at Demo Day. The reasons say as much about how YC has changed as about African tech.
In early-2022, Y Combinator’s Winter batch included 24 African startups, 18 of them from Nigeria. For the first time, an African country ranked third in a YC cohort, behind only the United States (US) and India. Lagos founders talked about the accelerator as a rite of passage, and the Paystack exit to Stripe made the path look repeatable.
Indeed, Disrupt Africa wrote articles around that time about the “cult of Y Combinator”, and the rave reviews the programme received from founders that participated in it.
That moment did not last. By Winter 2023 the African count had fallen to three, and Winter 2024 again admitted just three. Africa’s share of a batch had shrunk from about six per cent at the peak to around one per cent by Winter 2024. A search of the YC website for African startups for the 12 batches since then returns the message “sorry, no matching companies found”.
The pullback, however, is not a single decision made in San Francisco. It is the product of three things moving at once – a YC that has changed what it wants, an African funding market that cooled faster than most, and a portfolio record that has made the case for Africa harder to argue.
The numbers: from 24, to a handful, to none
YC’s African intake rose fast in the remote era and fell faster when it ended. The accelerator went fully remote from Summer 2020, ballooned its batches, and African founders who could never have relocated to San Francisco for three months suddenly could apply from Lagos or Nairobi. The Winter 2021 batch had ten African startups; Winter 2022 had 24.
Then came the correction. YC cut its Summer 2022 cohort to 240 companies from 414, citing the downturn and a changed venture market, and only eight African startups made it. Winter 2023 admitted three. Winter 2024 admitted four again – Nigerian fintechs Cleva and Miden, Kenyan travel-tech startup Triply, and Zimbabwe’s Ocular AI, out of 260 companies picked from more than 27,000 applications. There have been none since.
Across 14 years the picture is lopsided. YC has backed roughly 100 African startups since Wave in 2012, about two per cent of a portfolio of more than 4,600 companies. Nigeria accounts for around 40 per cent of them, Egypt about 15 per cent, and Kenya about 14 per cent, and more than half are fintechs. In other words, the surge in 2021 and 2022 was the anomaly, not the decline.
YC changed first
The biggest reason fewer African startups get in is that YC now wants something different, and wants it in San Francisco. Three shifts matter most.
The first is a return to physical programmes. Summer 2022 opened with an in-person kickoff, the first since Winter 2020. The programme now runs mainly on YC’s San Francisco campus for three months. For a founder in Accra or Kigali, that means a US visa, a quarter away from customers and staff, and San Francisco rents paid from a pre-seed budget. The remote years removed those costs; the return to campus put them back.
In addition, the type of company YC accepts has changed. Recent batches are dominated by AI companies selling to other businesses. In Spring 2026, 62 per cent of the cohort was B2B, and the Summer 2026 batch was focused on infrastructure for AI agents, with consumer companies at about five per cent. African YC alumni were overwhelmingly fintech and consumer-facing marketplaces built around local market gaps. That profile now sits outside what YC is hunting for.
In the meantime, YC raising the size of its cheque has set a higher bar, especially for African ventures. Its standard deal is now US$500,000 – US$125,000 for seven per cent, plus a US$375,000 uncapped SAFE. Companies must also incorporate in Delaware. A larger cheque on an uncapped note is a bet on US-scale outcomes, which raises the bar for businesses whose ceiling is set by Nigerian or Kenyan purchasing power.
YC did move to four batches a year in 2025, with smaller cohorts and more application windows. That gives African founders more shots, but it has not yet shown up as a visible rebound in African admissions. As previously mentioned, there have been none in that time.
Africa’s own downturn
The African side of the story made YC’s retreat easier. Startup funding on the continent fell by 27.8 per cent to US$2.4 billion in 2023, and a further 53.5 per cent in 2024, to US$1.12 billion.
When it recovered in 2025, to US$1.6 billion over the course of the year – note, 2026 is likely to be similar to this – the money went mostly to large rounds. The recovery has been real, but it has not been a seed-stage recovery. Average Series A and B cheques grew, while investors backed fewer companies. For YC, whose model depends on a deep pool of follow-on seed and Series A investors, that matters. A Demo Day company needs someone to lead its next round, and fewer global funds were writing early cheques into Lagos or Nairobi.
Currency made it worse. The naira lost most of its value against the dollar after Nigeria’s 2023 reforms, and Egypt’s pound was devalued repeatedly. A startup earning in local currency but valued in dollars watched its revenue shrink in the metric YC investors care about. Nigeria, which supplied 18 of the 24 African companies at the 2022 peak, took the hardest hit.
The portfolio record has not helped either. Of roughly 100 African YC companies, the ones that returned real capital or reached meaningful scale are a short list – Paystack, Flutterwave, Wave, Nomba and Reliance Health. Most of the rest are subscale, or shut down. Paystack’s US$200 million sale to Stripe in 2020 remains the benchmark exit, but it is six years old. At least five YC-backed African startups are formally inactive in YC’s directory.
What fills the gap
Fewer YC slots cost African founders more than US$500,000. The YC badge worked as a signal that let a first-time founder in Lagos raise from US investors who had never heard of them. Briter Bridges counted about US$1.3 billion in follow-on funding raised by YC’s African portfolio by 2021. Local alternatives can match the cheque, but not yet the network.
They are trying. Iyin Aboyeji’s Future Africa launched Accelerate Africa, openly pitched as a home-grown answer to YC. It takes no equity on entry and may invest US$250,000 to US$500,000 after due diligence. Madica writes up to US$200,000 on a SAFE, Katapult Africa invests US$150,000 to US$500,000 in agri-, food- and climate-tech, and Antler runs residencies in Nairobi and Lagos. Google’s equity-free Africa programme drew nearly 2,600 applicants for 15 places in 2026.
The broader accelerator map is shrinking, though. Techstars closed its Lagos programme in late 2024 after two cohorts, and the Founders Factory Africa venture studio shut in 2025 after its Mastercard Foundation partnership ended. The founders YC turns away are competing for a smaller set of local seats.
There is a quieter shift too. A growing number of YC’s African alumni now invest or build locally, and YC has kept supporting its earlier bets. In 2025 it took part in follow-on rounds for Nigerian food-delivery startup Chowdeck’s Series A and Egyptian grocery company Breadfast. YC is still in Africa. It is just backing what it already owns rather than buying new tickets.
A question of fit
Underneath the cyclical story is a structural one. YC’s model rewards companies that grow fast and reach liquidity within a decade. That works for payments, which is why Africa’s YC winners are almost all fintech startups. It fits poorly with the sectors where the continent’s infrastructure gaps are largest, such as energy, agri-tech, e-health, logistics, and last-mile delivery, which need longer runways, heavier regulation and less obvious exits.
There are reasons the numbers could tick up. Four batches a year means four chances rather than two, and smaller cohorts of roughly 100 to 125 companies may favour founders who were crowded out of the old twice-yearly rush. African teams building AI tools for global business customers fit YC’s current thesis far better than the marketplace startups of 2021. And the African funding market has been recovering in 2025 and 2026, even if the money is skewing late-stage.
The Fall 2026 Demo Day on December 2 will be one test of whether any of that is landing. But the more interesting question may run the other way. With local capital deeper, local accelerators more credible, and a generation of YC alumni now writing cheques at home, Africa’s next Paystack may not need Y Combinator at all. Whether YC can adapt fast enough to find it first is YC’s problem, not Africa’s.

articles.title: Google Search pourra fouiller votre Wallet et votre Drive pour personnaliser vos résultats
articles.text:
Google introduit une mise à jour majeure dans son moteur de recherche. La firme de Mountain View va vous permettre de connecter votre Google Wallet, votre Google Drive et même Gemini à son système Personal Intelligence.
Avec ce nouveau fonctionnement, les résultats de recherche fournis par Google Search seront personnalisés en tenant compte de vos habitudes. L’IA va ainsi s’appuyer sur vos documents, vos conversations récentes ou encore sur vos dernières dépenses pour vous proposer des résultats plus pertinents. Bonne nouvelle, vous pourrez garder le contrôle sur vos données. Google vous laissera en effet le choix de connecter ou non ces applications dans les paramètres de personnalisation.
Des données privées supplémentaires contre des résultats personnalisés
En connectant Google Search à votre Google Wallet, Google veut permettre à au mode IA de son moteur de recherche d’analyser vos habitudes de dépense. Le moteur de recherche pourra aussi suggérer d’utiliser une carte de paiement plutôt qu’une autre afin de maximiser les possibilités d’obtenir du cashback ou des points de récompense fidélité. Google précise que l’accès à votre Wallet se fait en lecture seule et que l’IA ne pourra jamais réaliser un paiement à votre place.
Dans le cas de Google Drive, l’accès à vos documents doit permettre au mode IA de Google Search de consulter et d’extraire des informations pertinentes de vos documents pour personnaliser les résultats de vos recherches.
Enfin, l’accès à vos conversations Gemini a pour objectif de maintenir la continuité de vos conversations. Vous pourrez ainsi continuer une recherche initiée dans Gemini directement dans le mode IA de Google Search sans avoir à réexpliquer le contexte.
Évidemment, permettre à Google Search d’avoir accès à ces données sensibles pose des questions de confidentialité. Pour vous permettre de garder un œil sur les données que Google utilise, une nouvelle icône Personnalisation affichée en dessous des réponses générées vous permettra de connaître les données personnelles ayant été utilisées.
Par ailleurs toutes ces intégrations ne sont faites que sur la base du volontariat. Google vous laisse un contrôle total sur ce que vous souhaitez activer ou non, avec la possibilité de changer vos paramètres à n’importe quel moment dans les paramètres de personnalisation de la recherche Google.

articles.title: Amazon discovers Falcon 9 and Ariane 6 can deliver when nobody else can
articles.text:
A European Ariane 6 launcher propelled 36 satellites into orbit for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation Tuesday, continuing the network’s build-out after 40 satellites were lost earlier this month during a failure of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket.
The launch was an important rebound for Amazon, bringing the Amazon Leo fleet to 432 satellites as the company seeks to fill the void left by the grounding of ULA’s Vulcan rocket, Amazon’s primary launch provider. Now, an Amazon official tells Ars it is accelerating several Falcon 9 launches the company has purchased from SpaceX, which also owns the Starlink satellite network that Amazon seeks to dethrone.
The next Falcon 9 launch for Amazon Leo is now planned for December, Amazon said, moved forward from its previous launch date next year. Several more Falcon 9s are scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites in rapid succession after the December flight.
Winners and losers
Amazon cast a wide net when it started signing deals for launch services five years ago, securing rides on 108 flights with every available medium- or heavy-lift rocket in the West to place a fleet of 3,232 satellites into low-Earth orbit. As of Tuesday, Amazon and its launch partners have completed 17 of those flights, with one mission failure.
Amazon executives initially bought up capacity from US-based United Launch Alliance, Europe’s Arianespace, and Blue Origin. Nearly all of those launch contracts depended on rockets still in development: ULA’s Vulcan, Europe’s Ariane 6, and Blue Origin’s New Glenn.
Each launch vehicle faced development delays, as all new rockets do. New Glenn has been grounded since May after an explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in Florida. ULA’s Vulcan will be sidelined for months after misfiring during a mission with Amazon satellites on November 15.

articles.title: 94% of India's most-used online platforms still use dark patterns: LocalCircles
articles.text:
94% of India's most-used online platforms still use dark patterns: LocalCircles
A LocalCircles study finds that 94% of India's 354 most-used online platforms continue to deploy dark patterns, with 37 of 45 sectors having no fully compliant platform.
As many as 94% of India's most-used online platforms continue to use deceptive design practices, commonly known as dark patterns, despite growing regulatory scrutiny, according to a new study by LocalCircles.
The study analysed 354 online platforms across 45 sectors and found that only 20 were free of dark patterns. Further, 37 sectors had no platform that fully complied with the dark pattern guidelines.
The findings come weeks before the amended Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2026, take effect on January 1, 2027. Under the new rules, e-commerce companies must conduct annual self-audits and prominently display certificates declaring their platforms free of dark patterns.
Dark patterns or Dark UX are user interface designs that trick users into taking unintended actions such as buying a subscription, making payments or sharing personal data.
The study also found gaps in the self-declaration process. Of the 31 companies that had submitted a 'dark pattern free' declaration to the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), platforms operated by 23 companies, or 74%, were still found to have dark patterns. Only eight companies were found to be compliant.
Among publicly listed companies, 102 of the 108 consumer-facing online platforms analysed continued to have dark patterns. This means 94% of the platforms operated by listed companies still had deceptive design practices.
Online grocery, food delivery, OTT platforms show zero compliance
The study found that 37 of the 45 sectors analysed had no fully compliant platforms. These included online grocery, food delivery aggregators, taxi aggregators, OTT platforms, edtech, online banking, airlines, railway ticketing, mobile telecom services, online gaming, insurance and AI platforms.
B2B business marketplaces recorded the highest compliance at 100%, followed by car rental at 25%, e-commerce inventory platforms at 19%, e-commerce at 17% and quick commerce at 14%. Online payments recorded 11% compliance, while travel booking and digital lending reported 10% and 3%, respectively.
Forced action and drip pricing remain common
Forced action was the most prevalent dark pattern, appearing on 237 platforms, or 67% of those analysed. Drip pricing, where additional charges are introduced during the purchase process, was found on 222 platforms (63%).
Bait and switch practices were identified on 178 platforms (50%), while interface interference appeared on 170 platforms (48%). Other common practices included nagging (36%), subscription traps (32%) and privacy zuckering (23%).
The study also identified basket sneaking on 11% of platforms and false urgency on 10%.
The findings are based on complaints and experiences shared by more than 250,000 consumers across 392 districts, LocalCircles' AI-powered detection technology and public social media complaints.
Regulatory action against dark patterns has also increased. The CCPA penalised nine digital platforms in August 2026. Meanwhile, SEBI's Common Advertisement Code, notified in October, prohibits regulated entities from using dark patterns listed in the CCPA guidelines. The RBI has also issued directions barring banks and their sales agents from deploying such practices, effective January 1, 2027.
LocalCircles has urged the Department of Consumer Affairs and the CCPA to make dark-pattern compliance mandatory across all consumer-facing online platforms, in coordination with sectoral regulators. It has also called for publicly listed companies to display dark-pattern-free certificates.

articles.title: YC-backed elbic raises €2.7 million to keep European customer calls off US servers with sovereign voice AI
articles.text:
elbic, a Berlin-based voice AI startup formerly known as KugelAudio, has raised €2.7 million in a pre-Seed round.
The round was led by London-based Repeat Ventures, with participation from San Francisco’s Rebel Fund, Y Combinator, and several business angels from the German scene, including fastgen founders Maik Mahlkow and David Nordhausen and voize co-founder Erik Ziegler. The raise follows the startup’s acceptance into Y Combinator’s programme in spring 2026.
“Voice is becoming the most important interface between companies and their customers. European firms need models they can run themselves, and Elbic’s founding team has the deep expertise in voice AI and model compression to deliver exactly that. Viktor and Kajo turned their research into models already running in production with lots of customers,” said Dan Jones, founder and managing partner of Repeat.
Founded in 2025 by Victor Presber and Kajo Kratzenstein, elbic builds its own speech models for telecom operators and contact centre vendors who want to keep customer call data off US servers. Kratzenstein studied computer science at the Hasso Plattner Institute in Potsdam, where he spent two years researching natural speech synthesis, work that produced the first model the company released as open source.
That model, the company says, has since been downloaded more than 150,000 times on Hugging Face. Presber previously co-founded software startup full-house.io, having started his first business, a video production company, at the age of 17.
The company says traditional phone AI systems work through three sequential steps: transcribing speech to text, generating a text reply, and then reading it aloud; elbic’s models streamline this into a single, uninterrupted exchange. Its newest model, Fluid, is a speech-to-speech system that takes in spoken language and responds directly in spoken language.
When the model needs to fetch additional information, say from a customer account, Fluid passes the query in the background to a text-based large language model of the customer’s choice, then speaks the answer back. In the cloud, the voice begins responding in under 100 milliseconds to avoid any perceptible pause on the call.
As of now, elbic offers four models: Fluid for live conversations, Kugel for text-to-speech, Ear for speech-to-text transcription, and Clarity for noise removal. These models serve telecom operators and contact centre software vendors who embed them in their phone assistants. elbic says its models support 24 languages and are built to handle the precise demands of a real phone call: contract information, IBANs, surnames, and regional dialects.
Düsseldorf-based telecom operator sipgate is already running elbic’s voice models in production on its own servers, while Deutsche Telekom also works with the startup.
“In our project, it was extremely important to us to choose a purely European solution. Elbic makes that possible, and in use, both the pronunciation and the range of European voices convinced us right away. We value the naturalness of the voices and the direction the product is taking,” said Sebastian Schumann, Senior Architect, Network & Services International at Deutsche Telekom.
On independent benchmarks, elbic says Fluid 1 ranks second globally among speech-to-speech voice agents, passing 84% of tasks on the τ²-bench voice comparison. It placed just behind OpenAI’s GPT Live 1 at 85%, and ahead of Google’s Gemini 3.8 Live and xAI’s Grok Voice.
“Companies that let an AI handle their customer calls don’t want to send those conversations through servers in the US, and the models have to really master German. With five people in Berlin, we’re showing that these models don’t have to come from Silicon Valley. We want to stay the smallest lab that builds its own speech models,” said Presber, co-founder of Elbic.
The fresh capital will go primarily into compute for the next generation of models and into deploying those models for enterprise customers across Europe. With its new name, chosen because it is short and easy to pronounce across languages, the company is also looking beyond Germany, and aims to become the go-to sovereign voice AI infrastructure for European businesses.

Un laptop pensé pour jouer plus que pour créer

Il faut quand même accepter un poids de 2,21 kg, une autonomie qui tourne autour de 5h en utilisation légère et un écran à la colorimétrie limitée si vous êtes un créatif exigeant.
RTX 5050 ou RTX 5060 : où se situe vraiment cet HyperX Omen ?
Cette version du HyperX Omen est une porte d'entrée intéressante s'il s'agit de votre premier laptop gaming, surtout avec une carte graphique Nvidia de la génération Blackwell. Mais il ne joue pas dans la même catégorie que les machines dotées d'une RTX 5060 ou d'une RTX 5070. Ces dernières offrent plus de marge pour les jeux plus costauds, tandis que la RTX 5050 présentée ici mise plutôt sur la polyvalence, pour jouer en Full HD+. Son écran à colorimétrie moyenne, son stockage de 512 Go et sa mémoire vive sur une seule barrette sont aussi des concessions à prendre en compte.

- La luminosité limitée à 300 cd/m²
- La couverture colorimétrique limitée à 62,5% du spectre sRGB
- Le SSD de 512 Go, limite pour les jeux volumineux
- La RAM sur une seule barrette
- L'autonomie

articles.title: Radware discloses breach exposing customer cloud access keys
articles.text:
Cybersecurity company Radware says attackers gained access to some of its customers' account details and cloud access keys through an unsecured internal Cloud WAF (Web Application Firewall) management API that was left exposed online.
Founded in 1996 and headquartered in Tel Aviv, Radware now provides application delivery and DDoS protection services to more than 12,500 enterprise and telecom carrier customers worldwide.
In a root cause analysis report shared by an anonymous source with BleepingComputer, Radware says it blocked the originating IP address and access to the internal management API. The company also revoked and replaced all internal account credentials after detecting the breach on Thursday, ten hours after the initial unauthorized API access.
"On 19 November 2026, an unauthorized party accessed an internal-only Cloud WAF management API that was reachable from the Public Internet without requiring authentication," Radware said.
"The confirmed information potentially accessed includes customer contact details, and for a subset of customers, the credentials configured for log export into their self-managed storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or SFTP)."
The company added that the breach did not expose WAF traffic inspection, certificates, end-users’ data, customer application traffic, or cloud DDoS services and data.
Customers advised to rotate exposed keys
It also "strongly" advised affected AppSec (WAF, BOT) customers to rotate Cloud WAF log export credentials (including Azure Blob Storage keys or SAS tokens, AWS S3 access keys, or SFTP credentials) as soon as possible and review access logs on their cloud storage accounts for unexpected access since at least November 19.
The company is still investigating the breach and whether any API keys or other customer information exposed in the incident were used without authorization, and said it has already received reports from customers about AWS alerts for an unfamiliar IP address attempting to access their log-export buckets.
"WAF traffic inspection and protection have continued without interruption, and we have not identified an impact on the availability or protection of customer applications and services," Radware added. "We have found no evidence to date of changes to customer security policies or of access to customer application traffic."
Radware has yet to issue a public statement regarding the incident or file a breach report with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
BleepingComputer also reached out to a Radware spokesperson with questions about the incident, but a response was not immediately available.

articles.title: Maniable et noté 5/5, ce nettoyeur Mova tombe à 129 € à l'occasion du Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : Le nettoyeur de sol Mova M10 "5 étoiles" à 129,00 € (-17%)
Actuellement noté 5/5 par notre rédaction, le nettoyeur de sol Mova M10 supprime efficacement les taches tout en passant sous les meubles grâce à sa tête maniable. Le Black Friday 2026 fait descendre son prix à 129,00 € chez Amazon, soit une baisse d'environ 17 % pour une économie de 26,67 €.
Mova signe avec le M10 un nettoyeur de sol conçu pour combiner aspiration et lavage tout en restant accessible. L'appareil est pensé pour passer sous les meubles, éliminer les cheveux emmêlés et laver son rouleau à l'eau chaude. Ce balai avait convaincu notre laboratoire lors de ses tests pratiques.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Mova M10 descend à 129,00 € chez Amazon, soit environ 17 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (155,67 €). Cette baisse de prix permet d'économiser 26,67 €.
Un nettoyage complet qui passe sous les meubles
Le Mova M10 supprime les taches sur les sols durs et aspire les saletés sans exiger un passage d'aspirateur préalable. Sa tête de lavage maniable épouse les bordures et se glisse sous le mobilier pour déloger la poussière accumulée. Le rouleau profite d'un système qui élimine les cheveux entortillés et d'un entretien automatisé à l'eau chaude sur sa base. Notre rédaction lui accorde la note maximale à ce jour dans nos tests, consultable dans notre test complet.
Mova M10
Points forts
- Excellentes performances de lavage et d'aspiration.
- Tête de lavage facile à manier : épouse bien le contour des meubles.
- Belles finitions.
- Balai qui ne pèse pas sur le bras.
- Très bonne autonomie.
- Bonne gestion de l’eau (évite de remplir ou vider les réservoirs régulièrement).
- Passe sous les meubles.
Points faibles
- On cherche encore…
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Une grande autonomie pour les pièces spacieuses
Ce modèle sans fil dispose d'une autonomie annoncée de 40 min, une durée confortable pour couvrir de grandes surfaces sans devoir s'interrompre. La gestion de l'eau optimise les flux pour éviter de remplir le réservoir d'eau propre ou de vider le collecteur d'eau sale trop souvent au cours d'une même session. Les points faibles restent quasiment inexistants d'après les relevés de notre laboratoire, ce qui conviendra à ceux qui cherchent un appareil efficace dès les premières minutes sans mauvaise surprise à l'usage.
Rowenta X-Clean 2 : l'autre option face au Mova M10
Le Rowenta X-Clean 2 avance une tête autotractée qui facilite le guidage au sol et assure un lavage correct sur les taches courantes. En revanche, son réservoir d'eau sale fait l'impasse sur la grille de retenue des déchets solides, compliquant son nettoyage après chaque passage face au système plus complet du balai Mova.
Le Rowenta X-Clean 2 est vendu 20,99 € plus cher et affiche une note actuelle de 3/5, tandis que le Mova M10 bénéficie d'une note actuelle de 5/5 tout en restant plus efficace sur les grandes surfaces à son prix du jour.
Rowenta X-Clean 2
Points forts
- Nettoyeur autotracté, facile à passer.
- Belles performances de lavage.
Points faibles
- Pas de crépinette dans le réservoir d'eau sale.
- Autonomie un brin limitée.

articles.title: 4 juegos gratis en Steam para PC: acción, música, terror y puzles para descargar sin pagar
articles.text:
Steam suma cuatro juegos gratis para PC con propuestas de acción, música, terror psicológico y puzles tridimensionales. Los títulos están disponibles desde el martes 24 de noviembre y se pueden añadir a la biblioteca desde la ficha oficial de cada uno, sin descuentos temporales ni pagos posteriores.
La selección amplía las opciones para quienes buscan juegos gratuitos en Steam sin necesidad de contar con un ordenador de altas prestaciones. Incluye tres experiencias completas y un primer capítulo gratuito que permite conocer una aventura narrativa mayor antes de la llegada de su versión definitiva.
Temporal Strike propone estrategia y disparos contra un ejército de orcos
Temporal Strike combina acción, disparos y estrategia dentro de una estructura roguelike. El jugador viaja 2.000 años al pasado con el objetivo de frenar a un ejército de orcos, en una batalla donde la supervivencia de la humanidad depende de resistir oleadas de enemigos.
El sistema permite lanzar unidades al combate, desbloquear mejoras y reforzar las habilidades a medida que avanzan los intentos. Cuenta con cinco tipos de soldados y un árbol de 38 mejoras, por lo que cada partida puede desarrollarse de forma distinta.
Las unidades admiten control directo, aunque también es posible dejar que ataquen de forma automática. Esa alternativa permite concentrarse en el posicionamiento, la selección de tropas y las decisiones de progreso durante los enfrentamientos.
MUPO transforma el teclado en un instrumento para competir y crear
MUPO se centra en música, ritmo y creatividad. El juego convierte el teclado en un instrumento: cada canción exige pulsar las notas correctas, superar dificultades y conseguir puntuaciones que permiten competir en clasificaciones mundiales.
Uno de sus elementos principales es el editor de niveles. La herramienta permite crear mapas musicales y compartirlos con otros jugadores, una función que amplía el contenido disponible más allá de las canciones iniciales.
El título incorpora modificadores de dificultad, está disponible en español y funciona en Windows, macOS y Linux. Su propuesta está dirigida a quienes buscan pruebas de precisión, retos musicales y opciones para diseñar experiencias propias dentro de la comunidad.
Agent of Strange: Arrival abre una ciudad marcada por secretos
Agent of Strange: Arrival es el único lanzamiento que no ofrece una aventura completa. Se trata del primer capítulo de una producción más amplia, pero funciona como una introducción gratuita a su universo narrativo y a sus mecánicas de decisión.
La historia se desarrolla en Brocken, una ciudad misteriosa de principios del siglo XX. El jugador controla a un conspirador que regresa al lugar y debe investigar secretos, enfrentarse a una familia poderosa y elegir entre varias formas de resolver los conflictos.
El juego combina exploración, diálogos, elementos de rol narrativo y terror psicológico. Las decisiones alteran el recorrido de la historia, por lo que el capítulo permite conocer el tono de la propuesta antes de que llegue la experiencia completa.
Horochi’s Challenge reúne 100 rompecabezas con gravedad en seis direcciones
Horochi’s Challenge plantea puzles tridimensionales centrados en el movimiento de esferas de cristal. El objetivo consiste en llevarlas hasta posiciones concretas mediante cambios de gravedad que pueden aplicarse en seis direcciones.
Los escenarios incluyen interruptores, plataformas flotantes, mecanismos relacionados con el agua y obstáculos que obligan a estudiar cada espacio antes de actuar. El juego contiene 100 niveles de dificultad diversa y propone completar cada desafío con el menor número posible de movimientos.
La ficha no detalla los idiomas disponibles ni presenta cifras de reseñas, por lo que esos datos no permiten anticipar la recepción del juego. Aun así, su estructura basada en lógica y planificación lo diferencia de las otras propuestas de la tanda.
Cómo descargar los cuatro juegos gratis en Steam
Para añadir los títulos a la cuenta, el proceso puede realizarse desde la aplicación de ordenador o desde el sitio web de Steam:
- Inicie sesión con su cuenta habitual.
- Escriba el nombre del juego en el buscador.
- Abra la ficha oficial y compruebe que el precio figure como 0,00 euros o la moneda local.
- Pulse “Añadir a la cuenta”, “Obtener” o la opción equivalente.
- Confirme la operación cuando la plataforma lo solicite.
- Revise la biblioteca para verificar que el juego quedó asociado a la cuenta.
- Descárguelo en ese momento o instálelo más adelante desde otro ordenador vinculado a la misma cuenta.
Antes de añadir un título, conviene comprobar si su gratuidad es permanente o forma parte de una campaña limitada. Steam permite comprar, descargar y actualizar videojuegos desde una sola cuenta, sin discos físicos ni tiendas especializadas. Ese formato digital facilita el acceso a catálogos internacionales y da visibilidad a estudios independientes que pueden pasar inadvertidos entre los grandes lanzamientos.

articles.title: La nueva vida de Beatriz Montañez, expresentadora de ‘El Intermedio’, viviendo en el bosque
articles.text:
Beatriz Montañez pasó cinco años presentando ‘El Intermedio’ junto al Gran Wyoming, pero en diciembre de 2011 decidió despedirse del programa para dedicarse a otros proyectos. Lo hizo después de convertirse en uno de los rostros más conocidos de La Sexta y, aunque todavía trabajó en televisión y cine durante algún tiempo, terminó cambiando los platós por una casa de pastores en mitad del bosque. Allí encontró una tranquilidad que, por mucho dinero que ganara, no había conseguido tener antes.
La periodista reconoció en una entrevista con la Cadena SER en 2021 que estaba completamente perdida cuando tomó aquella decisión. Había demasiado ruido en su vida y necesitaba alejarse para pensar con claridad. Entre medias había participado en programas como ‘Hable con ellas’ y trabajado como guionista en ‘Muchos hijos, un mono y un castillo’, documental ganador del Goya en 2018. Pero lo que realmente quería era otra cosa: silencio y una vida que pudiera llevar a su ritmo.
Vivir en el bosque con menos de 150 euros al mes para comer
Su nuevo hogar recibió el nombre de Niadela, el mismo que utilizó para titular el libro en el que relató su primer año de retiro. Durante su presentación explicó que vivía de los ahorros de su etapa televisiva y que había reducido los gastos al mínimo. Se hizo vegana, empezó a alimentarse principalmente de verduras, legumbres y semillas, y calculaba que gastaba menos de 150 euros mensuales en comida. Además, contaba con paneles solares para la electricidad y agua procedente de un pozo.
Su rutina también era bastante distinta de la que llevaba en televisión. Contó que salía a comprar aproximadamente cada 25 días y que viajaba a Madrid un par de veces al año para ver a sus amigos. El resto del tiempo lo pasaba en su casa, rodeada de naturaleza, una elección que resumió durante la promoción de su libro: «No hay dinero en el mundo que te pueda comprar la paz».
Pero aquella tranquilidad se vio alterada precisamente cuando decidió contar su historia. En julio de 2021, Montañez denunció públicamente que algunas personas habían acudido hasta su casa sin permiso, le dejaban notas y llegaban a observarla con prismáticos. La situación fue tan incómoda que, según explicó, tuvo que intervenir la Guardia Civil. Después de años buscando estar sola, se encontró con desconocidos que querían acercarse a la vida de la que tanto le había costado apartarse.

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy Fit4 : une fuite dévoile son prix en hausse pour la France
articles.text:
Samsung n’a pas renouvelé son bracelet connecté depuis le Galaxy Fit3, lancé en 2024 à 69,90 euros. Son successeur est pourtant en préparation depuis des mois. Dès juin, Samsung travaillait sur un nouveau bracelet connecté en plus de ses Galaxy Watch, et le Galaxy Fit4 s’est depuis montré sous tous les angles. Il manquait le prix. Ce lundi 23 novembre, Dealabs, le site communautaire de bons plans, affirme qu’il sera vendu 79,90 euros en France. Ce serait 10 euros de plus que le Fit3, soit une hausse de 14 %, pour un bracelet qui ressemble beaucoup à l’ancien.
L’information vient de billbil-kun, rédacteur de Dealabs Magazine, qui s’est fait une spécialité de révéler les prix et les dates en avance, surtout dans le jeu vidéo. Selon lui, le Galaxy Fit4 arrivera en Europe en trois coloris : noir, argent et vert. Ce vert correspond sans doute au vert-bleu clair visible dans les vidéos du Galaxy Fit4 qui ont fuité en octobre. Samsung, de son côté, n’a encore rien officialisé. Les signes d’un lancement proche s’accumulent pourtant. Le bracelet a passé la certification américaine FCC et des pages d’assistance à son nom sont en ligne sur les sites de Samsung en France et dans plusieurs pays européens. La fiche de l’application Galaxy Fit4 Manager montre aussi déjà des visuels du bracelet sur le Galaxy Store.
Un écran à peine plus haut, et toujours pas de GPS
Le 29 octobre, le site SammyGuru, spécialisé dans Samsung, a fouillé le code de cette application. L’application du Galaxy Fit4 a ainsi livré l’essentiel de sa fiche technique. Les cadrans trouvés dans l’application mesurent 258 x 428 pixels, contre 256 x 402 pixels pour l’écran AMOLED du Fit3. Si l’écran a la même définition que ces cadrans, il gagnerait 26 pixels en hauteur et 2 en largeur, pour un rectangle un peu plus allongé. Le bracelet pourra aussi afficher jusqu’à 12 tuiles (ces écrans de raccourcis qu’on fait défiler du doigt) et faire sonner le smartphone quand on l’a égaré.
Côté santé, la liste ressemble beaucoup à celle du Fit3 : fréquence cardiaque avec alertes si le rythme est trop haut ou trop bas, mesure de l’oxygène dans le sang, suivi du stress, phases de sommeil et coaching personnalisé après sept nuits. Surtout, SammyGuru n’a trouvé aucune trace de GPS intégré. Le bracelet ne pourra donc pas enregistrer seul le tracé d’un footing. Évidemment, à moins de 80 euros, on ne s’attendait pas à une révolution. Mais pour justifier une hausse de prix, un écran un peu plus haut fait léger.
Xiaomi aussi augmente ses prix, mais reste moins cher
Samsung ne serait pas le seul à augmenter ses tarifs. Xiaomi a lancé son Smart Band 11 en France mi-novembre à 59,99 euros, soit 10 euros de plus que le Smart Band 10. La version NFC, qui permet de payer sans contact, monte à 79,99 euros. À 79,90 euros, le Galaxy Fit4 coûterait donc 20 euros de plus que le bracelet standard de Xiaomi, et autant que sa version NFC.
    Pour aller plus loin

Samsung n’a encore communiqué ni la date de sortie ni la fiche technique officielle du Galaxy Fit4. En attendant, notre sélection des meilleurs bracelets connectés passe en revue les modèles déjà en vente.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
  November 17, 2026
- Source:
  University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
  A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

Associations of Physical Activity and Sedentary Time From Childhood to Adolescence With Cognition in Adolescence: The PANIC Study. Pediatric Exercise Science, 2026; 38 (3): 268 DOI: 10.1123/pes.2025-0083
