articles.title: Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming
articles.text:
Music streaming service Tidal said on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform. The company said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of tracks uploaded to its platform were generated by AI, and that was a major reason driving this decision.
Tidal said it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year. With the new rules in place, the platform said it will be rejecting roughly 80,000-85,000 tracks per day.
Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI.
The company said it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated.
The move comes as AI-generated music inundates streaming services across the board. Tidal is one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music outright. Deezer, which also provides detection tools to other streaming services, said that it will introduce a toggle to let users filter out AI music. Larger platforms like Spotify and YouTube Music have adopted a milder approach to this issue, choosing to label AI-generated music instead of offering filters or taking stronger measures.
Tidal started de-monetizing songs made using AI in June, but that did not prove enough of a deterrent, Tidal Music’s lead, Robert Anderson, said on X.
The company said that 27 million, or 6.3% of tracks on the platform, are fully AI-generated, but 96% of those have no streams.
“It’s true that not all songs catch on immediately, and artists should have time to build their fanbases. But this situation is different – at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried,” the company said in a post.
Meanwhile, music labels are trying to make money by partnering with platforms and AI model makers to sell their catalog for training or remixing features. Goldman Sachs estimates that by 2035, AI-related licensing tools and new monetization opportunities have the potential to improve record labels’ revenue by 10%.

articles.title: MTN Benin’s $215 million plan is running into a good problem with customers’ demand for more data
articles.text:
A jump in traffic is forcing MTN to spend faster than planned. Getting customers onto 5G will take more than building the network.
MTN Benin has a problem that most telecom operators would welcome: people are using its network more, and keeping up is proving expensive. But that extra usage has not brought a comparable jump in revenue.
The company’s third-quarter service revenue rose to R1.592 billion (~$91m) in 2026, from R1.562 billion (~$89m) a year earlier—an increase of R30 million, or about 1.9%. The longer view was less encouraging: service revenue for the nine months to September fell 6.1% in reported rand terms to R4.42 billion. Stripping out currency movements, the decline was 0.3%.
Those figures point to a business still working to turn growing network usage into sustained revenue growth. They do not establish how much additional revenue came directly from the traffic increase Ofodile described.
In January 2024, MTN Group pledged $215 million for infrastructure in Benin over three years. Now, chief executive Uche Ofodile expects the local operation to exceed that budget by early 2027, as demand forces it to bring spending forward.
The commitment is substantial for one market, though only a fraction of MTN’s wider investment bill. The group spent R38.5 billion (~$2.2bn) on capital expenditure, excluding leases, in 2025, equivalent to about $2.15 billion at its average exchange rate for that year. Benin’s entire three-year pledge is therefore roughly one-tenth of a single year’s group-wide spending.
“We’re probably going to outspend that,” Ofodile said in an interview with TechCabal on the sidelines of the Cyber Africa Forum, held between November 16 and 17, 2026, in Cotonou, the Republic of Benin.
Ofodile linked the spending pressure to a regulatory change in February, after which, she said, traffic grew by 100 per cent. She did not specify the comparison period or disclose how much of the investment pledge MTN has spent.
Her account highlights the difficult economics of cheaper connectivity: customers can consume more data without the operator earning proportionately more revenue, even as the operator needs additional capacity to serve them.
The original investment announcement also included a new office for MTN Benin. But Ofodile said unexpected demand had already pushed the company beyond its 2026 spending plans.
There is more to accommodate than heavier usage. Cotonou is growing, nearby communities are expanding, and MTN wants stronger coverage in the north. The question is where to build next, what customers can afford once the network arrives, and whether their spending can justify the investment.
The phones have to follow
MTN launched commercial 5G in Benin in November 2024, six years after Africa’s first commercial deployment in Lesotho, later followed by South Africa (2019), Seychelles (2020), Togo (2020), Mauritius (2021), and Botswana (2022).
Benin’s market shows why introducing a newer network does not immediately displace older technology. Regulatory figures for September 2026 show that 2G still held a narrow lead, accounting for 44% of mobile subscriptions, compared with 43.6% for 4G. Specifically for internet access, however, 4G accounted for 58% of mobile internet subscriptions in 2025. The September 2026 figures do not separately identify 5G subscriptions.
Ofodile expects MTN’s 5G network to expand beyond Cotonou in early 2027. She is, however, less interested in putting coverage everywhere before enough people have the devices to use it.
“I can have all the desire in the world to expand,” she said. “But if we don’t have enough devices, then… it makes it a bit difficult.”
It is an unglamorous hurdle for a technology usually sold on speed. A faster network does little for someone whose phone cannot connect to it.
Nigeria offers a cautionary example. By September 2026, 5G accounted for 5.05 per cent of mobile subscriptions, up from 2.81 per cent in April 2025, but still a small share of the market. High device costs have been a barrier to adoption. Nigeria’s figures do not describe Benin’s market, but they illustrate why building a network does not automatically bring customers onto it.
Ofodile said MTN Benin allows customers to pay a deposit for a phone and then clear the balance daily or weekly. Benin’s mobile penetration stood at 78.1 per cent at the end of 2025, representing about 10.3 million unique subscribers, although this measure reflects access to mobile services rather than smartphone ownership.
Elsewhere, MTN’s South African MoMo business introduced rent-to-own smartphones in July 2025, with advertised daily payments starting at R10 (¢57). But those terms apply to South Africa, not Benin.
Splitting a bill into smaller payments can help. It does not necessarily make the phone cheaper or the repayments manageable.
Following the customers
For now, businesses and households offer MTN another route to growing its network.
Ofodile said business customers are increasingly interested in fixed wireless access: broadband delivered over a mobile network, without running a physical connection to every building. It is particularly useful where fibre is unavailable.
New homes around Cotonou and Abomey-Calavi also mean potential customers. MTN wants to follow that growth, rather than expand 5G simply to claim more coverage.
Farther afield, the approach changes. Ofodile cited a rural-site partnership with Africa Mobile Networks Group (AMN) as an example of how to find infrastructure suited to the communities being served.
“I’m going to put the best technology for the environment,” she said. “Rural telephony, rural coverage.”
A rural community and an urban business district do not necessarily need the same setup, or generate enough revenue to justify the same costs.
Data prices, meanwhile, have fallen sharply. Government figures drawn from regulatory data put the average price at CFA995 ($1.66) per gigabyte in 2022 and CFA440 ($0.74) per gigabyte in 2024, down by roughly 56%.
For customers, lower prices mean their money can go further. For MTN, more usage means finding ways to carry the extra traffic while keeping costs down. Neither side of that equation disappears when the company switches on 5G.
The challenge, however, is making those investments pay without asking customers to shoulder prices that put connectivity beyond their financial reach.
The 83% question
Ofodile’s benchmark for success is not another generation of mobile technology. It is mobile money, and how thoroughly it has worked its way into everyday life.
According to the GSMA’s 2026 mobile-money report, global services processed over $2.1 trillion in 2025, driven largely by sub-Saharan Africa. Merchant payments grew fastest, jumping 42% to $155 billion as phones became tools for daily commerce rather than just transfers. Importantly, mobile money functions over USSD on basic phones, meaning deeper digital inclusion does not require 5G or smartphones.
“Mobile Money represents 83 per cent of the value of the transactions in the country,” Ofodile said.
Benin’s 2025 annual report from the Autorité de Régulation des Communications Électroniques et de la Poste (Electronic Communications and Postal Regulatory Authority) (ARCEP) gives MTN Mobile Money approximately 83% of mobile financial services revenue, from a total market of CFA82.5 billion.
Provider revenue is not the money customers transfer or spend. The report confirms MTN’s dominance by revenue; it does not independently establish Ofodile’s claim about transaction value.
Her wider point, though, is about what people do with the service. She remembers early mobile-money advertising that centred on a city worker sending money to a parent in a village. Today, its uses extend well beyond that transaction.
She wants connectivity to follow the same path: from something customers subscribe to, to something they rely on to work, trade, and improve their lives. Subscriber totals alone cannot tell her whether that is happening.
“We can count the customers all we want,” Ofodile said. “At the end of the day, if they’re not using digital services to grow the economy, to improve their own lives, then we haven’t done enough.”

articles.title: Engineering Around Non-Determinism: Evals, Grounding, and Release Gates for AI-Drafted Suspicious Reports
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- A drafting agent should refuse to draft when the evidence is missing. Stopping with an explicit "insufficient context" signal is safer than a fluent narrative built around gaps.
- An LLM judge is itself non-deterministic. Freeze its version and pair it with a deterministic fact-checker for names, dates, and amounts.
- Building agentic systems on probabilistic LLMs requires engineering around them: evals, context engineering, observability, regression runs, and human-in-the-loop controls contain the effects of randomness rather than removing it.
- Grounding the system in authoritative case evidence and a knowledge-augmented graph data system helps ensure that every material claim is supported by traceable data.
- Versioned models, prompts, policies, retrieval configurations, and reviewer actions make the system observable, reversible, and suitable for regulated production environments.
Investigative narrative drafting in a financial institution
Financial institutions must investigate potentially suspicious activity and prepare accurate, complete, and timely reports for Financial Intelligence Units. The process is sensitive, labor-intensive, and subject to strict deadlines. This article explains how non-deterministic Artificial Intelligence (AI) components can be incorporated into a dependable agentic system that reduces the cost of doing business, increases drafting and review speed, and maintains the quality of the final report.
What is a Suspicious Activity Report?
A Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) is a formal document submitted by regulated entities and financial institutions to law enforcement or financial intelligence units (such as the UK's National Crime Agency) to flag known or suspected instances of money laundering, fraud, or terrorist financing.
SARs should give a clear and concise explanation of the reason(s) for the suspicion, identifying:
- Who – the identity of the party, or parties involved
- What – the transaction they are involved in
- Where – a description of the criminal property
- How – a description of the prohibited act(s)
- Why – the criminal activity suspected
- When – any critical deadlines
The Inverted Pyramid Plot Model for SAR narratives organizes information from most to least important, much like a news article.
- The narrative opens with the lead, a short summary of the most noteworthy details and the main story event.
- It answers the five W questions: who, what, when, where, and why.
- Next comes the body, a series of crucial details that build up the main story event, supported by evidence, facts, and patterns.
- The narrative closes with the tail, which gives concluding remarks.
Because the structure moves from the broadest, most critical information down to the narrowest, a reader can grasp the core of the case from the opening lines alone and turn to the later sections only for supporting detail.
Risks and cost of non-compliance
- Regulators penalize institutions for systematic data deficiencies, missing narratives, or failing to report suspicious transactions adequately.
- Public enforcement actions can undermine the confidence of investors, business partners, and customers.
- Considering the sensitivity of data and investigations, typically these cases are investigated and reported by in-house employees in a very secure environment. If suspicious activity volumes increase, the cost of investigation and reporting increases as well. For example, If there are 10% of active customers who are detected, investigated, and reported, and each case takes $50 in human labour cost, there is a significant increase in the cost of doing business, which has to be eventually passed back to the customer.
Typical Deterministic System Architecture
In the following system context diagram, a human agent views the investigation notes prepared by another human agent and then drafts the suspicious activity report. Once the report is reviewed by another peer, it is submitted to a financial intelligence unit.
System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors)
In the following diagram, there are 4 key timelines of any investigation:
- Detection: Any suspicious activity is detected either through manual oversight or with the support of machine learning models.
- Investigation: Once suspicious activity is detected, it goes for thorough investigation and peer review to confirm the suspicion.
- Reporting: Any confirmed suspicious activity has to be reported to the national financial intelligence unit within a tight deadline. The report has to be factually correct, and the suspicion has to be clearly articulated.
- Further investigation by the Financial Intelligence Unit: All of these suspicious reported activities by all financial institutions enable the national intelligence unit to understand the complete web of illicit activities and intervene before they become a threat to national or international security.
High-level diagram of a traditional reporting system (Source: authors)
- The quality of the reports is directly proportional to the quality of investigation & editorial style of the human workforce. There is a lack of consistency.
- If there is an increase in suspicious activities, then the manual system can not keep pace with the increase in demand.
- There is a cost to the business and the customer for every suspicious activity investigation and reporting.
Non-Deterministic Agentic System Architecture
We propose improving the traditional reporting system by using AI to automate selected tasks and generate high-quality SAR drafts, followed by specialized human review and minor edits where necessary. The goal is to increase throughput, reduce cost per case, and decrease reporting failures.
In the following system context diagram, human agent effort is shifted to review/edit the AI-assisted report drafting and review.
System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors)
We changed the earlier design to support background automation of suspicious activity report generation. As soon as the investigation is complete, the case is sent to the queue for processing by the Agentic System. Before the human agent picks the case for drafting the report, the AI Agent has drafted the first version to speed up the report generation.
High-level diagram of an AI-powered reporting system (Source: authors)
The non-deterministic nature of AI, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), creates two central concerns:
- High-quality first-attempt drafts require strong control, evaluation, and monitoring of AI components.
- Low-quality drafts create repeated draft-and-review cycles and additional human editing, increasing the cost per report.
Multi-agent system for report generation
The proposed solution is a multi-agent system, with access to selected LLMs via a gateway, and supported by a tailored knowledge graph built from operational data.
Grounding is the foundation of trustworthy SAR generation. The system should make it easier to state only what the evidence supports, not merely make the prose more fluent.
High-level diagram of the agentic system (Source: authors)
- Preprocessed Event Plot Knowledge Graph: All the data is already tagged and collected by previous processes. There is an Event Plot Knowledge Graph already generated as part of detection and investigation.
- Data Query Planner Agent: fetches the quality data required to generate the report. If the data is not present, then we stop the agentic automation and give feedback to the user that Agents cannot generate the report as the data is not present.
- Data Reranker Agent: takes the data returned by Data Query Planner and re-ranks the data to ensure that data is relevant to the context.
- Drafter Agent: specialized agents produce a narrative from factual data, against a defined SAR schema, and cite supporting source identifiers.
- Judge Agent: deterministic checks and an independent judge assess factuality, completeness, consistency, and style.
- Coordinator Agent: Once the quality of the generated report is of decent standard, then the report is published for human review.
- Since the investigation of the network is already done, there is no need for community detection. Hence, the GraphRAG approach is not considered.
- We also need to ensure that security and privacy concerns of the cases are under consideration; hence, data is carefully labelled and collected.
- All the real-time updates are present in operational databases, which can be fetched by the agents if there are some updates for a particular user profile or transaction.
- Knowledge Graph of main and associate suspects are generated at a regular cadence through data pipeline jobs.
- If a case is investigated and reported, then data needs to be retained as per data retention policies of the jurisdiction.
Sequence diagram of Drafter agent, Judge Agent and Human (Source: authors)
High-quality report generation with Evals
Quality means more than well-written prose. It means a complete, internally consistent, reviewable narrative that meets institutional and jurisdictional requirements.
- Completeness against the required SAR narrative fields.
- Consistency across names, dates, amounts, accounts, locations, and transaction sequences.
- Clear separation of observed facts, analysis, and unresolved uncertainty.
- Appropriate tone and terminology without overstatement or unsupported conclusions.
- Traceable provenance for material statements and reviewer edits.
Unlike traditional software, LLM outputs are non-deterministic, and "quality" is subjective. In the case of report writing, "what does a good report look like?" becomes more subjective. Hence, there is a need to test the "subjective" aspects against "objective" metrics, and here the Eval shines.
Evals are like tests of regular software development practices, and they can be leveraged in the following processes:
- Initial development of the system
- Updates to the system when there is a change in the requirements
- Updates in the models
- Regular run on some percentage of production spans to assess overall drift in quality
- Any new release in any aspect of the AI system has to be gated with the Evals suite
Eval Creation
There are a few broad focus areas where the model output has to be tested on a continuous basis:
- Instruction following capability
- Generation capability
- Narrative-specific correctness
For example, Evals can be written to assess different aspects of the generated narrative like:
- Factual accuracy of the narrative
- Factual completeness of the narrative
- Name identification
- Timeframe of events
- Narrative follows the Inverted Pyramid Plot structure
- Narrative Articulation
- Narrative Coherence
- Narrative tone
- ..etc.
Sample Eval can look like this:
Sample Eval (Source: authors)
Once we have scores from all the evals, either we can use a weighted average or a simple average of all the individual scores to figure out the final grading criteria. This is how the Evals can be leveraged to grade the quality of generated output
Sequence diagram of Evals grading (Source: authors)
Regression Evals with Golden Data Set
Since the model and prompt are bound to change, this adds another dimension of non-determinism to the system. With any production system, we need to have a regression run of all evals against the golden data set before any model upgrade or prompt/config change happens.
The golden data set has to be collected initially with different edge cases with defined input and output. This will help in testing the system during development. The Golden Data Set can be augmented with human feedback in production where they love the output generated by the AI system.
Evals shall answer some of the generated report’s quality metrics like :
- Did the system provide a factually correct answer?
- Was the summary faithful to the source?
- Was the final response actually helpful to the user?
System Behavior observability
Traditional testing is a deterministic process of verification - it asks, "Did we build the product right?" against a fixed specification. This approach fails when a system’s core logic is probabilistic, because non-deterministic output may be more likely to introduce subtle degradations of quality that do not result in explicit crashes and may not be repeatable. Hence, it is important to monitor the decision-making trajectory, from initial intent to final outcome.
- LLM Model: We first check the core reasoning. Is the LLM Model itself the problem? Failures here include hallucinations, nonsensical or off-topic responses.
- RAG Performance: The response depends on the quality of its retrieved information. Failures include irrelevant document retrieval, fetching outdated or incorrect information, or the LLM ignoring the retrieved context entirely and hallucinating an answer anyway.
- System Failures: What happens when the Model is not able to find the right context or data? Does it make things up or throw the error? What happens when the underlying system is unavailable?
The system is gradually improved by generating telemetry, understanding the system, and patching the underlying issues.
Human-in-The-Loop Control
Human review remains a policy decision owned by the BSA/AML function. AI accelerates preparation; it does not replace accountable judgment.
- Risk-tiered routing: low-risk, familiar typologies may use sampling or streamlined review; novel, high-risk, multilingual, or low-confidence cases default to full review.
- Reviewer experience: show evidence beside each material claim, highlight uncertainty, and make changes explainable rather than forcing reviewers to rewrite from scratch.
- Review quality: evaluate human edits as well as AI output so reviewers correct errors without introducing unsupported statements.
- Accountability: the designated BSA/AML officer retains responsibility for filing decisions and approved risk thresholds.
Release Process
Treat models and prompts as regulated production changes. The release plane provides controlled progress rather than "ship and hope."
- Version: register the model, prompts, retrieval logic, data mappings, policies, and eval set with an owner and change rationale.
- Test: run deterministic factuality checks, rubric scoring, security and privacy checks, and jurisdiction-specific regression suites.
- Gate: require approval from engineering, Compliance/AML, Risk, and Legal according to the change type.
- Shadow and canary: compare the candidate with the incumbent before increasing traffic.
- Monitor: track factuality pass rate, judge scores, reviewer edit rate, latency, queue age, and escalation volume.
- Rollback: use configuration-based feature flags to revert to the previous model, stricter review, or full human drafting when thresholds are breached.
Engineering Trust Into AI-Drafted SARs
The bottleneck in drafting a quality Suspicious Activity Report was qualified personnel. LLM-based systems can reduce that dependency, but only if they're engineered for it, with grounding and evals as the substitute for the judgment of a qualified investigator.
The mechanism we've described treats non-determinism as an engineering problem rather than an excuse. Grounding drafts in a case-specific knowledge graph and operational data keeps the Drafter Agent grounded in evidence. A Judge Agent and deterministic fact-checker turn "does this read well?" into measurable checks against factuality, completeness, and the Inverted Pyramid structure the FIU expects. Evals and a golden dataset give these subjective judgments an objective, regression-testable backbone, the same way unit tests do for deterministic code. And a release process that versions models, prompts, and configuration, gated with shadow/canary rollout and feature-flag rollback, treats every change to the system as a production release
None of this shifts accountability away from the humans who own it. The BSA/AML officer still decides what gets filed; the agentic system's job is to make sure that when a human reviews a draft, the evidence is already assembled, the uncertain claims are flagged, and the reviewer's time goes to judgment rather than transcription. Risk-tiered routing means the system earns trust on familiar, low-risk cases before it is ever allowed near the ones that matter most.
SAR narratives can now be drafted at machine speed, by codifying what "good" looks like into evals a machine can check against. When a human reviews the output, they're not taking the narrative on faith; they can trace the reasoning and the evidence lineage behind it, and that traceability is what turns speed into trust.

articles.title: Google wants to create an AI-generated TV channel starring you, complete with ads
articles.text:
Through the looking glass: Companies that have invested millions or billions into AI aren't being discouraged by the "slop" label. Google, for example, has filed a patent application for an entirely AI-generated TV channel in which the main character is... you. If that doesn't sound off-putting enough, the content will be based on the data Google collects about you, and it will also feature customized ads.
First noticed by Patentlyze, Google's AI-generated channel, imaginatively called "My Channel," is described as an option in a TV app. The content it generates will be based on demographic data, device data, YouTube watch history, and any other information Google holds about the user, who will also be the protagonist in these shows.
Once someone clicks on the channel, they will be given options to watch a personalized show starring themselves. Examples include sci-fi adventures, fun romantic comedies, and an action/thriller experience, all featuring the user's own likeness and voice. These shows can be created with or without specific user requests.
One section describes how, if a person watched a lot of sports videos, such as the best moments of a particular player, the system could create a video of the player's highlights interspersed with footage of the user cheering in the stands. The user could even be shown "interacting" with the player – something that sounds a little concerning.
Not surprisingly, it's also suggested that the channel would be connected to an "advertising server," one that inserts ads into the personalized content. "An advertising stitcher included in the advertising server generates an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item," it reads.
An entirely AI-generated TV channel isn't new. In August, Fairground AI Creator TV launched, a free, ad-supported streaming channel that airs AI-generated films and series 24 hours a day. It lists Roku, LG, and Amazon among the platforms to watch the channel.
AI-generated movies and TV shows are still about as popular as the plague. China's first fully AI-generated movie recently flopped at the box office, pulling in just $270,000 over three weeks.
Google might think using your likeness as the star of the personalized shows will make the content more appealing, but most people will probably just find it creepy and a worrying illustration of just how much the company knows about them. There's also the fact that the more AI-generated slop proliferates across social media, the more people are pushing back against it. Instagram took note and recently made it harder for AI-generated personas to pass themselves off as real people.
The majority of patents don't become real products, of course. Let's hope this one never does.

articles.title: Drupal Flaw Found by Anthropic Scanner Exploited in Attacks
articles.text:
A recently patched Drupal core vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, according to the cybersecurity agency CISA and Drupal developers.
The vulnerability, CVE-2026-132165, can be exploited for remote code execution. It was patched on November 18, and Drupal’s advisory says in-the-wild exploitation began shortly after.
“The Security Team has received a report this was exploited on live sites as early as 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC,” Drupal noted.
The discovery of the flaw is credited to Anthropic’s OSS Scanner, a free opt-in service that regularly scans enrolled open source projects for vulnerabilities.
Anthropic has not said how many vulnerabilities OSS Scanner has found since its October launch, but as of early November, it reported disclosing more than 5,000 vulnerabilities overall, across 680 open source projects.
CISA added CVE-2026-132165 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 24, instructing federal agencies to address it by November 27.
No public information appears to be available on attacks exploiting CVE-2026-132165. It’s unclear how many websites are affected.
The security hole affects the installer that ships with Drupal core, which enables users to set up a new site. An unauthenticated attacker — under certain conditions — can abuse the installer to reinstall Drupal, which can allow them to hijack the website or execute arbitrary code.
“Some (but not all) exploit paths are mitigated if the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php. In addition to upgrading, the Drupal Security Team recommends securing the Drupal installer after installation,” Drupal said.
Patches are included in Drupal 11.4.13, 11.3.22 and 10.6.22; end-of-life branches will not get a fix.
It’s worth noting that Drupal raised the vulnerability’s rating to ‘highly critical’ (CMSS score of 20/25) after it learned of the attacks.
This is the third Drupal vulnerability exploited in the wild this year. Drupal warned in late October that CVE-2026-118539, a highly critical access bypass flaw in the Commerce Core module, had been exploited against online stores.
In May, security firms reported seeing attacks exploiting a vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-9082 against thousands of websites.
Related: Apache Patches Critical HTTP Server RCE Found by Anthropic, Google
Related: VMware Updates Patch Critical ESX, vCenter Vulnerabilities
Related: Check Point Security Management Servers Hacked in AI-Assisted Campaign

articles.title: Tech leaders call for action on scale-up capital, procurement, and government support
articles.text:
In 1714, the British Parliament offered up to 20,000 pounds, a fortune at the time (roughly $3.5 million in today’s Canadian dollars), for a reliable way to determine longitude at sea—a problem that was costing sailors their lives. The answer didn’t come from astronomers of the day; it was John Harrison, a self-taught carpenter and clockmaker, who developed the marine chronometer and made ocean navigation safer.
What could a prize like that help Canadian innovators solve today?
“Canada can’t grow the innovation economy with public money and regulation. It’s stifling, overly restrictive, and full of red tape.”
Fiona Simpson, BioMimir
Robert Kaul, CEO of remote patient monitoring company Cloud DX, would like to find out. In a MaRS pulse-check of 21 high-growth founders and executives looking at what it takes to scale a company in Canada, Kaul proposed putting up $100 million to incentivize startups to solve “the hardest problems the country faces,” from hospital overcrowding and lagging productivity to homelessness and substance addiction.
“The allure of a large monetary prize and ultimate prestige can generate more than 100 times [the investment],” he said.
Toronto-based MaRS Discovery District is marking 25 years as the anchor innovation hub for Canadian startups. Its fall snapshot (captured from October 23 to November 6) heard from founders and executives of 21 high-growth ventures in its portfolio. It captures both ambitious ideas, like Kaul’s, and concerns about whether companies can get the backing they need to succeed globally. With seven of the 21 respondents considering moving their headquarters abroad, the findings also raise the question of whether Canada can provide the support they need to stay at home as they grow.
Finding the money to grow
For startups ready to expand, financing is the most common concern respondents raised. Access to growth capital was a challenge cited in 17 of the 21 responses, with Canadian venture funding particularly limited for companies seeking $25 million or more in a single financing round.
Fiona Simpson, CEO of BioMimir, a Sherbrooke-based medtech company, called for more private investment in young startups.
“Canada can’t grow the innovation economy with public money and regulation,” she noted. “It’s stifling, overly restrictive, and full of red tape.”
She called for capital gains tax incentives to encourage more early-stage and seed funds to form and make more investments. Initial successes could build confidence in complex, high-risk fields such as medtech, deep tech, and AgTech, helping attract additional capital, retain Canadian talent, and recruit international expertise.
The federal government proposed a related measure in Budget 2026: the Canada Growth Incentive, which includes a tax exemption on up to $15 million in capital gains from eligible startup investments, along with more time to reinvest proceeds in qualifying Canadian businesses.
Finding customers at home
Convincing investors to take a chance on startups is easier with a paying customer on board, which presents another hurdle. Twelve of the 21 respondents identified slow procurement and difficulty finding Canadian customers as barriers to growth.
For deep tech and hard tech businesses, those first sales can be especially tricky, explained Vida Gabriel, COO of TerraFixing, an Ottawa-based company that develops cold-climate carbon capture technology.
“Investors want to see customers and market traction, but early-stage deep tech and hard tech companies have a hard time selling first-of-a-kind projects,” she said. If the government can help get tech from demonstration stage to full commercial readiness, “that would help.”
For Sam Mugel, CTO of Multiverse Computing, an AI and quantum software developer with an office in Toronto, Canadian corporations’ reluctance to adopt new technology makes it harder for businesses that sell it to grow at home. He wants the government to give buyers both direction and a financial incentive.
“Canada needs to send a clear message to its industrial sector to say these are the champions which I would like you to support; and I will finance your procurement if you’re procuring from these companies,” he said.
Choose a priority, and stick with it
Albert Tai, CEO of Toronto-based healthtech Hypercare, suggests concentrating that backing in a few industries, including healthcare IT, medical devices, and pharmaceuticals.
“We have world-renowned hospitals, but the majority of the hospital software systems are American,” he said.
Louis Brun, CEO of Montreal’s Sollum Technologies, which develops programmable LED lighting for greenhouses, also favours a focused approach, with a commitment to see it through. He suggests sustained public investment in priorities such as sustainable clean tech, sovereign AgTech, and applied frontier engineering.
“By locking in a multi-decade commitment that transcends election cycles, we [give] researchers, entrepreneurs, and global investors the policy stability required to build world-leading domestic industries from the ground up,” he said.
For Kaul, the value of a major innovation award is personal. Cloud DX, based in Kitchener, was Canada’s entry into Qualcomm Tricorder XPRIZE and in 2017 became the first-ever recipient of the XPRIZE Bold Epic Innovator Award. But he knows prizes alone won’t make Canada a better place to build a business.
“There’s no magic bullet,” he said. “We need the best rules and regulations, the fairest taxes, the best R&D partnerships, the best (and quickest) access to capital, the most trustworthy, low-friction legal environment, and the strongest commitment from government, the media, enterprise, and academia—all pulling together.”

articles.title: Vehicle-to-Grid: Great Idea or Unrealistic Dream?
articles.text:
You’re undoubtedly familiar with the idea of vehicle-to-grid (V2G) automobile energy transfer. It’s been a “hot” topic for the last few years, largely due to the number of pure electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid vehicles on the road. In the U.S., these EVs/HEVs account for roughly 8% to 10% of all new cars sold (but they are a much lower fraction of cars on the road, of course); the worldwide numbers are higher depending on the region.
What is V2G? In short, V2G enables the energy stored in car battery packs to become a part of the grid, using some percent of each battery’s energy storage capacity to meet grid-level peak demand (Figure 1).
V2G appears poised for increased adoption by automakers due to the release of a new certification program for V2G technologies based on the recently issued UL 1741 Supplement SC standard. (Note that one variation of V2G is V2H, or vehicle-to-home, but we’re focusing just on V2G here.)
This adjunct standard creates a formal testing and certification pathway for bidirectional electric vehicle supply equipment (BEVSE) under UL 1741, the primary North American safety and performance standard for inverters, converters, charge controllers, and interconnection system equipment (ISE) used in distributed energy resources (DERs), such as solar panels, wind turbines, and home battery-storage systems (Figure 2).
The certification program covers AC-based V2G connections, known as V2G-AC. Under this approach, EVs equipped with certified bidirectional onboard inverters can connect to the electric grid through AC wallboxes. The wallbox oversees the connection between the vehicle, home wiring, and grid rather than relying on an external inverter.
What’s the plan?
Since energy storage is one of the bigger challenges facing efficient and environmentally friendly energy generation and distribution, using cars for transitional storage of any excess energy can minimize the need to build new generating capacity. It can also help create a more resilient grid, in principle.
The premise of V2G is that many car owners usually use only a fraction of their battery capacity, so V2G lets them offer more “use” of their cars as battery energy storage systems (BESS). Vehicle owners who send their unneeded energy back to the grid get some payment.
I’m not going to delve into the operational details of the proposed V2G operation, as that information is widely available. The idea is simple in concept: A car that is connected to a home charger when not in use can either recharge or allow its “excess” stored energy (which is temporarily unneeded) to be transferred back to the grid.
This capability would be especially useful to bolster the grid when its capacity is low compared to demand. In operation, power would flow from the grid to the car or vice versa, depending on the supply/demand balance and energy pricing at that moment.
In engineering and economic terms, everything will be optimized: supply, demand, pricing, costs—you name it. On top of that, it comes with a host of “green” virtues. So, what’s not to like?
The second part explores some issues and concerns associated with V2G.

Dukosi Samples Contactless Battery Communication System for EVs, Grid Storage
Chasing the 1%: Power Electronics and the Modern Grid Ecosystem
Two Obvious problems
- What happens after the system temporarily drains the cars electicity, and owner has to go somewhere unexpectedly?
- An LiB can only drain and recharge so many times. Who pays for a new battery?

articles.title: Browser auf dem iPhone: Warum Mozilla und 55.000 andere Unternehmen die EU auffordern, gegen Apple vorzugehen
articles.text:
Browser auf dem iPhone: Warum Mozilla und 55.000 andere Unternehmen die EU auffordern, gegen Apple vorzugehen
Ein Bündnis aus Mozilla, dem E-Commerce-Anbieter Shopify und über 50.000 Firmen aus der EU fordert von der Europäischen Kommission ein Verfahren samt Strafen gegen Apple. In einem offenen Brief „für mehr Wettbewerb im Web“ und ein „stärkeres Europa“ sprechen die Unterzeichner Kommissionspräsidentin Ursula von der Leyen direkt an.
Worum es im Streit geht
Im Zentrum steht die sogenannte Browser-Engine – also der technische Unterbau, der Webseiten darstellt. Auf iPhone und iPad schreibt Apple außerhalb der EU und Japans vor, dass alle Browser Apples eigene Engine WebKit nutzen. Selbst Googles Chrome läuft dort deshalb mit Apple-Technik.
In der Europäischen Union ist das anders: Durch den Digital Markets Act (DMA), die EU-Regeln für besonders marktmächtige Plattformen, dürfen Entwickler seit knapp drei Jahren eigene Engines auf iOS und iPadOS anbieten. Apple ist dabei als sogenannter Gatekeeper reguliert. In Japan gilt eine ähnliche Regelung seit Dezember 2025.
Warum bislang niemand mitmacht
Genutzt hat die neuen Möglichkeiten bisher aber kein großer Anbieter. Der Grund: Es ist kompliziert. Mozilla kritisiert, Apples Bedingungen seien „nicht praktikabel“, weil Entwickler eigene App-Pakete allein für die EU bauen und pflegen müssten. Für Mozilla lohne es sich so nicht, einen echten Alternativbrowser umzusetzen. Das Projekt würde für Firefox gerne die hauseigene Gecko-Engine nutzen statt WebKit. Auch Google hat bislang keine Anstalten gemacht, Chrome auf iOS umzustellen, auch wenn der Internet-Konzern die entsprechenden Mittel sicher hätte.
Die Koalition verlangt nun, dass die EU-Kommission „den DMA endlich umsetzt“. Apple habe „technische und rechtliche Hindernisse“ errichtet, die die Ausübung der Rechte der Browser-Anbieter unmöglich machten und dadurch den Markt behinderten. Dadurch fehle Firmen und ihren Kunden die echte Wahlfreiheit bei Browsern und der Wettbewerb bei Web-Apps, den der DMA eigentlich ermöglichen sollte. „Die Zeit drängt“, heißt es im offenen Brief. Apple habe mehr als zweieinhalb Jahre Zeit gehabt, die Anforderungen zu erfüllen, doch die Hindernisse bestünden weiter, während das mobile Internet „an Boden verliert“. Eine Reaktion der EU-Kommission steht bislang aus.

articles.title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops
articles.text:
The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this “smoke taint” adversely affected not only local wine production, but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant.
That’s why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on the quantity of tainted hops that are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists.
As previously reported, the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, in 2018, OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper—identified the growing popularity of “dry hopping” (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon.
All beer contains hops, a key flavoring agent that also imparts useful antimicrobial properties. (Beer spoils quickly without them.) Brewers mash and steep grain in hot water, which converts all that starch into sugars. This is traditionally the stage where hops are added to the liquid extract (wort) and boiled to give the beer that hint of bitterness. During the boiling process, a portion of the resins (alpha acids) in hops isomerize into iso-alpha acids. That chemical rearrangement of the molecules is what produces bitterness. Yeast is then added to trigger fermentation, turning the sugars into alcohol.

articles.title: Gagner 720 € en laissant sa voiture électrique branchée : on a refait le calcul de Volkswagen
articles.text:
Une voiture électrique passe le plus clair de ses nuits immobile dans un garage, et Volkswagen a décidé de rémunérer cette inactivité. Seule condition : laisser le véhicule branché pour que sa batterie serve de réservoir tampon au réseau électrique pendant que vous dormez.
    Pour aller plus loin
Charge bidirectionnelle, V2L, V2X, V2G : qu’est-ce que c’est et à quoi ça sert ?
            
Être payé à ne rien faire a tout de l’arnaque de groupe Facebook, mais sur un coin de table, le calcul tient la route. En décembre, Elli (la filiale énergie du groupe Volkswagen) lance en Allemagne son offre de « vehicle-to-grid » (V2G), une recharge bidirectionnelle qui renvoie aussi de l’électricité vers le réseau.
    Pour aller plus loin
Des « batteries sur roues » : pourquoi les voitures électriques vont avoir un rôle crucial pour le réseau électrique européen
            
Au cœur du dispositif, la borne Elli BiDi Charger (facturée 1 995 euros TTC, hors pose) charge et décharge jusqu’à 11 kW. En coulisses, le partenaire The Mobility House agrège les batteries des clients en une « centrale virtuelle » qui absorbe le courant quand il abonde et le restitue lors des pics, avec environ un million de véhicules basés sur la plateforme MEB déjà prêts en Europe selon Volkswagen (dont 360 000 en Allemagne).
Le calcul, ligne par ligne
Particularité de l’offre : la prime ne rémunère pas l’électricité réinjectée, mais simplement le temps passé branché, à hauteur de 0,24 euro par heure (pour des sessions d’au moins trois heures, plafonnées à 250 heures par mois). Cela représente jusqu’à 60 euros par mois et 720 euros la première année, avant un éventuel paiement à 0,40 euro par kWh réinjecté évoqué pour plus tard sans calendrier.
Votre production solaire dépasse votre consommation ? Stockez le surplus au lieu de le revendre à bas prix. Le SolarFlow 2400 AC+ se branche sur votre installation existante, 100 % plug-and-play, et s’amortit plus vite grâce au Black Friday.
Voici ce que cela donne concrètement :
- Le plafond : 250 heures par mois correspondent à 8 h 13 par jour, week-ends compris. Une voiture branchée chaque soir de 19 h à 7 h atteint donc facilement le maximum.
- Un usage plus réaliste : quatre nuits de 10 heures par semaine (environ 173 heures mensuelles) rapportent 41,60 euros par mois, soit un peu moins de 500 euros par an.
- La promesse de Volkswagen : 720 euros couvriraient 15 500 km en ID.3 à 0,33 euro le kWh, un calcul qui suppose une consommation flatteuse de 14 kWh aux 100 km.
- L’amortissement : comptez 2,8 ans hors frais d’installation, à condition que la prime reste au plafond au-delà de la première année, ce que rien ne garantit.
Face à BMW (2 095 euros) et Mercedes (2 990 euros, ou 1 990 euros en offre de lancement), Elli se place dans la moyenne allemande.
    Pour aller plus loin
30 heures sans électricité : son Renault Scénic E-Tech alimente sa maison en ne perdant que 8 % de batterie
            
Ces bornes coûtent cher parce qu’elles fonctionnent en courant continu et intègrent la conversion habituellement assurée par le chargeur embarqué de la voiture, là où Renault a fait le choix inverse en plaçant cette électronique dans le véhicule pour proposer sa borne bidirectionnelle à 2 059 euros pose comprise en France.
Brancher, régler l’appli, et c’est tout ?
Avant de commander, Elli impose un diagnostic en ligne, un devis d’installateur, un compteur communicant et la souscription au contrat d’électricité V2G Flow pendant douze mois pour la maison et la voiture. Au quotidien, l’usage se veut transparent : on branche la voiture, on saisit l’heure de départ et le niveau de charge minimum dans l’application, et l’algorithme gère le reste (la borne respectant la norme ISO 15118-20, ce qui ouvre la porte à d’autres marques à l’avenir).
Toutes les voitures du groupe ne sont toutefois pas compatibles. Volkswagen cible les ID. équipés du logiciel 3.5 et d’une batterie d’au moins 77 kWh, ainsi que tous les modèles sous logiciel 6.
Sur l’usure de la batterie, le constructeur promet un impact « pas significatif » mais renvoie aux conditions de garantie, qui plafonnaient la quantité d’énergie déchargée sur les premiers modèles. Quant aux foyers équipés de panneaux solaires, Cupra prévient que le V2G ne sera débloqué que progressivement.
Et en France, c’est pour quand ?
Pas avant 2027 au mieux : Volkswagen cite bien la France parmi ses prochains marchés une fois les conditions techniques et réglementaires réunies, mais sans donner de date. Le compteur Linky coche pourtant déjà la case du compteur communicant.
Chez nous, Renault a déjà pris de l’avance en proposant son service V2G sur ses R5, R4, Twingo, Mégane et Scénic électriques, avec des gains directement déduits de la facture via un contrat opéré par The Mobility House, le même partenaire qu’Elli. Pour un conducteur français d’ID., le seul réflexe utile aujourd’hui reste de vérifier la version logicielle et la capacité de la batterie avant d’acheter.
Un pari malin, suspendu à la deuxième année
Rémunérer l’heure de branchement plutôt que le kWh réinjecté est une approche habile : le client comprend immédiatement ce qu’il gagne, et Volkswagen garde la maîtrise de la batterie.
Reste que 720 euros garantis la première année pour une borne à près de 2 000 euros hors pose ressemblent surtout à une remise étalée sur douze mois : toute la rentabilité se jouera sur le montant de la prime le jour où le contrat soufflera sa première bougie.
    Pour aller plus loin
Charge bidirectionnelle, V2L, V2X, V2G : qu’est-ce que c’est et à quoi ça sert ?

articles.title: Google corrige une rare faille critique dans Chrome, n'attendez pas pour mettre votre navigateur à jour
articles.text:
Google vient de corriger une vulnérabilité critique qui pourrait permettre à des pirates de contourner les protections de Chrome et d'exécuter du code malveillant sur votre ordinateur ou votre smartphone Android. Le déploiement automatique du patch pourrait prendre plusieurs semaines.
Les bulletins de sécurité de Chrome égrènent d’ordinaire une longue liste de vulnérabilités, mais une seule, extrêmement sérieuse, a motivé la mise à jour publiée ce lundi 23 novembre. Identifiée sous la référence CVE-2026-134401 et découverte par les équipes de Google fin août, la faille a été classée critique, soit le plus haut niveau de gravité que l'entreprise ne retient qu'en de rares occasions. Et pour cause, son exploitation pourrait permettre à un pirate de franchir la barrière de sécurité qui sépare les contenus web du reste du système d'exploitation, au risque de compromettre votre appareil tout entier.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Une faille critique au cœur du système d'expérimentation de Chrome
Dans le détail, la vulnérabilité touche Variations, le composant qui permet à Google de tester et de déployer de nouvelles fonctionnalités dans Chrome sans avoir à publier de mise à jour du navigateur. C'est grâce à lui que deux personnes utilisant une même version de Chrome peuvent, par exemple, disposer d'interfaces légèrement différentes. Pour piloter ces changements, le navigateur récupère auprès des serveurs de Google des données de configuration qui déterminent les fonctionnalités à activer ou à désactiver.
D'après la fiche technique de la vulnérabilité, le composant ne contrôle pas suffisamment la validité des données qu'il traite. Si Google n'a détaillé ni les données en cause ni les conditions exactes d'exploitation de la faille, l'entreprise indique qu'un pirate pourrait tirer parti de ce défaut à l'aide d'une page HTML piégée pour exécuter du code arbitraire en dehors de la sandbox de Chrome.
Or, pour rappel, cette sandbox permet d'isoler le traitement des contenus web du reste du système d'exploitation. Même lorsqu'un pirate parvient à exploiter une faille du moteur de rendu de Chrome, cette protection est censée limiter les dégâts en l'empêchant d'accéder à des ressources du système auxquelles il ne devrait pas avoir accès. S'en affranchir pourrait donc lui permettre de compromettre le PC ou le smartphone lui-même, et non plus seulement le navigateur.
Pourquoi il ne faut pas attendre la mise à jour automatique de Chrome
Si près de trois mois se sont écoulés entre la découverte de la vulnérabilité et sa correction, Google ne fait état d'aucune exploitation par des pirates à ce jour. Comme à son habitude, l'entreprise se réserve le droit de restreindre l'accès aux détails techniques de la faille tant que la majorité des internautes n'a pas installé le correctif, afin de limiter les risques d'exploitation.
Problème, Google prévoit d'étaler le déploiement de sa mise à jour sur plusieurs jours, voire plusieurs semaines. Au vu des risques encourus en cas de compromission (vol de documents personnels et d'identifiants, détournement de comptes en ligne, installation de logiciels espions ou encore de ransomwares), on ne saurait trop vous conseiller de forcer la mise à jour de Chrome sans attendre.
Sur Windows et macOS, rendez-vous dans la rubrique « À propos de Chrome » depuis les paramètres du navigateur, ou saisissez chrome://settings/help dans la barre d'adresse pour lancer la recherche de mises à jour. Sur Linux, passez par le gestionnaire de paquets de votre distribution.
Assurez-vous de disposer de la version 158.0.8127.88 ou 158.0.8127.89 sur Windows et macOS, ou 158.0.8127.88 sur Linux (ou d'une version plus récente), et n'oubliez pas de relancer votre navigateur pour appliquer le patch. Sur Android, le correctif est intégré à la version 158.0.8127.92 de Chrome, dont vous pouvez vérifier la disponibilité sur le Play Store.

articles.title: Payhawk and Dronamics backer Eleven secures €57 million first close of its fourth fund, targets €100 million
articles.text:
Eleven, the Sofia-based early-stage venture capital firm behind some of Europe’s most prominent startup success stories, has secured a €57 million first close for its fourth fund, targeting a final raise of €100 million.
The first close of its Fund IV drew strong support from existing limited partners, with 70% of Eleven’s LP base recommitting to the fund. The European Investment Fund (EIF) returns as an anchor investor for a third consecutive time and is now joined by the Hellenic Development Bank of Investments (HDBI). Fund IV’s investor base also includes more than 50 founders and operators who bring not just capital, but hands-on mentorship, global networks, and co-investment capacity.
“For us, a new fund isn’t a new start. We’ve invested continuously since 2012, and alongside we’ve built an ecosystem of founders, mentors and partners that early-stage companies can rely on,” said Ivaylo Simov, Founding Partner at Eleven.
Eleven (formerly Eleven Ventures) was founded in Sofia in 2012 as one of the region’s first accelerators, and it takes its name from escape velocity: 11.2 km/s, the minimum speed required to break free of gravity. The firm has backed more than 160 companies across Europe, operating with on-the-ground teams in Sofia, Athens, Warsaw, and Istanbul, with a Bucharest hub set to follow early next year. Its €60 million third fund brought investments to South-Eastern Europe.
Its portfolio includes some of Europe’s most recognised names, including Payhawk, Bulgaria’s first unicorn, which recently raised a €255.14 million ($280 million) Series C round at a €1.82 billion ($2 billion) valuation. Other prominent names include Dronamics, Europe’s first licensed cargo drone airline; eBag, which has surpassed €100 million in annualised revenues; and SMSBump and NitroPack, both acquired by global buyers.
According to PitchBook data, Eleven Fund I and Fund II rank in the top 5% of comparable global venture funds by TVPI for their respective vintage years, and the firm placed 12th in PitchBook’s 2025 Global Manager Performance Score League Tables.
With Fund IV, Eleven plans to lead or co-lead pre-Seed and Seed rounds across Europe, writing initial cheques of €300k to €1.5 million, with up to €5 million per company reserved for follow-on investment. At least 60% of the fund’s capital will be held back for follow-on investment.
Eleven expects to make around 40 investments over a five-year period, targeting rounds of up to €3 million. It says five investments in robotics, agentic FinTech, energy and applied AI across Bulgaria, Serbia, and Turkey are in advanced discussions and will be announced in the coming months.
“We’re in advanced discussions with founders building companies in robotics, energy, fintech and applied AI, which we’ll announce in the coming months. The new capital is more fuel for what already works: backing great founders and strengthening the ecosystems around them,” added Simov.
With Fund IV, Eleven plans to focus on FinTech, healthcare and the future of work, sectors being reshaped by AI ,but also broadening its target sectors to include cybersecurity, applied and physical AI, and energy. A platform team will work with every portfolio company from the moment a deal closes, addressing common failure points: product-market fit, go-to-market strategy, brand positioning, senior hiring, governance and fundraising readiness.
Eleven has proven its moat as one of Europe’s leading venture firms, with LPs from Bulgaria, Greece, Turkey, Romania, the UK, Switzerland, and the United States. Its fourth fund not only expands its sectoral focus but also bets that the next breakthrough will come not from established European tech capitals, but from Sofia, Athens, Warsaw, Bucharest, and Istanbul, cities it has called home from the beginning.

articles.title: The Download: AI’s gas power boom and a consciousness reality check
articles.text:
The Download: AI’s gas power boom and a consciousness reality check
Plus: Huang's Nvidia return has lifted markets and put Trump under fire.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
One of the biggest obstacles to building a data center is getting approval to connect to the grid, a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers won’t wait and are instead building their own off-grid gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.
As of October 2026, developers had announced plans for more than 100 such gas power plants at data centers in the US. But bypassing the grid brings its own problems, from worsening climate emissions to potentially higher energy bills for everyone else.
Find out how the push for gas power could shape the grid—and the climate—for decades.
—Casey Crownhart
A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility of AI consciousness as a risk factor for investors, warning that it might introduce new rules to protect its models. But that stance came under fire from an inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.
Thomas Nagel, best known for his essay about what it's like to be a bat, was blunt. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said. He argued that producing language isn't enough to establish consciousness. But other philosophers disagree.
Here's why language has become central to the debate over conscious AI.
—James O'Donnell
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Huang's Nvidia return has lifted markets and put Trump under fire
US stock indexes had their best day since April 2025. (NBC News)
+ Trump made up to $15 million on his Nvidia holdings. (Guardian)
+ He reportedly saw Huang as vital to US open-weight AI. (Reuters $)
+ The US has also finally blacklisted Megaspeed. (BBC)
+ Open-source advocates wanted Huang back. (MIT Technology Review)
2 COP31's collapse has revived calls to end the consensus rule
It effectively lets any single country block a deal. (Axios)
+ But changing the rule would itself require consensus. (Guardian)
+ Rare wins at the talks included a new electrification pledge. (Nature $)
+ Our climate models have a major blind spot. (MIT Technology Review)
3 Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite as soon as next month
The warning comes from intelligence shared among Nato allies. (BBC)
+ Such a weapon could destroy thousands of satellites at once. (FT $)
+ The Kremlin has dismissed the claims as propaganda. (Guardian)
4 Google wants to make a 24/7 AI TV channel starring you
Its new patent imagines shows and ads built around each viewer. (404 Media)
+ They would be generated from your viewing history. (Gizmodo)
5 Oregon and Virginia are suing SpaceX over Grok's sexualized images
Grok’s “spicy mode” produced explicit images of women and children. (NYT $)
+ Deepfake porn is stealing people’s bodies. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Prosecutors say an ex-OpenAI engineer bugged company meetings
One appears to have involved a foreign government. (Bloomberg $)
7 Signal has joined banks and airlines in blocking AI agents
It's urging Apple, Google, and Microsoft to give apps more control. (CNBC)
+ AI agents are not your “coworkers.” (MIT Technology Review)
8 An emerging technology could bypass government internet blackouts
It connects ordinary phones directly to satellites. (New Scientist $)
9 AI billionaires are fueling a new wealth tax debate
Proposals include new levies on net worth and extra income taxes. (CNN)
10 "Pervert glasses" is Australia's word of the year
The Macquarie dictionary picked it ahead of "nudify" and "AI;DR." (Guardian)
Quote of the day
“The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some f**king donation to his ballroom.”
—Senator Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) says on X that Donald Trump’s avarice is behind Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO.
One more thing
How gamification took over the world
It’s a thought that occurs to every video-game player at some point: what if the weird, hyper-focused state I enter in virtual worlds could somehow be applied to the real one?
For a handful of consultants, startup gurus, and game designers in the late 2000s, this state of “blissful productivity” became the key to unlocking our true human potential. Their vision became the global phenomenon of gamification—but it didn’t live up to the hype.
Instead of liberating us, gamification became a tool for coercion, distraction, and control. Find out why we fell for it—and how we can recover.
—Bryan Gardiner
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ Rural libraries are pioneering "extended access" hours schemes to stay open longer.
+ After three years of recovery from a brain injury, a dad surprised his children by walking again.
+ Can loo roll survive a blowtorch? The Hydraulic Press Channel’s latest experiment is wonderfully silly.
+ Artist Maya Barkai’s collection of pedestrian traffic signals shows every little green walking man has its own personality.

articles.title: ShinyHunters claims to return after FBI arrests, uses old PGP keys as proof
articles.text:
The ShinyHunters extortion gang claims to have returned in posts on a new data leak site after a series of arrests over the past two months targeting alleged members.
The new Tor site, launched on November 23, contains messages in both Russian and English announcing the group's return, distancing itself from alleged impostors, and denouncing a former member who was reportedly arrested and is cooperating with law enforcement.
The site also includes two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys dating back to 2020, including one previously used to authenticate communications with BleepingComputer in August 2025.
BleepingComputer confirmed that both messages were signed using known PGP keys associated with the ShinyHunters extortion gang, confirming that the new operators have access to private signing keys historically used by the group.
However, these keys do not confirm whether the individuals behind the new operation are the same people who previously controlled the group, as the keys have circulated among numerous people.
The announcement follows a series of law enforcement operations targeting alleged ShinyHunters members after the group claimed to have breached FBI systems in September using an Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability.
Later that month, Dutch police confirmed the arrest of a 24-year-old Amsterdam man suspected of involvement with ShinyHunters, who was identified in media reports as Pepijn van der Stap, previously known online as Umbreon.
In early October, another alleged ShinyHunters member known as Rey or Saif was reportedly detained in Jordan and is cooperating with law enforcement. Around the same time, Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested in Pennsylvania in an extortion investigation reportedly linked to ShinyHunters.
After the arrests, ShinyHunters' main representative, who had regularly communicated with BleepingComputer and other media outlets, abruptly stopped responding, and their Telegram account was deleted. Soon after, the group's data leak site went offline.
In the new statement, the purported ShinyHunters operators say they are returning after months of rumors and misinformation circulated about the group.
"We’re finally back. A lot has happened recently, and there’s still plenty going on right now," reads the English announcement.
"To be honest, there’s just too much nonsense going on. Everyone’s telling different stories, but no one is really explaining what’s been happening over the last few months."
The operators of the new data leak site say they will communicate exclusively through the Exploit hacking forum account, which they claim to have controlled since 2020, and through the new Tor site.
The statement also addresses the reported arrest of a hacker and ShinyHunters member known as Rey, Dedale, or Saif, who was reportedly detained in Jordan in late September.
According to the announcement, Rey previously collaborated with ShinyHunters but began operating independently, creating Telegram channels without the group's approval.
"As far as we know, he has already been arrested and is now "actively cooperating" with the authorities," reads the English message.
"We already rotated the PGP key that Rey used for DLS, since it has most likely been compromised."
The message also mocks two other individuals reportedly tied to the ShinyHunters investigation, Umbreon and Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky, referring to their arrests.
"It was a pleasure working with you. And it’s truly a shame that our guys got caught because of such silly mistakes, ones that could easily have been avoided if you fools hadn’t gotten involved with the wrong people," reads the post.
The operators say they plan to launch a new CDN for hosting stolen data and will no longer use any of the existing backup servers.
Old PGP keys used to authenticate new site
To attempt to prove their legitimacy, the operators published two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys created in January and August 2020.
The keys have the following fingerprints:
- ShinyHunters RaidForums PGP key: 1FC4D0B1DEE914BB05B57FABF1F1B98A51C989B3
- ShinyHunters Empire Market PGP key: 828537C15F43F135A8317153CD16A1660CC7CE51
BleepingComputer verified that both messages were signed using these known PGP keys associated with the ShinyHunters extortion gang.
PGP uses a pair of cryptographic keys: a public key that anyone can access and use to verify a message or data, and a private key used to create signatures. The private key must be kept secret to prevent others from impersonating the key's owner.
BleepingComputer previously verified a message received from ShinyHunters on August 26, 2025, using the 1FC4D0B1DEE914BB05B57FABF1F1B98A51C989B3 public key.
Successful verification of the November message with that same public key shows that whoever signed it had access to the same private signing key used in the earlier communications, linking it to the ShinyHunters operation behind the widespread data theft attacks in 2026.
However, both historical keys were revoked in March 2026, when ShinyHunters announced a replacement PGP key with the fingerprint F4953411767DE71BEDCDABCB76F4E26F7A20978A.
At the time, the group used both 2020 keys to authenticate the replacement and stated that the older keys would no longer be used for communications.
Despite this, the November 23 announcement once again uses the two revoked 2020 keys to authenticate another new PGP key, 27DA9D5B183247CADFC322880ABC63E30F73822E.
However, none of the November messages examined by BleepingComputer were signed using the March 2026 replacement key, leaving it unclear whether the new operators also have access to that private key.
Because it was rumored that numerous people had the original 2020 keys, these unfortunately do not prove with certainty that the ShinyHunters group has returned or that the brand has not been revived by imposters.
