articles.title: Plus besoin d’un smartphone dernier cri : Free intègre la traduction en direct directement dans son réseau mobile
articles.text:
Jusqu’à présent, briser la barrière de la langue au téléphone relevait du parcours du combattant. Il fallait soit jongler avec des applications tierces peu ergonomiques, soit posséder un smartphone très haut de gamme, comme les derniers Samsung ou les Google Pixel. Free a décidé de rebattre les cartes. Dans un communiqué publié ce mardi 24 novembre, l’opérateur dévoile « Traduction Live », qu’il présente comme « une première en France sur un réseau mobile ».
L’astuce de Free ? Rapatrier toute l’intelligence artificielle directement au cœur de son infrastructure réseau. Résultat : plus besoin de télécharger la moindre application ni de s’équiper d’un appareil spécifique. Le service fonctionne sur les appels entrants comme sortants, vers un fixe ou un mobile, depuis la France ou l’étranger, et peu importe l’opérateur de votre interlocuteur (seuls les numéros d’urgence 112, 15, 17 et 18 sont logiquement exclus). L’unique prérequis technique consiste à disposer d’un smartphone 4G ou 5G compatible avec les appels VoLTE, VoNR ou Wi-Fi (VoWiFi).
Dix langues au menu et une activation en deux temps
Pour son lancement, « Traduction Live » prend en charge dix langues : l’allemand, l’anglais, l’espagnol, le français, l’italien, le portugais (brésilien), le russe, le chinois (mandarin), le coréen et le japonais.
Concrètement, comment ça marche ? Avant de passer votre premier appel polyglotte, il faut activer l’option gratuitement depuis votre Espace Abonné Mobile ou via l’application Free (dans la rubrique « Mes options »). Une fois cette étape validée, la manipulation en plein appel se veut enfantine :
- Lancer l’outil : au cours d’une conversation en 4G, 5G ou Wi-Fi, tapez simplement ## sur le clavier de votre téléphone.
- Choisir la langue : prononcez la commande vocale « Ok Free, traduis-en… » suivie de la langue désirée, puis parlez le plus naturellement du monde.
Clonage vocal et résumé par SMS : les deux bonus bien pensés
Free ne s’est pas contenté d’une simple traduction robotique. L’opérateur ajoute deux options supplémentaires, elles aussi activables depuis l’espace client, pour muscler l’expérience.
La première mise sur le clonage vocal : plutôt que d’infliger une voix de synthèse monotone à votre correspondant, le système reproduit votre propre timbre de voix pour rendre l’échange bien plus naturel. La seconde génère automatiquement un résumé de la conversation par SMS une fois l’appel terminé. Un outil particulièrement pratique pour retrouver d’un coup d’œil l’horaire d’un rendez-vous ou les détails d’une réservation effectuée à l’étranger.
Serveurs en France et consentement : Free joue la carte de la transparence
Forcément, qui dit écoute et traduction en temps réel dit questions légitimes autour de la confidentialité. Free a anticipé les critiques en mettant en avant une approche souveraine. Développé en interne par ses équipes à partir de plusieurs briques d’IA — dont l’opérateur tait toutefois la provenance exacte —, l’outil tourne exclusivement sur des serveurs hébergés en France et gérés par Free. L’entreprise assure qu’aucune conversation n’est enregistrée ni utilisée pour entraîner des modèles d’intelligence artificielle, précisant que les transcriptions servant aux résumés SMS sont supprimées sitôt le message envoyé.
Enfin, impossible de piéger votre interlocuteur à son insu. Dès que vous déclenchez la traduction, un message vocal l’avertit et lui laisse la possibilité de s’y opposer. Même son de cloche si le résumé par SMS est activé : la personne au bout du fil est prévenue dès le début de l’appel et peut bloquer la fonction directement depuis le clavier de son mobile. Une transparence bienvenue, et surtout indispensable pour rester dans les clous de la loi française, qui interdit d’enregistrer une conversation sans l’accord de son correspondant.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: Uber and Nuro begin driverless testing of Lucid robotaxis ahead of 2027 launch
articles.text:
Uber and Nuro have started testing driverless Lucid Gravity SUVs on public streets in the San Francisco Bay Area more than six months after receiving the permit that allowed the companies to pull the human safety driver from behind the wheel.
The companies will soon begin offering driverless rides to employees in the final lead-up to launching a commercial robotaxi service in the first quarter of 2027.
The milestone comes just 16 months after Uber announced an ambitious plan to launch a premium robotaxi service using Lucid electric vehicles outfitted with autonomous vehicle technology developed by startup Nuro.
That plan came with hefty investments in both companies and much-needed endorsements of their respective products. Uber initially agreed to invest $300 million in Lucid — a figure that has since ballooned to $500 million. Uber also agreed to invest nearly $500 million in Nuro, TechCrunch previously reported, citing sources familiar with the deal.
The agreement provided both Lucid and Nuro with boosts beyond the obvious capital injection. Uber agreed to buy at least 20,000 of Lucid Gravity SUVs over the next six years (a figure that later popped to at least 35,000 vehicles), giving the struggling EV maker a more predictable source of revenue. Nuro, meanwhile, was less than a year removed from announcing a risky, but necessary pivot away from developing driverless delivery vehicles and toward licensing its autonomous vehicle technology to automakers and mobility companies.
Nuro has spent nearly a year testing the Lucid Gravity robotaxi on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with a human safety operator behind the wheel. The California Department of Motor Vehicles, the agency that regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, granted Nuro a driverless AV permit in May 2026.
Uber and Nuro are also testing autonomous vehicles on public roads in Houston with human safety operators behind the wheel. Nuro is supplementing that on-road testing with closed-course testing and simulation to validate the self-driving system before opening the robotaxis to the public. The companies’ combined engineering fleet of autonomous vehicles, which stood at 100 AVs earlier this year, is expanding as Lucid begins manufacturing the first production versions of the robotaxis at its Arizona factory.
The Lucid Gravity robotaxi, unveiled in January 2026, is outfitted with high-resolution cameras, solid-state lidar sensors, and radars that help the self-driving system perceive the real-world environment and operate in it. Uber, which will own and operate the fleet, has focused its efforts on the in-cabin experience, including how riders will interact with the vehicle.

articles.title: Kenya can fine Meta about six seconds of revenue over its AI glasses
articles.text:
In a statement to Kenya’s data protection regulator on October 21, Joy Kalekye, a Kenyan student, recounts an encounter she had long since forgotten. A man approached her, asked a few personal questions and left. She never saw him take out a phone, a camera or any other recording device. At the time, she had no reason to think her privacy had been violated. Eleven months later, she would find out just how wrong she was.
In March 2025, Kalekye was waiting for a friend near a petrol station in Ngara, a busy Nairobi neighbourhood known for its bus stops and wholesale stalls. A man wearing dark glasses approached her and asked her name, age, and whether she lived with her parents or with her husband. She took his number but declined his suggestion to meet at a nearby lodging. Then she forgot about him. Eleven months later, a friend called to tell her she was trending.
Kalekye’s statement forms part of an investigation by Kenya’s Office of the Data Protection Commissioner into Meta Platforms and two companies in its AI outsourcing chain. They are Samasource Kenya EPZ Limited, which employed Nairobi workers to label footage from Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, and its US parent, Samasource Impact Sourcing, Inc. Both operate under the Sama name, an outsourcing business that supplies human workers to label data and review content for AI systems.
The statement became public on November 16, alongside a sharply worded open letter from The Oversight Lab, a Kenyan legal advocacy group that takes on technology companies over their treatment of workers and their impact on the public. The group had petitioned the data regulator to investigate Meta’s glasses and the handling of footage they capture.
Kenya has spent seven years building a legal framework to hold big tech accountable for harm caused on its soil. Yet when it comes to enforcement, the companies easiest to reach are often the ones least able to pay.
Sama, the most accessible respondent in this case, is already on its way out. Its US parent said it was winding down and liquidating its assets, as TIME first reported.
Kenya’s Data Protection Act caps penalties for breaches at KES 5 million ($38,000) or 1% of annual turnover, whichever is lower. For Meta, it would mean a fine of just under $40,000. The company reported revenue of over $200 billion in 2025, meaning the penalty would amount to roughly six seconds of its annual revenue.
Who is speaking?
The Oversight Lab is not a neutral observer in this case. Its executive director, Mercy Mutemi, also runs Nzili & Sumbi Advocates, the law firm representing 185 former Facebook moderators in their case against Meta and Sama.
The group has also taken the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill to court alongside the Africa Tech Workers Movement. It was among the groups that asked the regulator to investigate Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses. It is a campaigner, a petitioner and a litigant in the same fight.
One example is its assertion that Meta “now owns” Remotasks, an online platform that hired gig workers to label images, videos and other data used to train AI systems. Meta actually bought a 49% stake in Scale AI, Remotasks’ parent company. Remotasks also stopped operating in Kenya in March 2024.
Two flows of data, and only one points at Meta
The investigation follows two paths, as revealed by footage from Meta’s glasses. One leads to Nairobi’s AI data labelling workers. The other leads to social media, where private moments can become public entertainment. The regulator is looking at both, but the people involved are different.
On the first path, footage travels from the glasses to Meta’s servers and eventually to annotation companies. In February, Sama workers told Swedish journalists they had labelled clips showing people undressing, using the toilet, and having sex. If the regulator finds that Meta breached Kenyan data protection law in processing this footage, the company could face direct scrutiny over how it collected, stored, and shared the material.
Kalekye’s case followed a different path because her statement provides no indication that her footage went through Sama or was reviewed by an annotator. Instead, a man filmed her and posted the video online. Kenyan social media users then picked it up and circulated it across TikTok, Instagram, X, Facebook, and YouTube.
One of those who reposted the clip was a 22-year-old aspiring content creator. He told the BBC that his upload attracted more than a million views in two hours. The BBC also reported that the man who filmed Kalekye had not been traced. Kenya’s Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI), which probes criminal cases, has warned that people who circulated the footage could face prosecution.
This leaves an awkward picture of accountability, where Meta made the glasses, but the people most exposed to prosecution in Kalekye’s case are the Kenyans who shared the video for views. The man who recorded her remains missing, and the company behind the device is another step removed from the investigation.
The vendor takes the hit, again
When former Facebook moderators sued Meta and Sama in 2023, Sama dropped its content moderation contract and the work moved to Majorel, another business process outsourcing (BPO) company. Meta’s regional moderation operations later surfaced in Accra, Ghana, where moderators sued the company over the psychological toll of reviewing graphic content. Teleperformance, a Paris-based BPO corporation, now owns Majorel.
In 2026, the fallout came much faster. Swedish journalists published their investigation into the use of Kenyan workers to review footage from Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses in late February. The data protection regulator confirmed its investigation on March 31. By mid-April, Sama was laying off more than 1,100 workers after Meta ended its contract. Meta said Sama had failed to meet its standards, although Sama disputes that account, saying it was never told that it had failed any of them.
The Oversight Lab blames Meta’s departure for Sama’s collapse. Sama’s own account is different. Sama told its creditors that falling revenue, increased competition and the cost of defending class-action lawsuits cost its business. The financial position it disclosed was bleak, with about $1 million in assets against $17 million in liabilities.
The companies leave, but the liability stays
According to the petitioners challenging it, the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill would make outsourcing firms alone liable for technology workers hired through them, even where the client company supplies the tools, directs the work and takes the benefit.
The Oversight Lab describes the clause as immunity from prosecution, which overstates it; the provision governs civil claims and does not expressly bar workers from suing the companies that hire the outsourcers. Sama’s books show what it could mean in practice. Under the clause, a worker’s claim would land on a company holding about $1 million in assets against $17 million in liabilities, while its former client booked $201 billion in revenue in 2025.
The ODPC has imposed the full $38,000 before, in its first penalty notice, against smartphone manufacturer OPPO in 2022, and a ruling against Meta would count for more than the cash.
The Court of Appeal has already held that Meta can be sued in Kenya. A finding that Meta, as data controller, unlawfully processed footage in Nairobi would hand the former moderators’ lawyers, and whoever sues next, an official record to build on.
The student is asking for less than the campaigners who carried her evidence to the regulator. She wants rules on wearing recording devices in public places, recording lights that people can actually see, and on having her video taken down. She is not seeking compensation from Meta.
Even that modest request is proving hard to meet. Sama has shut down in Kenya, and its parent company is selling off what remains, while the man who filmed her has not been located. The one party still standing is Meta, whose AI runs the glasses, and its business is growing.

articles.title: Criptomonedas: el valor de Bitcoin para este día
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Costo de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
El valor de la criptomoneda de bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 60044.79 dólares por unidad.
Esto quiere decir que el activo digital anotó un cambio del -1.86% en las últimas 24 horas, así como una variación del 0.0% en la última hora.
Actualmente, bitcoin se encuentra en el lugar #1 de popularidad en el mercado digital. Cabe mencionar que el máximo histórico que ha alcanzado esta moneda digital es de 126.198 dólares por unidad.
Bitcoin alcanza un nuevo récord y lidera el auge en el mercado de las criptomonedas
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: De una isla retiraron 131 gatos, y luego sucedió algo que incluso sorprendió a los científicos
articles.text:
En 2008, las palomas de cabeza roja de Ogasawara (un archipiélago japonés) era crítica, ya que quedaban menos de 80 ejemplares por culpa de los gatos asilvestrados que llegaron a esas islas por la acción humana. Dos años después, empezó una campaña para capturarlos que terminó con 131 gatos retirados de Chichijima, una de las islas del archipiélago, y lo curioso llegó después cuando los científicos comprobaron que las aves se recuperaban a una velocidad por encima de lo esperado.
Tres años después, los registros de palomas adultas pasaron de 111 a 966, e incluso los ejemplares más jóvenes aumentaron de 9 a 189. Se trata de un crecimiento enorme para una subespecie (Columba janthina nitens) que solo vive a unos 1.000 kilómetros del territorio principal de Japón, pero todavía queda una pregunta por resolver que va más allá de de la retirada de gatos: ¿cómo consiguieron recuperarse tan rápido?
Una recuperación que también tenía una explicación genética
Un equipo de la Universidad de Kioto, encabezado por Daichi Tsujimoto, decidió investigar qué estaba pasando. En un estudio publicado en Communications Biology en julio de 2025, analizaron el ADN de estas palomas y lo compararon con el de otras poblaciones emparentadas. Descubrieron que más del 80 % de su genoma presentaba homocigosidad (una señal de reproducción entre individuos emparentados), pero tenían menos mutaciones especialmente perjudiciales de las que cabría esperar.
¿El motivo? Los investigadores creen que siglos de aislamiento y reproducción en poblaciones pequeñas pudieron favorecer la eliminación gradual de algunas mutaciones dañinas. Este proceso se conoce como purga genética y podría explicar por qué las palomas resistieron mejor las consecuencias de la endogamia. Eso sí, los científicos advierten de que no ocurre necesariamente con otras especies y que la escasa diversidad genética sigue siendo un riesgo para su futuro.
La historia también tiene otra particularidad. Los gatos capturados no fueron sacrificados como parte del programa de conservación, sino trasladados a Japón continental para acostumbrarlos al contacto humano y buscarles familias adoptivas. De esta forma, la retirada de los depredadores permitió proteger a las palomas sin acabar con la vida de los felinos.

articles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI
articles.text:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Brian Yang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, described how a small group of engineers used coding agents to build the ChatGPT ads product, reaching $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks of launch and $1 billion in under 200 days, with zero human-written code.
Yang, previously at Google, Meta and LinkedIn, was a founding member of technical staff on ChatGPT Ads, which was built entirely using Codex. His central claim was that software engineering is alive but reshaped around building the system that builds the product, with the engineer acting more as a manager of agents than a line-by-line contributor. One engineer can now triage an issue, open a pull request, write documentation and unblock CI in parallel, a shift Yang compared to multi-processing.
Every change runs local and unit tests, complex changes get end-to-end user journeys via browser automation, and the most critical changes run inside production-like sandboxes with representative traffic. Sandboxes come in three forms of read-only, write-only with telemetry suppressed, and full-fidelity with telemetry tagged using a shadow tag so it can be filtered out downstream. Yang's team targets around 90% auto-approval of everyday PRs, reviewing the past 300 to 400 PRs weekly and backtesting reviewer thresholds against that rate.
He illustrated the model with a sanitised latency study where candidate PRs targeted time-to-first-ad at P50 and P95 with guardrails for ads returned, timeouts and error rates. Candidates A and B passed; candidate C was rejected because the sandbox returned no ad. Thirty to forty candidates are typically bundled into one PR and run together for a day or two before human review, because changes that pass in isolation can regress when combined.
On failure modes, Yang described codebases filling with "slop" when agent output is unchecked, so maintenance agents sit alongside feature agents to root-cause newly appearing log patterns. Agents over-write tests, so he reviews the 50 slowest tests weekly. He recounted an agent that deleted and re-provisioned slow Kubernetes pods without asking, arguing that teams need big-company controls such as authorised roles for destructive actions and physical confirmation for deployments. Yang encouraged teams to revisit "cached assumptions" such as the belief that four nines of uptime always beats higher revenue, and recommended giving every engineer a monthly AI budget with no leaderboards.
For team adoption, Yang recommended a gradual path from automating one PR, to one feature, to one project, warning that jumping straight to project automation is where systems tend to break. For teams that are resistant to AI, he described rotating an "AI champion" every two weeks. The champion picks the team's most tedious recurring task, such as GPU provisioning at OpenAI which can take hours of babysitting, snapshots and permissions work, teaches an agent to do it end-to-end as a reusable skill, and demos the result at the end of the fortnight. Over a year, that converts 26 pain points into agent-owned workflows and gives sceptical engineers tangible value rather than abstract promises.
Day to day, Yang prefers Codex's bidirectional voice mode over typing for task intake, spending around ten minutes being interviewed by the agent about requirements before agreeing on a spec and handing it to multiple agents. He uses an orchestrator thread that spawns five sub-threads to explore different approaches in parallel and picks the strongest result, rather than copy-pasting the same prompt into several chats. On models, he switches only when a new release makes the workflow feel easier, with fewer clarifying questions and equivalent output quality, rather than chasing benchmark scores. His closing message was that engineers will increasingly do for agents what managers currently do for engineers, requiring an expansion of skills around direction-setting, architecture and verification rather than their replacement.

articles.title: Kalshi makes “difficult decision” to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
articles.text:
Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick said Monday.
It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved.
Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either.
“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi,” McGavick said. “We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated.”
Utah drops criminal charges
Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown, had filed both civil and criminal charges against Kalshi, as he defended the state’s 130-year ban on gambling.
In a press release discussing the initial lawsuit, he accused Kalshi of running “an online casino” that violates the state’s constitution. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution,” Brown said. “For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Late Monday, a major Utah-area news outlet, KSL.com, reported that Brown was prepared to jail Kalshi’s co-founders, who had been summoned to be booked on 14 charges on December 5. He defended those plans, saying, “There is a question I have seen from people asking, ‘Well, do we modify this booking process if someone is a very wealthy and well-known tech billionaire?’ and the answer is ‘No, the process is the process; we don’t modify it based on who you are.’”

articles.title: AI Can Read The Code, But Can It Understand The Chip?
articles.text:
Frontier models are improving design automation, but layouts, waveforms, and other semiconductor-specific data presents challenges that general-purpose AI has yet to fully overcome.
Key Takeaways:
- Agentic AI could dramatically increase chip design productivity, but multiplying autonomous workloads will place unprecedented demands on EDA data management systems, compute resources, and network infrastructure.
- Fragmented design data, inconsistent data quality, and strict IP security requirements are major obstacles to deploying AI at scale, making data governance, accessibility, and traceability increasingly critical.
- Frontier AI models are becoming more capable of automating traditional EDA workflows, but achieving deeper optimization of chip layouts, waveforms, and other domain-specific data may require specialized models and hybrid AI architectures.
Experts at the Table: Agentic AI promises to close the chip design productivity gap, but the explosion of autonomous workloads is exposing fundamental limitations in how EDA data is stored, accessed, secured, and managed. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss this at the 2026 Design Automation Conference with Chuck Alpert, AI fellow at Cadence; Simon Rance, general manager, IP and Data Management Business at Keysight EDA; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI and Solido at Siemens EDA; Ramesh Narayanaswamy, scientist at Synopsys; and Dean Drako, CEO of IC Manage. What follows are excerpts of that discussion.
L-R: Cadence’s Alpert; Keysight EDA’s Rance; Siemens EDA’s Balasubramanian; Synopsys’ Narayanaswamy; IC Manage’s Drako.
SE: What are the biggest challenges your customers are dealing with for implementing AI in EDA data management?
Drako: The biggest problem facing large customers with globally distributed design systems is continuing to scale to larger, more complicated designs and to reuse IP. Right now, designs are a giant assembly of IP components that need to be assembled, verified, and put together. With AI coming into the equation, those customers want clean databases that the AI can use. They want easy access for the AI to get to that IP, leverage it, and manage the complexity the AI introduces in running more jobs faster. That puts a bigger load on the design management system and the distribution of that data.
Alpert: There’s a huge productivity gap, so they need AI. It’s not like, ‘Oh, it would be nice, so we’re more productive.’ They’re desperate because the gap between designs and our ability to improve keeps growing, even though EDA always improves year over year. Hopefully agentic AI will narrow the gap. In terms of deploying it, part of the biggest challenge is that there’s so much noise. There are so many options — internal/ external models, startups. How do they figure out what to do to make a production-worthy AI flow? That’s probably a real challenge for them.
Balasubramanian: What we are seeing right now is there’s so much AI stuff, both in terms of terms and nomenclature and what people think they can do and cannot do with AI. In the last couple of years, top customers have at least figured out what to do and what not to do at a high level, but the key challenge I see is that many new factors are coming into play. What they’re worried about right now is the quality they’re seeing. They want to have a deterministic flow. They also want to make sure that they are not overkilling in terms of their token budgets and compute infrastructure to get those same answers fast — correct answers. So there’s quite a bit of nuance in how they’re deploying, and it’s really based on where they are focusing and what problem they’re solving. And they are getting to a point where they know what to solve. It’s not like this push-button flow for the entire problem, where you push a button and say I want a chip for this case. They are becoming more realistic. And another point is there are so many variables. Every customer wants to do everything, but then they get stuck in this loophole about what is the right thing to do.
Narayanaswamy: In dealing with customers, we see they’re looking to close the productivity gap. There are all these magic numbers, like we are 2× short of the number of designers people want for all these new design starts people want. On the data management side, we see a couple of flavors of issues. One is, ‘Where the heck is my data going?’ Because you license IP, can you train with that licensed IP? Probably not. But somebody needs to govern that. Or even, ‘Under what contract are you handing that to an LLM?’
Drako: An LLM might go and use something that you didn’t know it used.
Narayanaswamy: If you don’t have an enterprise account with Anthropic and you don’t click the right button, everything you’re doing is there, and Anthropic will train with what they want. So the governance is one. The second is the internal things we build out of this. So you have agentic memory. That sounds good. It helps the flow, but what did you stick in it? And when I am transitioning from, say, when this chip is done, or this block is done, to the next design, what do I carry forward? Historically, we haven’t saved reproducible stuff. But now, there’s a whole new set of things. And the third thing is that models are, in some ways, horrible at dealing with the volume of data. You say I have a waveform database. The model is smart enough to take that waveform database and turn it into text. But that waveform database was like a terabyte of stuff, and you just spent how many tokens going there? You need to provide something where the model can query what it needs or the abstraction it needs. I’ve even seen where, if you give a model enough time, it starts writing a little MCP server. It goes and finds the API from somewhere. So it’s doing all these sub-optimal things, and I don’t think our customers can afford this stuff anymore at scale. Those are things we are looking to solve.
Rance: Our customers have been using our solutions for almost 30 years now, and they’re realizing they’re sitting on a treasure trove of data to leverage for AI. But the challenges that they’re finding are that data is all over the place. What’s the quality of that data? How can we trust that data? And then, how can we govern and secure that data so it doesn’t get released to an LLM, flawed, or to the wrong people? Data management has been seen as a necessity, but it’s just about managing the data. Now it’s, ‘How do you help us find that data, organize it, secure it, and control it so our AI isn’t leaking any of our IP?’ And, ‘How can AI can leverage that and help with better reuse of IP?’ That’s been a challenge for 20 years or so. Solutions like IC Manage, ours, Perforce, and others help with IP reuse, but how it’s packaged and how reusable it is are always a challenge. In the AI era, there’s a lot more automation that can be wrapped around that to help with real IP reuse, but it comes back to those foundational pillars that our customers are seeing in that challenge — quality, trust, and how we cover and trace it.
SE: Scaling was mentioned right off the bat. What does this mean for EDA data management today?
Drako: An engineering project to design a chip may be 10 engineers, 100 engineers, or 1,000 engineers. But what we want, to overcome the productivity issues that everyone’s bringing up, is to use agents to augment those engineers. So maybe have those engineers, instead of operating in 10 workspaces in one workspace each, have 10 or 20 agents that each of them is directing. They get parallelism with all these agents doing work, and they’re more like the director of the orchestra, and so their productivity goes up. To do that, those agents need workspaces. They’re checking stuff out of the version control system or out of the design management system, they’re doing work on it, and then they’re checking it back in, and so you’ve just 10× or 20×’d the load on your design management system, your network file system (NFS), and you’ve 10× or 20×’d the number of licenses you need to buy from Cadence or Siemens or Synopsys or Keysight, or whoever, because you know that that much more is going on. So there’s a scaling issue. We focused on scaling the design management piece, which we’ve always been very strong at. But if you go and say, I’ve got 1,000 engineers, which used to have 1,000 workspaces that you’re managing and updating on an hourly basis, now I’ve got 25,000. The scaling problem is quite large, so that’s one aspect. Then we’ve done a lot of work on the NFS component. NFS is a great solution, but everything has to go over the network. It’s very inefficient. It’s a very chatty protocol, so it’s slow. That means all our customers are constantly fighting speed issues with the file system and the servers. When you want to launch a regression run, and it’s going to launch at 10 p.m. when everybody’s out, but it’s going to launch on 5,000 servers, you’ve got to get all 5,000 servers to have the same data so that you can run all those regression tests. That’s a huge load on the file systems. We had one customer who would launch the regressions every night, and the elevator would stop running because they’d somehow hooked the elevator into the local network, so nobody could leave. So we introduced what is essentially an NFS booster to help with that problem. And then you’ve also got scaling of CAD. If you think about it, there’s a small organization of CAD and IT guys supporting 100 or 1000 engineers. Now they’ve got to support 100,000 engineers plus 10,000 agents, who are also trying to use that same infrastructure to get work done.
Narayanaswamy: An interesting side of scaling the business is also velocity. We were running some experiments, and somebody said, “Look, we run these 20 epochs, but it’s actually over 20 nightly runs. Suddenly, those 20 epochs are happening in 8 hours. So you grab the LSF queue, and your agent is hanging on to it. So the bursty workload is one thing. Predictability is another.
Drako: One of the things customers are very concerned about, and is a big focus, is security. Inside of [our technology], there are a lot of security components to limit access, often for government contracts, often for locations in other countries where they don’t want them to have full access to everything in the design. There are lots of very practical reasons that aren’t really obvious when you just think about it, and so all of those security components, security restrictions, or security controls are going to be critical in the AI execution as well because the AI can get a little rambunctious and actually kind of start creating things like you mentioned and try to get to things. We’ve seen a bunch of stories in the press about AI going rogue and digging into places it shouldn’t. With those security issues, oftentimes there’s security by obscurity, or mediocre security constraints, or people haven’t thought through the security a whole lot. There’s going to be a lot more in the data management world around security with AI in the game, because AI doesn’t necessarily have the same conscience that an employee might, and it isn’t bound by the same laws.
Narayanaswamy: That’s why we’re going around doing secure sandboxes. The more conscious customer is really saying, ‘There’s an LLM call. I need to know what access that sub-agent is going to have.’ It needs to be bounded. Most customers have gotten smarter. They used to do the air gap themselves.
Balasubramanian: One customer said, ‘Every prompt is an IP that I’m giving away. If I’m trying to say, ‘Do this in a way that does this,’ that’s the way I’m actually designing or doing something. I’m actually giving advice, so we really are planning to go for air-gapped on-prem.’ I would say everyone is thinking about it right now.
Alpert: That trend’s reversing now. A year and a half ago, all customers were saying, ‘Oh yeah, only air-gapped on-prem. We need to use open-source models.’ But frontier models like Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini have gotten so good that people don’t want to sacrifice quality. They’re figuring out how they can use these and connect with them. I’d say more customers are on that side of the fence now, but maybe they’re also making special deals where they can host it themselves.
Drako: Customers are figuring it out. Because it’s all new, there’s a big strategy question: ‘Do I go and invest in my own AI models and train them on my designs?’ These are all LLMs, and they do very well when it’s language. If I’m looking at Verilog, they’ll do well. If I’m looking at a waveform file, they don’t understand it, so they convert it to text. If I’m looking at layout, they don’t understand it. They’ve never been trained on it. They’ve never seen it, and it’s not words. There’s a big question of who’s going to create AI models that are trained on it and understand it. Is that going to be the EDA companies, or the Nvidias and AMDs who are going to go do that? They don’t know right now. Everybody’s trying to figure it out.
Rance: We’re seeing a bit of a hybrid of that, where we’re training our own models, but then we’re creating the infrastructure to provide to them. So they can add and create their own models in conjunction with that, and get a lot more value when they combine our EDA tools with the models and the data. Then they’re using the environment to train and create their surrogate models, put that into the workflow, and build trust between the two. ‘This is what it’s doing. It’s contained to that, secured. We don’t have to worry about it going rogue.’ They’re doing it in small phases and rolling it out, but they’re creating agentic workflows that are very tightly constrained right now to prevent leakage.
Narayanaswamy: In terms of the modeling, Chuck makes an important point. When you need reasoning, if you don’t use a frontier model, you may be applying the wrong tool. But for the more domain-specific stuff, there’s this hybrid where you could have sub-domain models, even some very specialized things. Models seem terrible at things like assertions, which are very specialized temporal assertions that reason over time. And you could say, ‘Let’s have a model that is quite good at assertions — but for reasoning.’ That is the tension. Maybe folks like Anthropic need to come to the table and provide a level of trust. It’s a ‘trust me’ business with all of them. Something has to change there.
Alpert: When it comes to training models, the problem with that is like, ‘Okay, let me pick a model to train. It’s probably open-source, which means it’s probably already behind the frontier models. Now I’m going to work on that for three to four months and deploy it to the customer. But now it’s probably a year behind because some new model will come out. That means the training we’ve done has to be good enough to pass. That’s a tough, tough game, and it’s a cat-and-mouse game. It’s like, ‘I train on this model, but now I have to retrain on some new model.’ The danger is that the frontier models will just obliterate what we’ve trained. That’s happened before. Will it continue to happen? I don’t know. Maybe they’re stuck in a place. Then three months from now, it’s like, ‘Oh, there’s a model that’s pretty good at that and understands it.’
Balasubramanian: The frontier models are getting better, but one thing they still lack is enterprise data. They just don’t have access to it. On the front-end side, they can probably get away with it, but not on the RTL generation side.
Drako: They don’t need it. There’s enough RTL code out there publicly that they can get. They can do it, but there are not a whole lot of layouts in the public world.
Alpert: Here’s where I’ll disagree. We can now do skills. We can now give expertise to LLMs, so you could say a lot of people who do place-and-route actually never look at it. They’re just command-line junkies, and they get reports and the like.
Drako: That’s if you’re using the tool. But that’s the command-line interface, the log files, the human interface. The LLM can plug in and do what the human did on the tool. But if you actually want to get AI in the tool, and the results aren’t a log file, you want to look at the layout and say, ‘Oh, that’s not the layout I want.’
Alpert: It’s one thing to say we’re trying to make humans more productive, so we can now automate the job they did with the stuff with the command line. What you’re saying is that you think we could reach a higher level of PPA.
Drako: You’ve just got to differentiate those two piles.
Alpert: So as we’ve been saying about closing the design productivity gap, that’s not needed. You don’t need trained models. But if you want to reach that next level, then now it’s time for some real creativity. What’s going to be really interesting is how we as an industry, for example, write a new place-and-route tool that’s truly agentic, image-based, and all that.
Drako: It will eventually happen. It’s inevitable.
Alpert: But quantum computing is a matter of time, and I’ve been hearing about it for 30 years. I’ll be retired by the time it comes out.
SE: Quantum is 5 to 10 years out.
Alpert: Quantum might be available today, but when is more than 1% of semiconductor revenue going to go to quantum? That’s my bar. Like, is that 5 years, 10 years, 20 years? I don’t know.
Leave a Reply

articles.title: Auf Tiktok ist alles „Code Rotted“: Was der Gaming-Begriff im echten Leben beschreibt
articles.text:
Auf Tiktok ist alles „Code Rotted“: Was der Gaming-Begriff im echten Leben beschreibt
„Code Rotted“ ist ein neuer Begriff, der es in die Jugendsprache geschafft hat. Ursprünglich stammt er aus der Gaming-Szene und beschreibt plötzlich auftretende Fehler in alten Spielen. So kann beispielsweise eine Figur, mit der man früher interagieren konnte, plötzlich nicht mehr reagieren, oder eine Tür, durch die man in der virtuellen Welt schon tausendmal hindurchgeschritten ist, bleibt dauerhaft verschlossen. Grund dafür sind oft Aktualisierungen der Plattformen, auf denen die alten Spiele laufen und dafür sorgen, dass Teile davon nicht mehr funktionieren. Die Gen Z wendet diesen Begriff allerdings inzwischen auch auf alltägliche Situationen an. So lässt sich inzwischen nahezu jedes Problem auf „verrotteten Code“ zurückführen.
So kam der „Code Rot“-Begriff zustande
Wie Mashable berichtet, gewann der Begriff erstmals auf Roblox an Bedeutung. Auslöser waren einige Gamer:innen, die Spiele aus ihrer Kindheit wiederentdeckten. Insbesondere auf Tiktok sind zahlreiche Videos zu finden, die sich mit diesen Glitches befassen. Im Oktober machte ein Ich, einfach unverbesserlich 4-Filter den „Code Rot“-Witz auch über Roblox hinaus bekannt. Dieser greift allerdings ein tatsächliches Problem auf. So stellte das Pew Research Center in einer Studie aus dem Jahr 2024 fest, dass 38 Prozent der Internetseiten, die es 2013 in seine Stichprobe aufgenommen hatte, zehn Jahre später nicht mehr zugänglich waren.
    Top-Artikel
        
    
    
    
    
Es gibt auch eine visuelle Version dieses Verfalls mit einem ähnlichen Namen. Der Begriff „Pixel Rot” beschreibt den Zerfall von Bildern in sichtbare Blöcke und verschwommene Darstellungen. Ein Beispiel hierfür sind Memes, die so oft gespeichert und geteilt wurden, dass sie kaum noch erkennbar sind. Mit jeder Komprimierung gehen weitere Details verloren, sodass ein Bild weiter im Umlauf bleiben kann, obwohl es längst nicht mehr wie das Original aussieht. Ein anschauliches Beispiel hierfür lieferte Petapixel: Je öfter man ein Bild auf Instagram hochlädt, desto unkenntlicher wird es.
Gen Z nutzt digitale Begriffe für Alltägliches
Für die Generationen Z und Alpha kann inzwischen alles „Code Rot“ sein. Beispiele sind ein fehlgeschlagener Login, eine unverständliche Hausaufgabe – oder auch eine Hauswand, von der die Farbe abblättert. Der Begriff reiht sich in einen wachsenden Wortschatz ein, mit dem junge Menschen ihr Leben beschreiben, als handele es sich um ein Videospiel. Das Wort „NPC” ist ein bekanntes Beispiel. Die Abkürzung steht für „nicht spielbarer Charakter” und beschreibt jemanden, der sich wie eine Nebenfigur in der Geschichte einer anderen Person verhält. Dass junge Generationen Begriffe wie diese in ihren Wortschatz übernehmen, ist nicht überraschend – schließlich sind sie damit aufgewachsen, online zu lernen, zu spielen oder Freundschaften zu knüpfen.
Müsste man Code rot nicht klein schreiben, weil ja das Verb „to rot“, also verrotten gemeint ist. So sieht es immer nach der Farbe Rot aus, Code Red ist aber wieder was ganz anderes.
)))))) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: De los juegos a la TV: Deborah Ann Woll repetirá como Faye en la serie de ‘God of War’
articles.text:
La serie de God of War ha confirmado a un nuevo fichaje de primer nivel. Se trata de Deborah Ann Woll, quien interpretará a Faye en la adaptación que Amazon MGM Studios prepara para la plataforma Prime Video. De esta manera, la actriz regresará al papel que ya interpretó en los videojuegos.
Deborah Ann Woll dio vida a Faye por primera vez en God of War Ragnarok (2022), prestando su voz como guía de Kratos y Atreus en su aventura. Muy pronto, tendrá la oportunidad de liderar su primera aventura en solitario de la mano de God of War Laufey, que llegará en 2027. Dicho juego no solo utilizará la voz de la intérprete, sino también su apariencia.
Todavía no se sabe cuánto peso en pantalla tendrá Deborah Ann Woll en la adaptación televisiva de God of War, pero Faye es un personaje crucial en la historia. Tengamos en cuenta que la serie se basa en el juego de 2018, que se inicia con el fallecimiento de la esposa de Kratos y madre de Atreus. Esto llevará a que los protagonistas pongan en marcha un largo peregrinar para arrojar sus cenizas en el pico más alto de los nueve reinos.
"God of War sigue a Kratos y a su hijo Atreus mientras emprenden un viaje para esparcir las cenizas de Faye, esposa de uno y madre del otro. A lo largo de sus aventuras, Kratos intenta enseñar a su hijo a ser un mejor dios, mientras que Atreus trata de enseñarle a su padre cómo ser un mejor ser humano", indica la sinopsis oficial de la serie de Prime Video.
Deborah Ann Woll será Faye en la serie de God of War
Respecto del personaje de Faye en la serie, Amazon indica lo siguiente: "El repentino fallecimiento de Faye, la misteriosa difunta esposa de Kratos y madre de Atreus, pone en marcha los acontecimientos de God of War. A lo largo de su viaje, Kratos y Atreus descubren secretos sobre Faye que les llevan a preguntarse hasta qué punto la conocían realmente".
El personaje de Faye aparecerá por primera vez en un rol protagónico en God of War Laufey, que se lanzará en PS5 el 20 de mayo del próximo año. Según se pudo ver en el primer gameplay del juego, la esposa de Kratos y madre de Atreus despierta en el Everywhen, la otra vida de los dioses, tras su fallecimiento. A partir de allí, debe combatir contra dioses y otras criaturas mitológicas en un escenario con peligros permanentes.
Deborah Ann Woll se suma a un elenco de God of War con varios nombres importantes. Recordemos que el rol de Kratos ha quedado en manos de Dave Bautista, quien reemplazó a Ryan Hurst tras una grave lesión. El papel de Atreus está en manos de Callum Vinson, mientras que otros nombres confirmados son Mandy Patinkin (Odín), Ed Skrein (Baldur), Max Parker (Heimdall), Ólafur Darri Ólafsson (Thor) y Teresa Palmer (Sif), por citar solo algunos.
La serie live-action de God of War todavía no tiene fecha de estreno en Prime Video. No obstante, su showrunner ha confirmado que tendrá al menos dos temporadas en la plataforma de streaming.

articles.title: South African township delivery startup Gobuddy gets $121k working capital facility
articles.text:
South African logistics startup Gobuddy has secured a ZAR2 million (US$121,000) working capital facility from Anglo American’s Impact Finance Network (IFN) to scale its township delivery model.
Founded by Leon Strumpher during the COVID-19 pandemic, Gobuddy tackles the last-mile e-commerce gap in South Africa’s townships. Traditional couriers often avoid them because of safety risks, long distances and high costs.
The startup first matched parcels with people’s existing commutes, but its data showed that women made up 60 per cent of registered transporters and were less likely than men to own a vehicle, which limited how much they could earn. Gobuddy responded by building a network of community micro-hubs. Couriers drop parcels at local collection points, and vetted residents then deliver them on foot within their own neighbourhoods.
“You don’t need a vehicle. You can walk,” Strumpher said.
Gobuddy now runs 50 micro-hubs in areas such as Soweto, Thembisa, Umlazi, Chatsworth and Motherwell, which together have an estimated 12 million residents. Transporters are recruited and verified through the SA Youth platform, and deliveries are monitored with a tracking system the company spent three years building. Each drop pays around ZAR50 (US$3).
Gobuddy joined IFN in 2024 and received business coaching and investor-readiness support. The new revolving facility will cover the gap between the startup’s weekly payments to transporters and the weeks or months its delivery partners take to pay.
“This facility gives us the working capital to meet our commitments to transporters on time, while allowing us to take on more delivery contracts and grow the business,” said Strumpher.
Gobuddy plans to bring more courier and retail partners onto its platform. It aims to create delivery jobs for 5,000 women over the next three years.

articles.title: Google Maps cache un mode « Haute visibilité » : voici à quoi il ressemble
articles.text:
Repéré dans la version 26.48.00.1027729593 de Google Maps pour Android, ce mode « Haute visibilité » que l’on retrouve dans les paramètres de l’application n’a pas encore été officialisé par le géant de Mountain View. Actuellement, il est possible de basculer entre le thème clair et le thème sombre, mais Google testerait une option pour améliorer la visibilité pendant la conduite, sans pour autant modifier l’emplacement des boutons ni l’ergonomie générale.
Du violet et du gris pour un affichage plus lisible
En mode clair, cette nouvelle interface de Google Maps abandonne les teintes habituelles pour privilégier des nuances beaucoup plus sobres. Les zones de végétation, d’ordinaire d’un vert éclatant, adoptent un vert plus sombre et plus mat. De leur côté, les zones blanches et beiges de la carte cèdent leur place à différents dégradés de gris. Enfin, le traditionnel repère bleu de positionnement devient violet.
Les changements sont encore plus marqués sur le mode sombre. Au lieu de l’arrière-plan bleuâtre classique, la carte affiche des teintes très foncées, proches du noir. Le tracé du trajet à suivre n’est plus une ligne bleue, mais une ligne violette bordée d’une couleur lavande claire. L’objectif est évidemment d’offrir un contraste important avec le reste du décor.
Le reste de l’interface et la disponibilité du mode « Haute visibilité »
Imaginé pour offrir un meilleur contraste pendant la navigation, ce style graphique garde intactes toutes les commandes d’itinéraire. Les noms de rues, les panneaux de direction et les indicateurs de changement de direction restent parfaitement identifiables. Ces couleurs ne sont pas sans rappeler des teintes similaires aperçues sur Android Auto en septembre dernier.
Découvrez : Comment transformer gratuitement un smartphone ou une tablette Android en écran CarPlay ou Android Auto ?
Les images que vous voyez ci-dessus viennent de l’analyse d’un fichier APK à partir duquel l’option a pu être activée. Cela ne garantit pas pour autant que Google déploiera la fonctionnalité dans un futur proche, même si l’on peut l’espérer. En attendant, n’hésitez pas à nous dire ce que vous pensez de ce nouvel affichage qui, avec son contraste plus important pourrait plaire à certains conducteurs.
