articles.title: Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers
articles.text:
The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.
“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”
It’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.
That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.
“Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he said. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”
Both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.
G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that company, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter said.
The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.
“The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter said. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”
In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a new generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio company Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.
Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter said they should start thinking about them now.
“It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he said.

articles.title: Tidal announces ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted
articles.text:
Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists.
Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn’t enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.
As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it’s only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.
Some people don’t particularly mind AI music, but the team at Tidal has come to believe the harm to artists is too great. AI models can pump out random noises faster than humans can create things of real value, which can mislead listeners and siphon royalty payments away from creators. There’s also an issue with AI uploaders who are actively attempting to steal royalty payments. Tidal says it has already removed about 66,000 tracks from its service for impersonating artists, which was against its AI policy even before this update.

articles.title: The Best CPUs - Late 2026 Update
articles.text:
If you're building a new PC or considering a platform upgrade, choosing the right CPU in late 2026 presents an unusual dilemma. There are plenty of good processors covering a wide range of prices, and some holiday deals, particularly on Intel CPUs, are outstanding. But with DDR5 memory prices through the roof and new processors from both Intel and AMD on the horizon, this might not be the best time to invest in an entirely new platform.
In fact, if you can afford to wait, that's exactly what we'd recommend. Intel's next-generation Nova Lake processors are expected in early 2027, potentially within the first quarter, with AMD's Zen 6 series likely following a little later. Faster CPUs are just around the corner, and their arrival should put downward pressure on pricing for existing hardware.
Of course, not everyone can wait. If you need a new PC today, there are some excellent deals worth considering, including a few that challenge our usual advice about avoiding dead-end platforms.
Intel's Core Ultra 5 250K Plus and Core Ultra 7 270K Plus are particularly attractive right now, with some frankly insane discounts. Amazon has been among those offering the most aggressive deals, though it's hard to say how long those will last. Availability and pricing vary considerably by region, however. In Australia, for example, the 250K Plus is still around $300 AUD, though that's considerably less than the Ryzen 7 9700X, which costs $385 AUD even after Amazon's discount.
As we've noted repeatedly, we normally wouldn't recommend investing in Intel's LGA1851 platform, given its limited upgrade path. But at current prices, you're effectively getting the motherboard for free compared to competing AMD configurations. The other major consideration is memory pricing. DDR5 has become painfully expensive, making older DDR4 platforms attractive again, especially for anyone who already owns a decent memory kit.
The AI bubble also looks like it might be losing some air, it's impossible to predict what will happen, but NAND flash prices have been dropping lately, falling by around 20% in recent weeks.
With all that in mind, we've updated our CPU recommendations to reflect current pricing and the unusual state of the market. We'll start with the best affordable DDR4 options, move on to DDR5, and then look at the processors offering the most performance for your money.
Best Entry-Level Platform Upgrade (DDR4)
Ryzen 7 5700X or Core i5-14400F
Let's start with the cheapest worthwhile hardware options available right now. The premise for this category is simple: you need a new PC or a complete platform upgrade, but don't want to pay current DDR5 prices, perhaps because you already own a decent DDR4 kit.
As it stands, a basic 16GB DDR5 memory kit costs roughly twice as much as DDR4, at around $260 versus $130. For budget builders who can get away with 16GB of memory, DDR4 is considerably more attractive, even if it means investing in older platforms such as AM4 or LGA1700.
So what are the options? As usual, availability and pricing will depend on your region, especially since many of these processors are quite old now.
Starting with AMD, the cheapest AM4 processor worth considering is the Ryzen 5 5600 or 5600X, whichever is cheaper or more readily available. The Ryzen 5 5500 has been a popular choice at $90. While its name suggests it's simply a slightly downclocked 5600, it's actually a much worse processor, featuring an entirely different design with just half the L3 cache. As a result, it performs more like a Ryzen 5 3600 than a 5600, making it difficult to justify the $45 saving over the 5600X.
Beyond the 5600 models, there's the Ryzen 7 5700X, currently on sale for $160, just $25 more than the 5600. Frankly, it's well worth coughing up the extra cash if you can. The 5700X packs two additional cores and is generally a little faster for gaming, while offering a much more substantial improvement in productivity performance. We should also point out that there's a Ryzen 7 5700 (non-X), which you should avoid like the plague. Essentially, it's an 8-core version of the Ryzen 5 5500, meaning it features a cut-down 16MB L3 cache rather than the 32MB found in the 5700X and 5800X.
Turning to Intel, your DDR4 options are limited to the LGA1700 platform, which supports 12th-, 13th-, and 14th-generation Core processors. Again, availability and pricing will vary considerably.
In the US, the Core i3-14100F costs around $105, but it's only a quad-core processor, so we'd avoid it. That leaves the Core i5-14400F at $155 as Intel's best budget DDR4 option. It packs six P-cores, four E-cores, and 20MB of L3 cache. The 14400F is slightly faster than the Ryzen 5 5600 for gaming while offering superior productivity performance, largely thanks to those additional E-cores. It currently costs about 15% more, but the extra performance helps offset the price increase.
Beyond that, you're looking at spending over $200 on something like the Core i5-14600KF at $230 or the Core i7-12700KF at $285, which is well beyond entry-level territory.
So which DDR4-compatible CPU should you buy for under $200? Your main options are the Ryzen 5 5600 at $135, the Core i5-14400F at $155, and the Ryzen 7 5700X at $160.
We think the 5700X is a better buy than the 5600 at those prices, so it really comes down to the 5700X versus the 14400F. There's no wrong choice here. They're quite similar in performance, especially for gaming, so the decision will largely depend on pricing and availability in your region.
Best Gaming Platform Upgrade (DDR4)
Intel Core i5-14600KF
What if you want to build the fastest gaming PC you can while still using DDR4 memory, either because you don't want to pay today's DDR5 prices or because you already own a good DDR4 kit?
Right now, the most viable options include the Intel Core i5-14600KF at $230, the Core i7-12700KF at $285, and the Ryzen 7 5800X3D at $320. In a normal market, the 14600KF at $230 wouldn't be particularly appealing. You'd be better off investing in AMD's AM5 platform or buying something even cheaper and slightly faster, such as the Core Ultra 5 250K Plus.
Sadly, we're not in a normal market, and those alternatives all require DDR5 memory. For anyone specifically looking for a DDR4 solution, the 14600KF is therefore extremely attractive and easily our top recommendation.
Overall gaming performance is very similar to the 5800X3D, but at almost a 30% discount, the Core i5 represents considerably better value. The 14600KF also outperforms the 12700KF, offering better single-core and multi-core performance, so there's little reason to spend another $55 on the older Core i7.
If you're after the best-performing processor that still supports DDR4 memory without breaking the bank, the 14600KF is the one to get. Obviously, the fastest LGA1700 processor is the Core i9-14900K, but even the KF variant starts at $430, and it's absolutely not worth paying almost twice as much as the Core i5-14600KF.
The 13th- and 14th-generation Core i7 and Core i9 processors have also been plagued by stability issues. While Intel has introduced fixes intended to address those problems, we can't say for certain that every affected processor is in the clear.
On that note, we strongly recommend avoiding second-hand 13th- or 14th-gen Core i7 and i9 processors. Many have suffered degradation that can lead to stability problems or poor performance, and there's no reliable way to know what you're getting.
Best Entry-Level Platform Upgrade (DDR5)
AMD Ryzen 5 7500F
Sadly, budget CPU options remain pretty miserable, especially if you want to move to AMD's or Intel's latest platform. On Intel's side, the Core Ultra 5 225F is its cheapest current-generation offering, and at $160, it's pretty horrible. Despite packing six P-cores and four E-cores, it only delivers multi-core performance comparable to the Ryzen 5 7500F while being considerably slower for gaming.
Several factors hurt the 225F's performance. One is its 4.9GHz boost clock, but the bigger issue is the measly 20MB L3 cache, the smallest cache capacity of any Core Ultra 200 series processor. That's a significant problem given that these CPUs aren't particularly impressive for gaming to begin with. Even if the 225F were considerably more competitive, you'd still have the problem of buying into a dead platform.
The LGA1851 socket won't support any future CPU architectures, making it effectively a dead end. Intel's upcoming Nova Lake-S desktop processors will use the new LGA1954 socket, which is incompatible with LGA1851.
So if you're building a new PC or performing a complete platform upgrade with DDR5 memory, it's difficult to justify investing in a platform with no future CPU upgrade path. That really leaves AMD's AM5 platform as the only viable option for budget builders right now.
This is why we continue to recommend the Ryzen 5 7500F for budget gamers, though the older Core i5 processors are potentially better investments for productivity workloads. For gaming, however, the 7500F is only slightly slower than those older Core i5 models, making it an excellent value choice, particularly given AM5's much stronger upgrade path.
The main downside is availability, as the 7500F isn't officially sold in every region. In the US, it's not generally available through local retailers, but you can order it from AliExpress for around $120. Alternatively, the Ryzen 5 7600X costs $185 at most retailers, although AMD's store on Amazon currently has it for just $165, making it a reasonable alternative to the imported 7500F.
Best CPU for ~$200
Intel Core Ultra 5 250K Plus
If we ignore future platform upgrades and simply focus on getting the most CPU performance for your money, there's one standout option that's become irresistibly cheap. Whether you're gaming, working, or doing just about anything else, the Core Ultra 5 250K Plus is the CPU to get right now.
Retailers such as Newegg have the 250K Plus for around $170, but Amazon is currently offering it for just $140 to eligible Amazon Visa cardholders, thanks to a $60 discount on its $200 list price. At that price, it's an absolute steal.
The 250K Plus packs six P-cores clocked up to 5.3GHz with a shared 30MB L3 cache, along with 12 E-cores. It also features a 43% increase in die-to-die frequency, jumping from 2.1GHz to 3GHz. This improvement addresses many of the latency issues found in the original Arrow Lake processors, leading to substantially better gaming performance.
AMD is currently floundering at this price point. While the Ryzen 7 9700X might deliver similar gaming performance, the 250K Plus is up to 50% faster in core-heavy productivity workloads.
To get comparable gaming and productivity performance from AMD, you'd need to spend at least $300 on the Ryzen 9 7900X, though that processor can be a bit sketchy for gaming at times. Ideally, you'd want the Ryzen 9 9900X, but that processor costs around $330, making it more than twice as expensive as the 250K Plus at Amazon's promotional price.
That means you can currently buy the 250K Plus along with a quality Z890 motherboard for roughly the same price as the Ryzen 9 9900X alone, making Intel's dead-platform issue a complete non-issue from a financial perspective. So while we normally wouldn't recommend investing in Intel's dead-end LGA1851 socket, especially with Nova Lake and its new socket expected in early 2027, the 250K Plus is cheap enough that the deal makes sense.
Frankly, at these prices, it's much better value than anything AMD has on offer right now.
Best Value Productivity CPU
Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus
If you have more than $200 to spend, the good news is that you don't actually need to spend much more than that on a CPU right now. In fact, Amazon is currently selling Intel's Core Ultra 7 270K Plus for just $221, which is complete madness.
The 270K Plus is a one-stop shop for just about any workload. Whether you're gaming or tackling demanding productivity tasks, if you want a CPU that handles everything with a high degree of efficiency, this is the one to get.
This model packs eight P-cores clocked at up to 5.5GHz, along with 16 E-cores that can reach 4.7GHz. There's also 36MB of L3 cache, and Intel has specified a maximum turbo power rating of 250 watts.
In multi-threaded, core-heavy productivity workloads, it performs within 2 – 5% of the AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, a processor that often retails for twice the price. That makes the 270K Plus, by far, one of the most cost-effective ways to get high-end workstation-class performance on a mainstream desktop.
Not only that, but unlike the original Core Ultra 7 265K, the Plus version addresses internal latency issues, greatly improving gaming performance to the point where it's no longer embarrassing.
Of course, AMD's X3D processors still hold the crown for pure gaming performance, but we think the 270K Plus is now close enough that the price savings make it more attractive for most people, especially if you're looking for strong performance across a variety of workloads.
The fact that you're getting productivity performance approaching that of the 9950X, along with very capable gaming performance, at a fraction of the price makes concerns about future platform support largely irrelevant. As with the 250K Plus, you're effectively getting the motherboard for free.
The cheapest Ryzen 9 9950X we could find at the time of writing was $490. Meanwhile, shoppers can get the 270K Plus at Amazon for just $221, along with a really nice $200 Z890 motherboard, for less than the price of the Ryzen 9 alone.
Once again, the motherboard is effectively free, and at that point, the lack of a future upgrade path becomes much less of a concern. For anyone who needs serious productivity performance without spending a fortune, it's an incredibly compelling deal.
Best Gaming CPU
AMD Ryzen 7 9850X3D or Ryzen 7 7700X3D
There's no debating which company makes the fastest gaming CPUs. AMD continues to dominate with its X3D processors, and the Ryzen 7 9850X3D remains the fastest gaming CPU money can buy.
What's changed in the last few months is pricing, and right now the 9850X3D is a much more attractive option. Amazon has discounted the 9850X3D to just $399, matching the price of the 9800X3D. Given that the 9850X3D is ~5% faster on average, there's really no reason to buy the 9800X3D at the same price.
Of course, that 4-5% improvement isn't exactly exciting, and as we found in our original review, the additional performance comes at the cost of substantially higher power consumption. Still, both processors are relatively efficient compared to Intel's previous flagships, and at identical prices, we'd take the extra performance.
The 9850X3D is also around 15% faster than the Ryzen 7 7800X3D in our CPU-limited gaming benchmarks, and a massive 40% faster than Intel's Core Ultra 9 285K. AMD's lead is particularly impressive in titles such as Baldur's Gate 3, Cyberpunk 2077, and Assetto Corsa Competizione, where the additional L3 cache makes a significant difference.
But do you really need to spend $400 on a gaming CPU? Absolutely not.
The older Ryzen 7 7800X3D remains an option at around $339. It's roughly 15% slower than the 9850X3D, but costs 15% less, making it a reasonable alternative. There's also the newer Ryzen 7 7700X3D, which launched in July at $329 and is currently available for $299. This is essentially a slightly downclocked 7800X3D, and in our 13-game benchmark we found it was just 7% slower on average, while trailing the 9800X3D by 15%.
At these prices, the 7700X3D is arguably the best-value X3D processor for gamers. It delivers excellent gaming performance, and you're saving $100 compared to the 9850X3D. All of these processors use AMD's AM5 platform, so you're also getting a much better upgrade path than Intel's current LGA1851 offerings.
One important consideration is that all these CPUs require DDR5 memory, which has become painfully expensive. The good news is that AMD's X3D processors aren't particularly sensitive to memory speed. In our testing, the 9850X3D lost very little performance when switching from DDR5-6000 CL30 to slower DDR5-4800 CL40 memory, making cheaper DDR5 kits a viable option.
For most gamers, our Core Ultra 7 270K Plus recommendation will be more than sufficient, especially considering its outstanding productivity performance and current pricing. But if gaming is your priority, AMD's X3D processors remain the top choice.

articles.title: Resumo do OD: bomba nuclear espacial; desculpas de Huang; guerra do delivery
articles.text:
O CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, pediu desculpas aos funcionários da empresa nesta terça-feira (24), durante sua primeira reunião geral desde que foi reconduzido ao cargo. O executivo reconheceu que violou o código de conduta da companhia, admitiu ter cometido erros pessoais e afirmou que está fazendo terapia. A reunião também foi marcada por declarações sobre seu retorno à liderança, a influência do governo de Donald Trump e a estrutura de comando da fabricante de chips.
Sucesso bilionário de GTA 6 esconde lado cruel da indústria dos games
O lançamento do Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) é um dos acontecimentos mais esperados da história dos videogames. Depois de mais de uma década de desenvolvimento, a expectativa é que o novo título da Rockstar Games movimente bilhões. Mas, por trás dessa produção de cifras astronômicas, existe uma realidade que contrasta com tanto sucesso: os profissionais que criam esses jogos enfrentam demissões, jornadas excessivas e insegurança no emprego.
Bomba nuclear russa no espaço pode deixar a Terra sem internet?
O secretário-geral da Otan, Mark Rutte, afirmou nesta terça-feira (24) que a aliança militar está preparada para se defender contra quaisquer ameaças no espaço. A declaração é uma resposta a uma investigação realizada pela imprensa da Alemanha com base em informações de serviços de inteligência ocidentais e que aponta que a Rússia estaria preparando o lançamento de uma bomba nuclear ao espaço ainda neste ano.
Mas o que aconteceria em caso de detonação em órbita? Este é o tema da coluna Fala AI, com Roberto Pena Spinelli, físico pela USP, com especialidade em Machine Learning por Stanford e pesquisador na área de Inteligência Artificial. 
Confira!
Correndo contra o relógio: como alertas e bônus dos apps pressionam entregadores nas ruas
Para quem trabalha com aplicativos de delivery, poucos minutos fazem uma grande diferença no rendimento ao longo do dia. Um atraso na retirada de um pedido pode significar perder uma corrida, deixar de ganhar um bônus ou, em alguns casos, até receber notificações cobrando rapidez. A pressão pelo cumprimento dos prazos, no entanto, levanta preocupações sobre a segurança dos entregadores no trânsito.
Saiba mais.
Hackers usam cada vez mais IA – e acordo bilionário tenta frear isso
Ciberataques sofisticados impulsionados por inteligência artificial (IA) estão cada vez mais comuns. Isso tem feito empresas reduzirem fornecedores de segurança cibernética na expectativa de reduzir margem para exploração de brechas. Com essa mudança de comportamento no radar, a CrowdStrike anunciou, nesta semana, a aquisição da Zscaler.
Falha em radar suspende voos para um dos aeroportos mais movimentados dos EUA
Uma falha em equipamentos de controle de tráfego aéreo levou os Estados Unidos a suspender temporariamente parte dos voos com destino ao Aeroporto Internacional O’Hare, em Chicago, nesta terça-feira (24). O problema atingiu um sistema de radar e rastreamento utilizado para monitorar aeronaves e veículos nas pistas do aeroporto.
Saiba mais.
Bruno Capozzi é jornalista, mestre em Ciências Sociais e editor executivo do OD.

articles.title: US financial crimes bureau discloses ‘cybersecurity incident’
articles.text:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it’s investigating a “cybersecurity incident.” The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it’s looking into an “incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It hasn’t offered any information about the full scope or source of the breach, but FinCEN has taken some systems offline as a precaution.
US financial crimes bureau discloses ‘cybersecurity incident’
FinCEN’s alert comes in the wake of a reported breach of unclassified information at US spy agencies, including the CIA.
The news comes hours after The New York Times reported that the Central Intelligence Agency and Office of the Director of National Security discovered a breach of an open source intelligence system, exposing unclassified information. The Department of Defense, whose National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was also reportedly impacted by the breach, declined to comment. The CIA and ODNI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s unclear if the FinCEN breach is related. Americans have been on high alert about security incidents after a series of seemingly unrelated outages earlier this month.
Americans have been on high alert about security incidents
FinCEN’s role is to protect the financial system from illegal activity, including by combatting money laundering and terrorism financing. The bureau maintains financial transaction data and distributes it for law enforcement purposes. FinCEN also houses reports of suspicious activity that financial institutions file as part of the Bank Secrecy Act.
FinCEN says in its alert that banks can still file reports about suspicious activity online, but some services may not be immediately available. Filers that need to expedite their reports in the meantime can still call the Financial Institutions Hotline, which it says was not impacted by the disruption.
Update, November 24th: Added response from Department of Defense.

articles.title: An Unclassified CIA System Was Breached in a Cyberattack, AP Source Says
articles.text:
An unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack, according to a person familiar with the incident who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity.
The breach did not involve any classified information and the issue has been resolved, said the person, who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The breach affected a system that handles open source intelligence, which involves the collection and analysis of publicly available data from sources including the internet, commercial satellites and private data brokers. Though the information is generally public or semi-public, open-source information can give intelligence analysts significant insight on its own or in combination with intelligence obtained from classified spying programs.
It was not clear what specific information was compromised or who was responsible.
The breach was first reported by The New York Times on Tuesday.
The incident comes to light following a series of highly disruptive system failures that unnerved many Americans. An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline for a time last week, and the FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains.
Those incidents followed a nationwide ground stop that snarled air travel after air traffic controllers struggled to communicate with pilots. Apple, JP Morgan Chase and Microsoft also had systems go down this month.
The incidents have put a spotlight on the vulnerabilities inside critical infrastructure, banking systems and the digital tools that millions of people use daily.
President Donald Trump’s administration says the series of outages is not part of a coordinated cyberattack and dispatched Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to calm Americans in appearances on Sunday morning news shows.
Clayton said the outages largely stem from the rush to patch and upgrade systems to stay ahead of hackers who are now empowered with sophisticated artificial intelligence tools to attack at an unprecedented scale.
Related: FBI Investigating Apparent Hack of Its Key National Criminal Justice Database, AP Source Says

articles.title: Why an international advocacy group is bringing its fight for safer social media to Canada
articles.text:
A UK-based digital advocacy group that has had high-profile spats with the likes of X and the US government is taking on Canada’s proposed Safe Social Media Act—arguing it doesn’t go far enough.
The news: The Center for Countering Digital Harm (CCDH), which recently rebranded from the Center for Countering Digital Hate, opened an Ottawa office in September. The organization currently has one Ottawa staffer working remotely, supported by research, comms, and advocacy teams in the US, EU, and UK.
CCDH is currently focused on Bill C-34, which the organization views as an opportunity to strengthen platform accountability and improve protections. It also plans to monitor policies and legislation that touch on issues like deepfakes, tech-facilitated gender-based violence, online fraud, election integrity, and consumer protection.
From the source: “Canada has an opportunity to lead the world in building a safer, more accountable digital ecosystem,” Nicole Fournier-Sylvester, Canada senior manager at CCDH, told BetaKit in an emailed statement. “As concerns about online harms, AI, and platform accountability grow, Canadians are looking for practical, evidence-based solutions.” She added that CCDH wants to bring “independent research and real-world evidence” to that conversation.
The context: CCDH’s Canadian expansion was first reported by the Globe and Mail. It’s being funded by the Ronald S. Roadburg Foundation, a private foundation established through the estate of the late Vancouver philanthropist and real estate mogul. The organization’s latest report found that safeguards in ChatGPT for teens are easily bypassed, giving users harmful responses about eating disorders, suicide, and substance abuse.
Final thought: CCDH was sued by X and accused of running a scare campaign in 2023 after CCDH used data scraping to report on disinformation spreading on the platform; the suit was dismissed. CCDH’s CEO was also denied a US visa last year, as US officials called the organization “radical” activists who aimed to censor US big tech companies.
Its focus in Canada, Bill C-34, is currently under review by a House committee. The bill aims to create a new digital super regulator and restrict social media accounts for youth under age 16 unless platforms establish safeguards. Open Media, a Canadian non-profit digital advocacy org, said on Tuesday in a post to its website that if done right, the bill “can be a win for both fundamental freedoms and common-sense regulation,” but “done wrong, it could become a blueprint for censorship and privacy violations dressed up as safety.”

articles.title: London-based Bound secures €45.68 million debt facility for its AI-powered FX risk management platform
articles.text:
Bound, a London-based AI-powered foreign exchange risk management platform for mid-market companies, has secured a €45.68 million ($50 million) three-year revolving debt facility.
The debt facility comes from Viola Credit, a global alternative credit manager specialising in funding Europe’s high-growth technology companies. It is structured as a warehouse facility, allowing the company to expand its trading book and offer clients more flexible credit terms and broader trading lines.
“We’re excited to partner with the Bound team through this $50 million warehouse facility. Our investment reflects our confidence in the business, its technology and the team’s vision of how businesses can optimise foreign exchange risk management. We look forward to supporting Bound as it continues to scale its platform,” said Conor Sheehy, Head of Asset Backed Lending, Europe, Viola Credit.
Founded in 2020 by Seth Phillips and Dan Kindler, Bound was built to address the persistent frustrations faced by finance teams when working with traditional FX brokers: opaque pricing, manual workflows, and rigid processes. The platform automates the execution of FX trades and monitors currency markets around the clock for emerging risks, enabling treasury and finance teams to manage hedging strategies without the need for dedicated FX specialists.
Bound says it currently serves over 200 businesses, handles more than 36 currencies, and integrates with accounting software such as Xero to automatically calculate FX exposure in real time. The company is FCA-regulated and ISO 27001 certified. Bound’s growth has been striking, with the company reporting transaction volumes of approximately €1.37 billion ($1.5 billion) in 2025, and the company is on track to surpass $6 billion in 2026.
“This facility bolsters our balance sheet so that we can support a larger trading book, and also offer better trading terms and protection for our customers. Bound has been growing rapidly in recent months and we’re excited to have the additional capital so we can expand further,” said Marita Cavalcanti, Chief Financial Officer of Bound.
The facility comes on top of Bound’s €20.7 million ($24.5 million) Series A equity round led by AlbionVC in February. The fresh capital will be deployed to extend Bound’s trading book and broaden access to its platform for mid-sized corporates and funds.
The company is targeting businesses processing between $10 million and $100 million in annual FX transactions. These businesses generally lack dedicated FX teams, making Bound’s automated, self-service model a compelling alternative to traditional broker-driven approaches.
“We’re really excited about this credit line as it fuels our ambitions and gives us the headroom to expand and onboard more customers. As market volatility and geopolitical instability becomes the norm, FX risk management cannot be left to chance, or spreadsheets. The old ways of booking trades over the phone with a broker, and leaving the positions unmonitored, won’t cut it if businesses want to protect themselves from market movements. Emerging risks need to be continually monitored, in real-time, 24/7,” said Phillips, co-founder and CEO of Bound.
In addition to expanding its trading book, the company is also looking at global expansion. It has already submitted a regulatory application to enter European markets, with plans to expand its platform to Asia and North America, while continuing to invest in its product capabilities.

articles.title: We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
articles.text:
We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in The Free Press entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?”
Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.
Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly.
There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream of the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problem lies.
Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, recoverability—these are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs.
More importantly, they are inefficient: costs that feel wasteful until something bad happens. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, squeeze all inefficiencies out of a company in pursuit of near-term profits. Competition, with multiple companies competing to do the same thing, is another inefficiency. Monopolization removes that in pursuit of near-term profits.
The result is brittle systems, single points of failure. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.
Fixing this is technical, but it’s political first. It requires changing incentives, and that involves regulation and control. “What to do” is easy; finding the political will to stand up to moneyed interests and do it is hard.
Untitled • November 24, 2026 7:49 AM
Your opening sentence cited Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA. Two of those five (FAA and NSA) are government-funded, not unregulated capitalism.
Politicians have different incentives than private corporations, but the outcome is much the same: maintenance is neglected in favour of eye-catching, glossy new initiatives.

articles.title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
articles.text:
Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom.
One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.
xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.
As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.
It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.
Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.
When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.
Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.
“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.
Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.
Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.
The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)
Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.
Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.
BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.
And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.
There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.
Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.
While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.
“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

articles.title: Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real
articles.text:
It wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.
That’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that’s usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.
So, for the company’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance.
Mid-engined? Mid-batteried.
That EV battery layout, stacked behind the two-seat cabin rather than sandwiched below it, isn’t novel. It’s the same setup that Tesla used on the original Roadster back in 2008. Back then it was done for cost reasons as much as anything, enabling Tesla to repurpose a Lotus chassis meant to hold an internal combustion engine in the middle.
For Porsche’s new Boxster (and the Audi Concept C, which is built on the same platform), that pack enables the low seating position and also delivers a rearward weight bias (40:60 front/rear) that’s in keeping with the last-generation 718 Boxster, the internal combustion model killed by EU cybersecurity regulations last year.

articles.title: Hope Is Not A Strategy: What First-Silicon Success Really Takes
articles.text:
Most re-spins are caused by logic and functional flaws, not hard-to-predict physical effects.
Only about one chip in twenty now works the first time it comes back from the fab. For an industry that invests years and millions in every tape-out, that is a disconcerting thought.
It was also the starting point for a recent episode of ‘Wearing Flip Flops’, where host Ronen sat down with Axiomise CEO Ashish Darbari. The conversation traveled from AI silicon and power bugs to the place of formal engineers in a verification team. But one idea ran through all of it: Hope is not a strategy. Determinism is.
Here is what that idea means in practice and why we believe it matters more today than ever.
The latest Wilson Research Group functional verification study puts first-silicon success at around 5%, down from 14% in 2024. At Axiomise, that number doesn’t surprise us.
Look at who is building chips. Two years ago, the survey was shaped by a wave of new RISC-V teams, where design was moving faster than verification could follow. Today it is the turn of custom AI silicon, built not only for hyperscalers but for phones and cars too. For verification, this is an unknown territory.
Formal is in more projects than ever, perhaps 30 to 40% of them. But “using formal” can mean very different things. It might be a lint or connectivity app, assertions that only ever run in simulation, or formal trusted to sign off functional verification. Only the last really improves the chances of success at tape-out.
By our estimate, fewer than a dozen of the world’s 200-plus silicon houses use formal as a sign-off criterion today. The appetite is growing fast: at DVCon US this year, NVIDIA’s VP of graphics predicted that formal will eventually replace simulation. Yet the journey has barely begun.
That 5% is the latest point in a long slide. For years, roughly three projects in ten got silicon right first time. The figure fell to 24% in 2022 and to 14% in 2024, which Harry Foster of Siemens EDA called the lowest point in more than twenty years of tracking. In 2026 it reached 5%, while around three in four projects are still missing their original schedules.
Every one of those failures means a re-spin: fixing the design and manufacturing the chip again. At 3nm, a mask set alone costs tens of millions of dollars, and a single re-spin at an advanced node can wipe out an entire product cycle. Half of all projects need more than one re-spin, and some large chipmakers now plan for as many as four.
The data also shows where the trouble starts. Logic and functional flaws remain the most common reason chips fail and around 70% of re-spins trace back to design errors caused by changing specifications. In other words, most re-spins are not caused by hard-to-predict physical effects. They are functional bugs that verification should have caught and that exhaustive methods such as formal are designed to find.
Back in the days of the 386 and the Pentium, life was simpler. A processor was built to run a known version of Windows, and everyone understood the scope of the job. Today, an AI chip must run models from OpenAI, Anthropic and many others, and those models change far faster than any hardware schedule.
The hardware has changed too. Many AI chips grew out of GPUs, which were originally designed for graphics, so older graphics hardware now sits alongside new AI-specific units. To squeeze out more speed, designers add layer upon layer of coherency, the mechanisms that keep every part of the chip working with the same up-to-date data: one coherent NoC, then another, then coherency across whole clusters. Every layer creates interactions that never existed before, and many are never reached in simulation.
Power adds its own surprises. One story from the episode stays with us: a GPU on a test chip that refused to start. The failure showed up at system, FPGA and OS level, but the root cause was an X value read from an uninitialized FIFO, left behind by a low-power optimization. A tiny functional bug had brought down the whole chip.
Clock gating tells a similar tale. On paper, proving that a gated design behaves exactly like its ungated twin is a well-defined problem, and one that formal sequential equivalence checking is built to solve. In practice, the constraints come from firmware and software, and on large designs they are hard to capture. So, clock-gating checks tend to land at the very end of sign-off, just when there is least time to deal with what they find. The answer is not a different tool, but bringing formal in earlier, with the firmware and software teams at the table.
The people behind the study are reaching a similar conclusion. Harry Foster argues that verification has succeeded for decades by splitting the problem into specialist domains and that the next challenge is interaction complexity: parts that work perfectly alone but fail together across hardware, firmware, power, safety and security.
At Axiomise, this is the problem we work on every day. Simulation samples behavior: it checks the scenarios someone thought to write. Interaction bugs live in the scenarios nobody thought of, such as an interrupt, a power transition and a coherency request arriving in just the wrong order. Formal starts from every possible input sequence and asks whether any of them can break the design. That is why we built our apps around the places where interactions hide: nocProve for networks-on-chip, formalISA for processors, floatrix for floating-point units and footprint for redundant logic.
None of this replaces simulation. It means using each method where it is strongest. Formal excels at concurrent, control-heavy logic such as NoCs, coherency, arbiters and FIFOs. Simulation and emulation remain essential for software, performance and end-to-end system behavior. Our role is to help teams combine them in the right measures, at the right time, for the right reason and to prove, with mutation and scenario coverage, that the formal part has truly done its job.
Formal has a measurement problem. With equivalence checking, the answer is clear: the proof converged, synthesis broke nothing, job done. Functional formal is less tidy. Some proofs are bounded rather than exhaustive, and any VP of silicon will reasonably ask: “If you haven’t got the proofs, what have you got?”
At Axiomise, we answer that question by measuring formal in six dimensions. Alongside the familiar counts of assertions written, passed and failed, and the coverage figures EDA tools already provide, two measures do the heavy lifting.
Mutation means planting bugs on purpose and showing that the checkers and constraints catch each one. If they don’t, you have found a gap before the silicon does.
Scenario coverage means proving that each scenario in the verification plan can happen and always happens. Instead of claiming “every RISC-V instruction works”, a team can show that debug was checked against interrupts, that loads and stores complete under every dependency, and that each result traces back to a requirement. We built this approach into formalISA, our RISC-V app, and it gives designers, verification engineers and managers something rare: a shared language.
Tying results to requirements matters more than ever. If around 70% of re-spins begin with a changing specification, verification that isn’t linked to requirements can quietly end up checking the wrong thing. With scenario coverage, a changed requirement points straight to the scenarios and proofs that need revisiting.
That matters, because today’s leaders receive formal numbers and simulation numbers that cannot easily be compared. Without a way to bring them together, the tape-out decision becomes “let’s try it and see.” And that is how you arrive at a 5% success rate.
The big three EDA vendors build excellent tools for linting, X-propagation, CDC and connectivity checking. These apps tend to sit at either end of a project. Axiomise works in the space between, using formal for full functional verification, safety and security.
Our apps run on the axiomiser platform and work together: nocProve for complete NoC grids, floatrix for floating-point units, formalISA for RISC-V processors and footprint for redundancy and power. Their strongest results come from designs that were already considered verified, where they still find bugs others missed.
A security core, and a fix that broke something else. cheriot-ibex, Microsoft’s CHERI-extended RISC-V core, had already been verified with both simulation and formal. Within days of integrating it with formalISA in 2024, a standard RTYPE check failed in JasperGold in 20 seconds. An illegal CHERI load was never squashed: it went out to memory and the data it brought back corrupted the AND instruction behind it, putting stores, and therefore memory, at risk too. The designers pointed us to a fix. On re-running, the load bug was gone, but bit-manipulation proofs that had previously passed now failed. A fix in one corner had opened a hole in another, exactly the kind of interaction that formal is built to catch.
A vector FPU in ninety minutes. On the Tenstorrent Ocelot core, floatrix was surfacing bugs within an hour and a half of cloning the repository, on a design that had already been extensively tested.
Late, but not too late. For Akeana, our team ran footprint before tape-out, covering unexpected scenarios. Redundancy is the bug nobody looks for. In one AI design, a control bug meant that each 512-deep FIFO in a chain only ever used a single location. Reachability analysis reported 99.998%, every flop toggled, and standard coverage saw nothing wrong. Yet the chip was burning area and power on storage it never touched. It is like renting an entire hotel for a single guest.
LLMs can now produce SystemVerilog assertions, constraints and even whole testbenches. That is a genuine productivity boost, and we use AI agents in-house at Axiomise. But walk the floor at DAC this year and one question came up again and again among experienced designers: how do we know we can trust it?
AI-generated checks still need auditing. Even when they produce proofs, someone has to confirm that every corner case was actually expressed. In inexperienced hands, AI can even slow a team down, because every line needs a human review.
This is where determinism earns its place. On every engagement, we build a full mutation coverage plan. Customers can plant bugs themselves without telling us, or hand us a plan to script into the environment, while we inject our own mutations independently to avoid shared blind spots. When every planted bug is caught, you have evidence rather than hope. Our rule is simple: if we can’t show that every bug that could be planted is caught, we won’t put our name to the result.
In many companies, “DV” still quietly means simulation, and formal engineers are called in late, as rescuers rather than partners. We would like to see a different picture: formal and simulation engineers sitting at the same table as architects, designers, and firmware and software teams, from the moment the specification is written.
For teams planning their next tape-out, that starts with a few practical shifts:
- Bring formal in at the planning stage, not only at the end.
- Agree what “formal” means on your project, from apps to full functional sign-off.
- Measure the quality of formal with mutation and scenario coverage, not proofs alone.
- Tie every result back to requirements, so formal and simulation can live in one plan.
- Treat AI-generated verification as a first draft and prove that it really catches bugs.
One chip in twenty is not a law of nature. It is the result of choices, and better ones are available. Hope is not a strategy. Determinism is.

articles.title: La A-63 de Asturias lleva casi tres décadas en obras: todavía quedan 12,5 km y un cuello de botella que no acaba
articles.text:
De los aproximadamente 49 kilómetros proyectados para la A-63 entre Oviedo y La Espina, unos 36,5 están abiertos al tráfico. Los 12,5 restantes siguen pendientes, y la fecha para ver finalizada por fin la autovía completa se sigue retrasando.
Por qué importa. La A-63 es la principal conexión por carretera entre Oviedo y el suroccidente de la región, y los colectivos locales sostienen que la supervivencia económica de la zona depende de ella. Y claro, con las elecciones acercándose y las autonómicas previstas para 2027, la autovía ha vuelto a la agenda política.
El estado. Tal y como comparten desde el medio La Nueva España, la autovía está totalmente operativa desde Oviedo hasta Cornellana, un tramo de unos 31 kilómetros abierto por fases entre 1999 y 2017. Otros cinco kilómetros entre Salas y el viaducto de El Regueirón están abiertos desde noviembre de 2022.
Todavía faltan los seis kilómetros entre Cornellana y Salas, la segunda calzada entre El Regueirón y La Espina, de algo menos de siete kilómetros, y la prolongación más allá de La Espina hacia Tineo, que aún ni siquiera ha llegado a la fase de proyecto, según afirma el medio.
El cuello de botella. Todo depende de Casazorrina, en el concejo de Salas, donde un gran deslizamiento de tierra en 2021 interrumpió la construcción del tramo Cornellana-Salas. La Nueva España informa de que más de cinco años y medio después el terreno sigue sin estar completamente estabilizado, y que las obras ya han absorbido más de 158 millones de euros.
La Radiotelevisión del Principado de Asturias (RTPA) señalaba en diciembre de 2025 que había maquinaria trabajando en el lugar, mientras que algunos viaductos del tramo ya estaban terminados. Aun así, el medio indicaba que nadie podía decir cuándo se abriría el tramo.
El último calendario. Según comparten desde La Nueva España, la información que circula ahora es que la zona de Casazorrina debería estar lista entre finales de este año y enero de 2027, y que el tramo Cornellana-Salas se abriría alrededor de mediados de 2027.
Según cuenta el medio, esa segunda fecha se ha pospuesto ya hasta unos seis meses después de que terminen las obras por el deslizamiento, mientras que desde la plataforma "El Suroccidente también es Asturias. Por unas carreteras seguras y modernas", aseguran que al principio les dijeron que seguiría inmediatamente.
Qué viene después de Salas. Una vez que Cornellana-Salas esté abierto, seguiría faltando la segunda calzada entre El Regueirón y La Espina. A partir de ese punto, tomaría el relevo el Gobierno regional. En marzo, se inició el proceso para un estudio informativo y de impacto ambiental para la primera calzada entre La Espina y Tineo. La Nueva España cuenta que se esperaba que la licitación tuviera un valor de 184.307 euros con un plazo de ejecución de nueve meses, y que el estudio daría a la administración una base técnica actualizada. El proyecto de presupuestos regionales de 2027, según la misma fuente, incluye dos partidas para el estudio, de 164.308 y 50.000 euros, que suman 214.308 euros.
José Luis Fernández Berguño, vicepresidente de la plataforma reivindicativa, le contaba al periódico que se decía que el proyecto estaba en marcha en 2025. Cree que sigue “en el punto cero” y que se ha perdido otro año.

articles.title: 12 startups named winners at 2026 South African Startup Awards
articles.text:
Twelve startups, including Community Wolf, WaFunda and VezoPay, have been named winners at the 2026 South African Startup Awards.
Run by Startup Club ZA and now in its fourth year, the South African Startup Awards held its awards ceremony at the Homecoming Centre in Cape Town’s District Six last week, attended by around 250 founders, investors and ecosystem players and livestreamed nationally.
This year’s awards drew 179 entries this year, with 51 finalists across 12 categories. Winners were chosen through a combination of 9,000 public votes cast over five days and scoring by a 24-strong judging panel that included the founders of iKhokha, Retail Capital, OrderIn and Payfast.
Community Wolf, which builds safety products that turn ground-level observations into usable intelligence, won the AI & Big Data category, while smart metering and energy trading startup Switch Energy took Climate & Sustainability. VezoPay, which makes battery-free payment wearables, won Consumertech, and AI-native energy management platform Tavas won Deeptech.
WhatsApp-based back-to-school concierge Zumii won Digital Commerce, learning resources provider Edufern took Edtech, and WaFunda – which helps graduates unlock qualifications withheld over unpaid fees through income share agreements – won Fintech.
Skills simulation platform LEVRA won Future of Work, clinical platform GreenNotes took Healthtech, and AskMandla, a WhatsApp service that helps households employ domestic workers legally, won the Informal Market category. CitiPods, which operates rest hubs for delivery riders and outdoor workers, won Mobility & Logistics, while mobile 3D mammography provider Radhiant Diagnostic Imaging was named People’s Choice.
“This year we saw a massive uptake in public participation, with public votes more than doubling, alongside a strong field of entries and real buy-in from key stakeholders across the country’s startup and venture capital ecosystem,” said Mathew Marsden, founder of Startup Club ZA.
The awards were presented in partnership with FNB, RMB, E Squared Investments, Canva Africa and the Western Cape Government, among others.

articles.title: Stealth Health launches direct-to-consumer clinic with MedExpress acquisition
articles.text:
A Canadian telehealth software provider is now spinning up its own online clinic.
The news: Toronto-based Stealth Health announced on Tuesday that it acquired the Canadian business of MedExpress from HeliosX, a United Kingdom-based digital healthcare company, in an all-cash deal. MedExpress is now operating as Mira Health, Stealth Health’s own online clinic that offers consultations and prescription treatment for weight management and sexual health. The purchase price was not disclosed.
Stealth Health said in a statement that the acquisition gives it an established Canadian patient business and a foundation to expand its own direct-to-consumer services, while HeliosX focuses on growing in the US and Europe.
From the source: Stealth Health co-founder and CEO Matthew Mazzuca said in a statement that his company’s goal is to become “the centre of longevity medicine in Canada and the United States.”
“We now have the technology, the clinical network and the pharmacy capability in one company, and we are going to keep building and acquiring until Stealth is the first place people on both sides of the border turn for their long-term health,” Mazzuca said.
The context: Stealth Health provides a white-label platform and pharmacy infrastructure to more than 200 third-party clinics and health brands in the US and Canada, Mazzuca told BetaKit in an email. The company said that acquiring an established patient business, MedExpress, brings those technology and operational offerings to a greater scale.
Stealth Health said it’s coordinating the handover of MedExpress with HeliosX, and that its patients will be transitioned to, and supported by, Mira Health following the acquisition. No employees are joining Stealth Health as part of the deal, Mazzuca said.
Final thought: Stealth Health is directly entering a market it supports with its own software as more telehealth providers specializing in weight loss and sexual health crop up in the Canadian market. Last year, similar platforms like Felix Health and Phoenix secured significant funding as weight loss drugs like Ozempic ballooned in popularity. After seven years of bootstrapping, Science&Humans, another telehealth platform, secured its first round of funding earlier this year as interest in its services heated up.

articles.title: Microsoft Teams va analyser vos appels avec une IA pour détecter les arnaques
articles.text:
Les numéros indésirables qui vous appellent quotidiennement sur votre smartphone pour tenter de vous arnaquer avec des voix générées par IA ne se cantonnent pas simplement au téléphone. Les escrocs utilisent tous les moyens possibles pour commettre leurs méfaits et se servent même parfois des outils de messagerie collaborative.
Si Microsoft a déjà renforcé la sécurité de Teams contre les cyberattaques, notamment en bloquant les fichiers suspects et liens piégés, l’entreprise compte désormais s’attaquer aux appels indésirables dans son application.
L’IA va analyser les conversations vocales pour bloquer les arnaques
Microsoft Teams va bientôt faire écouter vos appels à une IA pour vérifier que vous n’êtes pas en train de vous faire arnaquer. C’est en tout cas ce qu’indique la roadmap de la firme de Redmond qui indique l’arrivée d’une nouvelle fonction de détection de phishing vocal pour les appels externes dans Microsoft Teams.
« La détection du phishing vocal permet de protéger les utilisateurs de Microsoft Teams contre d’éventuelles escroqueries lors d’appels individuels avec des personnes extérieures à leur organisation. Grâce à l’IA, Teams analyse les conversations à la recherche de signes d’ingénierie sociale et alerte les destinataires lorsqu’une activité suspecte est détectée, les aidant ainsi à reconnaître les menaces potentielles et à décider comment procéder. » explique Microsoft sans donner plus de détails.
Car comme le relèvent nos confrères de Neowin, la question qui se pose désormais est de savoir comment l’analyse de ces appels va être réalisée par Microsoft Teams. Si l’IA analyse localement le contenu des appels vocaux externes, les problèmes liés à la confidentialité des échanges ne se posent pas. En revanche, si Teams s’appuie sur une IA dans le cloud, les échanges seront envoyés sur les serveurs de Microsoft afin d’y être analysés, avec tous les risques pour la confidentialité que cela peut engendrer.
La fonction, qui doit être rendue disponible sur Windows 11, macOS, Android et iOS sera déployée pour les utilisateurs du monde entier à compter de janvier 2027. Microsoft aura sans doute l’occasion de répondre à l’ensemble des interrogations qui entourent l’arrivée de cette fonction dans les prochaines semaines, la firme de Redmond ayant a priori prévu de déployer celle-ci en preview à compter de ce mois de décembre.

articles.title: 4TB SSD at Newegg costs just $75 per terabyte
articles.text:
Black Friday SSD deal: Newegg slashes $200 off the 4TB KingSpec P3, bringing it down to just $75 per terabyte
Big capacity without the equally big price tag
With SSD prices remaining stubbornly high amid the ongoing memory crisis, finding affordable high-capacity storage isn't easy. The 4TB KingSpec P3 offers plenty of room for creative projects, games, videos and personal files, provided you're happy with SATA rather than NVMe speeds.
Best For: Budget-conscious PC builders, creative types, gamers, and anyone looking to maximize storage capacity without paying over the odds.
The Deal: The 4TB KingSpec P3 SSD is now $300 (was $500) at Newegg for Black Friday, saving you $200 (40%) and bringing the cost down to just $75 per terabyte.
Today's best internal SSD
The 4TB KingSpec P3 2.5-inch SATA III SSD features 3D NAND flash, 550MB/s read and 510MB/s write speeds, TRIM support, wear leveling, 1,920TBW endurance, and a three-year limited manufacturer warranty.
Why we recommend it
The KingSpec P3 is a 2.5-inch internal SSD that uses a SATA III 6Gbps interface and 3D NAND flash memory. It delivers sequential read and write speeds of up to 550MB/s and 510MB/s, respectively, with random read and write performance of up to 65,000 and 70,000 IOPS.
While those speeds are far slower than modern NVMe SSDs, they're still a big improvement over mechanical hard drives. The drive supports TRIM, wear leveling, garbage collection, error correction, and S.M.A.R.T. health monitoring. KingSpec also lists a write endurance rating of 1,920TBW and backs the drive with a three-year warranty. Power consumption is rated at just 1.85W during active use and 0.41W when idle.
Price context & historical value
Newegg's $200 Black Friday discount brings the 4TB KingSpec P3 down to a penny under $300, or 7.5 cents per gigabyte. It's not the cheapest we've seen it however. It was on sale for $225 earlier in the year.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the KingSpec P3 SSD if...
Storage capacity is more important to you than outright speed, or you're replacing an older mechanical hard drive.
❌ Skip the KingSpec P3 SSD if...
You regularly transfer large files, work on demanding video projects, or want the fastest possible storage. In that case, you'll be better off with an NVMe SSD.

articles.title: Le clavier Logitech MX Keys S tombe à 69,99 € à l'occasion du Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : Le clavier Logitech MX Keys S Graphite à 69,99 € (-11%)
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le clavier Logitech MX Keys S passe à 69,99 € chez Amazon et Boulanger.com, soit une baisse d'environ 11 % et 8,93 € d'économie. Réputé pour sa frappe silencieuse et son rétroéclairage automatique, il affiche une note actuelle de 4,5/5 dans nos tests.
Logitech propose avec le MX Keys S une mise à jour par petites touches de son clavier bureautique de référence. Ce modèle sans fil complet conserve son format avec pavé numérique et ses touches à mécanisme ciseaux pour le travail au quotidien. Lors de son passage dans notre labo, il avait convaincu nos testeurs par sa frappe silencieuse et sa fabrication soignée.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Logitech MX Keys S descend à 69,99 € chez Amazon et Boulanger.com, soit environ 11 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (78,92 €). Cela représente une économie de 8,93 €.
Frappe fluide et rétroéclairage automatique pour la bureautique
Le Logitech MX Keys S s'appuie sur une structure robuste pour offrir un confort de frappe stable lors des longues sessions de saisie. Ses interrupteurs ciseaux assurent une frappe agréable et silencieuse, idéale pour travailler dans un espace partagé sans déranger son entourage. Comme le détaille notre test complet, l'appareil intègre également un rétroéclairage automatique qui s'ajuste tout seul à la lumière ambiante pour préserver la batterie sans sacrifier la lisibilité.
Logitech MX Keys S
Points forts
- Qualité de fabrication.
- Rétroéclairage automatique.
- Frappe agréable et silencieuse.
- Bonne autonomie pour un clavier sans fil rétroéclairé.
- Connexion à trois appareils possible.
Points faibles
- Sérigraphie à la fois Mac et PC qui fait fouillis.
- Inclinaison du clavier non réglable.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Connexion multi-appareils et concessions ergonomiques
Ce clavier bureautique permet de connecter jusqu'à trois appareils différents et de basculer de l'un à l'autre en appuyant sur une touche dédiée. Cette polyvalence s'accompagne d'une double sérigraphie Mac et PC sur les touches, qui peut sembler un peu chargée à l'œil, tandis que l'inclinaison du châssis reste fixe et ne propose aucun réglage en hauteur. Ces détails ne gênent toutefois pas la saisie standard si l'angle naturel du plateau convient à votre installation.
Logitech MX Keys Mini : l'autre option face au Logitech MX Keys S
Le Logitech MX Keys Mini reprend les mêmes qualités de fabrication et le toucher silencieux de son grand frère, mais fait l'impasse sur le pavé numérique pour réduire son encombrement sur le bureau. Alors que le MX Keys S est actuellement noté 4,5/5 par notre rédaction, la version Mini affiche une note actuelle de 4/5.
Le Logitech MX Keys Mini est vendu 5,00 € moins cher que le Logitech MX Keys S à son tarif remisé, mais ce dernier conserve l'avantage pratique de son pavé numérique complet pour les utilisateurs qui manipulent régulièrement des chiffres.
Logitech MX Keys Mini
Points forts
- Qualité et finition impeccables.
- Frappe agréable et réactive.
- Très compact.
- Bonne autonomie malgré le rétroéclairage.
- Connexion à 3 appareils possible.
Points faibles
- Sérigraphie Mac et PC qui fait fouillis.
- Inclinaison du clavier non réglable.
