articles.title: Black Friday: Diese Samsung-Angebote lohnen sich
articles.text:
Black Friday: Diese Samsung-Angebote bei Amazon und Mediamarkt lohnen sich
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Offiziell findet der Black Friday zwar erst am 27. November statt, die Preisschlacht hat aber schon jetzt begonnen. Besonders viel sparen können Schnäppchenjäger:innen dann, wenn mehrere Shops versuchen, sich mit ihren Rabattaktionen gegenseitig zu unterbieten. Aktuell ist das bei den Konkurrenten Amazon und Media Markt der Fall, die beide Samsung-Smartphones deutlich reduziert anbieten. Wir haben die Black-Friday-Deals geprüft und zeigen dir, wo du derzeit am meisten sparst.
Samsung Galaxy A18 jetzt noch günstiger
Samsung bietet mehrere Smartphone-Serien an, die sich in Ausstattung und Preis teils deutlich voneinander unterscheiden. Die A-Reihe umfasst günstigere und mittelpreisige Modelle. Sie richtet sich an Nutzer:innen, die ein solides Gerät für den Alltag suchen, aber auf teure Spitzenfunktionen verzichten können. Zu den günstigsten Einstiegsmodellen der Reihe zählt das Samsung Galaxy A18.
Es hat ein 6,7-Zoll-Display und 128 Gigabyte internen Speicher. Mithilfe des „RAM Plus“-Features soll das Smartphone auf bis zu vier Gigabyte virtuellen Arbeitsspeicher zusätzlich zu den festen vier Gigabyte RAM zugreifen können. Dabei greift das Gerät dann auf den Datenspeicher zu. Einen sehr großen Leistungsschub sollte man sich davon nicht erwarten.
Die unverbindliche Preisempfehlung liegt bei 279 Euro. Bei Amazon ist das Modell aktuell für 209 Euro erhältlich. Im Onlineshop von Mediamarkt ist das Galaxy A18 allerdings noch günstiger zu haben. Hier liegt der Preis bei 179 Euro. Wer jetzt zuschlägt, spart rund 36 Prozent gegenüber der Preisempfehlung. Laut etablierten Preisvergleichsportalen war das Smartphone bislang kaum irgendwo günstiger zu haben.
So viel kannst du jetzt bei Foldables sparen
Auch die Foldables von Samsung sind aktuell reduziert. Das Galaxy Z Flip 8 misst aufgeklappt 6,9 Zoll, das Frontdisplay 4,1 Zoll. Die Dualkamera kombiniert ein 50-Megapixel-Weitwinkel- mit einem 12-Megapixel-Ultraweitwinkel-Objektiv. Bei Amazon ist das Modell derzeit ausverkauft. Im Samsung-Shop kostet es mit 256 Gigabyte internem Speicher 1.069 Euro, bei Media Markt 749 Euro. Hier sparst du also 320 Euro beziehungsweise knapp 30 Prozent.
Auch das Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 ist jetzt günstiger. Es eignet sich für alle, die sich ein möglichst großes Display für Videos oder E-Mails wünschen. Das Frontdisplay misst 5,5 Zoll, aufgeklappt sind es 7,6 Zoll. Die Hauptkamera auf der Rückseite löst mit 50 Megapixeln aus. Laut Herstellerangaben ermöglicht der große Akku bis zu 26 Stunden Videowiedergabe. Bei Samsung kostet das Foldable mit 256 Gigabyte ab 1.799 Euro, bei Mediamarkt 1.649 Euro und damit 150 Euro weniger. Bei Amazon ist es ausverkauft.
Der Preisvergleich zeigt: Bei beiden Modellen fällt die Ersparnis geringer aus als von Mediamarkt angegeben. Der Händler legt eine höhere unverbindliche Preisempfehlung zugrunde, obwohl die Geräte beim Hersteller selbst günstiger sind. Auch ein Blick in etablierte Preisvergleichsportale lohnt sich: Laut Analyse sind beide Foldables in kleineren Onlineshops aktuell noch günstiger.
Galaxy A57: Warum sich der Vergleich lohnt
Auch das Samsung Galaxy A57 ist Teil der Black-Friday-Aktion. Das höherwertige Mittelklassemodell bietet mehr Leistung und eine bessere Kameraausstattung als das A18. Es unterstützt 5G und hat 256 Gigabyte Speicher. Das Display misst ebenfalls 6,7 Zoll, bietet aber eine Bildrate von 120 Hertz. Die 50-Megapixel-Hauptkamera verfügt über eine optische Bildstabilisierung. Dazu kommen eine 12-Megapixel-Weitwinkelkamera und eine 5-Megapixel-Makrokamera. Mit KI‑Funktionen wie dem Objektradierer, der störende Elemente aus dem Hintergrund entfernt, lassen sich die Bilder bearbeiten.
Bei Amazon zählte das Galaxy A57 über Wochen zu den meistverkauften Smartphones, inzwischen ist es dort vergriffen. Mediamarkt bietet es aktuell noch zum reduzierten Black-Friday-Preis von 379 Euro an. Das Angebot ist allerdings weniger gut, als der Händler suggeriert. Er nennt eine unverbindliche Preisempfehlung von 659 Euro, was eine Ersparnis von 42 Prozent bedeuten würde. Beim Hersteller selbst kostet das Modell aber nur noch 459 Euro.
Dass es sich nicht um ein einmaliges Schnäppchen handelt, zeigen auch Vergleichsportale: Laut ihrer Analyse ist das Modell in anderen Shops noch günstiger. Zudem lag der Preis vor einigen Monaten regelmäßig bei etwa 300 Euro. Zwar sparen Käufer:innen bei Media Markt jetzt 80 Euro gegenüber dem Herstellerpreis. Ein Preisvergleich zeigt aber, dass sich der Kauf im Rahmen der Black-Friday-Aktion nur bedingt lohnt.
Ist das Samsung Galaxy S26 wirklich günstiger?
Ähnliches gilt für das Galaxy S26. Bei diesem Smartphone handelt es sich um das aktuelle Premium-Modell von Samsung. Dessen Prozessor, der Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, ist speziell auf KI-Anwendungen ausgelegt und geht darüber hinaus zu den leistungsstärksten Chips in der Android-Welt. Das Smartphone ist in verschiedenen Ausführungen erhältlich. Das Standardmodell verfügt über ein 6,3-Zoll-Display und 256 Gigabyte integrierten Speicher. Die Dreifachkamera besteht aus einem 50-Megapixel-Weitwinkel-, einem 12-Megapixel-Ultraweitwinkel- und einem 10-Megapixel-Teleobjektiv.
Mediamarkt nennt für das Galaxy S26 eine unverbindliche Preisempfehlung von 1.099 Euro, der Hersteller verlangt inzwischen aber nur noch 699 Euro. Der Black-Friday-Nachlass fällt daher geringer aus als im Onlineshop angegeben. Statt der versprochenen 42 Prozent sparen Käufer:innen beim Angebot von 679 Euro nur 20 Euro, also weniger als drei Prozent. Laut Vergleichsportalen schwankte der Preis zuletzt stark und lag in anderen Shops oft bei 650 Euro oder weniger.
Black Friday: Lass dich nicht täuschen
Anlässlich der Black Week locken viele Onlineshops mit hohen Rabatten. Ein Preisvergleich zeigt allerdings, dass diese nicht immer so hoch ausfallen wie angegeben. Oft sind aktuelle Smartphones beim Hersteller günstiger, als die unverbindlichen Preisempfehlung suggeriert. Kaufinteressierte sollten sich daher nicht von vermeintlichen Schnäppchen blenden lassen. Ob ein Angebot wirklich gut ist, zeigt nur der direkte Preisvergleich.

articles.title: Anthropic Expands Enterprise Safeguards for Detecting AI Misuse
articles.text:
Anthropic on Monday announced the public beta of Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), a system designed to help organizations detect malicious use of AI.
Unveiled in September, EFS has been developed with input from over 100 Anthropic customers, with companies such as Stripe and Salesforce evaluating it in private beta. A quarter of Fortune 100 companies helped develop EFS.
According to Anthropic, existing Claude protections can identify potentially harmful requests made individually, but EFS adds a monitoring layer that can detect suspicious patterns across multiple requests that may appear benign when analyzed individually.
The system targets organizations that use Claude under zero data retention agreements and have so far relied only on classifiers that analyze each request in isolation.
EFS is designed to detect both deliberate misuse of AI, such as AI-powered cyberattacks, and incidents where AI agents go beyond what their operator intended, such as the cases where agents exploited vulnerabilities to gain access to real-world systems.
With EFS, organizations store conversation data in their own cloud and protect it with their own encryption keys and access policies.
Neither Anthropic nor its cloud providers retain copies of the conversation data after it’s transferred to the customer’s storage. Anthropic receives monitoring metadata, but not the content of conversations.
Security teams are provided reports on potentially harmful activity, which can be ingested via SIEM solutions. EFS is currently available via the Claude Platform, AWS, and Google Cloud, with Microsoft Foundry integration in the works.
Guide to securing enterprise coding agents
Anthropic on Monday also published a guide to securing enterprise coding agents, with a focus on risks associated with privilege abuse, credential exposure, risky dependencies, prompt injection, and data exfiltration.
Citing previously published testing results, the company said mechanisms designed to detect prompt injection reduced attack success rates from 90% to 28% on Fable 5.2 and from 55% to 11% on Opus 5.5.
Anthropic also highlighted the effectiveness of its auto mode classifier, which evaluates proposed actions against user intent.
In tests conducted this summer, auto mode, which is now enabled by default for interactive Claude Code sessions, blocked 89% of dangerous commands, compared to only 14% in the case of human reviewers.
However, Anthropic recommends requiring human approval for high-risk actions and enforcing additional controls, such as sandboxing and network access restrictions.
Related: Anthropic Rolls Out Mythos 5.2 With Improved Bug Hunting, Fewer Sandbox Escapes

articles.title: Anthony Vetro: From Video Coding Lab to Global R&D Leader At MERL
articles.text:
The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.
Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.
Anthony Vetro
Employer
Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.
Title
Member grade
Fellow
Alma mater
Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)
He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.
Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.
His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.
He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.
Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.
“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.
A multimedia pioneer
Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.
Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.
“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.
“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”
Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.
“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.
He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.
“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”
It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.
“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”
“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”
After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.
“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.
He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.
Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.
“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.
The road to management
After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.
“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”
He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.
Mitsubishi Electric’s first U.S. innovation hub
To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.
The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.
The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”
The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.
Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.
“Serendie Street [Boston] aims to strengthen the bridge between our global R&D efforts and real-world industry challenges. The hub is intended to bring our partners and customers together to engage in more cocreation activities, where we listen to their problems and work together to solve them,” he says. “I think the company has come to recognize that we can’t just do it all internally by ourselves.”
The technologies being worked on include robotics, energy solutions such as integrating renewable energy into the grid, and more energy-efficient data center systems.
The decision to colocate the hub with MERL offices was deliberate, Vetro says.
“The area has a very rich ecosystem,” he says. “We have Harvard, MIT, and many other universities a stone’s throw away.”
Strengthening IEEE’s involvement with industry
Vetro joined IEEE in 1992 as a student member during an event the Polytechnic’s student branch was holding. He enjoyed reading the IEEE Potentials student member publication and other periodicals, he says.
“In the earliest stages of my career, IEEE was a place where I could attend conferences, read journals, and stay on top of the latest research and trends,” he says. “Over the years, I was able to build a professional network, which has been helpful. That facilitated a lot of research collaboration with university professors attending the conferences.
“In more recent years, IEEE has provided a great platform for industry to exhibit thought leadership and discuss real-world problems we’re facing. I think these discussions may have even set some research directions among the academic community.”
Vetro is an active volunteer for the IEEE Signal Processing Society. He has chaired several of its technical committees and conferences, and he served as an associate editor for some of its journals.
He says he’s most proud of establishing the society’s industry board and serving as its inaugural chair. The board formed a corporate engagement program, launched the Industry Signals newsletter, developed short courses tailored to industry, and holds career fairs at the society’s flagship conferences.
Vetro also had a hand in MERL sponsoring two IEEE technical field awards: the Flanagan Speech and Audio Processing Award and the Fourier Award for Signal Processing.
“Industry-level engagement in IEEE is really very vital to the organization in maintaining its relevance to the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity,” he says.

She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

articles.title: Why Canada invested in Cohere
articles.text:
Today we have another edition of what is becoming a quarterly accountability check-in with Canada’s AI Minister, Evan Solomon.
“Simply put, Canada is not gonna wait for others to build the AI—maybe people we don’t know or don’t trust. We’re gonna build it now.”
The last time the minister was on the podcast, it was shortly following the release of Canada’s AI strategy. This time, we’re checking in right after Budget 2026, and we talk through some of the budget components the minister is most passionate about in their support of entrepreneurs. We also cover how some of those steps are designed to help prevent more AI companies like Taalas and Tenstorrent from being acquired or fleeing south—for his part, Minister Solomon said it’s his job to give those companies reasons not to leave.
But we also talk about the big news that dropped right before the budget: the federal government’s investment in AI champion Cohere. If you’ve seen the minister on The BetaKit Podcast before, or are familiar with BetaKit’s coverage generally, this news should not surprise you.
But public investments in private companies are relatively novel in Canada, and now that every Canadian has skin in the game, they’re coming armed with a lot of questions. As Build Canada’s Lucy Hargreaves put it, “Ottawa is becoming the owner, the funder, the customer and the regulator of the same companies.” How is that going to work?

I put the question to the minister directly alongside these two: why did the feds choose this approach, and how much can Canadians expect to know about their growing tech portfolio?
Do you want to know the answers? Let’s dig in.

articles.title: Meta integra Muse ao Instagram e prepara terreno para novas vendas
articles.text:
A Meta está levando seu agente pessoal de inteligência artificial (IA) Muse para dentro do Instagram. A novidade permitirá que usuários organizem publicações salvas e conversem com o assistente diretamente pelo Direct. Por trás da integração, porém, existe também uma estratégia comercial: transformar o interesse dos usuários em produtos e conteúdos em novas oportunidades de vendas e publicidade.
A empresa começará a incentivar o uso do Muse quando as pessoas salvarem publicações no Instagram. Nos Estados Unidos, usuários também receberão sugestões para organizar conteúdos em coleções específicas, como receitas e vídeos de viagens.
A integração estará disponível para quem conectar suas contas do Instagram e do Muse. O assistente também ganhará presença própria nas mensagens diretas, permitindo iniciar conversas a partir de conteúdos encontrados na rede social.
Como o Muse vai funcionar no Instagram?
- Uma das principais funções será organizar publicações salvas ao longo do tempo. Em vez de procurar manualmente um vídeo ou uma imagem entre dezenas de itens armazenados, o usuário poderá pedir ao Muse que agrupe os conteúdos por assunto;
- A ferramenta também poderá ajudar em tarefas relacionadas às publicações e conversas do Instagram. Por exemplo, será possível enviar conteúdos sobre destinos turísticos para que o agente pesquise informações para uma viagem ou pedir que ele procure produtos específicos;
- A integração, entretanto, terá algumas limitações. A experiência dentro do Instagram será mais restrita do que a oferecida pelo aplicativo ou pela versão web do Muse. Para acompanhar determinadas tarefas e visualizar resultados mais completos, ainda poderá ser necessário acessar essas plataformas;
- O novo assistente também não substituirá o chatbot Meta AI, que continuará disponível nas mensagens diretas. Enquanto o Meta AI funciona como ferramenta mais generalista para responder perguntas, o Muse terá proposta de assistente pessoal, com foco em tarefas e atividades do usuário.
Meta quer transformar o Muse em ferramenta de compras
A expansão do agente para o Instagram também tem objetivo comercial. A rede social é uma das principais fontes de receita publicitária da Meta e a empresa pretende aproveitar os hábitos de navegação e consumo dos usuários para estimular compras.
Segundo informações obtidas pela CNBC, aproximadamente 20% dos usuários diários do Instagram salvam pelo menos uma publicação por dia. Uma parcela significativa desses conteúdos envolve produtos que podem ser comprados ou anúncios.
O Muse pode facilitar o retorno a esses itens e reduzir etapas entre o interesse inicial e a compra. Um executivo da Meta afirmou à CNBC que, mesmo sem exibir publicidade própria, o agente já contribui para os negócios de anúncios da companhia ao aumentar as conversões dos anunciantes.
A lógica é simples: se o assistente ajuda alguém a encontrar um produto, organizar referências e concluir uma compra, a empresa pode gerar mais resultados para marcas que já investem em publicidade no Instagram.
Além disso, as informações sobre os produtos procurados e comprados por meio do Muse podem ajudar a Meta a compreender melhor os interesses dos consumidores e direcionar anúncios com maior precisão.
Leia mais:
- Meta abre código do Muse para você criar seu próprio gadget de IA
- Meta lança IA de peso aberto que roda em Macs; veja como funciona
- Meta quer colocar sua IA em chaveiro com internet 5G
Meta já domina compras realizadas por agentes de IA
Os números apresentados pela CNBC indicam que o Muse está ganhando espaço no comércio realizado por meio de agentes de IA.
Durante a última teleconferência de resultados da Meta, o CEO Mark Zuckerberg afirmou que 25% dos usuários do Muse utilizam a ferramenta para fazer compras. Essa é a atividade mais comum entre os usuários do agente, e o valor médio das compras ultrapassa US$ 200 (cerca de R$ 1.100).
Zuckerberg também afirmou que a empresa pretende cobrar uma pequena taxa sobre as transações realizadas pela plataforma.
Outro levantamento, da empresa de análise de comércio eletrônico Forter Intelligence, apontou que o Muse respondeu por 51% dos pedidos feitos por agentes de IA na semana encerrada em 22 de novembro.
No mesmo período, o Grok, da xAI, ficou com 24%, enquanto o ChatGPT, da OpenAI, respondeu por 22%. Google e a startup Instinct dividiram os 3% restantes.
Os números indicam que a Meta está conquistando espaço em mercado no qual assistentes de IA começam a assumir etapas que tradicionalmente eram realizadas diretamente pelos consumidores em lojas virtuais.
Meta ainda pode incluir anúncios diretamente no Muse
Apesar de já contribuir indiretamente para a receita publicitária da companhia, o Muse ainda não exibe anúncios próprios.
Segundo fontes ouvidas pela CNBC, a Meta deve eventualmente testar publicidade dentro do agente, mas não estaria sob pressão financeira para acelerar essa estratégia.
Uma possibilidade seria inserir anúncios diretamente no feed do Muse, que funciona de maneira mais próxima a um mural de publicações do que a uma interface baseada exclusivamente em perguntas e respostas.
A empresa costuma priorizar o crescimento da audiência antes de introduzir mecanismos de monetização em seus produtos. Com a integração ao Instagram, a Meta ganha mais uma oportunidade de atrair usuários para o Muse e ampliar sua presença no comércio digital.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship, strikes cargo ships from Mediterranean to Baltic
articles.text:
Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland.
The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press. Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones launched from a mother ship to target the Merkury, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara.
Zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that currently controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli.
Casualties from the strikes included at least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, Libyan National Army officials told The Associated Press. They also mentioned some wounded crew members of the Russian warship being transferred to local hospitals.
Merkury was a Steregushchiy-class missile corvette, designated by Russia as Project 20380, that can carry both anti-ship and air-defense missiles. They are also armed with torpedoes to counter submarines and have a naval cannon mounted on the deck.
Corvette-class warships are typically smaller than the destroyers or frigates that often act as workhorses of modern navies, although NATO has designated Russian missile corvettes such as the Merkury as being equivalent to frigates.
Merkury was originally meant to join Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. But after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Russian warship was unable to enter the Black Sea because Turkey invoked the 1936 Montreux Convention to restrict warships from entering or leaving the Black Sea. Instead, the Merkury mainly operated from Russia’s Northern Fleet bases in Arctic waters, according to naval analyst HI Sutton.

articles.title: La película live-action de ‘Naruto’ ficha a Hiroyuki Sanada para un papel clave
articles.text:
La película live-action de Naruto acaba de cerrar uno de sus primeros fichajes. Y se trata de un nombre de muchísimo nivel. Hiroyuki Sanada, legendario actor de series como Shogun o películas como El Último Samurai, John Wick 4 o Mortal Kombat, se une a las filas de este esperado remake en imagen real. Además, ya se ha revelado el papel que interpretará y, desde luego, no podían haber elegido a nadie mejor.
Tal y como ha informado Deadline, Hiroyuki Sanada será Hiruzen Sarutobi en la película live-action de Naruto. Sarutobi era el Tercer Hokage de la Aldea Oculta de la Hoja. Es decir, el líder ninja del pueblo natal del joven protagonista. Conocedor de las cinco naturalezas del chakra, se trata de uno de los personajes más poderosos e importantes de todo el manga y el anime.
Por el momento, Hiroyuki Sanada se ha convertido en el primer actor confirmado para el reparto de la película live-action de Naruto. Con su fichaje, el proyecto gana no solo a uno de los mejores y más queridos actores japoneses del mundo, sino a un auténtico experto en el cine de artes marciales.
Se sabe también que el director de la película live-action de Naruto será Destin Daniel Cretton. El cineasta es conocido por el gran público gracias a su trabajo en Marvel. En dicha saga ha dirigido Shang-Chi y la Leyenda de los Diez Anillos, la serie de Wonder Man y, sobre todo, la reciente Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Y, además, el joven actor Charles Melton (Riverdale) está en negociaciones para unirse al filme, aunque todavía no hay nada cerrado.
De qué va Naruto
Naruto fue publicada entre 1999 y 2014 en la popular revista Shonen Jump y ha vendido más de 250 millones de copias en todo el mundo. Su trama sigue la historia de un muchacho huérfano que vive en la Aldea Oculta de la Hoja. En su interior vive encerrado el espíritu de un temible demonio, el Zorro de las Nueve Colas. Un monstruo que años atrás atacó y arrasó la aldea. Por eso mismo, Naruto Uzumakivive marginado y aislado.
Ante esta situación, el protagonista se lanza a cumplir su sueño. Para ganarse el respeto y la admiración de todos, deberá convertirse en Hokage, el líder ninja de la aldea. Pero si quiere conseguirlo, deberá entrenar muy duro y sortear todo tipo de aventuras. Entre sus aliados encontrará a Sasuke y Sakura, que le ayudarán a hacer frente a las misiones y amenazas que se crucen en su camino.

articles.title: The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
articles.text:
Weeks before the end of the legislative session, some members of Congress are scrambling to reauthorize a controversial warrantless wiretapping authority, possibly by attaching it to a must-pass military spending bill. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politicothat Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) could be attached to the National Defense Authorization Act. It’s the latest in a grueling fight over a major spying rule that hasn’t technically lapsed.
The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
Warrantless wiretapping proponents are rushing to beat the looming blue wave.
“We don’t have two weeks to work just on FISA,” said Rounds, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “But if it’s amended onto the NDAA then you can move it forward and get that done in time.”
FISA allows for the warrantless surveillance of certain foreigners’ communications, ostensibly on national security grounds. In part because of FISA’s broad scope, Congress revisits it every few years, both to reauthorize the authority and to reform it. The last effort to do both failed. Despite pressure from President Donald Trump, Congress failed to reauthorize FISA over the summer, in part because leadership wouldn’t allow any amendments — particularly attempts to limit its sweeping scope — to be debated or introduced. (Trump didn’t help matters when he made Bill Pulte the acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, who reportedly bragged about purging one-third of the DNI staff, is now the director of federal housing.) But the surveillance authority didn’t actually lapse because the FISA court rectified surveillance under Section 702 back in March, meaning the surveillance state can keep chugging along as is for another four months.
So why the urgency? If you haven’t heard, there’s about to be a new Congress in town — one that is even less likely to give Trump seemingly unlimited spying powers without some semblance of reform.
Support for — and opposition to — FISA isn’t a clear-cut partisan issue. Last time around, a bipartisan coalition led by House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT), the ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, led the campaign for a “clean” reauthorization of FISA. Their efforts were defeated largely because of holdouts from the Freedom Caucus, whose privacy concerns echoed those of liberal lawmakers. FISA’s critics wanted reform, not abolition. Their goal was to make it harder for intelligence agencies to use the statute, which is intended for foreign targets, to access Americans’ communications.
“It was remarkable watching two dozen House Republicans stand up to the establishment, stand up to Mike Johnson, and fight to reform FISA,” said Michael Baick, an organizer with the OpenAI boycott campaign QuitGPT, which has been advocating for FISA reform to stop AI surveillance. “This has always been a bipartisan issue where Americans of all stripes can agree, and trying to make deals with the establishment to maintain the status quo, while the ground is shifting, is just short-sighted and missing what this moment really is.”
“I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time.”
Johnson and Himes were adamantly opposed to any reining in of Section 702, stressing the need for a so-called “clean reauthorization.” Both claimed there had already been reforms. “It ain’t the same FISA,” Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) declared in April.
But the changes reformers most wanted were missing. Among them were a warrant requirement and an end to what critics say are major loopholes. Under Section 702, intelligence agencies can pull the communications of non-US persons not in the United States — that is, foreign nationals outside the country. But federal agencies like the FBI and NSA can buy Americans’ data from private brokers, a practice FBI director Kash Patel admits is ongoing. And intelligence agencies can use Section 702 to obtain the communications of non-US persons who are communicating with Americans — a workaround known as the “backdoor search loophole.”
“I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time,” Don Bell, senior policy counsel at the Constitution Project of the Project on Government Oversight, told The Verge. “This is something everyone knew was coming down the pike. There have been months to do this, and I don’t think anyone is saying don’t reauthorize at all. The argument is this is an incredibly powerful surveillance tool, and there needs to be guardrails in place to protect people’s constitutional rights.”
Himes, arguably the Democratic Party’s biggest champion of FISA, seems willing to give Trump one more win before the blue wave crashes down in Washington. “I made it clear to some very senior administration officials that they should get this thing done in the lame-duck,” he told The Hill, “because it’s, you know, going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.”
But Himes didn’t have the votes this summer, and it’s even less likely that he’ll have the votes for a clean reauthorization now.

articles.title: Vale, Chris Dickman: Australian science grieves the loss of a giant of ecology and conservation
articles.text:
Australia has lost one of its most distinguished ecologists and conservation champions, Emeritus Professor Chris Dickman.
Chris’s achievements and legacy are vast, much like his beloved Simpson Desert that he and his research team – known as “the ratcatchers” – have studied for well over 30 years. He and his team would camp out under the stars, carefully trapping and monitoring the desert’s animals and plants.
Without Chris, we wouldn’t know just how important even small but ferocious predators are in structuring ecological communities. One example is the brush-tailed mulgara, which preys on and regulates numbers of other predators, including the lesser hairy-footed dunnart.
Chris touched many in both his personal and professional roles. The authors of this article each knew Chris for many years.
Chris was honoured in a celebratory forum and festschrift, a collection of written tributes, in June that was attended by about 200 people and another 140 online. He died on November 17, 2026.
Science and service
Chris’s impressive career was marked by a dedication to the scientific field and service to the wider community.
He was an internationally renowned leader in wildlife conservation who studied everything from the small marsupial Antechinus to dunnarts, long-haired rats, mulgaras, quolls, sandy inland and spinifex hopping mice and the Tasmanian devil, to name but a few species.
His work shed light on the remarkable lives these animals lead as well as the challenges they face, including feral cats and foxes. Chris was among the first to draw attention to the contentious issue of dingo management by bringing experts together for a scientific forum.
With Lily van Eeden, Chris also led a team of researchers who first estimated three billion animals had been affected by Australia’s 2019-20 bushfire crisis, garnering global attention.
A living legacy
What follows are our personal reflections about Chris. We hope they help convey who he was, both as a person and a professional.
Glenda Wardle
Professor of Ecology and Evolution, University of Sydney
Chris was a true intellect, polymath and gentleman of science. He welcomed me to the University of Sydney in 1995 and led by example in all aspects of academic life. It would be hard to find a better role model.
Over several decades we shared a commitment to discovering the ecological secrets of the red sand country of the Simpson Desert. We faced adversity in the field through floods, fires and flies, but would always smile and keep working.
I will miss the hilarious stories we shared around campfires with the many wonderful students and volunteers that joined our research efforts. Together, we would dig and delight in the way the desert came to life, particularly after big flooding rains. I will miss Chris’s writing, which was both edifying and entertaining. I will remember him when listening to the Simon and Garfunkel song, The Sounds of Silence.
Aaron Greenville
Senior Lecturer of Spatial Agricultural and Environmental Sciences, University of Sydney
It was 1998 and I was a young second-year zoology student. We had just finished a lecture that sounded like an in-person BBC wildlife documentary. The lecturer was Chris Dickman.
Soon after, Chris encouraged us students to join the Royal Zoological Society of New South Wales and I promptly signed up. Little did I know that moment would change my life.
His enthusiastic, kind and generous nature has supported many a student, colleague and friend. His door was always open, regardless of how busy he was. Chris’ passion for the Simpson Desert was contagious and persuaded many people, including myself, to make a trip to the desert year after year. Chris led by example, creating a supportive and caring environment that has ultimately shaped how I lead my own research and teaching programs.
Chris was a true gentleman scientist, mentor and friend. I will miss him greatly.
Euan Ritchie
Professor of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, Deakin University
As a young PhD student, I attended the 2003 annual scientific meeting of the Australian Mammal Society in Sydney. At the time, Chris Dickman was president of the society. I was instantly struck by a few of his qualities, which in the years since have greatly shaped my own career.
Chris and his team were diligently uncovering the dynamics of the mighty Simpson Desert. Their work underscored the importance of long-term, systematic monitoring of wildlife to documenting the complex lives of mulgaras, dunnarts, native rodents and other sand-dwelling denizens. This is no mean feat, especially in an environment as unpredictable and ever-changing as the Simpson.
Chris was also a master communicator. He spoke with such clarity and with his distinctly dulcet tone, both qualities that gave his science such impact.
Most notably, Chris was incredibly generous with his time. He would ask me about my research and was always genuinely interested in what I had to say. He made young scientists like myself feel like we belonged, particularly in academia where imposter syndrome is rife. His mentorship and kind, thoughtful and supportive nature has helped me and many others pursue careers in ecology and conservation. For this, we are all forever grateful.
Thomas Newsome
Associate Professor of Global Ecology, University of Sydney
I was so lucky to have Chris as a lecturer during my undergraduate studies at The University of Sydney.
I fondly remember my first field trip with Chris, which involved sampling small mammals in the ancient forests of Barrington Tops in New South Wales, also known as Dungog. My peers and I slid around in the mud, attempting to reach the sampling sites, and learnt about the history of the area and its inhabitants. These early experiences shaped me as an ecologist.
I also had the privilege of working with Chris as a masters and then PhD student. I would approach him with so many ideas, some better than others. Chris always listened but, in his own style, would gently guide me in the right direction and towards fascinating topics. In our time together, we asked and answered questions about dingoes in the Tanami, foxes and cats in the Simpson, wolves in the United States and scavengers in Australia.
I owe Chris so much for his time and support. And I will forever treasure the memories of our adventures, alongside an appreciation for his knowledge and kindness.
Vale, Chris, our dear friend, mentor and colleague.
We farewell Chris here with an excerpt from his forthcoming festschrift, a collection of reflections written in his honour:
For science at its very best is not a solitary quest — It helps us see, to care and to learn what we all share
Know that in the shimmering moonlight on a distant dune crest or beside a dry creek’s trace,
The scientist with the stellar moustache was listening, and learning, with patience, skill and grace.

articles.title: ¿Qué pasa en una casa inteligente cuando se cae internet?
articles.text:
¿Qué pasa en una casa inteligente cuando se cae internet?
Una avería en la fibra no tiene por qué dejar fuera de juego toda la domótica, pero sí puede impedir controlar luces, cámaras o electrodomésticos
Televisores, altavoces inteligentes, termostatos, cámaras de vigilancia, electrodomésticos… Cada vez utilizamos más dispositivos conectados y pocas veces nos paramos a pensar qué pasaría en caso de producirse un fallo con la conexión a internet. ¿Seguirían funcionando como si nada? ¿Podríamos controlarlos de alguna manera? Lo cierto es que no hay una respuesta universal, y al final todo depende del producto concreto y del tipo de conexión que se use para configurarlos en la red doméstica.
Lo primero que hay que tener en cuenta es que, aunque a menudo hablamos de internet (o la conexión) y del Wi-Fi como sinónimos, la realidad es que no son lo mismo: internet es la red global que permite acceder a páginas web, plataformas y servidores externos, mientras Wi-Fi es la tecnología que conecta nuestros dispositivos con la red local del hogar sin cables. ¿Por qué es importante esta diferencia? Porque una avería en la conexión de fibra óptica puede dejarnos sin acceso a internet, pero si el router sigue encendido y funcionando, la red doméstica puede seguir comunicando los dispositivos entre sí, siempre que estos dispongan de una vía de comunicación local. En cambio, si el router deja de funcionar, los dispositivos que dependen de él para comunicarse pueden perder esa conexión, aunque algunos sistemas con un concentrador o una red propia podrían seguir funcionando.
Luces, enchufes y termostatos
La iluminación inteligente es uno de los ejemplos más claros: cuando usamos bombillas conectadas a una plataforma que necesita comunicarse con sus servidores para ejecutar órdenes, la caída de internet impedirá que las controlemos desde la aplicación o mediante asistentes de voz. Sin embargo, será posible hacerlo desde los interruptores físicos o los mandos compatibles.
Algo parecido sucede con los enchufes inteligentes, que permiten encender y apagar los aparatos conectados a ellos —o programar su funcionamiento— desde el móvil. Si la aplicación depende de la nube, puede dejar de enviar órdenes cuando no hay internet, pero un enchufe que tenga programaciones almacenadas localmente podría mantenerlas.
Por otro lado, los termostatos inteligentes plantean una situación interesante: aunque perdamos el control desde el móvil, es fácil encontrar modelos que permiten seguir controlando la temperatura desde el propio dispositivo y mantienen su funcionamiento básico. Otra cosa es que se mantengan las automatizaciones, los ajustes inteligentes o las funciones que necesitan consultar servicios externos.
¿Qué ocurre con las cámaras, alarmas y asistentes de voz?
Cuando hablamos de seguridad doméstica, perder la conexión puede tener consecuencias más importantes que van más allá de la imposibilidad de encender una bombilla desde el móvil: las cámaras conectadas suelen depender de servidores externos, así que sin internet no se podrán consultar imágenes en directo, recibir alertas o acceder a grabaciones desde una aplicación. En función del modelo, incluso se interrumpiría la grabación en la nube. Esto no ocurre con las que incorporan una tarjeta de memoria para guardar los vídeos; en este caso, aunque no fuera posible acceder para ver el vídeo en directo, la cámara seguiría encendida y grabando localmente.
Con las alarmas sucede algo similar y, si no hay conexión, se puede dar el caso de que detecte una intrusión y se active la sirena, pero el aviso nunca llegue al móvil del propietario. Para evitarlo, algunos modelos incorporan una conexión alternativa, como la red móvil, que permite transmitir avisos si falla internet.
Los altavoces inteligentes también pueden perder parte de su utilidad en caso de fallo de internet. Si las órdenes de voz necesitan llegar a un servicio en la nube para ser interpretadas —algo habitual—, funciones como consultar el tiempo, pedir información o controlar dispositivos con comandos de voz dejarán de estar disponibles, del mismo modo que no será posible reproducir contenidos en streaming.
La clave está en la nube y en el control local
Con todos estos ejemplos, queda una cosa clara: no hay una respuesta general para todos los dispositivos conectados del hogar, porque depende mucho de cómo se comuniquen y de dónde se procesen las órdenes. En los sistemas basados en la nube, la orden pasa por un servidor externo antes de llegar al dispositivo o de activar la función solicitada. Por eso, si se interrumpe la conexión a internet, ese intercambio deja de ser posible. En cambio, en los casos en los que todo se procesa de manera local, las funciones compatibles se seguirán ejecutando dentro de casa, siempre que los dispositivos, el controlador y la red necesaria continúen funcionando.
Dicho esto, ¿podemos hacer algo para preparar la casa para una caída de internet? Lo esencial sería identificar qué dispositivos utilizamos a diario y qué ocurriría si perdiéramos la conexión. Por eso, al elegir un producto inteligente, no basta con comprobar si es compatible con Alexa, Google Home o Apple Home; es recomendable saber qué funciones mantiene sin conexión, si necesita un concentrador (un dispositivo que coordina la comunicación entre los equipos) y si las automatizaciones se ejecutan localmente o en servidores externos. También conviene comprobar si dispone de controles físicos o de alguna alternativa para seguir utilizando sus funciones esenciales cuando falla la conexión.

articles.title: A Link Is Not Architecture: Why Multi-Die Systems Need More Than Die-to-Die Connectivity
articles.text:
Maintaining consistent communication behavior, integration, and security across configurations.
The system-on-chip (SoC) transformed semiconductor design by bringing the major functions of an electronic system onto one die, an integration that shaped chip architecture for years. Multi-die design is now changing the model again, distributing system functionality across multiple dies within a single package.
While this approach gives engineers greater flexibility to align semiconductor design with system requirements, bringing these designs to life takes more than a die-to-die link to transport transactions across the package. It requires a system architecture that manages how data moves between dies.
In AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems, multi-die architectures enable teams to scale compute and select an appropriate process technology for each part of the design. These partitioning choices determine which transactions remain within a die and which must cross die boundaries. Treating each boundary independently increases integration and verification effort, complicates performance management, and reduces the practical value of chiplet reuse.
Still, managing communication across these die boundaries requires a clear separation between the physical interface that transports transactions and the system architecture that manages them. Extending the system’s data-movement architecture across die boundaries allows engineers to repartition or scale designs without rebuilding the entire communication architecture.
The die-to-die controller and PHY provide transport between dies: the controller handles protocol functions, while the PHY provides the electrical interface. The link does not automatically preserve the traffic management, quality of service (QoS), routing, address handling, and observability established by the network-on-chip (NoC). These functions remain part of the system architecture above the physical interface.
Getting transactions across a die boundary is only part of the challenge. Those transactions must also compete for shared bandwidth, often with different performance and latency requirements. QoS manages how bandwidth is allocated across die boundaries, preserving traffic priorities as the system architecture evolves.
In architectures that implement end-to-end QoS, service can be coordinated for each transaction along its route, from initiator to target. Arbitration and packet-level priorities determine which traffic advances when demand changes, while bandwidth controls regulate how much capacity each source can consume. Coordinating these mechanisms across the NoC ensures that each traffic class receives its configured service level, while the physical link is responsible for transport.
A multi-die package can carry coherent shared-memory traffic alongside non-coherent data and control flows. Coherent interconnects support data sharing across dies, while non-coherent interconnects serve paths that do not require shared-memory coherency. These different traffic requirements call for different interconnect capabilities, with Arteris addressing both coherent and non-coherent communication through its multi-die IP portfolio.
FlexGen Multi-Die smart interconnect IP provides non-coherent NoC connectivity for AI and HPC architectures. It extends NoC connectivity and QoS across chiplet boundaries, enabling traffic management across the multi-die system. FlexGen Multi-Die supports bidirectional transactions over a single UCIe PHY, reducing PHY area, power, and I/O requirements by up to 50 percent.
Ncore Multi-Die interconnect IP addresses cache-coherent compute architectures. It extends cache coherency and data sharing across dies, enabling software to see the multi-die assembly as a single piece of silicon.
Magillem integration automation supports IP, chiplet, and hardware-software integration as the number of components and interfaces increases. This reduces the engineering effort and complexity associated with assembling a growing set of reusable components.
As a multi-die system adds interfaces between dies, the number of trust boundaries increases. Security assurance must therefore extend beyond individual dies to cover the interfaces and trust boundaries.
Cycuity hardware security assurance helps teams uncover vulnerabilities, identify weaknesses, and verify security requirements.
Bringing these capabilities together requires coordination across the multi-die system. As chiplet configurations evolve, engineers must manage a changing combination of components and interfaces while maintaining the system’s communication, integration, and security requirements.
These products operate within a broader ecosystem because no single layer defines the complete multi-die stack. Arteris focuses on interconnect, data movement, integration, and assurance while engineering teams select the controller, PHY, package, and surrounding tools for their design. Standards-aligned integration helps preserve those technology choices, while co-optimization balances system performance and power. As controller, PHY, packaging, and tool roadmaps change, engineers must evaluate how those changes affect the complete design.
The next phase of multi-die design will depend on preserving system intent across all physical partitions. As chiplet combinations and interface technologies evolve, engineers must maintain consistent communication behavior, integration, and security across configurations. The goal is to give designers the freedom to partition systems according to their requirements without having to rethink the entire architecture each time the physical implementation changes.

articles.title: OpenAI, Cisco Unveil Open Source Tool to Shield Unpatched Linux Systems
articles.text:
OpenAI and Cisco on Monday unveiled Shirudo, an open source security platform that uses AI agents to prevent the exploitation of vulnerabilities in Linux systems and applications.
The project is an AI-focused rewrite of Cisco-owned Isovalent’s Tetragon runtime security platform. Tetragon was open-sourced in 2022, and it also powers Cisco’s Live Protect vulnerability mitigation technology.
Shirudo is designed to help defenders address the challenges introduced by AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation, which is increasing pressure on organizations to deploy patches quickly.
The tool leverages eBPF technology to modify Linux kernel behavior without restarting the OS.
According to Cisco and OpenAI, agents can analyze vulnerability information, generate so-called ‘shields’ to prevent exploitation, and test their effectiveness without disrupting important services. Security teams still retain control over which shields are deployed.
Protections are digitally signed and verified before deployment, with mechanisms designed to prevent even attackers with root privileges from disabling kernel-level enforcement.
In a controlled test targeting the recent Java4Shell vulnerability, a shield generated using OpenAI’s Codex blocked an exploitation attempt targeting an Elasticsearch instance without requiring a restart.
Shirudo is currently in pre-release development and not ready for production use. The tool requires specific Linux kernel capabilities, additional kernel patches, and TPM 2.0.
OpenAI and Cisco hope that down the line Shirudo shields can be distributed alongside vulnerability disclosures to give organizations temporary protection until they can install permanent patches.
Amiram Shachar, CEO and co-founder of cloud security firm Upwind, commented, “Writing the most sensitive kernel code on the fly and deploying it straight to runtime is a very risky concept. I love the idea, but doing it with open source is very risky.”
“There are countless Linux versions and distributions this has to work across. It needs to be tested, packaged and automated before anyone should trust it in production,” Shachar added.

articles.title: Moins de 3 secondes de 0 à 100 km/h et faux son de 6 cylindres : la Porsche 718 Boxster électrique promet des sensations fortes
articles.text:
Le Boxster électrique se fait attendre. Après les nombreux bruits de couloir, Michael Leiters, président du directoire de Porsche, avait confirmé en août l’arrivée de la 718 électrique, puis la marque a annoncé le 7 octobre que les prochains 718 Boxster et Cayman abandonneraient définitivement l’essence.
Sauf qu’il manquait encore du concret, et Porsche a enfin donné quelques os à ronger ce mardi 24 novembre 2026 dans un communiqué. Ce sera la première sportive deux portes 100 % électrique de la marque. Le communiqué ne dit rien du Cayman, pourtant lui aussi confirmé en version électrique.
Une architecture spéciale pour la 718 électrique
Porsche a surtout travaillé l’emplacement de la batterie, qui fonctionne en 800 volts. Sur la plupart des voitures électriques, elle est posée sous le plancher. Sur la 718, elle se loge juste derrière les sièges, à la place de l’ancien moteur thermique. Porsche appelle cette architecture « E-Core ». Selon Porsche, elle permet de garder une position de conduite basse et une répartition des masses identique à celle d’une sportive à moteur central, avec 40 % sur l’avant et 60 % sur l’arrière.
Le châssis reprend aussi beaucoup de pièces de la 911, comme la direction, dérivée de la version Carrera GTS, ou le différentiel piloté « PTV+ » qui répartit la force entre les roues arrière pour mieux tourner. Pour la première fois sur un Boxster, des roues arrière directrices font leur apparition. La 718 électrique ne devrait donc pas avoir de mal à enchaîner les virages.
Plus vif qu’un Spyder RS, mais plus lourd
Au rayon des performances, Porsche annonce moins de 3 secondes pour abattre le 0 à 100 km/h, avec les seules roues arrière motrices. À titre comparatif, le 718 Spyder RS, le Boxster thermique le plus radical avec son six-cylindres de 500 ch, met 3,4 secondes. Comme Porsche promet la 718 la plus puissante de l’histoire, la version électrique devrait donc dépasser les 500 ch. En revanche, la vitesse de pointe s’arrête à « plus de 250 km/h », alors qu’un 718 Boxster GTS 4.0 en boîte PDK atteint 288 km/h et le Spyder RS 308 km/h.
Pour le poids, Porsche se contente d’annoncer un total « comparable à celui des modèles 911 Cabriolet actuels équipés du groupe motopropulseur T-Hybrid », le système hybride de la 911. Or, une 911 Carrera GTS Cabriolet pèse 1 675 kg à vide, soit 240 kg de plus qu’un Boxster GTS 4.0 PDK (1 435 kg). Les chiffres qui comptent pour une voiture électrique manquent toujours à l’appel : capacité de la batterie, autonomie et temps de recharge.
Une boîte PDK virtuelle et un six-cylindres reproduit
Tous les Boxster électriques auront de série le système E-Shift. Un bouton active une boîte PDK virtuelle à sept rapports, du nom de la boîte à double embrayage des Porsche thermiques, avec des passages automatiques ou manuels via des palettes. La voiture diffuse alors le son d’un six-cylindres à plat, inspiré du Boxster GTS de génération 981 (celle qui précédait la 718).
Porsche assure que les performances ne changent pas, que le mode soit activé ou non, grâce à un surplus de couple au moment des changements de rapport. Quand le E-Shift n’est pas activé, les palettes servent à choisir entre trois niveaux de récupération d’énergie.
Le reste des détails suivra lorsque Porsche présentera le 718 Boxster 100 % électrique au premier trimestre 2027. La production se fera dans son usine historique de Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen.

articles.title: Affaire des puces NVIDIA : Washington met sur liste noire sept sociétés soupçonnées d'alimenter la Chine
articles.text:
Le département du Commerce américain ajoute Megaspeed et six sociétés liées à l'Entity List. Toute livraison de produits soumis au contrôle des exportations américain exigera désormais une licence, que l’administration compte refuser par principe.
En juin 2025, NVIDIA avait inscrit Megaspeed sur sa liste interne d’entreprises à qui elle refuse de vendre. Le 23 novembre, le département du Commerce américain a rendu publique sa décision d’inscrire le groupe singapourien sur son Entity List, la liste noire commerciale américaine. La mesure coïncide avec le retour de Jensen Huang à la direction de NVIDIA, onze jours après l’annonce de sa démission.
Une licence pour les exportations de puces
Le Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), rattaché au département du Commerce, a inscrit sept sociétés sur l’Entity List. Le texte les répertorie sous Singapour, la Malaisie et la Thaïlande. Parmi elles figurent Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd., la filiale malaisienne Speedmatrix et Megaspeed (Thailand) mais aussi Apex Enterprise Solutions, filiale d’Alibaba. Le BIS invoque un risque important de détournement de matériel de calcul avancé vers des utilisateurs ou des usages non autorisés.
La mesure s’applique à tous les produits qui relèvent des Export Administration Regulations (EAR), la réglementation américaine sur les exportations. Lorsqu’une des sept sociétés intervient dans une exportation, une réexportation ou un transfert à l’intérieur d’un pays, ces produits sont soumis à licence. Le BIS examine les demandes avec une présomption de refus. Le texte prévoit une clause transitoire pour certaines expéditions qui étaient déjà en route.
Selon Reuters, Washington n’avait ajouté aucune société à l’Entity List depuis octobre 2025. L’agence avait rapporté en juin que l’administration Trump avait notamment différé l’inscription de DeepSeek, spécialiste de l’IA, et de CXMT, fabricant de puces mémoire, pour éviter d’attiser les tensions avec Pékin.
Washington enquête sur Megaspeed depuis 2024
Les autorités américaines cherchent à établir si Megaspeed a détourné des puces d’IA vers la Chine. L’entreprise affirme respecter les contrôles à l’exportation. Le 24 novembre, le Premier ministre de Singapour, Lawrence Wong, a confirmé que son pays poursuivait sa propre enquête pour déterminer si Megaspeed avait enfreint le droit singapourien.
L’affaire a pris un tour politique avec la révélation de la liaison de Jensen Huang avec Alice Huang, ancienne dirigeante de Megaspeed qui, selon l’entreprise, a quitté ses fonctions en août 2025.
D’après le New York Times, les services américains soupçonnent Alice Huang d’avoir transmis des renseignements à Pékin. Les autorités chinoises contestent toutefois cette accusation. Selon Lawrence Wong, les investigations singapouriennes n’ont pas permis de poursuivre Alice Huang. Celles-ci portaient sur de possibles fausses déclarations liées à des achats de serveurs, et non sur l’espionnage, précise d’ailleurs le ministère de l’Intérieur singapourien.
Le 13 novembre, le secrétaire américain au Trésor Scott Bessent avait publiquement reproché au département du Commerce de tarder à inscrire Megaspeed sur la liste. Il s’était aussi interrogé sur les vérifications menées par NVIDIA auprès de son client. Le fabricant a depuis annoncé la création d’un comité de son conseil d’administration chargé de superviser le respect des contrôles à l’exportation et les risques liés à la sécurité nationale.
Pour les puces fabriquées à l’étranger, les autres contrôles comptent aussi
L’inscription de Megaspeed sur la liste noire soulève toutefois un débat sur les puces fabriquées hors des États-Unis. La Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR) permet à Washington de contrôler certains produits fabriqués à l’étranger à l’aide de technologies ou de logiciels américains. Mais la décision ne comporte pas la mention qui aurait étendu spécifiquement ce dispositif aux entreprises visées.
Pour Chris McGuire, ancien responsable des politiques technologiques à la Maison-Blanche, cette absence réduit fortement l’efficacité de la mesure. Le BIS conteste cette lecture : selon lui, les règles existantes permettent déjà de contrôler les ventes de puces d’IA avancées fabriquées à l’étranger.
Ces règles ont notamment été renforcées le 19 novembre, avec une obligation de licence pour certaines livraisons de puces avancées vers Singapour, la Malaisie et la Thaïlande. L’inscription de Megaspeed à cette liste noire vient donc s’ajouter à des restrictions déjà en place. Quelques jours après les sourires du sommet de Shenzhen, Washington resserre un peu plus ses contrôles sur les puces d’IA susceptibles de finir en Chine.
Source : Computerbase

articles.title: J’ai testé l’ouverture de ma serrure Nuki avec Google Wallet : enfin la simplicité que j’attendais sur Android avec le Keypad 2 NFC
articles.text:
En domotique, la frontière entre le gadget et l’objet indispensable tient souvent à un détail : la friction à l’usage. Si vous avez déjà pesté devant votre porte d’entrée avec les bras chargés de courses parce que le Bluetooth mettait trois secondes de trop à réagir, vous voyez bien de quoi je parle.
Fin mars 2026, le spécialiste autrichien Nuki frappait un grand coup en lançant le Keypad 2 NFC, le tout premier clavier résidentiel certifié Aliro, ce nouveau standard créé pour harmoniser la communication entre nos smartphones et nos serrures connectées.
Toutefois, l’exécution était assez chaotique. La compatibilité se limitait aux smartphones Apple et Samsung, chacun avec son propre hub (Apple Home ou SmartThings). La mise en route sur les appareils Samsung était en plus complexe.
Avec l’arrivée d’une intégration officielle de Google Wallet Home Keys, la configuration devient beaucoup plus simple. Il m’a suffi d’ouvrir l’application Google Home pour ajouter mes clés, sans avoir à me soucier d’utiliser le portefeuille numérique de Samsung.
Une configuration ultra simple qui fait oublier l’application Nuki
Le principe du Tap to Unlock n’est pas nouveau, mais son arrivée dans Google Wallet l’ouvre à tous les smartphones Android équipés du NFC et tournant sous Android 9 ou plus récent, quelle que soit leur marque. Plus besoin de déverrouiller son smartphone, d’ouvrir l’application Nuki et d’appuyer sur un bouton. On approche simplement le dos du téléphone du clavier, et le verrou s’actionne dans la foulée.
Là où j’avais trouvé l’expérience Samsung déjà convaincante une fois mise en route, cette intégration Google Wallet m’a bluffé par sa fluidité dès la mise en route. Tout se pilote directement depuis l’application Google Home : en quelques secondes, la clé numérique est générée et ajoutée au portefeuille Google. Comme chez Apple et Samsung, un hub reste obligatoire. Il faut une Nuki Smart Lock compatible Matter (quatrième génération ou plus récente), un hub Google qui sert de routeur de bordure Thread (Nest Hub de deuxième génération, Nest Hub Max, Nest Wifi Pro ou Google TV Streamer) et un smartphone Android avec NFC équipé des applications Google Home et Google Wallet.
Grâce à l’approche modulaire de la marque, où la serrure et le clavier fonctionnent comme deux appareils indépendants, faire évoluer une installation existante en ajoutant simplement le Keypad 2 NFC sur sa porte prend à peine quelques minutes. Au quotidien, le geste devient aussi naturel que de payer sa baguette sans contact.
Six façons d’entrer chez soi : le clavier le plus polyvalent du marché ?
Avec cette nouveauté, Nuki transforme son Keypad 2 NFC en véritable couteau suisse de l’accès résidentiel, au point qu’il devient pratiquement impossible de se retrouver bloqué dehors, quel que soit l’équipement des membres du foyer. Le boîtier réunit désormais six méthodes d’ouverture distinctes : en plus de Google Wallet Home Keys, il prend déjà en charge Apple Home Key, Samsung Digital Home Key, le déverrouillage Tap to Unlock classique via l’application Nuki, le lecteur d’empreintes digitales et le clavier à code.
Ces six méthodes ne se cumulent pas toutes. Nuki impose de choisir entre le mode Smart Home, qui passe par les portefeuilles Apple, Samsung ou Google, et le mode application Nuki : on ne peut pas mélanger les deux. En mode Smart Home, chaque utilisateur s’ajoute depuis l’application de son écosystème. Un possesseur d’iPhone ne peut inviter que d’autres utilisateurs d’iPhone, et il en va de même chez Samsung et Google. Les codes et les empreintes se gèrent en revanche pour tout le monde depuis l’application Nuki.
Cette polyvalence s’accompagne d’une capacité d’accueil taillée aussi bien pour les familles nombreuses que pour les invités de passage, puisque le clavier peut mémoriser jusqu’à 20 empreintes digitales, 35 clés numériques Tap to Unlock et 200 codes d’accès personnalisés. Comme le souligne Martin Pansy, cofondateur et PDG de Nuki, cette ouverture concrétise la promesse d’une maison intelligente véritablement unifiée, où un utilisateur de Pixel, un adepte de Galaxy et un possesseur d’iPhone profitent exactement de la même expérience transparente sur la même porte.
Bien entendu, la serrure Nuki peut également se piloter depuis l’application de la marque, mais aussi à distance grâce aux intégrations Google Home, Alexa, Home Assistant et Matter.
Une disponibilité en bêta pour l’instant
L’intégration Nuki et Google Wallet Home Keys est disponible dès maintenant pour les inscrits au programme Public Preview de Google Home, que Nuki appelle « Google Home Beta ». Google promet un déploiement pour tous « dans les semaines à venir », sans date précise, et n’a pas publié la liste des pays concernés. Les montres Wear OS ne sont pas prises en charge au lancement.
Si vous ne faites pas encore partie du programme, il suffit de le rejoindre depuis l’application Google Home, en appuyant sur votre photo de profil en haut à droite de l’écran, puis sur Public Preview.

articles.title: NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO; Sarvam unveils upgraded model amid Token Factory row
articles.text:
NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO; Sarvam unveils upgraded model amid Token Factory row
Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as its president, CEO, and board director, less than two weeks after his resignation from the company. In other news, Sarvam’s new AI model promises better performance at a lower cost.
Dear Reader,
In a quick turn of events, Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as its president, CEO, and board director.
This development comes less than two weeks after Huang’s resignation from the company. It follows discussions between Huang and the board, alongside inputs from senior US government officials, the company said.
In other news, Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu has said AI is transforming coding and intellectual work the way mechanisation impacted farming and weaving.
Backing an observation by AI researcher Subbarao Kambhampati, Vembu said, in a post on X, “What happened to farmers and weavers and carpenters and ironsmiths in the waves of mechanization and automation is now starting to happen to mathematicians and programmers.”
Amid the backlash over hosting Chinese models on its Token Factory platform, Sarvam has clarified its AI strategy.
Co-founder Pratyush Kumar said a model’s country of origin and the location of the infrastructure on which it runs are two different matters. He also emphasised that building inference infrastructure does not diminish Sarvam’s core focus on its own models.
The company has released an upgraded model that it says delivers better performance at a lower cost. More on that below.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Home Affairs has urged users to log out after using WhatsApp Web to prevent account hijacking. An advisory issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre says active WhatsApp Web sessions could be misused to access private messages, impersonate users, and carry out cyber fraud.
In today’s newsletter:
- Sarvam’s new AI model promises better performance at lower cost
- Digital Naaris: A network of women micro-entrepreneurs
Here’s your trivia for today: What does ‘dim sum’ mean in English? (Scroll down for the answer)
Artificial Intelligence
Sarvam’s new AI model promises better performance at lower cost
Sarvam AI has released Sarvam-105B-1711, a model designed for businesses handling large volumes of customer queries, phone calls, and software-based tasks. The company says the updated version of its 105B model follows instructions more reliably, uses digital tools better, and handles Indian languages more effectively, all at a lower cost.
The latest release is part of a broader push by Sarvam to build models for different applications. It follows Sarvam Prism, a model designed to make quick, straightforward decisions; Bulbul V4 Flash, which turns written text into natural-sounding speech; and Saaras V4, which converts spoken language into text across 22 Indian languages.
More for less:
- Sarvam-105B-1711 was trained on Nvidia’s Blackwell B200 chips, powerful processors built for AI calculations. The model’s architecture activates only selected parts to generate each response, reducing computing requirements.
- Potential uses include customer-service chatbots, AI voice assistants that speak with callers, and digital assistants that use software to complete tasks.
- Sarvam is making the model’s learned settings, known as ‘weights’, available for download. Businesses with suitable computers can run the model themselves rather than relying entirely on Sarvam’s online service.

In-focus
How PayNearby is building a network of women micro-entrepreneurs
PayNearby was founded in 2016 to enable neighbourhood stores to offer digital banking and financial services. As its reach expanded over the years, the company noticed that more men were accessing its services than women.
So, in 2024, the fintech platform launched Digital Naari to train women as financial and digital service providers serving other women in their communities. The company says the initiative now reaches women across more than 15,000 pin codes, helping them earn through transaction-based commissions.
Key takeaways:
- A Digital Naari is a banking touchpoint within a community, operated by a woman agent. After training, agents use a mobile phone to provide services such as banking, insurance, credit, bill payments and telehealth.
- PayNearby says about 80% of the women joining the programme are first-time entrepreneurs. Participants include women from low-income households, single mothers and widows supporting their families.
- Digital Naari not only creates an income opportunity for women, it also makes financial services more accessible to other women within their communities.

articles.title: Le clavier Razer Joro passe à 54,18 € (-29 %) pour le Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : Le clavier Razer Joro à 54,18 € (-29%)
Actuellement noté 4/5 par notre rédaction, le clavier Razer Joro séduit par son format léger facile à transporter et sa frappe réactive. Le Black Friday 2026 est l'occasion de se l'offrir moins cher : il passe à 54,18 € chez Amazon, soit une baisse d'environ 29 % et 22,19 € d'économie.
Razer propose avec le Joro son premier modèle nomade à mécanisme à ciseaux, pensé pour les joueurs qui se déplacent souvent. Ce clavier compact au format 75 % sans pavé numérique combine une double connexion sans fil Bluetooth 5.0 et 2,4 GHz, une configuration qui avait convaincu notre laboratoire lors de son passage sur le banc d'essai.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Razer Joro descend à 54,18 € chez Amazon, soit environ 29 % de moins que son prix moyen du mois écoulé fixé à 76,37 €. Cela représente une économie de 22,19 € sur ce modèle actuellement noté 4/5.
Une frappe réactive au format compact
Le Razer Joro s'adresse directement aux utilisateurs nomades grâce à son format 75 % qui supprime le pavé numérique pour libérer de la place dans un sac. Notre équipe a pu apprécier la réactivité de ses interrupteurs à ciseaux, qui assurent une saisie rapide et agréable en jeu comme en bureautique, comme le détaille notre test complet. Sa double connectivité sans fil permet de basculer facilement entre le Bluetooth 5.0 pour la bureautique et la liaison 2,4 GHz pour réduire la latence.
Razer Joro
Points forts
- Frappe réactive et agréable.
- Design élégant.
- Léger et transportable.
- Belle autonomie en mode économie d'énergie.
Points faibles
- Plastique ABS des touches.
- Connectivité 2,4 GHz sous conditions.
- Rétroéclairage qui handicape l'autonomie.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Une autonomie dépendante des réglages
Ce modèle présente toutefois quelques concessions matérielles, à commencer par des touches en plastique ABS plus sensibles à l'usure que le PBT. L'activation du rétroéclairage réduit également la durée de la batterie par défaut, ce qui oblige à activer le mode d'économie d'énergie pour préserver une autonomie confortable. Ces limites demandent quelques ajustements de réglages, mais ne gênent pas l'usage régulier d'un joueur en déplacement.
